{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:51:00.241593+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ec83e8838255549a30a7a891bd8b4e6575b0da6a976936f541e4fe7a1ce1727","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem Varadhan of arXiv:2604.23751, 'Large deviation principles for pattern-avoiding permutations, and limit shapes for constra'] For any $n\ge 1,$ let $\mu_n$ denote the distribution of $X_n$ and assume that $(X_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good rate function $I.$ Let $F:E \rightarrow \mathbb R$ be a bounded continuous function. Let the distribution $\nu_n$  be defined as follows:
 \[ \mathrm{d}\nu_n(x) := \frac{1}{Z_n} \textup{e}^{a_nF(x)} \mathrm{d}\mu_n(x),\]
 where $Z_n$ is a normalizing constant such that $\nu_n$ is a probability measure.
 Then we have
	\[ \lim_{n \rightarrow \infty} \frac{1}{a_n} \log Z_n = -  \inf_{y\in E} (I(y)- F(y)). \]
	Moreover, if we let $Y_n$ have distribution $\nu_n$,
the sequence $(Y_n)$ satisfies an LDP at speed $a_n$ with good rate function $J$
 given by
 \[ \forall x\in E, \quad J(x) = I(x) - F(x) - \inf_{y\in E} (I(y)- F(y)).\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.476426+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ec925087e3f2cc19b7ae358770a7b52bed6d90cf6961fa65158b244c9a52032","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] \label[lemma]{lem:Zp_symmetrizer_space}
For $f \in_R \mathbb{Z}_{2q+1}$ ($q \ge 1$),
\[ \Sym(f) = 
    \{ g \in_R \mathbb{Z}_{2q+1}
    \mid \forall x \in [q] \quad
    \sum_{i=-q}^q (f(x-i) - f(-x-i)) g(i) = 0 \}.
    \]
In particular, $\dim(\Sym(f)) \ge q$. 
\begin{proof}
We identify the elements of $\mathbb{Z}_{2q+1}$ with $[-q,q] \cap \mathbb{Z}$ so that inverses are obvious. 
By direct computation, $\Sym(f)$ is the set of random vectors $g  \in \mathbb{Z}_{2q+1}$  such that for all integers $x \in [-q,q]$, $(f * g)(x) = (f * g)(-x)$, i.e.
\[    \sum_{i=-q}^q (f(x-i) - f(-x-i)) g(i) = 0 \}.    \]
But the condition corresponding to $x=0$ is vacuous, and for all $x \in [q]$ the conditions produced by $x$ and $-x$ are identical. 

To see the dimension, note that the simplex of probability measures on $\mathbb{Z}_{2q+1}$ has dimension $2q$, and we have imposed $q$ linear constraints. 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:50:26.915932+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ecc4bb4c4cf4e7d19657604145f7214bfb3037b64ce05bbe6e34eb0f59480d6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:Buse_basic_properties of arXiv:2505.09604, 'Exceptional force, uncountably many solutions in the KPZ fixed point'] [Busa-Sepp-Sore-22a] 
On the probability space of the directed landscape $\mathcal{L}$, there exists a process
\[
\Bigl(W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,s;y,t): \xi \in \mathbb{R}, {\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{-,+\}, (x,s;y,t) \in \mathbb{R}^4\Bigr)
\]
satisfying the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), font=\normalfont]
\item{\rm(Continuity)}   As an $\mathbb{R}^4 \to \mathbb{R}$ function,  $(x,s;y,t) \mapsto W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,s;y,t)$ is  continuous. 
 \item {\rm(Additivity)}  For all $p,q,r \in \mathbb{R}^2$, 
    $W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(p;q) + W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(q;r) = W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(p;r)$.   In particular, \\ $W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(p;q) = -W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(q;p)$ and $W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(p;p) = 0$.
    \item {\rm(Monotonicity along a horizontal line)}
     Whenever $\xi_1< \xi_2$, $x < y$, and $t \in \mathbb{R}$,
    \[
    W^{\xi_1 -}(x,t;y,t) \le W^{\xi_1 +}(x,t;y,t) \le W^{\xi_2 -}(x,t;y,t) \le W^{\xi_2 +}(x,t;y,t).
    \]
    \item {\rm(Evolution as the KPZ fixed point)} For 
    all $x,y \in \mathbb{R}$ and $s < t$,
    \begin{equation}
    W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,s;y,t) = \sup_{z \in \mathbb{R}}\{W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(x,s;z,s) +
 \mathcal{L}(z,s;y,t)\}.
    \end{equation}
    \item  {\rm(Law and asymptotic slope)} For fixed $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$, $W^{\xi} := W^{\xi +} = W^{\xi -}$ with probability one, and for each $t \in \mathbb{R}$, the random function $x \mapsto W^{\xi}(0,t;x,t)$ is a two-sided Brownian motion with variance $2$ and drift $2\xi$. Furthermore, on a single event of full probability, for all $t \in \mathbb{R},\xi \in \mathbb{R}$, and ${\scaleobj{0.9}{\boxempty}} \in \{-,+\}$,
    \[
    \lim_{|x| \to \infty} \frac{W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(0,t;x,t)}{x} = 2\xi.
    \]
    \item {\rm(General Busemann limits)} for all $\xi \in \mathbb{R}$, $t \in \mathbb{R}$, $x < y$, and sequences $\mathbf v_n = (x_n,t_n)$ with $t_n \to -\infty$ and $\frac{x_n}{|t_n|}\to \xi$,
\begin{align*}
W^{\xi-}(x,t;y,t) &\le \liminf_{n \to \infty} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf v_n;y,t) - \mathcal{L}(\mathbf v_n;x,t) \\&\le \limsup_{n \to \infty} \mathcal{L}(\mathbf v_n;y,t) - \mathcal{L}(\mathbf v_n;x,t) \le W^{\xi +}(x,t;y,t).
\end{align*}
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:22:48.891671+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5eda076fdfc115741b99a18fadcf755c648bf420abf206f1adef867240486756","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 38 of arXiv:2608.29157, 'Dilator-based analysis of $\KP$'] A sentence in the language of $\RS$ is \emph{axiomatic} if it is one of the following: 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item Extensionality:
        \begin{equation*}
        \forall x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \forall y\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega
        \left[
          \neg\left(
            \forall z\in x\, z\in y
            \wedge
            \forall z\in y\, z\in x
          \right)
          \vee x=y
        \right].
        \end{equation*}
        
        \item Pairing:
        \begin{equation*}
        \forall x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \forall y\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \exists z\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega
        \left(
          x\in z\wedge y\in z
        \right).
        \end{equation*}
        
        \item Union:
        \begin{equation*}
        \forall x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \exists y\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \forall z\in x\,
        \forall w\in z\,
        w\in y.
        \end{equation*}
        
        \item Set Induction:
        \begin{equation*}
        \neg
        \forall x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega
        \left(
          \neg\forall y\in x\,A(y)\vee A(x)
        \right)
        \vee
        \forall x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega A(x).
        \end{equation*}
        
        \item Infinity:
        \begin{equation*}
        \exists x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega
        \left[
          \exists y\in x\, y\in x
          \wedge
          \forall y\in x\,\exists z\in x\,y\in z
        \right].
        \end{equation*}
        
        \item $\Delta_0$-Separation:
        For every $\Delta_0$-formula $A(x,\vec a)$,
        \begin{equation*}
        \forall b\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \forall \vec a\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \exists c\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \forall x\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega
        \left[
          \left(x\notin c\vee
            \left(x\in b\wedge A(x,\vec a)\right)
          \right)
          \wedge
          \left(
            \neg\left(x\in b\wedge A(x,\vec a)\right)
            \vee x\in c
          \right)
        \right].
        \end{equation*}
        
        \item $\Delta_0$-Collection:
        For every $\Delta_0$-formula $A(x,y,\vec a)$,
        \begin{equation*}
        \forall b\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega\,
        \forall \vec a\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega
        \left[
          \neg\forall x\in b\,\exists y\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega A(x,y,\vec a)
          \vee
          \exists c\in \ttL(u)_\ttOmega
          \forall x\in b\,\exists y\in c\,A(x,y,\vec a)
        \right].
        \end{equation*}
    \end{enumerate}

    A sequent $\Gamma$ in the language of $\RS$ is \emph{axiomatic} if $\Gamma$ contains one of the following subsequent:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item An axiomatic sentence.
        \item $A,\lnot A$ for some formula $A$.
        \item $s\notin s$ for some set term $s$.
        \item $s\subseteq s$ for some set term $s$.
        \item $s\neq t, \lnot A(s),A(t)$ for some set term $s$, $t$, and some formula $A$.
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:54:15.646407+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5edc8a26f66303d2c7da24534f5f0c4bccff5a5da69488a16d39844f0d3a78c5","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 101 (Second-chaos factorization and the point-evaluation gap) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] For $i<j$, let
\[
 \Xi_{ij}(t)=t^{-1}\left(
  \int_0^tW_s^i\,\mathrm dW_s^j-
  \int_0^tW_s^j\,\mathrm dW_s^i\right).
\]
The active family $(\Xi_{ij}(t))_{c_ic_j>0}$ is orthonormal in
$L^2(\Omega)$, and second-chaos radonification defines an isometry
\[
 \operatorname{Rad}^{(2)}_{\Xi,t}:
 \mathcal S_2(\mathfrak h_{2,C},E)\longrightarrow L^2(\Omega;E).
\]
Moreover
\begin{equation}
 \alpha_{A_t^C}
 =\operatorname{Rad}^{(2)}_{\Xi,t}(K_{C,t}),
 \qquad
 \operatorname{Cov}(\alpha_{A_t^C})
 =K_{C,t}K_{C,t}^*=\frac{t^2}{4}\Lambda^2C.
 
\end{equation}
If $C$ has infinite rank, then almost surely algebraic point evaluation on
the active chaos space has no bounded extension to its $L^2$ closure.
Thus \eqref{eq:compact-second-chaos-factorization} is an $L^2$
radonification identity, not a bounded samplewise contraction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:53:51.329480+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ee09064a4b508c5845c52974eacc742d355aa824bb70e6cba053e8e75ba80d9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main-intro of arXiv:2605.03703, 'Scaling Limits of Bivariate Nearly-Unstable Hawkes Processes and Applications to Rough Vol'] Under Assumption~(ass:kernels of the paper),
the bivariate renormalized intensity process $(V^{T,1},V^{T,2})_{T\geq 1}$
converges weakly in $C([0,1];\mathbb{R}^2)$
to the unique triangular weak solution $(V^1,V^2)$
(Definition~(def:triangular-solution of the paper)) of the coupled stochastic Volterra system.
Set
\[
\nu_i=(m_i\lambda_i)^{-1/2},\qquad
\gamma_{12}=\frac{m_1}{m_2\lambda_1},
\qquad
L_{12}:=b_\infty^{12}\|\psi^{12}\|_1(K_1*K_2).
\]
Then
\begin{align}
V_t^1 &= b_1(t)
  + \nu_1\int_0^t K_1(t-s)\sqrt{V_s^1}\,d\beta_s^1,
\\
V_t^2 &= b_2(t)
  + \nu_2\int_0^t K_2(t-s)\sqrt{V_s^2}\,d\beta_s^2
  + \gamma_{12}\nu_1
    \int_0^t L_{12}(t-s)\sqrt{V_s^1}\,d\beta_s^1,

\end{align}
where $\beta^1,\beta^2$ are independent standard Brownian motions,
$b_1$ is defined by~(equation eq:b1-def of the paper), and $b_2$ is defined by~(equation eq:b2-full of the paper).

The limiting process has the following properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] \textbf{Heterogeneous roughness.}
Set $H_i:=\alpha_i-\tfrac12\in(0,\tfrac12)$.  Almost surely, $V^i$ is
H\"older continuous of every order $\gamma<H_i$, and the exponent is
sharp: away from the time origin, the mean-square increments satisfy
$\mathbb{E}[(V^i_t-V^i_s)^2]\asymp(t-s)^{2H_i}$
(Proposition~(prop:regularity of the paper)).  In this sense each $V^i$ has Hurst
parameter $H_i$, and $H_1<H_2$: the components carry distinct
roughnesses.

\item[\textup{(ii)}] \textbf{Covariance formula.}
The exact covariance of the limit process is
\[
\mathrm{Cov}(V_t^1,V_t^2)
= \gamma_{12}\nu_1^2
  \int_0^t K_1(t-s)\,L_{12}(t-s)\,b_1(s)\,ds,
\]
where $b_1(s)=\mathbb{E}[V_s^1]$.
In the stationary regime $b_1(s)\equiv\bar V^1$, this simplifies to
$\gamma_{12}\nu_1^2\bar V^1\int_0^t K_1(u)L_{12}(u)\,du$.
The effective cross-kernel is $L_{12}:=b_\infty^{12}\|\psi^{12}\|_1\cdot(K_1*K_2)$,
with $(K_1*K_2)(t)\sim C_{12}\,t^{\alpha_1+\alpha_2-1}$ as $t\downarrow 0$
(Proposition~(prop:main of the paper)).
\end{enumerate}

A self-contained statement with all explicit constants appears as
Theorem~(thm:main-final of the paper). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:29:21.935843+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5ee0b14ac38b0293255ee1c978583a5c49649d3eccaaed32e8c99e73b4ec3728","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 22 of arXiv:2608.01516, 'Nondegeneracy and regularity of polynomial pushforwards'] Let $n,d,k\in\mathbb N$ and assume that $n\ge k$. There exist two functions
\[
\alpha_{n,d,k}\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty)
\quad\text{and}\quad
\beta_{n,d,k}\colon(0,\infty)\to(0,\infty),
\]
with the following property.

Let $\mu$ be an isotropic log-concave measure on $\mathbb R^n$,
and let
$f=(f_1,\ldots,f_k)\in \mathcal P_d(\mathbb R^n;\mathbb R^k)$
be such that
\[
\operatorname{Var}_\mu(f_j)>0,
\quad
\forall j\in\{1,\ldots,k\}.
\]
Then, for every $a>0$,
\[
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Delta_{\hat{f}}\,d\mu\ge a
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge \beta_{n,d,k}(a),
\]
and, for every $b>0$,
\[
\det \Sigma_\mu^d(f)\ge b
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\int_{\mathbb{R}^n} \Delta_{\hat{f}}\,d\mu\ge \alpha_{n,d,k}(b).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:42:55.336181+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5f0e952d941d177740f1f2076523227062a98369675a5f42efc9c13c4bd8845d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 22 of arXiv:2609.02416, '2609.02416'] The exponential criteria used to close the simplicity argument are the following.

\textup{(i)} Assume the hypotheses of Lemma~\ref{thm:growth}. Let $\lambda_p=\Lp(\R)$ and choose $\beta>\gamma_H$. If
\[
\limsup_{|x|\to\infty}\left[a(x)+\lambda_p+d\big(M_J(\beta)-1\big)+q_1\beta\right]<0,
\]
where $M_J(\beta)=\int_\R J(z)e^{\beta|z|}\,dz$, then $W(x)=e^{\beta\sqrt{1+x^2}}$ satisfies $(\cA_\R+\lambda_p)W\le-\delta W$
outside a compact interval for some $\delta>0$. Every positive eigenfunction associated with $\lambda_p$ is $o(W)$. Consequently $\lambda_p$ is simple in the positive cone.

\textup{(ii)} Let $\lambda_p=\Lp(\R)$. Assume that every positive principal eigenfunction satisfies the exponential Harnack bound of Lemma~\ref{thm:growth} with exponent $\gamma_H$. Suppose there exist $\beta_+,\beta_->\gamma_H$ such that
\[
\limsup_{x\to+\infty}\left[a(x)+\lambda_p+d(M(\beta_+)-1)+q(x)\beta_+\right]<0
\]
and
\[
\limsup_{x\to-\infty}\left[a(x)+\lambda_p+d(M(\beta_-)-1)-q(x)\beta_-\right]<0,
\]
where $M(\beta)=\int_\R J(z)e^{\beta z}\,dz$; symmetry makes $M$ even. Then $\lambda_p$ is simple in the positive cone.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:55:37.821202+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5f2c32f0ccf474377351410d1758eb7ae4d9cbff1962ba674141db669a1f19e2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defstar def:boundary of arXiv:2605.06488, 'Continuous-state branching processes with L\'evy-Khintchine drift-interaction: Laplace dua'] Let $\Delta \in \{0,\infty\}$.

\begin{enumerate}[(a)]
	\item
	$\Delta$ is \textbf{instantaneous} if
	\[
	\mathbb{P}_{\Delta}(T_\Delta=0)=1,
	\qquad 
	T_\Delta:=\inf\{t>0: X_t\neq \Delta\}.
	\]
	Equivalently,
	\[
	\mathbb{P}_{\Delta}\big(\forall t>0,\ \exists s\in(0,t): X_s\neq \Delta\big)=1.
	\]

\item   
$\Delta$ is \textbf{continuous} if, under $\mathbb{P}_\Delta$, the process is either identically equal to $\Delta$ (absorbing case) or leaves $\Delta$ without a jump, that is, the jump measure of the process vanishes at~$\Delta$.

Equivalently, in the non-absorbing case, if one denotes by $G$ the set of strictly positive left-end points of excursion intervals away from $\Delta$, then
\[\mathbb{P}_{\Delta}\left( \forall s\in G, \ X_s=\Delta \right)=1.\]
\item  $\Delta$ is \textbf{non-sticky} if
\begin{equation}
\mathbb{P}_x(X_t=\Delta)=0,\ \forall t\in (0,\infty), \ x\in [0,\infty].\end{equation}
Equivalently, the Lebesgue measure of the $\Delta$-level set $\{t\geq 0: X_t\in \Delta\}$ is zero. 
\item $\Delta$ is \textbf{regular-for-itself} if 
\begin{equation}\mathbb{P}_{\Delta}(R^{\Delta}=0)=1, \text{ with } R^\Delta:=\inf\{t>0: X_{t-}=\Delta \text{ or } X_t=\Delta\}.
\end{equation}
In words, the process started from $\Delta$, returns immediately to $\Delta$. 
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.350738+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5f326bd75e71195d7f640a685c64c7480c53a128fca3265a09b7ec89b7e3e77a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition D:prelandscapes of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] A random function $\mathcal{M}^\rho: \mathbb{Q}^4 \cap \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow \to \mathbb{R}$ is a \textbf{(half-space) pre-landscape} with parameter $\rho \in \mathbb{R} \cup \{-\infty\}$ if the following three conditions hold:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item (Triangle inequality) For any $o = (x, s)$, $p = (y, r)$, $q = (z, t) \in \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0} \times \mathbb{Q}$ with $s<r<t$, we have
				$\mathcal{M}^\rho(o; p) + \mathcal{M}^\rho(p; q) \le \mathcal{M}^\rho(o; q)$.
				\item (Independent increments) For any $s_1<s_2<\cdots<s_k \in \mathbb{Q}$, the increments $\mathcal{M}^\rho(\cdot, s_i; \cdot, s_{i+1}):\mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}^2 \to \mathbb{R}, i\in\llbracket1, k-1 \rrbracket$ are independent.
                \item (KPZ fixed point marginals) Recall that $\NW_{+}$ is the set of all $f \in \operatorname{UC}_+$ such that $\text{supp}(f) = \{x : f(x) > -\infty\}$ is finite. Consider any function $f \in \NW_{+}$ with $\text{supp}(f) \subset \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}$ and $f(\mathbb{R})\subset\mathbb{Q}\cup\{-\infty\}$.  Then for any $t, s \in \mathbb{Q}$, $s > 0$ and any finite set $Y \subset \mathbb{Q}_{\ge 0}$ we have that
				\[
				 (f \diamond \mathcal{M}^\rho(\cdot, t; y, t + s) : y \in Y)
				\stackrel{d}{=} (\mathfrak{h}^\rho (t, y; f) : y \in Y).
				\]
                Here the right-hand side above is given by Theorem (T:half-space-fixed-point of the paper).
\end{enumerate}
Moving forward, we will use the notation $\mathcal{M}^\rho_{s, t}(\cdot, \cdot) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(\cdot, s; \cdot, t)$ for the increment in a pre-landscape from time $s$ to time $t$, and the notation $\mathfrak{h}^\rho_t f = \mathfrak{h}^\rho (t, \cdot; f)$, which will help emphasize the semigroup structure under metric composition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.439794+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5f4af5adc6e4e41366e9b00d46119beb9eda65a949ed7c916e8d6c4a81573dda","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 143 (Exterior Chen representation of the geometric state) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] For $x\in H$ and $A\in\mathcal S_2(H)_{\rm sk}$, define
\begin{equation}
 
 \mathscr E(x,A):=\exp_\wedge(x+2\alpha_A).
\end{equation}
Then the following hold.

\textup{(i)} The series belongs to $\mathscr F^\wedge(H)$ and satisfies
\begin{equation}
 
 \|\mathscr E(x,A)\|_{\mathscr F^\wedge}^2
 \le(1+\|x\|^2)\exp(4\|\alpha_A\|^2).
\end{equation}

\textup{(ii)} If
\[
 (x,A)\star(y,B)
 =\bigl(x+y,A+B+\Anti(x\otimes y)\bigr),
\]
then
\begin{equation}
 
 \mathscr E\bigl((x,A)\star(y,B)\bigr)
 =\mathscr E(x,A)\wedge\mathscr E(y,B).
\end{equation}
Thus the exterior product is closed on $\mathscr G_2^\wedge(H)$ and
$\mathscr E$ is a topological group isomorphism from the geometric step-two
state group onto its exterior Chen image, with the transported topology in
\eqref{eq:exterior-Chen-image-group}.  Its degree-one and degree-two coordinates
recover $x$ and $A$.

\textup{(iii)} Writing
$\mathscr E(x,A)=\sum_{k\ge0}\Xi_k(x,A)$ by homogeneous degree,
\begin{equation}
 
 \Xi_{2N}(x,A)=\frac{2^N}{N!}\alpha_A^{\wedge N},
 \qquad
 \Xi_{2N+1}(x,A)=\frac{2^N}{N!}
 x\wedge\alpha_A^{\wedge N}.
\end{equation}
For a state $z=(x,A,q)$, the joint map
\[
 z\longmapsto(\mathscr E(x,A),q)
\]
is a continuous lossless group isomorphism onto
$\mathscr G_2^\wedge(H)\times\mathcal S_1(H)_{\rm sa}$, where the second
factor is additive.  The covariance channel is exactly the information
forgotten by the exterior factor alone.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:32:34.741534+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5f4b9bbdc53e8751152c2e2e9776f2f49ee00f5cf2548a7cba7b2b11c0edf1ab","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:tropp_bound of arXiv:2411.07878, 'Bernstein-type and Bennett-type inequalities for unbounded matrix martingales'] Let $\mathbf{X}_1, \dots, \mathbf{X}_n \in \mathbb{H}(d)$ be a sequence adapted to a filtration $\mathscr{F}_1 \subset \mathscr{F}_2 \subset \dots \subset \mathscr{F}_n $.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:05:57.773836+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5f8868a42d13ebb2ff93c562dce5b2bea2e14dd0c637ba56c274bd6eb7787056","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 9 of arXiv:2608.30549, '\vspace{-1cm}Maximally Spread Out Measures and Implications\\{} for Phase Transitions in A'] Let $(\XX, d)$ be a quasi-metric space.
  Let $\emptyset \ne \SC \subset \XX$ be bounded.
  Then, writing $\CR^\ast := \bigl(\umd(\SC)\bigr)^{-1}$, the following holds:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item \emph{(A suitable codec sequence achieves every rate below $\CR^\ast$)}
          There exists a codec sequence ${\mathscr{S}^\ast = ( (E_n^\ast, D_n^\ast) )_{n \in \N}}$
          for $\SC$ such that for every $0 \leq \CR < \CR^\ast$,
          there exists $C(\CR) > 0$ satisfying
          \[
            \delta (E_n^\ast, D_n^\ast) \leq C(\CR) \cdot n^{-\CR}
            \qquad \forall \, n \in \N
            .
          \]
          In particular, $\mathcal{R}^\CR (\mathscr{S}^\ast, \SC, \XX) = \SC$.
  \end{enumerate}
  Now, assume that $\mu$ is a probability measure on $\XX$ that is critical for $\SC$,
  and set
  \[
    \CR^\sharp
    := \bigl(\lmd(\SC)\bigr)^{-1}
    .
  \]
  Then the following hold:
  \begin{enumerate}[resume,label=(\roman*)]
    \item \emph{(quantitative bound relating approximation error and number of bits)}
          Let $\CR \in (\CR^\sharp, \infty)$.
          Then there exist $c = c(\CR) > 0$ and $\eps_0 = \eps_0 (\CR) > 0$
          such that for every $n \in \N$ and every $n$-bit codec $(E_n, D_n)$ for $\SC$,
          we have
          \[
            \mu^\ast
            \Bigl(
              \bigl\{
                x \in \SC
                \,\,:\,\,
                d\bigl(x, D_n(E_n(x))\bigr) \leq \eps
              \bigr\}
            \Bigr)
            \leq 2^{n - c \cdot \eps^{-1/\CR}}
            \qquad \forall \, \eps \in (0, \eps_0)
            .
          \]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:30:07.875164+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5f8b705fc516590889d83aebde3fd231888bcdf436c6f2b07c84193c3171fc22","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def_triangle of arXiv:2608.09105, 'Longest convex chains with i.i.d.\ points'] Let $f\colon[a,b]\to\mathbb{R}$ be continuous and convex.
Let us write $\mathsf{A} = (a,f(a))$ and $\mathsf{B} = (b,f(b))$.
\begin{itemize}

\item (Typical case) 
If $\partial^+f(a) < \partial^-f(b)$ and at least one of these two derivatives is finite, then we denote by $\mathsf{Tri}_f(a,b)$ the triangle bounded by the following three lines: the tangent line of $f$ at $a$ with slope $\partial^+f(a)$, the tangent line of $f$ at $b$ with slope $\partial^-f(b)$, and the secant line of $f$ between $a$ and $b$.
The vertices of $\mathsf{Tri}_f(a,b)$ are thus $\mathsf{A}$, $\mathsf{B}$, and the unique intersection point of the two tangent lines.
See Figure~(fig_tangency_triangle of the paper) (left).

\item (Degenerate case 1: flat)
If $\partial^+f(a)=\partial^-f(b)<\infty$, then we let $\mathsf{Tri}_f(a,b)$ denote the line segment between $\mathsf{A}$ and $\mathsf{B}$.

\item (Degenerate case 2: doubly infinite)
If $\partial^+f(a)=-\infty$ and $\partial^-f(b)=\infty$, then we let $\mathsf{Tri}_f(a,b)$ denote the infinite region below the secant line, defined in (equation below_secant of the paper).
\hfill\ensuremath{\square}

\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:54:28.137902+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5fa30900af4833ec201f0263cd03614eb4aace2b90bfae026ea8f9167b970214","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Gluing of arXiv:2608.13716, 'Graph Causal Optimal Transport \\ and Wasserstein Distances'] Let $\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{B}, \mathcal{C}$ be Polish spaces and let $\pi_1 \in \probabilities{\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{B}}$, $\pi_2 \in \probabilities{\mathcal{B} \times \mathcal{C}}$ such that $\pushforward{\proj{\mathcal{B}}}{\pi_1} = \pushforward{\proj{\mathcal{B}}}{\pi_2} \eqqcolon \nu \in \probabilities{\mathcal{B}}$. Let $\pi_2$ be disintegrated as $\pi_2(db, dc) = \nu(db) \otimes \kappa(dc \mid b)$ for a stochastic kernel $\kappa$.

    Then $\bigglue{\pi_1}{\pi_2}$ is defined as the measure 
    $$\bigglue{\pi_1}{\pi_2}(da, db, dc) \coloneqq \pi_1(da, db) \otimes \kappa(dc \mid b) \in \probabilities{\mathcal{A} \times \mathcal{B} \times \mathcal{C}},$$ 
    and is called the \emph{conditional independent product} of $\pi_1$, $\pi_2$. Its $\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{C}$ marginal, $\pi_1 \mathbin{\mathop{\circ}\limits_{\raisebox{1ex}{$\scriptstyle \mathfrak{g}$}}} \pi_2 \coloneqq \pushforward{\proj{\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{C}}}{\bigglue{\pi_1}{\pi_2}}$ is called the \emph{gluing} of $\pi_1$, $\pi_2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:21:56.725427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5fa50b6d9eb23d576a6ebc9570f25f4a2b299e78684391b5facd201d2bb8460b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary co:close_geodesic_small_parts of arXiv:2507.15589, 'Tightness of approximations to metrics on non-simple conformal loop ensemble gaskets'] There exist $c>0$ and $\zeta>0$ (not depending on $M,a,a_1,a_0$) such that the following is true. When C_X <= C_Y pointwise (or the relevant difference has a consistent sign) and F is chosen with matching sign of mixed partials, this yields a comparison inequality between functionals of X and Y, an approach that both generalizes Slepian-type comparisons and, in the Gaussian multiplicative chaos literature, is used to show that different regularizations of a log-correlated field, such as the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, converge to the same limiting chaos measure regardless of the approximation scheme, a key technical step in constructing Liouville quantum gravity measures. It does not apply to non-Gaussian fields, the interpolation is built from independent copies of the two fields (always available, since only their laws are compared; a dependent coupling adds cross-covariance terms to the derivative), and the sign or convexity conditions on F needed to obtain a clean inequality must be verified case by case rather than assumed. Typical failure: Running the interpolation on a dependent coupling of the two fields while dropping the cross-covariance terms, or to a family of regularizations whose covariance difference does not have a consistent sign across the whole index set, which is common when comparing regularizations of a log-correlated field near its singular set; either error breaks the monotonicity the interpolation is meant to exploit, and the resulting comparison can go in the wrong direction with no explicit error term to control it. Canonical reference: Kahane, 1986, Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec; Robert and Vargas, 2010, Comptes Rendus Mathematique; Berestycki, 2017, Electronic Communications in Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space and A is self-adjoint on it","psi lies in the absolutely continuous subspace of A and its spectral density is bounded by M almost everywhere","K is Hilbert-Schmidt (in particular compact); boundedness alone is not enough","the Fourier convention is exp(-i t lambda), which fixes the constant 2 pi","the estimate is uniform in psi given the density bound and in K given its Hilbert-Schmidt norm"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.091166+00:00","domain":"spectral theory, scattering theory, trace class perturbations","id":"claim_5fbe9483d9083c1e18b3ec600c653d4f2d8f70dfbfef14f47a1428b1b63ecc4f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"CAUTION ON THE NAME: 'Rosenblum's argument' is used for at least two different results of M. Rosenblum; this entry is the scattering-theory one, the Plancherel estimate that drives the Kato-Rosenblum theorem on trace class perturbations and the standard existence proofs for wave operators. STATEMENT: let A be a self-adjoint operator on a Hilbert space H with spectral measure E, let psi in H be a vector whose spectral measure mu_psi(S) = <psi, E(S) psi> is absolutely continuous with respect to Lebesgue measure with density bounded by a constant M (that is, d mu_psi / d lambda <= M almost everywhere), and let K be a Hilbert-Schmidt operator on H. Then the map t -> K exp(-i t A) psi is square integrable on R as an H-valued function and the integral over R of the squared norm of K exp(-i t A) psi dt is at most 2 pi M times the square of the Hilbert-Schmidt norm of K. Consequently the quantity tends to 0 along a sequence of times, and combined with Cook's criterion this is what produces existence of wave operators for perturbations that factor through Hilbert-Schmidt operators; note that the bound is UNIFORM over all vectors psi with the same density bound M, which is how the estimate is bootstrapped from a dense set of vectors to the whole absolutely continuous subspace. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) the bounded density is essential. If psi has any point mass, for instance if psi is an eigenvector of A, then the norm of K exp(-i t A) psi equals the norm of K psi for all t and the time integral is infinite unless K psi = 0. The lemma is a statement about the absolutely continuous subspace with a locally bounded density, not about arbitrary vectors. (ii) 'Hilbert-Schmidt' cannot be relaxed to 'bounded': taking K the identity makes the left-hand side the integral of a positive constant over R, which diverges. (iii) The constant 2 pi is tied to the Fourier convention; with the kernel exp(-2 pi i t lambda) the constant is 1. (iv) Nothing is claimed about the pointwise decay of the norm of K exp(-i t A) psi in t; only its square integrability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:06:21.735352+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5fcfc0feb9dc35e944330ccce0420c886c81d2f14d332c6bb8f3cc4b3277b0d2","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 22 of arXiv:2607.21374, 'Local structure at the maximum and sharp persistence asymptotics of rough fractional Brown'] Put
\begin{equation}
  \Gamma_\rho(t,u)
  :=K_H(t,u)-\frac{K_H(t,\rho)K_H(u,\rho)}{|\rho|^\alpha}.
  
\end{equation}
Fix \(0<a<R<\infty\) and \(r_*>0\).  There are
\(\rho_0,C>0\) such that, if \(0<|\rho|\leq\rho_0\),
\(s,t\in[a,R]\), and \(u\notin\{0,\rho\}\), then
\begin{equation}
  |\Gamma_\rho(t,u)-\Gamma_\rho(s,u)|
  \leq C|t-s|^\alpha\Gamma_\rho(r_*,u).
  
\end{equation}
If instead \(r_*<0\), the reflected estimate holds for
\(s,t\in[-R,-a]\), with the same quantifiers.

If \(v=1/\rho\) and
\begin{equation}
  \overline\Gamma_v(t,u)
  :=K_H(t,u)-\frac{K_H(t,v)K_H(u,v)}{|v|^\alpha},
  
\end{equation}
then, for every \(\bar r_*>0\), there are \(v_0,C>0\) such that
\[
 |\overline\Gamma_v(t,u)-\overline\Gamma_v(s,u)|
 \leq C|t-s|^\alpha\overline\Gamma_v(\bar r_*,u)
\]
whenever \(|v|\geq v_0\), \(s,t\in[a,R]\), and
\(u\notin\{0,v\}\).  The reflected far-pin estimate holds for
\(\bar r_*<0\) and \(s,t\in[-R,-a]\).  Every reference kernel on the
right is strictly positive on its displayed domain.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:50:30.562116+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5fd3759c1f9fa289614d9d03edcd0d47c7624e755b3c2343bce202ef0a224ee0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 14 of arXiv:2605.30560, 'Projected McKean--Vlasov Dynamics for Entropic Weak Optimal Transport'] A weak solution of \eqreftag{eq:Fokker-planck-a} is a weak continuous flow
$
    (\P_t)_{t\ge0}\subset\Pc(\Xc\times\R^d),
$ 
$
    \P_0=\pi_0,
$
together with a Borel vector field
$
    \hat A:\R_+\times\R^d\longrightarrow\R^d,
$
such that the following conditions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*), ref=(\roman*)]
    \item 
    There exists \(p>1\) such that, for every \(T>0\),
    \[
    \int_0^T
    \int_{\Xc\times\R^d}
    \left|
    \hat A(t,y)
    -
    a\bigl(t,x,y,(\P_t)_x\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(y)
    \right|^p
    \P_t(dx,dy)\,dt
    <\infty.
    \]

    \item 
    For every \(t\ge0\) and every
    \(h\in C_b(\Xc\times\R^d; \R)\) such that
    \(h(x,\cdot)\in C_c^\infty(\R^d; \R)\) for all \(x\in\Xc\),
    \begin{align*}
    \E^{\P_t}[h]
    =&
    \E^{\P_0}[h] 
    +
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\P_s}\!\Big[
    \nabla_y h(X,Y)\cdot
    \big(
    \hat A(s,Y)
    -
    a\bigl(s,X,Y,(\P_s)_X\bigr)
    -
    \nabla_y V(Y)
    \big)\Big]ds
    \\
    &+
    \int_0^t
    \E^{\P_s}\!\Big[ \Delta_y h(X,Y)
    \Big]ds .
\end{align*}

    \item[(iii)] 
    For a.e. \(t\ge0\),
    \[
    \hat A(t,y)
    =
    \E^{\P_t}\!\left[
        a\bigl(t,X,y,(\P_t)_X\bigr)
        \mid Y=y
    \right],
    \qquad
    \P_t\text{-a.s.}
    \]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","T is densely defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.770065+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, unbounded operators","id":"claim_5fd3ebada06c815bb9dfcb5498aec75ad7cf012d7bf00e5e5fbacea33bb264f4","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a complex Hilbert space and T: D(T) ⊂ H → H densely defined. Then: (a) T* is closed. (b) T is closable if and only if D(T*) is dense, and in that case T̄ = T**. (c) If T is closable, (T̄)* = T*. (d) ker T* = Ran(T)^⊥, and if T is closed also ker T = Ran(T*)^⊥ provided T* is densely defined (true for closed densely defined T). (e) If S ⊂ T (both densely defined) then T* ⊂ S*. (f) If B is bounded and everywhere defined, (T + B)* = T* + B*. In general only inclusions hold for sums and products: (S + T)* ⊃ S* + T* when S + T is densely defined, and (ST)* ⊃ T*S* when ST is densely defined; equality in (ST)* = T*S* holds if S is bounded and everywhere defined.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:47:12.027894+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_5fdcb2ecb1e257e1cc6d2577a65cb0dc245af7f45b91bbf2e5e38ff92f453ac4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:8 of arXiv:2512.09219, 'Strong confluence of geodesics in Liouville quantum gravity'] ([GM21])
  
  For a GFF plus a continuous function $\mathtt{h}$, there exists a unique (up to a deterministic multiplicative constant) random metric $D_{\mathtt{h}}$ on $\mathbb{C}$ which is measurable with respect to $\mathtt{h}$ and satisfies the following almost sure properties.
  \begin{enumerate}
  \item 
 \textbf{Length space}: Almost surely, for all $u,v\in \mathbb{C}$, $D_\mathtt{h}(u,v)=\inf_{\eta}\ell(\eta;D_\mathtt{h})$, where the infimum is over all paths $\eta$ connecting $u,v$.
  \item 
   \textbf{Locality}: For any deterministic set $U\subseteq \mathbb{C}$, consider the induced metric $D_{\mathtt{h}}(\cdot,\cdot;U)$ defined by $D_{\mathtt{h}}(u,v;U)= \inf_{\eta\subseteq U} \ell(\eta; D_{\mathtt{h}})$,  where the infimum is taken over all paths contained in $U$. Then, for any fixed open set $U\subseteq \mathbb{C}$, the induced metric $D_{\mathtt{h}}(\cdot,\cdot;U)$ is measurable with respect to $\mathtt{h}\lvert_U$. 
  \item 
  \textbf{Weyl scaling}: For a continuous function $f\colon \mathbb{C}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$, consider the metric $e^f\cdot D_h$ defined by $e^f\cdot D_h(u,v)=\inf_{\eta}\int_{0}^{\ell(\eta;D_h)}e^{f(\eta(t))}dt$, where the infimum is over all paths $\eta$ from $u$ to $v$. Then, for $\xi=\gamma/d_\gamma$, with $d_\gamma$ denoting the fractal dimension of $\gamma$-LQG as defined in [DG20], we a.s.\ have the equality $e^{\xi f}\cdot D_{\mathtt{h}}=D_{\mathtt{h}+f}$ simultaneously for every continuous function $f\colon \mathbb{C}\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$.
  \item 
   \textbf{Coordinate change formula}: Fix a deterministic $z\in \mathbb{C}$ and $r>0$. With $Q$ defined by $Q=\gamma/2+2/\gamma$ and the field $\mathtt{h}'$ defined by $\mathtt{h}'(\cdot)=\mathtt{h}(r\cdot+z)+Q\log r$, almost surely, for all $u,v\in \mathbb{C}$, we have $D_\mathtt{h}(ru+z,rv+z)=D_{\mathtt{h}'}(u,v)$.

  \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:59:24.046016+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60161bb2972a1dbe1ce60aec1739e7a31e35a3c16ff820456f3cd7a87edc4309","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:weighted-collar-monotonicity of arXiv:2608.30700, 'Convex hulls and area minimizing currents in asymptotically locally hyperbolic manifolds'] Let
    \[
        \delta(r) := C_0 e^{-r}, \qquad
        w(r) := \exp(-qC_0e^{-r}),
    \]
    and let $Z$ be an integral $p$-current of finite mass such that its associated varifold $|Z|$ is stationary in $\{a<r<t\}$. Define
    \[
        B(s):= \int_{\{a < r < s\}} w(r)\,d\left\lVertZ\right\rVert_g.
    \]
    Then $s\mapsto e^{-qs}B(s)$ is nondecreasing on $(a,t)$. Equivalently, for every $a<s<u<t$,

    \]

{"assumptions":["Positive rational conductances and a finite connected graph.","For the stated extension, the optimizer is determined by a rational linear system."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364347+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60176608d5f28c8e19a49da0bfef4ae2de0694d33b62884c8abe186b56a4fe41","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked only, no independent read.] This is the energy-flow extension of the restricted negative answer to the question in Chapter 4 of David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html), recorded as intake row I0024. That question asks whether the relaxation time can be characterized exactly as an infimum over flows. Let G be a finite connected undirected graph with positive rational conductances c_e on its edges and distinct vertices a,b. Orient the edges arbitrarily and minimize E(f)=sum_e f_e^2/c_e over real flows f with divergence +1 at a, -1 at b, and zero at all other vertices. The minimum is the effective resistance R_eff(a,b). It is rational, because the electrical-flow optimality equations are a rational linear system. More generally, the same rationality conclusion holds for attained convex quadratic flow programs with rational data whose optimizing point is determined by a rational linear system. Therefore these minimum-energy constructions cannot universally return the relaxation time tau_2=1/(1-lambda_2) on rational reversible chains, since the simple random walk on the six-vertex path has tau_2=3+sqrt(5). This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The graph and intersection numbers satisfy the preceding definitions.","Only indices j<d occur in denominators b_j."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364578+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60217221b746575a4336b4914953ec24ff5ce593b2b8b5eae703154f9a276c88","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked against a direct linear-algebra solve on twelve graphs, with the complete graph and the cycle as independent controls at the two extremes.] This is a sufficient-condition reduction of Open Problem 7.31 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html), which asks for tau_0=O(n) uniformly over distance-regular graphs other than cycles. Let G be a finite connected simple distance-regular graph with n>=2 vertices, valency k, and diameter d: for vertices at distance i, the numbers of neighbors one step closer to or farther from the target are constants c_i and b_i depending only on i. Use c_1=1, b_0=k, b_d=0. Let k_i be the number of vertices at distance i from a fixed vertex, so k_0=1, k_1=k, k_{i+1} c_{i+1}=k_i b_i, and n=sum_{i=0}^d k_i. For the simple random walk, let T_y be the first hitting time of y, measured in steps, and define tau_0=max_{x,y} E_x[T_y]; here tau_0 is the maximum mean hitting time, not the spectral Kemeny sum. Define the tail count T_i=sum_{j=i}^d k_j and u_i=k/(k_i c_i). The intersection recurrence gives u_1=1 and u_{i+1}=u_i c_i/b_i for 1<=i<d, hence tau_0/n=sum_{i=1}^d (T_i/n) product_{j=1}^{i-1}(c_j/b_j) <= sum_{i=1}^d product_{j=1}^{i-1}(c_j/b_j), where an empty product is one. A uniform bound on the last sum over noncycle distance-regular graphs would prove the requested O(n) estimate. The campaign does not prove this uniform bound, and the sufficient criterion is not asserted to be necessary. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.910032+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60407aba2411982292872c5fc9dd447cde72fe1513962b40ef890be048b0e2ed","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:global-decay of arXiv:2608.26745, 'Moderate Deviations for the Largest Eigenvalue of a Randomly Deformed Gaussian Unitary Ens'] Let $a_j=w_N-\xi_j$.  For $j=1,2$, define
\[
 g_j(t)=\Re\{f_N(C_j(t))-f_N(w_N)\},
\]

\[
 g_j(t)=-\Re\{f_N(C_j(t))-f_N(w_N)\}.

Then

 g_1'(t)=g_2'(t)
 &=-\sum_{k=1}^N
 \frac{2t^2}{a_k\{(a_k+t)^2+t^2\}},                    \\

Consequently, uniformly over all truncated configurations (and hence on

 &&\frac{w_N}{2}\le t<\infty.                                  
\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:13:21.347303+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_604aa7f098076089375c70f46d2aab5517018fa11619882a6c9907c5da7f6780","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 (Continuity of blocking probability) of arXiv:2609.01559, 'Erlang Loss Model with Energy Constrained Servers'] Let $F_n$ be a sequence of service distributions such that
\[
F_n \Rightarrow F, \quad \mathbb{E}[S_n] \to \mathbb{E}[S].
\]
Then
\[
B(F_n) \to B(F).
\]
\begin{proof}
Let $Y^{(n)}$ and $Y$ denote the steady-state number in system for the $M/G/\infty$ systems with service distributions $F_n$ and $F$, respectively. By the standard results on Poisson driven infinite server queues \citet{eick1993physics, massey1993networks}, we have
\[
Y^{(n)} \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda \mathbb{E}[S_n]), \quad
Y \sim \mathrm{Poisson}(\lambda \mathbb{E}[S]).
\]
Since $\mathbb{E}[S_n] \to \mathbb{E}[S]$, the Poisson parameters converge, and hence
\[
Y^{(n)} \Rightarrow Y.
\]
Therefore,
\[
\mathbb{P}(Y^{(n)} \ge k) \to \mathbb{P}(Y \ge k).
\]
Using the representation $B(F_n) = \mathbb{P}(Y^{(n)} \ge k)$ and $B(F) = \mathbb{P}(Y \ge k)$ completes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.358526+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_604e25d183e41a15c5ac833de73b0908d48aca0128f87c6071e1c3bd7b1396ef","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 5 of arXiv:2604.21143, 'Quantitative homogenization for the critical long-range random conductance model'] For $u, v \in \Zd$ with $u \ne v$, let $\gamma_{v \to u}$ be the nearest-neighbour path from $v$ to $u$ obtained by changing coordinates one at a time in the order $1, \ldots, d$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.688604+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6085b334d4b6820f213d11f46457a0a30308a6645db37ab85484727c8640806f","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 100 (Triangular mixed rough--Young closure) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Fix $N\ge2$ and $R<\infty$.  Suppose
\[
 \|\mathbf x^S\|_{\eta;[s,T]}+|q|_{2\eta;[s,T]}\le R.
\]
Set $U^{(-1)}:=0$, $U^{(0)}:=1$, and define recursively
\begin{equation}

 U^{(k)}_{s,t}
 :=\int_s^t U^{(k-1)}_{s,r}\otimes\dd\mathbf x^S_r
   -\frac12\int_s^t U^{(k-2)}_{s,r}\otimes\dd q_r,
 \qquad 1\le k\le N.
\end{equation}
Then every level is well defined and
$U^{(k)}_{s,\cdot}$ is $x$-controlled with Gubinelli derivative
\[
 h\longmapsto U^{(k-1)}_{s,\cdot}\otimes h.
\]
For fixed $N$ the controlled norms of all levels are bounded by a constant
$C_{N,R}$, uniformly in the restart time $s$.  On bounded sets, the map
$(\mathbf x^S,q)\mapsto(U^{(1)},\ldots,U^{(N)})$ is locally Lipschitz in the
rough-path/controlled-path metric and the $2\eta$-H\"older norm of $q$.

The same conclusions hold in variation topology: if $2<p<3$ and
$1\le\nu\le p/2$, then on sets with bounded rough $p$-variation norm of
$\mathbf x^S$ and bounded $\nu$-variation norm of $q$, the solution map is
locally Lipschitz for the rough $p$-variation metric and the
$\nu$-variation norm, with all levels controlled in the $p$-variation sense.
On the common domain the H\"older and variation constructions coincide by
levelwise uniqueness.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-11-02T23:15:00.787949+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_60879b4ea19c5f59cebf5a301f68617a860dc3812429293d95f201af04bf71bb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Publication record. Y. Shmalo, The layer distribution of the random recursive tree and the minimum of the Poisson-weighted infinite tree (2026). The layer of a vertex of a tree is the number of rounds of leaf removal after which it is a leaf. Stepanyants, Krapivsky, Hartle and Krioukov (arXiv:2608.04303) showed that the limiting proportion of vertices at layer at least k in a random recursive tree is lbar_k = int_0^inf s_k(y) e^(-y) dy with s_0 = 1 and s_i(y) = 1 - exp(-int_0^y s_(i-1)), and conjectured that the proportion l_k at layer exactly k is exp[-k/e - (3/(2e)) log k - O(1)]. The paper proves lbar_k e^(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> C_* in (0, inf) and l_k e^(k/e) k^(3/(2e)) -> (1 - e^(-1/e)) C_*. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357787+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_609dfc8cf45f5e2feb97bcaeeb540a60ec4dfbdc71b507fea46e181996aee986","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 244 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp} and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}. We then have
	\begin{align*}
	\max_{\sigma\in\{\RomII,\RomIII\}}

	&\le L^{O(1)}\,,\\
	\max_{i\in[N]}
	\E\bigg[ \max_{0\le d\le\dmax}
	X^\Ising(q_d,i)^8\bigg] 
	&\le L^{O(1)}\,,
	\end{align*}
with the estimates holding uniformly in $N$.

\begin{proof} First consider $X^{\RomII}(q_d,a)$ for fixed $a\in[M]$, as a process indexed by time $q_d$ with $0\le d\le \dmax$. For the purposes of the proof let us abbreviate
		\[
	\frac{\Delta X^{\RomII}(q_d,a)}{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	\equiv 
	\mathfrak{y}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\bar{\bg}^a(q_d), \by(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}
	\,.
	\]
 Note that for fixed $a\in[M]$, $X^{\RomII}(q_d,a)$ (indexed by time $q_d$) is a martingale with respect to the filtration $\cG(q_d)$. Define a modified version similarly to the argument of  Lemma~\ref{l:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound}: let
	\begin{align}\nonumber
	\tilde{\bg}^a(q_d)
	&\equiv
	\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)
	\min\bigg\{1,\frac{2N^{1/2}}{\|\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)\|}\bigg\}\,,\\ \nonumber
	\tilde{\by}(q_{d+1})
	&\equiv
	\by(q_{d+1})
	\min\bigg\{1,\frac{2N^{1/2}}{\| \by(q_{d+1})\|}\bigg\}\,, \\
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)}{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	&\equiv 
	\tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)
	\equiv \frac{(\tilde{\bg}^a(q_d), \tilde{\by}(q_{d+1}))}{N^{1/2}}
	\,.
	\end{align}
We note that we have
$\tilde{\bg}^a(q_d)=\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)$ and 
$\tilde{\by}(q_{d+1})=\by(q_{d+1})$ on the event
	\[\cE\equiv
	\cE(q_d,a) 
	\equiv \bigg\{ 
	\frac{\|\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)\|}{2N^{1/2}} \le1 ,
	\frac{\| \by(q_{d+1})\|}{2N^{1/2}} \le1
	\bigg\} \,.
	\]
It follows from Lemma~\ref{l:y.subgaus} and standard estimates that the event $\cE(q_d,a)$ fails with probability $e^{-cN}$. We then argue similarly as in the proof of \eqref{e:lip.alg.l2.l4.bound.l4.step2}: the random variables $\mathfrak{y}^{\RomII}$ and $\tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomII}$ always have the same sign, with $|\tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomII}| \le |\mathfrak{y}^{\RomII}|$, and they agree on the event $\cE\equiv\cE(q_d,a)$: therefore,

	- \tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)
	\Big)^8
	\bigg]\bigg|
	\le \E[\mathfrak{y}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)^8;\cE^c]
	\le \E[\mathfrak{y}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)^{16}]^{1/2}
	\P(\cE^c)^{1/2}\\
	&\qquad\le
	\frac{\E[ \|\bar{\bg}^a(q_d)\|^{32}]^{1/4}
		\E[ \|\by(q_{d+1})\|^{32} ]^{1/4}}{N^4}
	\P(\cE^c)^{1/2}
	\le e^{-cN}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Essentially the same argument as for \eqref{e:RomII.tilde.discrepancy.second.mmt.bound} also gives
	\beq
	\E\bigg[ \Big\| \by(q_{d+1})-\tilde{\by}(q_{d+1})\Big\|^8\bigg]
	\le \E\Big[ \| \by(q_{d+1})\|^8 ; \cE^c \Big]
	\le e^{-cN}
	\eeq
Now let $\tilde{X}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)$ be the process started from zero with increments $\Delta\tilde{X}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)$. (Again, we consider this for fixed $a\in[M]$, as a process indexed by time $q_d$.) It follows from  \eqref{e:RomII.tilde.discrepancy.second.mmt.bound} above that
	\beq

	\Big(X^{\RomII}(q_d,a)
		-\tilde{X}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)\Big)^8\bigg]
	\le o_N(1)\,.
	\eeq
Note also that $\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)$ is a Lipschitz function of the gaussian input, with Lipschitz constant $L^{O(1)}(\delta_d)^{1/2}$.
Next define the re-centered increments
	\begin{align*}
	\frac{\Delta \bar{X}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)}{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}
	&\equiv
	\frac{\Delta \tilde{X}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)}{[\delta_d p(q_d)]^{1/2}}

		\bigg]\\

	-\E\Big[\tilde{\mathfrak{y}}^{\RomII}(q_d,a)
		\,\Big|\,\cG(q_d)\Big]\,.
	\end{align*}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:55:42.251467+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_609e1200a6ef58ddef16049323908117ce186f9c280acbb68a46eccb43306a9c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:determined of arXiv:2411.16398, 'Large Deviations of Cover Time of Tori in Dimensions $d\\geq 3$'] For a path $\\overline{\\omega} \\in \\overline{\\Psi}(\\mathcal{A})$ and a mapping $\\mathsf{Obj}(\\cdot)$ with domain $\\mathcal{A}$ (e.g., $\\mathcal{L}_{\\boldsymbol{F}}^{\\beta_N}(\\cdot)$, $B(\\cdot)$ in (equation eq: loops to be inserted in STEP1 of the paper), or the mapping that maps $\\omega\\in \\mathcal{A}$ to the loop insertion process described in (equation eq: inserting loops STEP 1 of the paper) etc.), we say that $\\mathsf{Obj}(\\cdot)$ is \\emph{determined} by $\\overline{\\omega}$ if $\\mathsf{Obj}(\\omega)$ is identical for all $\\omega \\in \\mathcal{A}$ satisfying $\\overline{\\omega} \\in \\overline{\\Psi}(\\omega)$.\n    With slight abuse of notation, we also say that $\\mathsf{Obj}(\\omega)$ is determined by $\\overline{\\omega}$ if we assume $\\overline{\\omega} \\in \\overline{\\Psi}(\\omega)$ and the mapping $\\mathsf{Obj}(\\cdot)$ is determined by $\\overline{\\omega}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["central sections (linear subspaces)","Q_n = [-1/2,1/2]^n","the density statement is for the uniform distribution on the cube only"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T01:01:03.840385+00:00","domain":"convex geometry","id":"claim_60a0a21170034ccb810c9ec9bf50076c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let Q_n = [-1/2,1/2]^n and 1 <= k <= n. For every k-dimensional linear subspace H of R^n: vol_k(Q_n \\cap H) <= min{ (n/k)^{k/2}, 2^{(n-k)/2} }. The first bound is attained when k divides n (H spanned by the sums of the coordinate vectors over k disjoint blocks of size n/k); the second is the smaller one and is attained when k >= n/2. Equivalently, a central section of codimension m has volume <= min{ (n/(n-m))^{(n-m)/2}, 2^{m/2} }, with 2^{m/2} attained when m <= n/2. Probabilistic form: if U is uniform on Q_n and P is the orthogonal projection onto an m-dimensional subspace E, the density of PU is largest at 0, where it equals vol_{n-m}(Q_n \\cap E^perp); hence it is at most min{ (n/(n-m))^{(n-m)/2}, 2^{m/2} } <= 2^{m/2}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:53.184789+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60ea7137d71e72118b919b8690b19d30d0e9abb6c125b298a7c286ad72fbf6c8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 14 (Endpoint-safe phase-bin package) of arXiv:2606.11758, '2606.11758'] For every \(\xi\in\mathbb R^2\setminus\{0\}\), the following conclusions hold.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item Partition of unity.  The functions above satisfy
\[
    \chi_{\xi,0}(t)
    +
    \chi_{\xi,1}(t)
    +
    \chi_{\xi,\mathrm{sd}}(t)
    +
    \sum_{d\in\mathfrak D_\xi}\chi_{\xi,d}(t)
    =
    1
    \qquad (0\le t\le1).
\]

\item Size of the safe region.  Let
\[
    E_\xi
    =
    \operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,0}
    \cup
    \operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,1}
    \cup
    \operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,\mathrm{sd}}.
\]
Then
\[
    |E_\xi|\le C_\gamma|\xi|^{-1/2}.
\]

\item Localization of each derivative band.  For each
\(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi\), set
\(
    S_{\xi,d}=\operatorname{spt}\chi_{\xi,d}.
\)
Then
\[
    S_{\xi,d}
    \subset
    \left\{
        t\in[0,1]:
        C_\gamma^{-1}d
        \le
        h_\xi(t)^{1/2}
        \le
        C_\gamma d
    \right\}.
\]

\item Phase-derivative bounds on each band.  For each
\(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi\), one has
\[
    c_\gamma|\xi|d
    \le
    |\varphi_\xi'(t)|
    \le
    C_\gamma|\xi|d
    \qquad (t\in S_{\xi,d}).
\]

\item Range and number of active dyadic scales.  The active dyadic scales
satisfy
\[
    C_\gamma^{-1}|\xi|^{-1/2}\le d\le C_\gamma
    \qquad (d\in\mathfrak D_\xi),
\]
and
\[
    \#\mathfrak D_\xi
    \le
    C_\gamma(1+\log(2+|\xi|)).
\]

\item Thickening estimate for each band.  For every \(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi\)
and every integer \(\ell\ge0\),
\[
    \left|
    \left\{
        t\in[0,1]:
        \operatorname{dist}(t,S_{\xi,d})\le2^{-\ell}
    \right\}
    \right|
    \le
    C_\gamma(d+2^{-\ell}).
\]

\item Bounded-variation integration-by-parts estimate.  For every
\(d\in\mathfrak D_\xi\),
\[
    \int_0^1
    \frac{|\chi_{\xi,d}'(t)|}{|\varphi_\xi'(t)|}\,dt
    \le
    C_\gamma(|\xi|d)^{-1}.
\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:52:32.333436+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60fcdebf44f7289647883a134f1d1e057e3090f40a3b289872a5566c397a7415","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:restrictedtraceoperators of arXiv:2609.03980, 'Decay Rates and Domain Dependence of a Coupled Wave-Heat System with Spatially Dependant H'] Let $\Gamma$ be a relatively open subset of the boundary $\partial \Omega$ of some bounded Lipschitz domain $\Omega \subset \mathbb{R}^n$.
 
 \begin{enumerate}
     \item  The restriction of ${\operatorname{tr}}(f)$ to $\Gamma$ for $f\in H^1(\Omega)$ induces the restricted trace operator 
    $${\operatorname{tr}}^{\Gamma}:H^1(\Omega)\to H^{1/2}(\Gamma), f\mapsto {\operatorname{tr}}(f)|_{\Gamma},$$
    which is again bounded and surjective, see e.g.  Proposition 1.2.60 in [Meinlschmidt].
    \item We define the Lions-Magenes space $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ as the subspace of functions $f\in H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$, for which the extension by zero $\Tilde{f}$ to $\partial\Omega$ is again an element of $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$. If $n=1$, one clearly has $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma) = H^{1/2}(\Gamma)$. If $n\geq 2$, then $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ is an intrinsic, i.e., independent of $\partial\Omega$, Hilbert space when equipped with the norm
    \begin{align*}
        \|f\|_{H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)}  \coloneq  \left(\|f\|_{H^{1/2}(\Gamma)} +\int_\Gamma  \frac{|u(x)|^2}{\dist(x,\partial \Gamma)} \;\mathrm{d} x\right)^{1/2},
    \end{align*} see e.g.\ Chapter~33 in [tartar2007introduction].
    This norm is equivalent to the $H^{1/2}(\partial\Omega)$-norm of the zero extension $\Tilde{f}$.
    Additionally, denote by $H^{-1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ the dual space of $H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$.
    \item We define the restricted normal trace operator
    $${\operatorname{tr}}^{\Gamma}_N:H^{\operatorname{div}}(\Omega)\to H^{-1/2}_{0}(\Gamma), f\mapsto \left( H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)\to \mathbb{C}, g\mapsto
    \duality{{\operatorname{tr}}_N(f)}{\Tilde{g}}\right),$$ where 
    $\Tilde{g}$ denotes the extension by zero to $\partial\Omega$ of an element $g\in H^{1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$.
    
    The restricted normal trace operator ${\operatorname{tr}}^{\Gamma}_N:H^{\operatorname{div}}(\Omega)\to H^{-1/2}_{0}(\Gamma)$ is well-defined, bounded and surjective, see Lemma~(lem:normaltracesurj of the paper).
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.696523+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_60fd8a2a114e1494985da199b55e960f57466fdc983c5520b03f39cd28f13559","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:first-exit of arXiv:2609.00645, 'Global persistence of nearly radial concentrated vortices in a bounded domain'] Let $V\subset\mathbb R^m$ be bounded and open, and suppose that
$w\in C(\overline V)$ has a unique minimum point
$\mathbf p_*\in V$ on $\overline V$.  Let
$d:\mathbb R\to[0,\infty)$ be continuous, and let $S$ be a set-valued
map from $\mathbb R$ to $\mathbb R^m$ with nonempty compact values.  Fix
$\delta>0$.  Then there exist $\eta_*,r_*>0$, depending only on $V,w,\delta$,
with the following property.

Assume that $S$ is upper semicontinuous\footnote{As in
(lem:centers of the paper)(vi), this means that, for every $t_0\in\mathbb R$ and every open
set $O\subset\mathbb R^m$ with $S(t_0)\subset O$, there exists $\sigma>0$ such that
$S(t)\subset O$ whenever $|t-t_0|<\sigma$.} and that
\[
  \operatorname{diam}S(t)\leq r_*
  \quad\text{whenever }d(t)\leq\delta,
\]
and that
\begin{equation}
  d(t)+\sup_{\mathbf b\in S(t)}[w(\mathbf b)-w(\mathbf p_*)]
  \leq\eta_*
\end{equation}
whenever $S(t)\subset\overline V$ and $d(t)\leq\delta$.
Then $S(0)\subset V$ and $d(0)<\delta$ imply that
$S(t)\subset V$ and $d(t)<\delta$ for every $t\in\mathbb R$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["h is a Gaussian free field with Dirichlet (or otherwise precisely specified) boundary conditions on domain D","U is a deterministic, or at least suitably measurable stopping-domain, subdomain of D","the Green's function and harmonic measure for D and U are well defined, requiring sufficient domain regularity","correct identification of phi_U as harmonic in U with boundary values equal to h on the boundary of U"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.988093+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_611d06babfa0bac3e6ad00051e94ec2a9160b2c2c47e76bdc0ac9037b7eb263d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). Let h be a (discrete or continuum) Gaussian free field on a domain D with Dirichlet boundary conditions, and let U be a deterministic subdomain of D. The Gibbs-Markov (domain Markov) property states that h decomposes as h = h_U + phi_U, where h_U is a zero-boundary Gaussian free field on U, phi_U is the harmonic extension into U of the values of h on the boundary of U, h_U and phi_U are independent of each other, and phi_U is measurable with respect to the sigma-field generated by h restricted to the complement of U. This is the discrete and continuum analogue of the strong Markov property for Brownian motion and harmonic functions, and it is the fundamental tool enabling induction-on-scale arguments, the theory of local sets, and the construction of conformally invariant objects such as Liouville quantum gravity from the field. It does not hold for general non-Gibbsian or non-Gaussian log-correlated fields without separate verification, and it requires exact specification of the domain and boundary conditions, since the decomposition depends on the harmonic extension operator for the particular pair (D,U) being used. Typical failure: Applying the plain Gibbs-Markov decomposition with U chosen depending on the field h itself, such as a random subdomain determined by a level set or an exploration process, without checking that U is a valid stopping domain for the field's filtration; naively random domains destroy the independence between h_U and phi_U, and the correct fix requires the more delicate theory of local sets developed by Schramm and Sheffield, not the plain domain Markov property. Canonical reference: Sheffield, 2007, Probability Theory and Related Fields; Schramm and Sheffield, 2013, Probability Theory and Related Fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:06:21.678290+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_612d004af7a82a0706428c51dc3c37064ef488932cfce8c110e2a102dfb08a9c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 51 (Finite-order uniform form of the chain density estimate) of arXiv:2607.20882, 'An Eyring--Kramers Law for the Hypoelliptic Third-Order\\ Langevin Diffusion'] Fix the chain length $n=3$, the block dimension $d$, and $T<\infty$.
Fix also $p>2$ and an inverse-moment order $q<\infty$.  There is an integer
$N=N(d,p,q)$ with the following property.  Consider a family of smooth
third-order chain diffusions in the block order
$X^1,X^2,X^3$, centered at the deterministic trajectory as in
\cite[(D2)]{Pigato2022}.  Suppose uniformly over the family that:
\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(P\arabic*)},leftmargin=2.6em]
\item the initial points and initial drift values are bounded;
\item the weak H\"ormander matrix in hypothesis \textup{(H1)} of
\cite{Pigato2022} has smallest singular value at least $\lambda_0>0$;
\item all positive-order spatial derivatives of orders $1,\ldots,N$, together
with their first time derivatives, are bounded on
$[0,T]\times\R^{3d}$;
\item the diffusion coefficient is bounded together with the derivatives
through the same order.
\end{enumerate}
Let
\[
\mathsf T_t
:=\operatorname{diag}\left(t^{1/2}I_d,t^{3/2}I_d,t^{5/2}I_d\right)
\]
and let $\Gamma_t^{\rm sc}$ be the Malliavin covariance of the centered,
scaled variable $\mathsf T_t^{-1}(X_t-\vartheta_t)$, where
$\vartheta_t$ is the deterministic trajectory from \cite[(D2)]{Pigato2022}.
Then
\begin{equation}

\sup_{0<t\le T}\E\!\left[
\lambda_{\min}(\Gamma_t^{\rm sc})^{-q}\right]\le C_q,
\end{equation}
where, for a symmetric non-negative matrix $M$,
$\lambda_{\min}(M):=\inf_{|v|=1}v^\top Mv$
denotes its smallest eigenvalue.
For the same statement, after taking $N$ to be the maximum of the finitely
many orders used in the two conclusions, the transition density
$q(t,\xi,y)$
satisfies
\begin{equation}

q(t,\xi,y)
\le
\frac{C_p t^{-9d/2}}
{1+|\mathsf T_t^{-1}(y-\vartheta_t)|^p},
\qquad 0<t\le T,\quad y\in\R^{3d}.
\end{equation}
The constants depend only on
$d,T,p,q,\lambda_0$ and the finitely many coefficient bounds above.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:06.980171+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6132a6727715a5fe5011f77aaea2e2ab6686a303f46bc391bad4b388e631a6a4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm2_3 of arXiv:2607.26169, 'Scaling and partial universality of the height zero probability in the 2D Abelian sandpile'] Let $U\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a bounded connected region satisfying Assumption (a:U of the paper)(i). Let \(g : W\rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) be a $C^1$ function on an open set \(W\) containing \(\partial U_\epsilon\) for all \(\epsilon > 0\) sufficiently small. Let \(u : U \cup \partial U \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) denote the solution to the Laplace equation on \(U\) with Dirichlet boundary condition \(g\). For \(\epsilon > 0\) such that \(\partial U_\epsilon \subset W\), let \(u_\epsilon : U_\epsilon \cup \partial U_\epsilon \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) denote the solution to the discrete Laplace equation on \(U_\epsilon\) with Dirichlet boundary condition \(u_\epsilon = g\) on \(\partial U_\epsilon\). \\
    (i) The family of functions \((u_\epsilon)\) satisfy
    \[
        u_\epsilon = u + \mathcal{O}(\varepsilon) \; \text{ as } \epsilon \downarrow 0,
    \]
    where the error term is locally uniform. Moreover, the error term is also uniform 
    in $U$, as long as $|g|$ remains under a fixed bound, and the distance from 
    $\partial U$ is bounded away from $0$.\\
    (ii) Furthermore, for \(z \in U\) and \(e \in \varepsilon \mathcal{E}\) an edge incident 
    with $z_\varepsilon$, we have 
    \[
        \partial_e u_\epsilon(z_\epsilon) 
        = u_\epsilon(z_\epsilon + e)-u_\epsilon(z_\epsilon)
        = \varepsilon \tilde{e} \cdot \nabla u (x) + O(\varepsilon^2), \; \text{as } \epsilon \downarrow 0,
    \]
    where $\tilde{e} = e/\varepsilon$ is the corresponding vector in $\mathcal{E}$. 
    The error term satisfies the same uniformity statement as in part (i). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["All explicit definitions in proofs/BOUNDED_RELU_PAIRED.md","Even width; independent Gaussian hidden-weight pairs with equal hidden weights and opposite heads +/-nu, nu fixed in (0,1]; neurons are not iid","Unit-norm centered ReLU teacher with a nonzero interaction Walsh coefficient on the support","Noise standard deviation c_e=e^2/sqrt((1+e^2+e^4)(1+e^2)) tends to zero; n=4 stratified training and uniform test support","Risk averaged over sixteen independent label-noise sign patterns; GD step 1/2; width limit precedes feature-scale limit"],"created_at":"2026-10-22T00:34:14.190364+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_6150b2543bd28a2853e880d5bd25f8624c1e1b6cb15383b4cea07167bb4daeae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"# Unit-norm nonlinear ReLU teacher with paired initialization

T267 / Target 1 / C010 / proof draft (unaudited); novelty unestablished.

This removes the diverging teacher norm in C009, at the price of paired
initialization and noise that shrinks with the signal. It is a restricted
four-point, stratified-design, noise-averaged theorem. It does not establish
the generic iid Gaussian-input target or a fixed-positive-noise result.
The hardest remaining target step is sign-level population-risk control
for a genuinely sampled nonlinear model beyond this finite-support
infinite-width construction.

## Statement

Fix nu in (0,1]. For 0<e<1/4 let D=1+e^2+e^4 and use the same four inputs
x_(s,t)=(1,e s,e^2 t)/sqrt(D), s,t in {-1,1}. Training contains each once;
the test law is uniform on these four points. Let

u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2),
c_e=e^2/[sqrt(D)*sqrt(1+e^2)], alpha_e=c_e/2,
g_e(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-E_X ReLU(u_e.X).

The vector u_e has norm one. On this support u_e.x=c_e(s+t), so

g_e(x_(s,t))=alpha_e(s+t+st).

Thus the teacher is genuinely nonlinear even when restricted to the
support: no affine function of x has a nonzero st Walsh coefficient.
The centering constant is the population mean c_e/2. Labels are g_e(x_i)
plus independent equiprobable noise +/-c_e, so the noise standard deviation
is c_e, not a fixed positive constant as e decreases.

Take even width m=2N and initialize each independent pair by
w_(2j-1)=w_(2j)=W_j iid N(0,I_3),
a_(2j-1)=nu, a_(2j)=-nu.
Pairs are independent; the individual neurons are NOT iid. Initially f=0
exactly. Train both layers of every neuron by simultaneous GD at step 1/2,
loss ||f(X)-y||^2/(2n), n=4, with f=m^(-1/2) sum a ReLU(w.x) and gate
convention 1_{z>0}. No symmetry is imposed after initialization.

Let Q_(m,e)(k) be clean population squared risk, averaged over the sixteen
training-label-noise patterns, conditional on initialization. Let b_h be
C009's rates for the full initial tangent kernel h_nu=k+nu^2 g1, with mode
indices 0,1,2,12. Set

k0=ceil(e^(-1/2)), k1=floor(log(2)/b1),
k2=ceil(e^(-3/2)), k3=floor(log(2)/b2),
B=log[b1/(b2+b12)].

In the iterated limit m=2N->infinity first, then e->0, the probability of
failure of the strict witnesses

Q(k0)>Q(k1)<Q(k2)>Q(k3)

tends to zero. More precisely the four risks divided by alpha_e^2 converge
in probability, in that iterated sense, to 4,7/2,4,3.
For every fixed delta>0, every maximizer k_peak on the integer interval
I_e=[floor((B-1)/b1),ceil((B+1)/b1)] is interior and satisfies
|b1 k_peak-B|<delta with probability tending to one in the same iterated
sense. Consequently

k_peak ~ (4*pi/nu^2) e^(-1) log(1/e).

This localizes a central local peak, not a global maximum or all extrema.

## 1. Teacher identity and exact initialization

ReLU(s+t) takes values 2,0,0,0, whose mean is 1/2. Its centered version is
(s+t+st)/2. The unit norm and displayed teacher identity follow directly.
The nonzero interaction coefficient rules out an affine teacher on the
four inputs, even though two projections lie exactly at the teacher's
ReLU kink. No differentiability of the teacher is used in training.

Each pair has exactly cancelling outputs. Its two readout-Jacobian Gram
summands are identical. Its two hidden-Jacobian Gram summands are also
identical because their readout factors are squared. Dividing by m=2N
therefore gives the same expected full kernel as in C009:

C_(nu,e)(i,l)=[k(x_i.x_l)+nu^2 g1(x_i.x_l)]/4.

Strong laws apply to the N independent pairs. No independent-neuron
concentration or centered independent readout-sign argument is needed.

## 2. Transfer from the actual nonlinear GD

Here we specify why C009 Section 3 applies despite correlated pairs.
For e<1/4, c_e<e^2<1/16. The largest absolute teacher value is 3c_e/2;
the largest label magnitude is at most 5c_e/2<5/32. Thus ||y||<5/16<2.
The actual initial output is identically zero; use M=0 and R_0=2 in the
deterministic finite-horizon recurrences of C009 Section 3. Those bounds
are neuronwise and use no independence. They hold separately for both
members of every pair, even after their hidden weights separate.

The empirical mean of initial squared hidden norms converges almost surely
to 3 by the pairwise strong law. The weighted initial gate-band mass is
now exactly the mean over N independent W_j of
(1+||W_j||)^2 1{min_i|W_j.x_i| <= D_* (1+||W_j||)/sqrt(2N)}.
It tends to zero by the same rational-band strong-law and dominated-
convergence argument as C009. The initial kernel converges entrywise to
C by the pairwise strong law. These are the only probabilistic inputs to
the instantaneous-kernel and exact discrete-step remainder bounds in C009.
Their finite-horizon telescoping proof therefore gives

max_(k<=T) ||f_actual(k)-f_frozen(k)|| -> 0 in probability

for every fixed e,nu,T, uniformly over all sixteen noise patterns. The
frozen iteration starts at zero exactly. Here and below T may depend on e;
width tends to infinity separately for each fixed e. This does not claim a
uniform feature-scale rate or a feasible numerical width.

## 3. Risk margins

All three nonconstant teacher Walsh coefficients are alpha=alpha_e.
Independent +/-c_e label noise has Walsh variances c_e^2/4=alpha^2.
Parseval and the zero initial prediction give the exact frozen risk

Q_e^0(k)/alpha^2 = (1-q0^k)^2
                 + sum_(h=1,2,12) [q_h^(2k)+(1-q_h^k)^2],
q_h=exp(-b_h).

C009 Section 2 supplies b1~nu^2 e/(4pi), b2~nu^2 e^2/(8pi),
b12/b2->1, and b0 bounded away from zero. At k0 all nonconstant modes
remain unlearned, giving 1+1+1+1=4. At k1 the fast component has q1->1/2
and the two slow components remain at one, giving 1+1/2+1+1=7/2.
At k2 the fast component has q1->0 while slow components remain at one,
giving 4. At k3 both slow components have q->1/2, giving 1+1+1/2+1/2=3.
The three strict limiting margins are 1/2,1/2,1. For fixed e, alpha>0 and
the finite-horizon transfer changes risk by o_P(1), hence by o_P(alpha^2)
as width grows; division by a fixed positive alpha^2 is legitimate.
Then let e decrease. This proves the four strict actual-risk witnesses.

## 4. Central peak

Interpolate the frozen curve continuously and put z=(B+s)/b1 with
B=log[b1/(b2+b12)]. Uniformly for s in compact intervals,

(Q_e^0)'(z)/[2 alpha^2 (b2+b12)] -> exp(-s)-1,
(Q_e^0)''(z)/[2 alpha^2 b1 (b2+b12)] -> -exp(-s).

Indeed each nonconstant mode contributes 2 alpha^2 b_h q_h(1-2q_h).
The fast term contributes exp(-s); its quadratic correction is
O((b2+b12)/b1). The two slow terms contribute -b2/(b2+b12) and
-b12/(b2+b12), up to errors O(((b2+b12)/b1) B). The constant-mode
term and its derivatives vanish faster than any polynomial of e.
The same estimates after one further differentiation give the stated
second derivative. Thus the frozen central peak has scaled coordinate
s_e->0 and a strict value gap away from any fixed delta neighborhood,
of order alpha^2 (b2+b12)/b1, by integrating the derivative on [-1,1].
The grid spacing b1 tends to zero, so discrete maximizers obey the same
localization. When delta>=1, the conclusion follows from any smaller
positive delta, and interval endpoints are excluded as well.

For each fixed e the interval is finite and its positive peak gap is a
fixed positive number. Section 2 therefore transfers the maximizer
localization to the actual risk with probability tending to one as width
grows. No random initial-output perturbation occurs. Finally
b1/(b2+b12)~1/e and b1~nu^2 e/(4pi) give the peak asymptotic.

## Scope and dependencies

This proof depends on the unaudited deterministic bounds and Gaussian
kernel asymptotics in C009, not on an independent audit or a floating-point
fit. Pair cancellation is only an initial condition, not frozen weights.
The centering offset is part of the single-index link ReLU(z)-c_e/2.
The teacher has uniformly unit norm and is nonlinear on the support;
its variation and the label-noise standard deviation both vanish as e^2.
The design remains stratified, finite support, with every test input in
training, and risk averages over labels. No fixed-noise, iid-design,
macroscopic feature-learning, full-target or novelty claim is made.
Primary kernel source: Heckel--Yilmaz arXiv:2007.10099v2 Section 3 K1/K2.
The existence of two noise thresholds in Stephenson--Lee 2108.12006 is not
used to infer that this model has the same noise window.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:52:17.372527+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6155a0d96c1f2a7df9adb75c5625d18e43954de54d37afea2a85c30cdc936d58","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 5 (Breuer-Major in rough Hölder topology) of arXiv:2606.04179, 'Functional Scaling Limits of Interpolated Correlated Random Walks in Hölder Topology'] Assume the correlation \(\rho\) satisfies
    \[
        \tag{summable ``thin tail''}

    second level is given by the Stratonovich integral. Specifically define the scaled

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:44:17.439469+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_615bb5c1701bd2d226fd69ca98ed6ef67afcf4fe82e9b9a550ed52f8bc7fdd0b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:chernoff of arXiv:2608.24087, 'Knowing When to Ask for Help: Bayesian Self-Escalation in Hierarchical LLM Agents'] Assume a finite signal alphabet and let
\begin{equation}
  C \;=\; -\log\ \min_{s\in[0,1]}\ \sum_{k} f_0(k)^{s} f_1(k)^{1-s}
\end{equation}
be the Chernoff information of $(f_0,f_1)$, with $C>0$ iff $f_0\neq f_1$. Then
for every fixed $\tau\in(0,1)$ there is a constant $A_\tau<\infty$, independent
of $t$, such that
\[
  \mathbb{P}\big(B_t\le\tau \mid Y=1\big)\;\le\;A_\tau\,e^{-tC},
  \qquad
  \mathbb{P}\big(B_t\ge\tau \mid Y=0\big)\;\le\;A_\tau\,e^{-tC}.
\]
Consequently $B_t\to\mathbf{1}\{Y=1\}$ almost surely, and the oracle's step-$t$
thresholded decision errs with probability at most $A_\tau e^{-tC}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.359970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_6164626031dbe84f0438c1f9ea9bb51a2b7ef90083e022c246bbf50fd4cd46c1","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 250 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Suppose the random vector $\bX$ in $\R^N$ is \emph{subgaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$}, meaning that $(\theta,\bX)$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$ for all $\theta$ in the unit ball $B_N\subset\R^N$. Then
    \[
    \P\bigg(\frac{\|\bX\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge t\bigg)
    \le \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{16\sigma^2} \bigg\}
    \]
provided $t\ge 6\sigma$. It follows that
$\E(\|\bX\|^p) \le  C_p \sigma^p N^{p/2}$
where $C_p$ is a constant depending only on $p$.

\begin{proof}
To bound the norm of a random vector $\bX$ in $\R^N$, the standard argument is to let $N_{1/2}$ be a $1/2$-net of the unit ball $B\subset \R^N$, and note that
    \begin{align*}
    \|\bX\|
    &= \sup \Big\{
    (\theta,\bX) : \theta\in B\Big\}
    \le 
    \sup\bigg\{
    (\theta_1+\theta_2,\bX):
    \theta_1\in N_{1/2},
    \theta_2\in \frac12 B\bigg\} \\
    &\le
    \sup\Big\{(\theta,\bX) :\theta\in N_{1/2}\Big\}
    + \frac{\|\bX\|}{2}
    \equiv S + \frac{\|\bX\|}{2} \,.
    \end{align*}
Rearranging the above gives
    \[\|\bX\|
    \le 2\sup\Big\{(\theta,\bX) :\theta\in N_{1/2}\Big\}
    = 2S\,.
    \]
We can arrange for $|N_{1/2}| \le 6^N$. If $(\theta,\bX)$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $\sigma^2$ for all $\theta\in B_N$, then a union bound over the net $N_{1/2}$ gives
    \beq
    \P\bigg(\frac{\|\bX\|}{N^{1/2}} \ge 2t\bigg)
    \le \P(S \ge N^{1/2} t)
    \le 6^N 
    \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{2\sigma^2}\bigg\}
    \le \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{4\sigma^2}\bigg\}\,,
    \eeq
where the last bound holds provided
$t\ge 3\sigma$. Integrating (similarly to \eqref{e:subgaus.mmt}) gives the moment bound
    \beq
    \frac{\E[ \|\bX\|^p]}{N^{p/2}}
    \le
    \frac{2^p \E(S^p)}{N^{p/2}}
    \le (6\sigma)^p
    +2^p \int_{3\sigma}^\infty
    pt^{p-1}
    \exp\bigg\{ -\frac{Nt^2}{4\sigma^2}\bigg\}\, dt
    \le C_p \sigma^p
    \eeq
for a constant $C_p$ depending only on $p$.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
