{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:33.595011+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_780a34cf99432152b10899cdd580dbdd2b800f24e54f58db93caaf547e75a987","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Abstract of arXiv:2609.02362, '\\textbf{Farthest-cell triplet entropy: high-dimensional shell limits and hyperbolic...'] We introduce farthest-cell triplet entropy, the conditional Shannon entropy of the farthest-prototype label given three random prototypes. For independent queries and prototypes, its estimator records only the farthest label, not coordinates or numerical distances. The statistic is bounded by $\\log 3$, is invariant under common strictly increasing transformations of the dissimilarities, and has an exact mutual-information interpretation. In high-dimensional isotropic radial models $X_d=R_dU_d$, the Euclidean ordering reduces to scores $\\lambda_d\\xi_{i,d}-Z_i$, where $\\lambda_d=\\sqrt d\\,\\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\\E R_d$ and the $Z_i$ are independent standard Gaussian variables. This gives angular-dominated, intermediate, and radial-dominated entropy limits $\\log 3$, $\\Hinf(\\lambda;F)$, and $0$. In hyperbolic space of curvature $-\\kappa_d^2$, the same master curve appears at $\\lambda_{d,\\mathbb H}=\\sqrt d\\,\\tau_d A(s_d)$, where $\\tau_d=\\operatorname{sd}(R_d)/\\E R_d$, $s_d=\\kappa_d\\E R_d$, and $A(s)=s\\coth s$. With a calibrated radial law and $\\tau_d$, and a monotone operating interval, entropy inversion identifies the scale-invariant target $s_d^2$; absolute curvature requires an external length unit. CPU simulations give Euclidean and hyperbolic master-curve RMSEs of $0.0164$ and $0.0209$. Inversion from observed synthetic latent coordinates has a median relative error in $\\kappa$ of $6.6\\%$, while angular anisotropy increases this error to $68.9\\%$. Thus the entropy statistic is comparison-based, whereas curvature recovery remains model-calibrated, is not graph-only, and is not robust to anisotropy.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f(t, .) is mu-integrable for every t in the open interval I","t -> f(t, omega) is differentiable on I for mu-a.e. omega","a single g in L^1(mu) dominates |d_t f(t, omega)| for ALL t in I (or on a neighbourhood of each point of I)"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.751130+00:00","domain":"measure theory","id":"claim_7822c113585052dd029ffd5524924ae4013b85f7e3c8560bfcb2f576ac848d43","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, F, mu) be a measure space, I a nonempty open interval of R, and f : I x Omega -> R with: (i) for every t in I the function omega -> f(t, omega) is mu-integrable; (ii) for mu-almost every omega the map t -> f(t, omega) is differentiable on I, with derivative d_t f(t, omega); (iii) there exists g in L^1(mu) with |d_t f(t, omega)| <= g(omega) for all t in I and mu-almost every omega. Then F(t) = integral f(t, omega) dmu(omega) is differentiable on I and F'(t) = integral d_t f(t, omega) dmu(omega). It suffices to have (iii) LOCALLY: for each t_0 in I a neighbourhood J of t_0 and g_{t_0} in L^1 dominating |d_t f| on J x Omega, since differentiability is local. The dominating function must dominate the DERIVATIVE and must not depend on t; a bound |f(t, omega)| <= g(omega) on the function itself is not enough. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.881531+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78322578f68fa80283707170c6e3d2fafa0ea032a9c87780340bca030a8bfd83","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let  $(X,\mathcal{X},\mu,\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ be a Dirichlet structure. The \emph{generator} $A:D(A) \to L^2(X,\mu)$ is the linear operator with domain
		\[
		D(A):= \{ f\in \mathcal{F} \vert \mbox{there exists $C>0$ such that $\abs{\mathcal{E}(f,g)} \le C \norm{g}_{L^2(\mu)}$ for all $g \in \mathcal{F}$}\}.
		\]
		For any $f \in D(A)$, the element $A(f) \in L^2(X,\mu)$ is defined by
		\[
		\mathcal{E}(f,g)= -\langle A(f), g \rangle_{L^2(\mu)}.
		\] 
		
		We define the \emph{energy measure} as $\Gamma(f,g)= \gamma(f,g)\cdot \mu$ for all $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$, where $\gamma: \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{F} \to L^1(X,\mu)$ is the associated carr\'e du champ.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377679+00:00","domain":"set theory","id":"claim_783ee34fc14e104fa620373620d7e9f6dc197a014b894eb8ac44b832183c96a2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Two sets A and B are equinumerous (have the same cardinality, written |A| = |B|) when there exists a bijection from A onto B. One writes |A| <= |B| when there is an injection from A into B. Equinumerosity is an equivalence relation, and <= is reflexive and transitive; by the Schroder-Bernstein theorem it is antisymmetric up to bijection (|A| <= |B| and |B| <= |A| imply |A| = |B|), all without the axiom of choice. With the axiom of choice any two sets are comparable (trichotomy), and every set is equinumerous with a unique initial ordinal, its cardinal number. A set is finite if it is equinumerous with {1, ..., n} for some natural number n; countably infinite if equinumerous with the set N of natural numbers; countable if finite or countably infinite; uncountable otherwise. Strict inequality |A| < |B| means |A| <= |B| and there is no bijection between A and B.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:02:06.330894+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_784ec7e2ed65fb70a81235dc60632904164a652abe4233610a860a630d9bf272","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 4 (Cameron-Martin) of arXiv:2607.06745, 'Regularization and asymptotic behaviour of Ornstein-Uhlenbeck evolution operators in infin'] \textcolor{red}{ }Let $a\in X$ and $Q\in\mathcal{L}\left(X\right)$

\[

iii)\  & \gamma\circ\widehat{h}^{-1}\sim\mathcal{N}\left(0,\left|Q^{-\frac{1}{2}}h\right|_{X}^{2}\right).
\end{align*}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:48:45.325887+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78698a32534138f93485047001179ba5571382992d7a76530f6981165ef357f2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition p:StandardCyl of arXiv:2411.14936, 'Massive Particle Systems,\\Wasserstein Brownian Motions,\\ and the Dean--Kawasaki Equation'] Fix~$\pi\in\msP(\mbfT_\circ)$.

Then,
\begin{enumerate}[$(i)$]
\item the space of cylinder functions~$\FC{\msA}{}$ is a Markovian subspace of~$\msD(\widehat\mcE_\pi)$;
\item the quadratic form~$\tparen{\widehat\mcE_\pi,\FC{\msA}{}}$ is closable on~$L^2(\mcQ_\pi)$.
Its closure \linebreak $\big({\mcE_\pi,\msD(\mcE_\pi)}\big)$ is a conservative strongly local Dirichlet form;
\item the form~$\big({\mcE_\pi,\msD(\mcE_\pi)}\big)$ is $\tau_\mrmn$-regular if and only if~$(M,\tau)$ is compact;
\item if additionally~(equation eq:QPP of the paper) holds, then~$\big({\mcE_\pi,\msD(\mcE_\pi)}\big)=\big({\widehat\mcE_\pi,\msD(\widehat\mcE_\pi)}\big)$ and the identity map $\id\colon (\msP,\tau_\mrma)\to(\msP,\tau_\mrmn)$ is a quasi-homeomorph\-ism.
In particular, the form is additionally $\tau_\mrmn$-quasi-regular.
\end{enumerate}

\begin{proof}
(i:p:StandardCyl:1 of the paper) Since~$\msR_0$ separates points from open sets, by Stone--Weierstra\ss\ Theorem it is dense in~$\mcC_0((0,1])$.
Thus, we can find a sequence~$\left(\varphi_n\right)_n\subset\msR_0$ satisfying~$\lim_{n} \varphi_n=1$ locally uniformly on~$(0,1]$.
Fix~$u=F\circ\mbff^\star\in\FC{\msA}{}$ with~$\mbff=\left(f_1,\dotsc, f_k\right)$, set~$\hat\mbff_n\eqdef \left(\varphi_n \otimes f_1, \dotsc, \varphi_n \otimes f_k\right)$, and~$u_n\eqdef F\circ \hat\mbff_n$.
It follows from~(equation eq:l:DiffusionP:0.1 of the paper) that the function~$\mu\mapsto\widehat\mcG(u_n)_\mu$ is uniformly bounded in~$n$ and converges pointwise on~$\msP$ to a function~$\mu\mapsto \widehat\mcG_\pi(u)_\mu$ defined by the right-hand side of~(equation eq:l:DiffusionP:0.1 of the paper) with~$\mbff$ in place of~$\hat\mbff$.
Thus,~$\widehat\mcG_\pi(u)\in L^1(\mcQ_\pi)$ by Dominated Convergence, and therefore~$u\in \msD(\widehat\mcE)$.
This shows that~$\FC{\msA}{}\subset \msD(\widehat\mcE_\pi)$.
As for its Markovianity, it suffices to notice that~$\FC{\msA}{}$ is closed under post-composition with smooth functions.

Since~$\car\in \FC{\msA}{}$, (i:p:StandardCyl:2 of the paper) is a standard consequence of~(i:p:StandardCyl:1 of the paper), see e.g.~[BouHir91].

(i:p:StandardCyl:3 of the paper)
It is readily seen that~$\FC{\msA}{}$ is a unital point-separating sub-algebra of~$\mcC_b(\tau_\mrmn)$, which proves~(i:d:QuasiReg:2 of the paper) since~$\FC{\msA}{}$ is dense in~$\msD(\mcE_\pi)$ (by definition of the latter).

If~$(M,\tau)$ is compact~$(\msP,\tau_\mrmn)$ too is compact.
Thus~$\FC{\msA}{}$ is uniformly dense in~$\mcC_c(\tau_\mrmn)=\mcC_b(\tau_\mrmn)$ by the above reasoning and Stone--Weierstra\ss\ Theorem.
Again since~$\FC{\msA}{}$ is dense in~$\msD(\mcE_\pi)$, it is a core for~$\big({\mcE_\pi,\msD(\mcE_\pi)}\big)$ which shows that the latter form is $\tau_\mrmn$-regular.

If otherwise~$(M,\tau)$ is not compact, then~$(\msP,\tau_\mrmn)$ is not locally compact, thus~$\big({\mcE_\pi,\msD(\mcE_\pi)}\big)$  is not $\tau_\mrmn$-regular.

(i:p:StandardCyl:4 of the paper) In order to show the equality it suffices to show that~$\hCylP{}{0}\subset\msD(\mcE_\pi)$.
This requires the capacity estimates in Appendix~(app:Capacity of the paper) and is eventually shown in Lemma~(l:CoincidenceDomains of the paper).

Since~$\big({\widehat\mcE_\pi,\msD(\widehat\mcE_\pi)}\big)$ is $\tau_\mrma$-quasi-regular, it admits a $\tau_\mrma$-compact $\widehat\mcE_\pi$-nest~$\left(\mcK_n\right)_n$.
Since~$\tau_\mrmn$ is coarser than~$\tau_\mrma$, the identity~$\id\colon (\msP,\tau_\mrma)\to(\msP,\tau_\mrmn)$ is continuous.
In particular, it is continuous and bijective on the compact Hausdorff space~$(\mcK_n,\tau_\mrma)$ with values in the Hausdorff space~$(\mcK_n,\tau_\mrmn)$.
It is then a standard topological fact that~$\id\colon (\mcK_n,\tau_\mrma) \to (\mcK_n,\tau_\mrmn)$ is a homeomorphism, and that~$\mcK_n$ is $\tau_\mrmn$-compact, hence in particular $\tau_\mrmn$-closed.
Since $\left(\mcK_n\right)_n$ is an $\widehat\mcE_\pi$-nest, it follows that~$\id\colon (\msP,\tau_\mrma)\to(\msP,\tau_\mrmn)$ is a quasi-homeomorphism.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:43:55.659303+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78777a494d1ebb937c61f3d2519ec1a462cfff8698b75503205e420678fb79a0","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem LAN of arXiv:2604.07183, 'Stopping on the last success with unknown odds: asymptotic minimax optimality of the plug-'] Fix~$h>0$ and an integer~$k\ge2$, let
$$
p_n^\pm:=\frac1k\pm\frac{h\sigma_k}{\sqrt n},
\quad
\textrm{with } 
\
\sigma_k:=
\sqrt{\frac1k\Big(1-\frac1k\Big)}
,
$$
write~$N:=n-k$, and let~$\mathbb P^\pm_N$ denote the law of~$(X_1,\ldots,X_N)$ under~$\mathbb P_{p_n^\pm}$, with likelihood ratio~$L_N:=d\mathbb P^+_N/d\mathbb P^-_N$. Then, (i) one has
$$

\textrm{under }\mathbb P^-_N
,
$$
so that, as~$n$ diverges to infinity, the local experiments~$(\mathbb P^-_N,\mathbb P^+_N)$ converge to the Gaussian shift experiment~$(\mathcal N(-h,1),\mathcal N(h,1))$; (ii) if~$Q_n^\pm$ denotes the law of~$(X_1,\ldots,X_N,U)$ under~$\mathbb P_{p_n^\pm}$, where~$U$ realizes the possible internal randomization of a rule (independent of the~$X_t$'s, with a \mbox{$p$-free} distribution), then
$$
1-\mathrm{TV}(Q_n^+,Q_n^-)
\to

$$
as~$n$ diverges to infinity (recall that~$\mathrm{TV}$ denotes the total variation distance).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-02T00:34:53.671792+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_78a165aff9dee2f512703489fc9be11da81a4a7bddf3fb18ed42eadd81d0c818","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Ising model, named after the physicists Ernst Ising and Wilhelm Lenz, is a mathematical model of ferromagnetism in statistical mechanics. The model consists of discrete variables that represent magnetic dipole moments of atomic \"spins\" that can be in one of two states. The spins are arranged in a graph, usually a lattice, allowing each spin to interact with its neighbors. Neighboring spins that agree have a lower energy than those that disagree; the system tends to the lowest energy but heat disturbs this tendency, thus creating the possibility of different structural phases. The two-dimensional square-lattice Ising model is one of the simplest statistical models to show a phase transition. Though it is a highly simplified model of a magnetic material, the Ising model can still provide qualitative and sometimes quantitative results applicable to real physical systems, and in general, it can be seen as a specialization of Stanley's n-vector model for n = 1.","status":"unverified"}

\prod_{i=1}^mf_i(x_i)^{\lambda_i} &\leq \Omega(-c(x_1,\dots,x_m)) \text{ for all } 
\\

one has

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.197231+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78b5f2af63677a8e0ff36d9d7c03fa4cefc36487dd925193649690b73fcabe8d","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 117 (temporal smoothing of budget constraint) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Analogously to \eqref{e:budget.constraint.Ising.plus.coarse} and the bound from Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}, with high probability we have 
	\begin{align*}
	\breve{C}^N(t)
	- \frac{\bar{W}^N(t)^2}{\alpha} 
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}
	+ 3\epsilon^\circ
	\end{align*}
for all $t\in[q_*,1]$. Additionally, with $J^N\equiv J(p^N,\tep,\lambda)$ as  defined by \eqref{e:bad.times.J}, we have
	\[
	\Big|\breve{C}^N(t)
	-\bar{C}^N(t)
	\Big|
	\le \bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}
	\]
for all $t\in[q_*,1] \setminus J^N$.

\begin{proof}
We continue to use the abbreviations introduced above. The function $\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}$ is convex on the expanded domain $\{(b,v,u) : v \ge u^2-2\bar{\lambda}\}$. Recall $\tGam^N\equiv(\tbbb,\tvvv,\tuuu)^N$
and $\TGam^N\equiv(\Tbbb,\Tvvv,\Tuuu)^N$: we have from Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} that
(with high probability)
 $\TGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times \R$, while
$\tGam^N(t,y)$ lies in the expanded domain for all $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$. Lemma~\ref{l:t.smooth.domain} implies, for $(t,y)\in ([q_*,1]\setminus J^N)\times \R$,
	\[
	\bigg|
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \tGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	-\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big( \TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\bigg|
	\le
	\bigg(\frac{ \trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2
	\lambda^{1/2}\,.
	\]
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_{\vY,N,t}*\sphi(y)}\,dy$ proves the second conclusion. For all $(t,y)\in[q_*,1]\times\R$, we can bound
	\begin{align*}
	& \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}
	\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	=
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\bigg( \tE \Big[\sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big]\bigg) \\
	&\qquad\le \tE\bigg[
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big( \sGam(t-\sss,y)\Big)\bigg]
	= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\,.
	\end{align*}
Integrating with respect to $\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy$ gives
	\begin{align*}
	&\breve{C}^N(t)
	=
	\int_{\R} \Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}\Big(\TGam^N(t,y)\Big)
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy
	\le
	\int_{\R}
	\bigg[
	 \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )\,ds\bigg]
	\overline{\varrho_t*\sphi}(y)\,dy \\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg[\int_{\R}
	\Cost_{2\bar{\lambda}}( \sGam(s,y) )
	\overline{\varrho_s*\sphi(y)} \,dy\bigg]\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{C}^N(s)\,ds
	+O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N
	\tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\,,
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate uses the bounds on $\sGam=(\sbbb,\svvv,\suuu)$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.reg}, along with the regularity of the map $t\mapsto \overline{\varrho_s*\sphi}$ proved in Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. 
 Similarly, note that
	\[
	S_t(w)
	\equiv
	\bigg( \int_{\R} w(y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\]
is a concave function. It follows that
	\begin{align*}
	&\bar{W}^N(t)^2 
	=\bigg(\int_{\R} \twww(t,y)^{1/2} \varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	= S_t\bigg(\tE\Big[ \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big]\bigg)
	\ge \tE\bigg[ S_t\Big( \swww(t-\sss,\cdot)\Big)\bigg]\\
	&\qquad= \int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_t*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2\,ds\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\bigg( \int_{\R} \swww(s,y)^{1/2} 
		\varsigma_s*\sphi(y)\,dy\bigg)^2
	\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\\
	&\qquad=
	\int_{\R} \tphi(t-s)
	\tilde{W}^N(s)^2\,ds
	+
	O\bigg[ \bigg(\frac{\trK L}{\sep}\bigg)^{O(1)} 
	(\MAX_N)^2 \TMAX_N \tep^{1/2}\bigg]
	\end{align*}
where the error estimate again follows from Lemmas \ref{l:sp.smooth.reg} and \ref{l:sp.smooth.cty}. The claim then follows by combining with
Lemma~\ref{l:sp.smooth.budget}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:31:49.903450+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78b8151fd8a506bf10bc33657c81d9bd8f046318b73a8610cc25eb24ce0b1758","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma of arXiv:2608.25065, 'Detection of first homology via random geometric graphs in the thermodynamic regime'] \label[lemma]{induction}
    Let $\mathcal{O}, L, \Delta$
    be as in the statement
    of (decomposition of the paper), and
    assume $L \ge (\Delta + 1)4Q\rho r|\log r| + 2r$,
    $r$ satisfies
    (equation r small enough of the paper), and
    the event $A_{Q,\rho}(r)$ holds.
    To reduce clutter, 
    write $K = 4Q \rho r|\log r|$.

    Suppose we are given $\mathcal{D} \subseteq \mathcal{O}$,
    $z \in Z_1(\mathring{G}^n_M(r))$,
    and $\sigma \in C_2(M)$
    such that the following holds:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $\partial \sigma = z$.
        \item For any $x \in |\sigma|$,
        there exists
        $V \in \mathcal{O} \setminus \mathcal{D}$

        \[
            \bar{B}(x, L - d(x)K)

        \[

            \exists U_1,...,U_m \in \mathcal{D} \mbox{ distinct, } x_1,...,x_m, x_{m+1}\in M \\
            \mbox{
            with } x_{m+1}=x, \mbox{ such that for all } 1 \le i \le m, \\
            x_i \in U_i
            \mbox{ and }
            d_M(x_i, x_{i+1}) \le K

            \right\}.

        \mathcal{D}' = \mathcal{D} \cup \{W\},
    \]
    we have:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item $|z - z'| \subseteq W$.
        \item $\partial \sigma' = z'$.
        \item For any $x \in |\sigma'|$,
        there exists
        $V' \in \mathcal{O} \setminus \mathcal{D'}$

            \bar{B}(x, L - d'(x)K)

            x_i \in U_i
            \mbox{ and }
            d_M(x_i, x_{i+1}) \le K

{"assumptions":["G countable, connected and locally finite","p_c(G)>0","Independent bond retention and independent subsequent thinning"],"created_at":"2026-10-10T10:10:00.547767+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78dd3cd1b51d06c4f712031aed8ab877687e0f268587065835d3460c5c471786","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Independent review pending. Let G be a countable connected locally finite graph with p_c(G)>0 and sample iid Bernoulli bond percolation at p_c(G). Almost surely every infinite open component C, regarded as a fixed graph after conditioning on the sampled field, has quenched bond threshold p_c(C)=1. For rational r<1, independent r-thinning of the sampled open bonds is unconditionally iid bond percolation at p_c(G)r<p_c(G), so its probability of any infinite component is zero. Conditioning, then intersecting over rational r and using monotonicity, proves simultaneous failure of percolation below r=1 on every C. Infinitude of C alone therefore supplies no robustness under thinning.","status":"unverified"}

where $e \sim e'$ means that the edges are adjacent in $G$ (and, if $P$ is a cycle, we also have $e_n \sim e_1$), such that the following hold:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.451152+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78e7f9001e04ec0a27742070218a07fa32e55e4e094660e1750dd00ce2833cd7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:conditional-transfer}
For all sufficiently large \(N\), suppose
\(\widehat Q_{N,L}\) and
\(\widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\) are finite for every
\(\varepsilon,\eta>0\).  Suppose also that there exist \(\Phi\in\mathbb R\) and a
function \(F\) on \((0,\infty)^2\) such that
\begin{equation}
 \widehat P_{N,L}(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow F(\varepsilon,\eta)
 \quad\text{for every fixed }\varepsilon,\eta>0,
 \qquad
 F(\varepsilon,\eta)\longrightarrow\Phi
 \quad\text{as }(\varepsilon,\eta)\to(0,0).
\end{equation}
Then
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\le\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\widehat Q_{N,L}
 &\ge\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V).
 
\end{align}
Consequently,
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\le
 \max\{\Phi+\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{up}}(V),
            \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &\ge
 \max\{\Phi-\delta_{L,\mathrm{dr}}^{J,\mathrm{low}}(V),
            \underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}.
 
\end{align}
If both de-regularization defects vanish, then
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N
 \log\widehat{\mathscr C}_{N,L}^J(V)=\Phi
\end{equation}
and the exact identities
\begin{align}
 \limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\},
 \\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)
 &=\max\{\Phi,\underline\Lambda_L^J(V)\}
 
\end{align}
hold.  In particular,
\begin{equation}
 \lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log\mathscr C_N^J(V)=\Phi
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 \overline\Lambda_L^J(V)\le\Phi.
\end{equation}

A concrete sufficient condition for (equation eq:abstract-pressure-bridge of the paper)
is that, for any fixed \(L>0\), the disorder array and \(V\) satisfy the
hypotheses of (thm:bulk-universality of the paper) with \(m=2\).
Indeed, (equation eq:point-Haar-zero-cost of the paper) is automatic.  In this concrete
case,
\[
 \Phi=\Phi_p^{\rm bulk}(V)
 =\sup_{u\in\mathbb R}\{\theta_p(u)-V(u)\}.
\]
When the two de-regularization defects vanish,
(equation eq:exact-universality-iff-localized-defect of the paper) therefore gives a
criterion for the localized branch that is both necessary and sufficient. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:15:34.568719+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_78ed1dffa9492905d1d41734bf53bbc50888f05b16f33564366fe3a65e4bd0dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 60 (singularity models of the two-nut case) of arXiv:2609.03332, 'Singularity Models of Finite-Time K\"ahler-Ricci Flows'] Let $\big(\widehat{M}$, $g (t)\big)$ be as in Theorem \ref{thm:twonut_typeI}, rescaled at the Type I rate as in \S\ref{sec:limits}. According to the first singular time, the pointed Cheeger--Gromov limits are:

\emph{(i) Fiber collapse}, $T = T_F'' < \min_{k \geq 3} \{ T_k^0, T_k^\ell \}$: with arbitrary base points,

\[
\big( \mathbb{CP}^{m_0 + m_\ell + 1} \times \mathbb{C}^{n''} , \; g_{FS} (t) \oplus g_{\mathbb{C}^{n''}} \big) \,, \qquad n'' \;=\; \sum_{k \geq 3} \dim_{\mathbb{C}} N_k \,,
\]

the shrinking Fubini--Study soliton on the fiber times a static flat factor.

\emph{(ii) Contraction at $Q_0$}, $T = \min_{k \geq 3} \{ T_k^0 \} < \min \big\{ T_F'', \min_{k \geq 3} \{ T_k^\ell \} \big\}$: let $\mathcal{I}_0 := \{ k \geq 3 : T_k^0 = T \}$; then $0 < ( m_0 + 1 )\, q_k < p_k$ for every $k \in \mathcal{I}_0$, and with base points on $Q_0$ the limit is

\[
\big( \operatorname{Tot} ( E_{\mathcal{I}_0} ) \times \mathbb{C}^{n''} , \; g_E (t) \oplus g_{\mathbb{C}^{n''}} \big) \,, \qquad E_{\mathcal{I}_0} \;=\; \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{I}_0}^{\oplus ( m_0 + 1 )} \,, \quad c_1 ( \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{I}_0} ) \;=\; - \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_0} q_k\, a_k \,,
\]
where $E_{\mathcal{I}_0}$ is the restriction of the normal bundle $\mathcal{N}_{Q_0}$ to $\prod_{k \in \mathcal{I}_0} N_k$, $g_E (t)$ is the Dancer--Wang shrinking K\"ahler--Ricci soliton of ansatz form \cite[Theorem 3.36]{DW2011}, and $n'' = m_\ell + \sum_{k \geq 3, \, k \not\in \mathcal{I}_0} \dim_{\mathbb{C}} N_k$: the $\mathbb{CP}^{m_\ell}$-factor of $Q_0$ does not contract, and flattens into $\mathbb{C}^{m_\ell}$.

\emph{(iii) Contraction at $Q_\ell$}: the mirror of (ii) under $( s, q_k, m_0 ) \leftrightarrow ( \ell - s, - q_k, m_\ell )$, with $\mathcal{I}_\infty := \{ k \geq 3 : T_k^\ell = T \}$, $0 < - ( m_\ell + 1 )\, q_k < p_k$ for every $k \in \mathcal{I}_\infty$, and limit $\operatorname{Tot} \big( \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{I}_\infty}^{\oplus ( m_\ell + 1 )} \big) \times \mathbb{C}^{n''}$, where $\mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{I}_\infty}^{\oplus ( m_\ell + 1 )}$ is the restriction of $\mathcal{N}_{Q_\ell}$ to $\prod_{k \in \mathcal{I}_\infty} N_k$, $c_1 ( \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{I}_\infty} ) = \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}_\infty} q_k\, a_k$, and $n'' = m_0 + \sum_{k \geq 3, \, k \not\in \mathcal{I}_\infty} \dim_{\mathbb{C}} N_k$.

\emph{(iv) Borderline}, $T = T_F'' = \min_{k \geq 3} \{ T_k^0, T_k^\ell \}$: let $\mathcal{I} := \{ k \geq 3 : T_k^0 = T \} = \{ k \geq 3 : T_k^\ell = T \}$; then $- \frac{p_k}{m_\ell + 1} < q_k < \frac{p_k}{m_0 + 1}$ for every $k \in \mathcal{I}$, and with arbitrary base points the limit is $\widehat{Z} \times \mathbb{C}^{n''}$, where

\[
\widehat{Z} \;:=\; \widehat{M} \Big|_{\prod_{k \in \mathcal{I}} N_k} \;=\; \mathbb{P} \big( \mathcal{O}^{\oplus ( m_0 + 1 )} \oplus \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{I}}^{\oplus ( m_\ell + 1 )} \big) \,, \qquad c_1 ( \mathcal{L}_{\mathcal{I}} ) \;=\; \sum_{k \in \mathcal{I}} q_k\, a_k \,,
\]
carrying its unique compact shrinking K\"ahler--Ricci soliton of ansatz form (uniqueness by Tian--Zhu \cite{TZhu}), and $n'' = \sum_{k \geq 3, \, k \not\in \mathcal{I}} \dim_{\mathbb{C}} N_k$. When $\mathcal{I} = \{ 3, \cdots, r \}$, we have $\widehat{Z} = \widehat{M}$ and the flow is the Fano canonical-class case.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:56.812556+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_791254e7e399998717c9474dc5f2a0192ed4c0f3ea1d23ff076ae18a74577e6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition Separating_Surface_Prop of arXiv:2603.28520, 'The Supercritical Loop O(1) and Random Current Models: Uniqueness and Mixing'] Let $q\in\mathbb{N}_{\geq 2},$ $G=(V,E)$ be a graph and let $E_1,E_3\subseteq E$ be disjoint. \begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]
    \item $E_1$ and $E_2$ are finite.
    \item The induced graph $G(E_2)$ is connected.
    \item Any path $(\gamma_j)_{1\leq j\leq n}$ in $G$ with $\gamma_1\in G(E_1)$ and $\gamma_n\in G(E_3)$ must have a $1<j<n$ with $\gamma_j\in G(E_2).$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.188849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7921c02af68dc652942368cd5bb06586646634155ca82d789995c416a9b6cf61","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 101 (coordinate sum) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For any measure $\rho$ on $[0,1]\times\R^d$, let $\bar{\rho}$ be the measure on $[0,1]\times\R$ that satisfies
	\[
	\int_{t,y} f\bigg(t, \sum_{i=1}^d y^i\bigg)
	\,\rho(dt\,dy)
	= \int_{t,x} f(t,x)
	\,\bar{\rho}(dt\,dx)\,,
	\]
where $t\in[0,1]$, $y\in\R^d$, and $x\in\R$.
As above, let $\vY$ be an $\R^d$-valued semimartingale with drift $\vD$ and covariation $\vQ$. We now consider the one-dimensional projections
	\[
	Y = \sum_{i=1}^d Y^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i=1}^d D^i\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d Q^{ij}\,.
	\]
Then $Y$ is a (one-dimensional) semimartingale with drift $D$ and covariation $Q$. We hereafter abbreviate $\rho\equiv\rho_{\vY}$ for the occupation measure of $\vY$ defined in Definition~\ref{d:intro.cts.occ}.
Then the occupation measure of $Y$ is $\bar{\rho}$. The occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $Y$ are
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{D^i}\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\bar{\rho}_{Q^{ij}}\,.	
	\]
Let $\hvY$ be as defined by Lemma~\ref{l:ideal.smoothed.occ.msr},
and let $\iY$ be the one-dimensional projection, so $\iY(t)=Y(t-\sss)+\mathfrak{x}$ where $(\sss,\mathfrak{x})\sim\bar{\varphi}$ (the density $\varphi$ integrated over $x^1 + \ldots + x^d=\mathfrak{x}$). It follows that $\iY$ has occupation measure $\overline{\rho*\varphi}=\bar{\rho}*\bar{\varphi}$. Similarly, the occupation measures associated to the drift and covariation of $\iY$ have densities
	\[
	\sum_{i=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}
	\,,\quad
	\sum_{i,j=1}^d
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}
		*\varphi}\,.	
	\]
Then, analogously to \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.drift} and \eqref{e:intro.occ.ratio.qv}, we define (with $x$ now a scalar)
	\begin{align}
	
	B(t,x) 
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{D^i}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
		{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,,\\
	A(t,x)
	&\equiv
	\sum_{i,j=1}^D \frac{
	\overline{\rho_{Q^{ij}}*\varphi}(t,x)
	}
	{\overline{\rho*\varphi}(t,x)}\,.
	
	\end{align}
Let $\iX$ be the solution to the (one-dimensional) SDE
	\[
	d\iX(t)
	= B(t,\iX)\,dt
	+A(t,\iX)^{1/2}\,dW(t)\,,
	\]
where $W$ is a one-dimensional standard Brownian motion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.234443+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_792986087db3bc5424c0820217b456467a0df89076a5769424f84da4d611fe3c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 40 (The one-dimensional Stokes tree) of arXiv:2608.14475, '\vspace{-1.2cm}\textbf{Finite Gaussian Reconstruction of Polynomial Orbits:\\ From Correla'] Let \(F\) be a tame Morse polynomial of degree \(m\) in one variable and
fix an admissible direction.  Denote by
\[
 E_0,\ldots,E_{m-1}
\]
the \(m\) decay sectors at infinity.  There is a canonical boundary
isomorphism
\begin{equation}
 \partial:
 H_1^{\mathrm{rd}}(F;\mathbb Z)
 \xrightarrow{\ \simeq\ }
 \widetilde H_0(\{E_0,\ldots,E_{m-1}\};\mathbb Z).
 
\end{equation}
If \(\Gamma_1,\ldots,\Gamma_{m-1}\) is a distinguished integral thimble
basis, join two vertices whenever the corresponding thimble has its two
ends in those sectors.  The resulting oriented graph \(T\) is a spanning
tree.

Let \(\gamma\) be an admissible contour directed from \(E_p\) to \(E_q\).
Then
\begin{equation}
 [\gamma]
 =
 \sum_{e\in[p,q]_T}
 \epsilon_e(p,q)[\Gamma_e],
 \qquad
 \epsilon_e(p,q)\in\{-1,1\},
 
\end{equation}
where \([p,q]_T\) is the unique path from \(p\) to \(q\), and the sign is
positive precisely when the orientation of \(e\) agrees with that path.
Thus the physical Betti row is obtained by a finite path search and all
of its entries belong to \(\{0,\pm1\}\).  If the contour lies on a Stokes
direction, the two lateral trees give the two lateral rows, related by
\eqref{eq:Betti-wall-crossing}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:24:34.416482+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_792a9b1ccd9c07e75edb60d9ee4b32c646efd874e5013dba3626cea525458c6b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 4 of arXiv:2608.31145, 'Gauge-compatible tensors on statistical manifolds: splitting and submanifold geometry'] Let $(M,g,\nabla,\nabla^{*},\Theta)$ be a $\Theta$-statistical manifold. Then
\[
R^{\nabla}(X,Y)\Theta Z
=
\Theta\,R^{\nabla^{*}}(X,Y)Z,
\]
for all $X,Y,Z\in\Gamma(TM)$.

If $\Theta$ is invertible, then
\[
R^{\nabla}(X,Y)
=
\Theta\circ R^{\nabla^{*}}(X,Y)\circ\Theta^{-1}.
\]

Moreover, for every piecewise smooth loop $\gamma$ based at $p$,
\[
\mathcal{P}^{\nabla}_{\gamma}\circ\Theta_p
=

{"assumptions":["a sequence of (random) rooted graphs with controlled local neighborhoods, such as bounded degree, sufficient for tightness","existence of a limiting infinite, typically unimodular, random rooted graph as the local weak limit","the functional of interest is expressible as, or well approximated by, a sum or average of local, root-based quantities","for extensive functionals: an additional argument, such as subadditivity or concentration, to pass from the local limit to a law of large numbers for the global sum"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.994267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_793f7dca888660c8d4669b9e22cd3be3e733262e6b2906c64e5ca49d47cf39e4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For a sequence of finite, possibly random, rooted graphs G_n, local weak (Benjamini-Schramm) convergence means that for every finite radius r, the distribution of the isomorphism class of the r-ball around the (uniformly, or otherwise canonically) chosen root converges weakly to that of a limiting, typically infinite, random rooted graph (G*, o). The objective method, due to Aldous and Steele, is the broader program of analyzing this limiting infinite object directly, such as a Poisson weighted infinite tree or a unimodular Galton-Watson tree, to compute limiting constants for combinatorial optimization functionals on the finite graphs, such as the minimum spanning tree constant or the limiting value in the random assignment problem, by solving a recursive distributional (fixed-point) equation on the infinite limit rather than working with finite-n computations directly. It does not by itself establish that a given sequence converges locally weakly, which typically must be separately verified via a subsequential compactness argument together with uniqueness of subsequential limits, and it does not directly give convergence of global, extensive functionals without an additional concentration or summation argument beyond the purely local statement. Typical failure: Assuming that local weak convergence of the underlying random graph automatically implies convergence of a global extensive functional, such as the total weight of a minimum spanning tree, at the same per-vertex limiting rate; local convergence controls only typical local neighborhoods, and passing to a global average requires an additional uniform-integrability or concentration argument, often the genuinely hard part of an objective-method proof, which is easy to overlook once the local limit has been identified. Canonical reference: Benjamini and Schramm, 2001, Electronic Journal of Probability; Aldous and Steele, 2004, in Probability on Discrete Structures, Springer; Aldous and Lyons, 2007, Electronic Journal of Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, M) is a measurable space","mu and nu are positive measures on M (for signed or complex measures the definition is applied to their total variations)","the separating set E is required to belong to M"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:13:10.402012+00:00","domain":"measure theory, decomposition of measures","id":"claim_7949ee76619d07edbf68d03f6116561c0881f49a0a0bfc5d35c33818a908ff98","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, M) be a measurable space and let mu and nu be positive measures on M. One says that mu and nu are MUTUALLY SINGULAR, written mu perp nu, if there exists a set E in M with mu(E) = 0 and nu(X minus E) = 0; equivalently, X splits into two measurable pieces, one carrying all of nu and mu-null, the other carrying all of mu and nu-null. The relation is symmetric. For signed or complex measures the definition is applied to the total variations: mu perp nu means |mu| perp |nu|. Basic consequences: mu perp mu holds if and only if mu = 0; if nu is absolutely continuous with respect to mu (nu << mu) and nu perp mu, then nu = 0; if nu_1 perp mu and nu_2 perp mu then (nu_1 + nu_2) perp mu. CAUTIONS. (1) Mutual singularity is much stronger than 'nu is not absolutely continuous with respect to mu': a measure can fail to be absolutely continuous without being singular, and in general a measure splits into an absolutely continuous and a singular part (Lebesgue decomposition). (2) Singularity is a measure-theoretic, not a topological, smallness statement: the measure sum over n of 2^(-n) times the Dirac mass at the n-th rational is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure on R yet has full support, and the Cantor-Lebesgue measure is mutually singular with Lebesgue measure while being atomless. (3) The witness set E must be measurable; without that requirement the notion is vacuous or ill-posed. (4) Mutual singularity is not preserved by arbitrary uncountable sums of measures.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:37:51.453104+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7957edfb35ce949aef2271108b1b57bd76ff843c44188e8d8db4a0cd9cf76213","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 33 of arXiv:2604.03213, 'Asymptotic expansion for transport maps \\ between laws of multimatrix models'] Let $\cX$ be a Banach space, and fix $x_0 \in \cX$, $r > 0$, $a \in \R$, and $T_0 > a$.
Suppose $f \colon [a,\infty) \times C_r(x_0) \to \cX$ is a continuous function such that for all $T > a$, there exists a $c_T < \infty$ such that
\[
\sup_{a \leq t \leq T} \norm{f(t,x) - f(t,y)}_{\cX} \leq c_T\norm{x-y}_{\cX} \qquad (x,y \in C_r(x_0)).
\]
Define
\[
M \coloneqq \sup_{(t,x) \in [a,T_0] \times C_r(x_0)} \norm{f(t,x)}_{\cX} < \infty.
\]
If $a < T < \min\left\{T_0,a + r/(2M)\right\}$ and $c \colon [a,T] \to C_{r/2}(x_0)$ is continuous, then there exists a continuous function $y \colon [a,T] \to C_r(x_0)$ such that
\begin{equation}
    y(t) = c(t) + \int_a^t f(s,y(s))\,\d s \qquad (a \leq t \leq T).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

  u_h^{(\varepsilon)} \;:=\; \mathcal{T}^{*}\,(\gamma_F + \varepsilon I)^{-1}\,h, \qquad u_h \;:=\; \mathcal{T}^{*}\,\gamma_F^{\dagger}\,h, \qquad \varepsilon > 0,

and assume:

A rank-one bounded PSD kernel on [-1,1], k(x,xprime)=1{x>=0}1{xprime>=0}, with observation noise variance 1, prevents every continuous raw-input Gaussian predictor from achieving uniform forward KL below log(9/8)/4 > 1/36. An empty context, or one observation (-1,0), yields predictive variances 1 left of zero and 2 at zero. Status: proof (unaudited), T336-w727-C003 v1. Complete theorem, constants and scope:
# Raw-input obstruction for Target 1

Claim T336-w727-C003 v1. Status: proof (unaudited). This is a scope obstruction to the literal bounded-kernel raw-input statement; it does not contradict C002's supplied-feature theorem. No novelty or Lean certification is claimed.

## Statement

There is a rank-one bounded positive-semidefinite kernel on the compact raw-input domain [-1,1], observation-noise variance s=1, and bounded context labels, such that every predictor with continuous Gaussian output parameters (mu(x),v(x)), v(x)>0, has worst-case noisy predictive forward KL at least

    c0=(1/4) log(9/8)>1/36.

The conclusion applies in particular to every finite transformer whose raw-input encoding and subsequent operations are continuous and whose output is a Gaussian with positive continuous variance. It applies to normalized ReLU attention and softmax attention under these conditions. Therefore boundedness, compactness, finite rank, and positive observation noise alone cannot imply the raw-input version of Target 1 for arbitrarily small eps.

## Kernel and posterior

Define phi(x)=0 for x<0 and phi(x)=1 for x>=0. Set k(x,x')=phi(x)phi(x'). For any finite coefficients a_i,

    sum_{i,j} a_i a_j k(x_i,x_j)=(sum_i a_i phi(x_i))^2>=0.

Thus k is positive semidefinite, bounded by 1, and of rank exactly one (because k(0,0)=1). The GP can be represented as f(x)=Z phi(x), with Z~N(0,1). Observations add independent N(0,1) noise.

Use the empty context if allowed. Alternatively, for any n>=1 use one observation at x=-1 with label y=0, which satisfies every B>=0. This observation is pure noise independent of Z, so the posterior law of Z remains N(0,1). For either context, the new noisy predictive distribution is

    P_x=N(0,1) for x<0; P_x=N(0,2) for x>=0.

Hence the example does not rely on whether a context of length zero is included.

## Continuity forces two incompatible approximation requirements

Fix this context and any continuous output mu(x),v(x)>0. Let E=sup_x KL(P_x || N(mu(x),v(x))). If E is infinite the bound is immediate. Otherwise put mu0=mu(0),v0=v(0)>0. At x=0,

    D_2:=KL(N(0,2)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

Take x_j=-1/j tending to zero from below. Since mu,v are continuous and v0>0, the explicit Gaussian KL formula is continuous along this sequence; all denominators remain positive near the limit. Therefore

    D_1:=KL(N(0,1)||N(mu0,v0))<=E.

No dominated convergence, probabilistic conditioning argument, or exchange of a supremum with a limit is used: every term in this deterministic convergent sequence is <=E.

For a>0 define

    D_a=(1/2)(log(v0/a)+(a+mu0^2)/v0-1).

Writing w=3/(2v0)>0 and combining logarithms gives the exact identity

    (D_1+D_2)/2
      = (1/4)log(9/8)+(1/2)(w-1-log w)+mu0^2/(2v0).

The inequality log w<=w-1 follows by integrating 1/t from 1 to w, separately for w>=1 and 0<w<=1, or by differentiating w-1-log w. Both additional terms are nonnegative. Consequently

    E >= (D_1+D_2)/2 >= (1/4)log(9/8).

Finally log(9/8)=integral_1^{9/8} dt/t > (1/8)(8/9)=1/9, since 1/t>8/9 except at the right endpoint. Thus c0>1/36. Every denominator and logarithm argument above is strictly positive.

## Interpretation for the dossier

C002 supplies phi as an input, so its input encoding itself is discontinuous as a function of raw x in this example; the continuity hypothesis here then fails. There is no contradiction. To close Target 1, the architecture must explicitly permit the fixed feature map in the input representation, or the theorem must add assumptions that make raw-input feature computation possible and account for its cost. Merely calling the kernel finite rank does not settle this issue.

The example is an obstruction to a named target interpretation, not a claimed solution of the entire T336 problem. The remaining feature-input theorem C002 and this obstruction both await independent review.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564661+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7994b8eb14afe8df4ccbb96e64ddbced16fb44ee3fe5f57fd62aa626e183d505","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 17 (Inversion of the surrogate objectives) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] Regard both distortions as functionals of the transformed energy vector $v$ at
fixed $E=\sum_k v_k$, the shared-scale one on a \emph{uniform} grid.
\begin{itemize}
\item The \textbf{allocation-flexible} coding surrogate (\Cref{sec:classical})
$D_{\mathrm{vr}}(v)\propto(\prod_k v_k)^{1/d}$ is the geometric mean, the form the
variable-rate distortion takes while every coordinate draws positive rate
(\Cref{prop:schur}(i); once the water level of \Cref{prop:waterfill} rises above a
coordinate's energy the true distortion is floored by the un-coded coordinates' energy,
so the vanishing limit below is an idealization of the surrogate). It is strictly
Schur-\emph{concave} wherever all coordinates are positive and identically zero elsewhere; it decreases under majorization, so it is driven down by
\emph{concentration}, the direction in which the KLT moves the profile, reaching the
majorization-maximal \emph{reachable} one, the spectrum (\Cref{thm:klt}).
\item The \textbf{shared-scale AbsMax} surrogate (\Cref{sec:inv-flatness})
$D_{\mathrm{fr}}(v)=\sum_g\max_{k\in g}v_k$ obeys the max-vs-mean bound of
\Cref{prop:schur}(ii), so among all $v$ of fixed sum it is minimized at the
\emph{flat} $v$, the direction in which incoherence processing and the Hadamard move the
profile (\Cref{prop:rht}), and maximized under within-group concentration.
\end{itemize}
Over all $v$ of fixed total energy, then, the two surrogates are driven apart. The
geometric mean is strictly Schur-concave on the positive orthant, so every majorization
step toward concentration strictly lowers $D_{\mathrm{vr}}$ while every coordinate remains
positive, and it is maximized at the flat $v$;
while $E/G\le D_{\mathrm{fr}}\le E$, the lower bound attained exactly when every group
is internally uniform and the upper bound when each group's mass sits on a single
coordinate. Concentrating energy \emph{within} a group therefore strictly lowers the first whenever every coordinate remains positive, and never lowers the second, strictly raising it as soon as the group maximum rises; flattening within groups does the reverse. Along no \emph{within-group} step of the order do the two objectives move the same way.","status":"unverified"}

  \;=\;
  \sup

    \sum_{j=1}^\infty \bigl\lvert \mu(E_j)\bigr\rvert
    \,\colon\,
    \{E_j\}_{j=1}^\infty \text{ is a Borel partition of } E
  \Bigr\},
  \quad
  E \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["The converse is explicitly a sketch, with a missing uniform estimate.","The claimed converse concerns the positive-infinity end only."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.363786+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_79d6f4cce6edf1f0f5f53b75138f63a88e6154f64713766db080a20a4b5e8768","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author_checked_criterion_controlled_against_the_papers_own_deterministic_benchmark] This is the broader partial answer reported for both cases of the open question in Remark 5.3(ii) of arXiv:2607.07410. Let V be a two-sided (r_0,alpha)-semi-selfsimilar Levy process with alpha in (0,2), whose value at time one has positive probability of each sign, and let nu be its Levy measure. For delta > 0 consider the two diffusion forms with reference densities exp(-|x|^delta - V(x)) and exp(|x|^delta - V(x)), each with energy (1/2) integral |f'|^2 times the corresponding density. The record claims noncompactness, with essential-spectrum bottom zero, for every delta, when nu has negative jumps in the first case or positive jumps in the second. The written quiet-window proof covers delta > 1; the paper's Proposition 5.2 covers 0 < delta <= 1/alpha. Together these give all delta when alpha <= 1, which includes alpha < 1, where nu must charge both half-lines. For alpha in (1,2) and 1/alpha < delta <= 1 the claim is not established by the written argument. For alpha > 1, delta > 1 and no negative jumps, the record also sketches compactness at the +infinity end of the first diffusion via the bound B_l(x) <= C^2 x^(2-2delta). Here B_l is the integral of the reciprocal density from a fixed positive x_0 to x times the integral of the density from x to infinity, and C is a finite path-dependent constant. The record explicitly leaves the uniform near-field estimate unwritten, so this converse is a sketch. Compactness at one end does not by itself establish compactness of the full two-sided operator. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T : X -> X is continuous and surjective","the definition quantifies over all nonempty OPEN subsets U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090776+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, mixing properties of non-invertible maps","id":"claim_79ea44cf7b3dcd7452df709c8e293198d63314337814289a89d9a84e9a0edffe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space and T : X -> X a continuous surjection. T is TOPOLOGICALLY EXACT, also called locally eventually onto, if for every nonempty open set U there is an integer n >= 1 with T^n(U) = X. Two consequences are what proofs actually use. (a) UNIFORMITY IN n: if T^n(U) = X then T^m(U) = X for every m >= n, because T is onto; hence for each nonempty open U there is N with T^n(U) = X for ALL n >= N. (b) DENSE BACKWARD ORBITS WITH ALL LARGE PERIODS: for every x in X and every nonempty open U there is N with U intersect T^{-n}(x) nonempty for every n >= N; in particular the full backward orbit of any point is dense. Property (b) is a genuine aperiodicity statement that topological transitivity does not give and that even topological mixing of an invertible system cannot give. Relations: topological exactness implies topological mixing, which implies topological transitivity; the converses are false. An invertible map is never topologically exact unless X is a single point, since T^n(U) = X forces U = X for a homeomorphism, so exactness is a hypothesis reserved for genuinely non-invertible maps: expanding maps of the circle or of a compact manifold, one-sided mixing subshifts of finite type, and Chebyshev-like interval maps are the standard examples.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:58:01.575452+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_79efc22e2efdf6b3517514085c1069b95d1e98df1cf7e1f83fb4c240025e816a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2608.27372, 'Universality and sharp thresholds for ellipsoid fitting'] Let $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}\in \R^d$ be i.i.d. random vectors such that $x_1=(x_{1j})_{1\leq j\leq d}$ has indpenedent coordinates satisfying
	\begin{equation}
		\E[x_{1j}]=0,\qquad \E \left[x_{1j}^2\right]=1,\qquad
		\E \left[x_{1j}^4\right]=\kappa,\qquad \sup_{j\le d}\|x_{1j}\|_{\psitwo}\le K_x,
	\end{equation}
    where $\kappa>1$ and $K_x>0$ do not depend on $n,d$. Let
	$n,d\to\infty$ with $n/d^2\to\alpha\in(0,\infty)$.  There is an explicit
	threshold $\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:alpha-star-def},
	which depends only on $\kappa$, such that the following holds.
	\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
		\item If $\alpha<\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one, there exists an ellipsoid fitting all $(x_i)_{1\leq i\leq n}$:
		\[
		\exists R\succ 0,\quad\textnormal{such that}\quad x_i^{\top}R x_i=1\quad \textnormal{for all}\quad 1\leq i\leq n.
		\]
		Moreover, such $R\in \R^{d\times d}$ can be chosen to be well-conditioned: $\lambda_{\max}(R)/\lambda_{\min}(R)=O(1)$. 
		\item If $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, then with probability tending to one
		there is no $R\succeq0$ such that $x_i^\top R x_i=1$ for all $1\leq i\leq n$. Moreover, the optimal squared fitting error converges in probability:
		\begin{equation}
			\Gamma_X:=\inf_{R\succeq0, \operatorname{Tr}R=d}\,\inf_{r\geq 0}\,
			\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n\left(\frac{x_i^\top Rx_i}{\sqrt{d}}-r\right)^2
			\pto e_\star(\alpha,\kappa),
		\end{equation}
        where $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)$ is defined in Eq.~\eqref{eq:optimal-fitting-error-main}. For $\alpha>\alpha_\star(\kappa)$, $e_\star(\alpha,\kappa)>0$ holds, thus an approximate ellipsoid fitting is not possible with any $R\succeq 0$ with $\Tr R=d$.
	\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

(b) [minimal-time / control representation] d(x) = inf { T ≥ 0 : there is an absolutely continuous ξ: [0,T] → ℝⁿ with |ξ'(s)| ≤ 1 for a.e. s, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K } = inf { ∫_0^T |ξ'(s)| ds : ξ absolutely continuous, ξ(0) = x, ξ(T) ∈ K, T ≥ 0 } — the distance is the value function of the minimal-time problem for the control system ξ' = α, |α| ≤ 1, with target K, and the straight segment from x to a nearest point of K is an optimal trajectory. (c) [variational characterization] d is the largest 1-Lipschitz function that is ≤ 0 on K: if u: ℝⁿ → ℝ is 1-Lipschitz and u ≤ 0 on K then u ≤ d everywhere, and d itself is admissible; equivalently d(x) = max { u(x) : u 1-Lipschitz, u ≤ 0 on K }. (d) [eikonal equation] d is a viscosity solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in the open set ℝⁿ \\ K, and a viscosity subsolution of |Du| − 1 ≤ 0 on all of ℝⁿ. Sharp edges. (2) Uniqueness of viscosity solutions of |Du| = 1 in ℝⁿ \\ K vanishing on K FAILS without a sign or growth restriction: for K = {0}, the function u(x) = −|x| is a classical (hence viscosity) solution of |Du| − 1 = 0 in ℝⁿ \\ {0} with u(0) = 0, different from d(x) = |x|. The distance is singled out among solutions by (c), or by nonnegativity/boundedness-below conditions that this lemma does not assert. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:17:04.322958+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a112d984414996beb1871b3c4a78c359f37fdfc7dd3eb7542762ba4b443e657","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2606.01683, 'Singular-value gap of nonreversible Markov processes'] For a Banach couple $(E_0, E_1)$, denote by $\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)$ the class 
    of functions $F: \Bar{S} \to E_0 + E_1$ satisfying
    \begin{itemize}
        \item $F$ is continuous on $\Bar{S}$ and analytic on $S$
        \item $F(it) \in E_0$ and $F(1+it) \in E_1$ for all $t \in \mathds{R}$
        \item $\|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)} \coloneqq 
        \max \Big\{ \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(it)\|_{E_0}, \sup_{t \in \mathds{R}} \|F(1+it)\|_{E_1}           \Big\} < \infty$ 
    \end{itemize}
    Then, for $0 \leq \theta \leq 1 $, the \textbf{complex interpolation space} $[E_0, E_1]_\theta$ is the 
    Banach space defined by
    \[
        [E_0, E_1]_\theta \coloneqq \{h \in E_0 + E_1: h = F(\theta) \ \ \text{for some} \ F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)\}
    \]
    equipped with the norm
    \[
        \|h\|_{[E_0, E_1]_\theta} \coloneqq \inf_{\substack{F \in \mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1) \\
        F(\theta) = h}} \|F\|_{\mathcal{F}(E_0, E_1)}
    \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.740358+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a118bd39237e36f9cf206734f90190f5bd46dea6d841e3f5d3c658a95681f87","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 104 (Passage of finite propagation to the cutoff limits) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $(\chi_1,\rho_1)$ and $(\chi_2,\rho_2)$ be adapted to $(K,T_0)$, and let

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:56:36.587912+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a13d8024428def817be185b12010821d20c2bbe75867199b2938a788f55a9d2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn defi_kin_sol of arXiv:2608.30548, 'Finite speed of propagation and waiting time phenomena for stochastic porous media equatio'] Let $u_0\in L^1(\mathbb{T}^d)$ be non-negative and assume  (equation equation_n_m_together of the paper)  and (equation Eq_ass_B1 of the paper)--(equation Eq_ass_B3 of the paper). 		\mathrm{d} s

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:32:20.700746+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a27de1a472a2e9c77ede654fb36c9aed79863034186b287fd8b0de5df60d21d","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 7 of arXiv:2609.00254, 'On the geometry and cohomology of almost abelian solvmanifolds'] Let $K\subset \bigwedge^\bullet T^*_M\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$ be a line sub-bundle which is

    \left(T_M\oplus T_M^\ast\right)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C\longrightarrow
    \left(T_M\oplus T_M^\ast\right)\otimes_{\mathbb R}\mathbb C$$
    denote the projections onto $L$ and onto $\bar L$ associated with this splitting, so that
    $v=\mathrm{pr}_L(v)+\mathrm{pr}_{\bar L}(v)$ for every

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:47.659910+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a37ce8165404fc566d24822af83b22605397f94fcfe11efc17e4145e45ac5d6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 20 of arXiv:2605.08844, 'Signature Kernel and Schwinger-Dyson Kernel Equations as Two-Parameter Rough Differential '] For every \(n\in [1:\kappa+\zeta]\), let \(\ell=\lceil n/2\rceil\). Then the homogeneous components of the Schwinger--Dyson kernel satisfy
\begin{equation}
K_0(s,t)=1 +  \int_s^t  K_{1}(s,u) d\mathbf{X}_u du,
\qquad
K_n(s,t)
=
-\int_s^t \sigma_n\bigl(K_{\ell-1}(s, \cdot),K_{n-\ell}(\cdot, t)\bigr)_u\,d\mathbf X_u .
\end{equation}
Here, for every word \(I=i_1\cdots i_n\) over the alphabet \(\{1,\dots,d\}\), we set
\(
\tilde I:=i_1\cdots i_{\ell-1},\,
\hat I:=i_{\ell+1}\cdots i_n,
\)
and,given a basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) of \(V\), define
\begin{align*}
&\sigma_n:
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(\ell-1)},\mathbb R\bigr)\boxtimes
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V^{\otimes(n-\ell)},\mathbb R\bigr)
\to
\mathrm{Hom}\bigl(V,\mathrm{Hom}(V^{\otimes n},\mathbb R)\bigr),\\
&\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_I)
=
\sigma_n(\eta,\xi)[e_j](e_{\tilde I}\otimes e_{i_\ell}\otimes e_{\hat I})
=
\eta(e_{\tilde I})\,\delta_{i_\ell j}\,\xi(e_{\hat I}),
\end{align*}
for every word \(I\) of length \(n\), and extend linearly on \(V^{\otimes n}\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:29:35.074214+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a39b5e7291a8d7b501d4280b30d7ed0d078312db894b022e4ecf41e31d0ca83","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2609.03784, '2609.03784'] Let $m\ge2$, $d\ge7$, and let $b\in B$ be very general. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:19:56.712514+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a49b705a1eff1d6d56361f2585346d775af33fe4ef1039f67e9fc5640c798e0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 26 of arXiv:2608.30991, 'A block-Toeplitz approach to the spectrum of the Neumann-Poincaré operator on self-similar'] Let $a:\mathbb{T}\to\mathcal{L}(X)$. A \emph{right Wiener--Hopf factorisation} of $a$ with respect to the unit circle $\mathbb{T}$ is a representation
	\[
	a(z)=a_-(z)\Lambda(z)a_+(z),
	\qquad z\in\mathbb{T},
	\]
	in which $a_+$ and $a_+^{-1}$ extend holomorphically to the interior unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, $a_-$ and $a_-^{-1}$ extend holomorphically to the exterior domain $\mathbb{E} = \{z : |z| > 1\} \cup \{\infty\}$, all four with continuous boundary values on $\mathbb{T}$, and
	\[
	\Lambda(z)=I-\Pi+\sum_{j=1}^{J}z^{\nu_j}\Pi_j,
	\qquad
	\Pi:=\sum_{j=1}^{J}\Pi_j,
	\]
	where $\Pi_1,\dots,\Pi_J$ are rank-one idempotents with $\Pi_i\Pi_j=0$ for $i\neq j$ and $\nu_1,\dots,\nu_J\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}$ are the \emph{non-zero partial indices}, not necessarily distinct. The factorisation is \emph{canonical} if $J=0$, that is $\Lambda\equiv I$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.153335+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a4b687052c31d21a374350800babbe1e0bb54804bb21e625501c86003d4f73f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2608.29406, 'Partially Totally Real Submanifolds of Sasakian Manifolds'] A submanifold $M$ of a Sasakian manifold, tangent to $\xi$, is called a \emph{partially totally real (PTR) submanifold} if there exists a nonzero constant-rank totally real distribution $\Dperp\subset TM\cap\ker\eta$, i.e.
\[
 \phi\Dperp\subset\Tperp.
\]
If $\Dtilde$ denotes the orthogonal complement of $\Dperp\oplus\langle\xi\rangle$ in $TM$, then
\begin{equation}
 TM=\Dperp\oplus\Dtilde\oplus\langle\xi\rangle.
\end{equation}
Following the K\"ahler PTR terminology, $\Dtilde$ is called the
\emph{ambiguous distribution}.  The PTR structure refers to this chosen
decomposition; maximality of \(\Dperp\), when needed, is imposed later
and is not part of the definition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.538462+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7a97ad96f4b81f30399ab986caeac2453c3307cc069e9dec1196571c81a009e1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 5 of arXiv:2603.28702, 'Distribution of the magnetization of the critical Ising model on sparse random graphs'] \begin{itemize}
\item 
Let $G$ be a graph with vertex set $V$. The Ising model on this graph with inverse temperature $\beta$ is the probability measure $\mu$ on $\{-1,1\}^V$ satisfying
$$\mu_{\beta}(\sigma)=\dfrac{1}{Z_{\beta,G}}\exp\left(\beta\SL{u\sim v}\sigma_u\sigma_v\right).$$
\item
Fix a measure $\nu$ on $\{-1,1\}^V$. For a configuration $\sigma\in\{-1,1\}^V$ and for some $v\in V$, let $\sigma^{\oplus v}$ be the configuration $\sigma$ in which the spin at vertex $v$ is flipped. For two configurations $\sigma,\tau\in\{-1,1\}^V$, we write $\sigma\sim\tau$ if $\tau=\sigma^{\oplus v}$ for some $v\in V$. The continuous time Glauber Dynamics on $G$ for $\nu$ at rate 1 is a Markov chain with transition rates, for $\sigma\neq\tau$, equal to
$$q(\sigma,\tau)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{\nu(\tau)}{\nu(\sigma)+\nu(\tau)},\ \ \text{if}\ \ \sigma \sim \tau
\\ \\
0,\ \ \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}$$
Informally, every vertex gets updated at rate one, and the update happens conditionally on the configuration in the rest of the vertices.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

Furthermore, let $X$ be any random variable under $\PP$.  Then there exists a map $\mu:E\times \mathcal{B}_\mathbb{R}\to [0,1]$ such that: (i) $\mu(\cdot,A)\in \EE/\mathcal{B}_{[0,1]}$ for each $A\in \mathcal{B}_\mathbb{R}$; (ii) $\mu(e,\cdot)$ is a probability on $\mathcal{B}_\mathbb{R}$ for each $e\in E$; and (iii) $\PP[f(X,Z)\vert Z]=\int f(x,Z)\mu(Z,\dd x)$ a.s.-$\PP$ for all $f\in (\mathcal{B}_\mathbb{R}\otimes \EE)/\mathcal{B}_{[-\infty,\infty]}$ for which $\PP[f(X,Z)^+]\land \PP[f(X,Z)^-]<\infty$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:02:17.985904+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7abd5943eeca0508bf674af20b2bef2fa66b54442080048fa79fc8c4ef9c274c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:standard-twostream of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix $\lambda \in (0,1)$
and a \emph{send sequence}  
$\overline{p}$ with $p_0=1$.
Let $Z=(Z^A,Z^B)$ be the two-stream process with birth rate~$\lambda$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and start time~$0$  
where for all $D\in \{A,B\}$ and all
positive integers~$k$,
$\mathbf{arr}_k^{Z^D}(\tau) = \emptyset$. 
Let $X$ be the backoff process with birth distribution~$\mathsf{Po}(\lambda)$, send sequence~$\overline{p}$, and cohort set $\mathcal{C}=\{A,B\}$ (Definition~(def:backoff-cohorts of the paper)).
The standard coupling of~$Z$ and~$X$ has the following invariants for every $i\geq 1$ and $t\geq 1$.
\begin{description}  
\item  [Inv-$b_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{b}_i^{Z^D}(t-1) \subseteq \mathbf{b}_i^{X^D}(t-1)$.
\item  [Inv-$B_i(t)$:] For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\item [Inv-$s_i(t)$:] 
For each stream $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t)$.
\end{description}
Initially, Inv-$b_i(1)$ holds for every $i\geq 1$ since all of these sets are empty.

For any $t$ assuming Inv-$b_i(t)$, the coupling at step~$t$ proceeds as follows.
For each $D\in \{A,B\}$, $\mathbf{n}^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{n}^{X^D}(t)$, so for all $i\geq 1$, 
Inv-$B_i(t)$ holds.
For every   
$D\in \{A,B\}$ and
$i\geq 1$, $\mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t)$ is formed by including each ball in 
$\mathbf{B}_i^{X^D}(t) \setminus \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t)$ 
independently with probability~$p_i$.
Then $\mathbf{s}^{X^D}_i(t) = \mathbf{S}^{X^D}_i(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^D}_i(t)$, establishing Inv-$s_i(t)$.

 
  

  
The assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t)$ follow deterministically, using  Definition~(def:backoffasgen of the paper)
and the assignments to $\mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$  are chosen  following Definition~(def:two-stream of the paper).

Since $\mathbf{s}_i^{X^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{B}_i^{Z^D}(t) = \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, Inv-$b_i(t+1)$  follows from  
$ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) \subseteq \mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t)$, which holds:
If a ball~$\beta$ is in $ \mathbf{s}_i^{Z^D}(t) \cap \mathbf{e}_i^{X^D}(t) $ then
$\mathbf{s}^{X^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{X^B}(t)= \{\beta\}$ so
$\mathbf{s}^{Z^A}(t) \cup \mathbf{s}^{Z^B}(t) = \{\beta\}$ so 
$\mathbf{e}_i^{Z^D}(t) = \{\beta\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:59:24.052460+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7acf4cebcdf3320b4a885a7f1398cec5bd1f2ceb7be521f238958e306f2b4758","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:pathbound of arXiv:2608.30888, 'Three-term asymptotics for discrete\\ Hardy--Rellich constants in high dimension'] Fix $J$ and two finite sets of partitions.  Uniformly for $0\leq j\leq J$ and
for all partitions $\lambda,\mu$ in those sets or reachable from them in at

\begin{equation}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:56:37.651622+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ad26847ff861be199c6bd05ca3ce9408dd4e7aec539420e2a44e52a20c91d27","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:openpath of arXiv:2608.24830, 'Motion helps the contact process: survival below\\ the percolation threshold on Poisson Br'] Let $\lambda\in(0,\infty]$, $\mu\in(0,\infty]$ and $\mathfrak r\in\{\mathrm{u},\mathrm{i}\}$. An \emph{open
path} from $(u_0,t_0)$ to $(u_n,t_{n+1})$ consists of particles $u_0,\dots,u_n$, such that
consecutive particles are distinct, and times $t_0<t_1<\dots<t_{n+1}$, such that
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item for $1\le j\le n$ there is an active transmission mark from $u_{j-1}$ to $u_j$ at time
  $t_j$; when $\lambda=\infty$ this says that $u_{j-1}$ and $u_j$ are in contact at $t_j$;
\item for $0\le j\le n$ there is no effective recovery mark of $u_j$ in $(t_j,t_{j+1}]$.
\end{enumerate}
Its \emph{trace} is the c\`adl\`ag path $\gamma$ on $[t_0,t_{n+1}]$ given by $\gamma(t)=X_{u_j}(t)$
for $t\in[t_j,t_{j+1})$ and $0\le j\le n-1$, and by $\gamma(t)=X_{u_n}(t)$ for
$t\in[t_n,t_{n+1}]$. Its jumps have size at most $2r$. The path is \emph{contained} in a
space-time region $D$ if $(\gamma(t),t)\in D$ for every $t\in[t_0,t_{n+1}]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:47:32.861305+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b04438f4566f1287283f6effd1ea2497d7145b382a434a36ed88b006ffdd697","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 22 of arXiv:2609.02423, '2609.02423'] For $\ell=0,1,2,3$, set
\[
	V_{\nu,N,\ell}
	=\Op\bigl(|v_\nu|^{1/2}\Theta_{\nu,N,\ell}\bigr).
\]
	For a $y$ chart, define
	\begin{equation}
		\mathcal P_{\nu,N,\ell}(T)
		=\sup_{y_0\in\R}\frac\mu R
		\int_0^T\!\!\int_{\R^2}
		a'\left(\frac{\mu(y-y_0)}R\right)
		|V_{\nu,N,\ell}z_N|^2\dd x\dd y\dd t,
	\end{equation}
	and use the analogous definition on an $x$ chart, with
	$\lambda\simeq N$ and the supremum taken over $x_0\in\R$.
	For $\ell=0,1,2$, the construction
	\eqref{eq:mN}-\eqref{eq:bN}, applied with
	$\Theta_{\nu,N,\ell}$ in place of the original chart cutoff, produces
	symbols $m_{N,\ell}$ and $b_{N,\ell}$, cubic corrections
	$\mathcal C_{N,\ell}$, normal commutator terms
	$\mathcal T_{N,\ell,2}$, cross terms $\mathcal X_{N,\ell}$, and
	quartic remainders $\mathcal R_{N,\ell}$.  The identity
	\eqref{eq:C-identity} holds with these level indices.  The resonance estimate,
	the high-variable symbol bounds, the boundary-correction estimate,
	and the quartic estimate below hold uniformly for
	$\ell=0,1,2$.  At the last level,
	\begin{equation}
		\mathcal P_{\nu,N,3}(T)
		\lesssim_R N^2T\norm{z_N}_{L_T^\infty L^2}^2.
	\end{equation}
	Indeed, on a $y$ chart,
	\[
	\frac\mu R\norm{V_{\nu,N,3}z_N}_2^2
	\lesssim_R
	N^{1/2}N^{3/2}\norm{z_N}_2^2
	=
	N^2\norm{z_N}_2^2,
\]
	while on an $x$ chart the corresponding bound is
	\[
	\frac\lambda R\norm{V_{\nu,N,3}z_N}_2^2
	\lesssim_R
	NN\norm{z_N}_2^2
	=
	N^2\norm{z_N}_2^2.
\]
	Here the $x$-chart bound uses the defining property of
	\cref{def:chart-ladder}: every auxiliary level $\ell\ge1$ is
	confined to the enlarged transition band, where $|v_x|\simeq N$.
	This is why the present $N^2$ bound is stronger than the crude
	level-zero estimate \eqref{eq:positive-finite}, for which
	$|v_x|$ may reach size $N^2$ on the full chart.
	Integration in time proves \eqref{eq:P3-crude}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:15:54.983664+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b1174403ad43db638eb1b9310108ffb2faefa813439da61246dbc94ae3e0994","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:prenosil-diamond of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] {simpson_proof_1994}}] 
  On an f-model $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, \sqsubset, V)$, consider the diamond clause
  \[
    x \Vdash^{\mathrm p}_\mathfrak{M} \Diamond \varphi
    \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;}
    \exists x', y \in W \,
      (x' \leq x \mathrel{\text{\&}} x' \sqsubset y \mathrel{\text{\&}} y \Vdash^{\mathrm p}_\mathfrak{M} \varphi).
  \]
  Thus $\Diamond \varphi$ holds at $x$ when $\varphi$ holds at an ${\sqsubset}$-successor
  of some ${\leq}$-predecessor of $x$.
  Simpson attributes this clause to unpublished work of Plotkin and Stirling.
  P\v{r}enosil later developed the corresponding operation on upsets [prenosil_duality_2014].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:51:33.328314+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b14ba8e7a519cb2c92fc84c492075b65cc6993ff31e0c70e5ca58cea8478ba7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma detect-pointed-presheaves of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] Let ${\mathcal{C}}$ be a cocomplete, pointed, and locally small $\infty$-category. Let ${\mathcal{I}}\subset{\mathcal{C}}$ be a small full subcategory containing the zero object and satisfying the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item For any $I\in{\mathcal{I}}$, the unique lift ${\mathcal{C}}\to\Spc_*$ of ${\textup{Hom}}(I,-)$ is cocontinuous.
        \item The functors ${\textup{Hom}}(I,-)\colon{\mathcal{C}}\to\Spc$ are jointly conservative.
    \end{enumerate}
    Then ${\mathcal{I}}\hookrightarrow{\mathcal{C}}$ extends to an equivalence $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\mathcal{C}}$.
    \begin{proof}
        As ${\mathcal{C}}$ is cocomplete and locally small, the inclusion extends to a functor $\Lambda\colon\PSh({\mathcal{I}})\to{\mathcal{C}}$ left adjoint to the restricted Yoneda embedding $\Upsilon$. By what it means to be a zero object, ${\textup{Hom}}(0,x)\simeq1$ for all $x\in{\mathcal{C}}$, i.e.\ $\Upsilon$ factors through $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})$, so we obtain a restricted adjunction $\PSh^0({\mathcal{I}})\rightleftarrows{\mathcal{C}}$. It remains to show that this is in fact an adjoint equivalence. As our second assumption guarantees that $\Upsilon$ is conservative, it will suffice for this that the unit $\eta\colon\textup{id}\to\Upsilon\Lambda$ is invertible. 

        Since ${\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}}$ has a zero object, postcomposing with the forgetful functor induces an equivalence ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc)$. Moreover, the full subcategory ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)\subset{\textup{Fun}}({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)$ is closed under colimits (as any colimit of initial objects is initial), so that colimits in ${\textup{Fun}}^0({\mathcal{I}}^{\textup{op}},\Spc_*)$ are computed pointwise. Thus, our first assumption guarantees that the right adjoint $\Upsilon$ is cocontinuous, so that the class of all pointed presheaves $X$ for which $\eta_X$ is invertible, is closed under colimits. It will therefore suffice to show that the unit $\eta_X$ is invertible whenever $X=\Upsilon(I)$ is representable. If we now let $Z\in{\mathcal{C}}$ arbitrary, then the composite
        \[
            {\textup{Hom}}(\Lambda(X),Z)\xrightarrow{\;\Upsilon\;}{\textup{Hom}}(\Upsilon\Lambda(X),\Upsilon(Z))\xrightarrow{\;{\textup{Hom}}(\eta,\Upsilon(Z))} {\textup{Hom}}(X,\Upsilon(Z))
        \]
        is invertible as it is just the adjunction equivalence. By assumption, $\Lambda(X)\simeq I\in{\mathcal{I}}$; if also $Z\in I$, then the first map is an equivalence by the Yoneda lemma, so that also the second map is an equivalence by $2$-out-of-$3$. We conclude that ${\textup{Hom}}(\eta_X,\Upsilon(Z))$ is an equivalence for every $Z\in I$. As $\eta_X\colon \Upsilon(I)=X\to \Upsilon\Lambda(X)\simeq\Upsilon(I)$ is a map in Yoneda image, this implies that $\eta_X$ is an equivalence.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.420239+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b25ee3e400161990fdf7639b1ad6dc25de6b9392775d9e0c962056d2dbbf3b4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 of arXiv:2605.16733, 'Concentration Inequalities for Sample Cross-Covariances'] Let \((X_i,Y_i)_{i=1}^N\) be i.i.d. copies of a centered random vector
\((X,Y)\in\mathbb R^{d_X+d_Y}\). Assume that \(X\) and \(Y\) are
sub-Gaussian random vectors with covariance matrices \(\Sigma_X\) and
\(\Sigma_Y\), and sub-Gaussian constants \(K_X,K_Y\). Set
\[
r_{X}:=\frac{\tr(\Sigma_X)}{\|\Sigma_X\|},
\qquad
r_{Y}:=\frac{\tr(\Sigma_Y)}{\|\Sigma_Y\|}.
\]
For every \(u\ge 1\), it holds with probability at least \(1-\exp(-u)\) that
\[
\bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y_i^{\top}-\E X Y^{\top}\bigg\| \lesssim K_{X}K_{Y}(\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}+u}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{(r_{X}+u)(r_{Y}+u)}}{N}\bigg).
\]
As a corollary,
 \begin{align*}
\E \bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y^{\top}_i-\E X Y^{\top}\bigg\| \lesssim K_{X}K_{Y} (\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{r_{X}r_{Y}}}{N}\bigg).
 \end{align*}
Moreover, if $(X,Y)$ is jointly Gaussian, then
\begin{align*}
\E \bigg\|\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} X_i Y^{\top}_i-\E XY^{\top}\bigg\| \asymp (\|\Sigma_{X}\|\|\Sigma_Y\|)^{1/2} \bigg(\sqrt{\frac{r_{X}+r_{Y}}{N}}+ \frac{\sqrt{r_{X}r_{Y}}}{N}\bigg).
\end{align*} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.363364+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b262947ed144307f28c9e91556faeae15d903118928cde119af3ffc21efb8ba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The following happen:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:58:09.906820+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b278a004a7c424df5a2cbef9a2782626f3fbb3b5c7a1a35691b03820a4c4781","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi The modified transition kernel $Q_{n,t}$ of arXiv:2607.19658, 'Hitting time mixing for random $k$-cycles'] For $t\ge t^*$, set
$$
C_t=(|M_t|-1)_{k-2},
\qquad
q_t=\frac{|M_t|}{|M_t|+1}
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}.
$$
If $k$ is odd, then the kernel $Q_{n,t}$ is defined by
\[
Q_{n,t}=\begin{cases}
(i\cdots i) & \text{with probability } C_tq_t \ \text{for } i\in S_t,\\[6pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } q_t\ \text{for } i_1\in S_t,\ i_2,\ldots,i_k\in M_t,\\[6pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } \left(\dfrac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}\ \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]
If $k$ is even, then the kernel $Q_{n,t}$ is defined by
\[
Q_{n,t}=\begin{cases}
(ab)(i\cdots i) & \text{with probability } \dfrac{C_tq_t}{\binom{|M_t|}{2}}
\ \text{for } i\in S_t,\ \{a,b\}\subset M_t,\\[8pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } q_t\ \text{for } i_1\in S_t,\ i_2,\ldots,i_k\in M_t,\\[6pt]
(i_1\cdots i_k) & \text{with probability } \left(\dfrac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}\ \text{otherwise}.
\end{cases}
\]

Here $(i\cdots i)$ is a labelled dummy move. In the odd case it acts as the identity. In the even case $(ab)(i\cdots i)$ acts on the permutation as the transposition $(ab)$ and carries the label $i$, which indicates the element to be marked. Throughout the marking argument we restrict to the event $|S_{t^*}|\leq \log n$, whose complement will be handled separately. Under both marking schemes the number of unmarked elements never increases, so for all sufficiently large $n$ we have $|M_t|\geq n-\log n$ for every $t\geq t^*$. Hence all quantities appearing in the definition of $Q_{n,t}$ are well-defined.

Let us check that $Q_{n,t}$ is indeed a probability kernel. The total mass assigned by the original uniform $k$-cycle kernel to cycles with exactly one element in $S_t$ is
$$
|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot(|M_t|-1)_{k-2}
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}=|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot C_t\cdot
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1}.
$$
Under $Q_{n,t}$, this mass is replaced by two contributions. The ordinary one-unmarked $k$-cycles have total mass $|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot C_t q_t$,
while the dummy moves have total mass
$|S_t|\cdot C_t q_t$ in the odd case, and
$$
|S_t|\cdot \binom{|M_t|}{2}\cdot\frac{C_tq_t}{\binom{|M_t|}{2}}=|S_t|\cdot C_t q_t
$$
in the even case. Hence the total replacement mass is
$$
|S_t|\cdot (|M_t|+1)\cdot C_tq_t=|S_t|\cdot|M_t|\cdot C_t
\left(\frac{n!}{k(n-k)!}\right)^{-1},
$$
by the definition of $q_t$. All other $k$-cycles retain their original mass. Therefore the total mass of $Q_{n,t}$ is indeed one.","status":"unverified"}

For each finite set $S \\subset T$, we write \\[S \\cup R = \\{s_1^0 < \\dots < s_{k_0}^0 < r_1 < s_1^1 < \\cdots < s_{k_1}^1 < r_2< \\cdots < s_1^{m-1} < \\cdots < s_{k_{m-1}}^{m-1}< r_m < s_1^m < \\cdots < s_{k_m}^m\\}\\] and \\[\\mu_S := \\textnormal{proj}^S_{\\#}[ P^{s_1^0,\\dots,s^0_{k_0},r_1} \\circ P^{r_1, s_1^1 , \\dots, s^1_{k_1},r_2} \\circ \\dots \\circ P^{r_m,s_1^m,\\dots, s_{k_m}^m}].\\] Denoting by $\\mathcal{S}$ the class of finite subsets of $T$, it is readily verified that $(\\mu_S)_{S \\in \\mathcal{S}}$ is a consistent family of measures. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.420730+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b3d69ebdd6cf81ce87818913bb35f34aae570e772cd0755f5ff67246f03def7","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:interval-counterexample of arXiv:2605.17513, 'Nonconcentration of hitting times for random walks on graphs'] There exist bounded-degree trees \(T_m\), vertices \(x_m,y_m\in T_m\), integers
	\(t_m>|V(T_m)|\), and a universal constant $c>0$, such that, writing \(n_m:=|V(T_m)|\),
	\[
	\mathbb P_{x_m}\left(t_m\le \tau_{y_m}\le t_m+n_m\right)
	\ge
	\frac{c}{\sqrt{\log n_m}},
	\qquad 
	\frac{n_m}{t_m}\asymp \frac{1}{\log n_m}.
	\]
	Consequently, (equation eq:interval-conjecture of the paper) cannot hold uniformly over finite
	Markov chains, even restricted to simple random walk on bounded-degree trees.","status":"unverified"}
