{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:39:18.538886+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b4bf2829b98c27088f397ce4eec0cdc1f624077b2b228b49a9855acc2bd5072","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 4 of arXiv:2609.02331, 'Metastability of Interacting Stochastic Systems with Countably Many Metastable States: Bey'] Suppose that Assumptions \ref{assu:U} and \ref{assu:M}
are in force. Then, the diffusion process $\{X_{\epsilon}(t)\}_{t\ge0}$
is metastable in the following sense:
\begin{enumerate}
\item (Mixing) The process satisfies the local mixing condition: For each
$n\in\mathbb{Z}$, $\mathfrak{m}_{n}$ is the attractor, i.e., for
any collection $(x_{\epsilon})_{\epsilon>0}$ in $\mathcal{E}^{n}$,
\[
\lim_{\epsilon\to0}\mathbb{Q}^{\epsilon}_{x_{\epsilon}}\left[\mathcal{H}_{\mathfrak{m}_{n}}>\mathcal{H}_{\mathcal{E}\setminus\mathcal{E}^{n}}\right]=0.
\]
\item (Convergence in law) For any $n\in\mathbb{Z}$ and $(x_{\epsilon})_{\epsilon>0}$
in $\mathcal{E}^{n}$, the trace laws ${\bf Q}^{\epsilon}_{x_{\epsilon}}$
converge weakly to the limit law ${\bf Q}_{n}$ as $\epsilon\to0$.
\item (Delta-negligibility) The excursions outside $\mathcal{E}$ is negligible,
i.e. for each $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, $(x_{\epsilon})_{\epsilon>0}$ in
$\mathcal{E}^{n}$, and $T>0$,
\[
\lim_{\epsilon\to0}{\rm E}^{\mathbb{Q}^{\epsilon}_{x_{\epsilon}}}\left[\int^{T}_{0}{\bf 1}\left\{ X_{\epsilon}(t)\notin\mathcal{E}\right\} {\rm d}t\right]=0.
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:54:28.005892+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7b4df4a17ba80b1a38ccb6de635f0dfebd68046dad4ee53e9f58069de0850150","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.07042, 'Limit Points of Reflow with Minibatch Optimal Transport'] We call a set $A\subset\mathbb{R}^d\times\mathbb{R}^d$ $N$-cyclically monotone for $N\geq 2$ if it holds for all $(x^{(i)},y^{(i)})\in A$ and

$$
\sum_{i=1}^N \|x^{(i)}-y^{(i)}\|^2\leq \sum_{i=1}^N \|x^{(i)}-y^{(\tau(i))}\|^2.
$$

if $\mathrm{supp}(\gamma)$ is $N$-cyclically monotone.","status":"unverified"}

Method: Express the escape probability through the branching-process representation for the one-cookie deterministic case. Result: In the deterministic environment with one cookie of strength p at each site (M = 1, delta = 2p - 1... transient iff delta > 1 which needs more than one cookie; take M = 2 cookies of strength p each, delta = 2(2p - 1) > 1 iff p > 3/4). The event of never returning to 0 after the first step: the walk must never come back, which in the branching-process picture (right excursions counted by the number of down-crossings of each edge) means the branching process with migration started from the edge (0,1) never produces a down-crossing of (0,1) into 0... the escape probability equals the probability that the total number of down-crossings of the edge (0,1) is zero, which is P(the branching process with migration started at 1 individual at level 1 has zero descendants at level 0) - not directly a standard extinction probability but a hitting probability of the time-reversed process. For the source's example [Zer05, Th. 18] the closed form exists; for general bounded stacks the escape probability is the solution of a finite-dimensional fixed-point equation obtained by conditioning on the first cookie stack at sites 1, 2, ...: define q_k = P(never return to 0 | walk currently at k, all cookies at sites >= k intact, cookies at sites < k in their post-visit states); the states of the sites already visited matter only through the remaining cookie counts, which for M bounded is a finite vector, and the walk's returns to 0 require descending through all visited sites; the escape probability then equals the probability of survival of a Markov chain on finite cookie-count vectors, computable numerically for given (M, p) but with no closed form in general. Recorded: reduction to a finite-state escape problem; closed form only in special cases. Obstruction: No closed form beyond special cases; the reduction gives a numerical procedure only.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["transversal Volterra quadratic stochastic operator with a finite fixed-point set","the object asked for is a periodic ITINERARY, a symbol sequence, not a periodic orbit","m = 3 for the affirmative half; m = 4 for the negative half"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869055+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_7b99ec5d60dc0898696527f9d4720a213936d1742c23a4204d7ba8866f289a8e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: unreviewed - author-checked against the source's exact wording; verification unreviewed] For a transversal Volterra quadratic stochastic operator the ITINERARY of a trajectory is the sequence of fixed-point neighbourhoods it visits; Rozikov (2009, p. 4) asks whether some trajectory has a periodic itinerary. CLAIM, in two halves. (i) YES at m = 3, by an example already in the literature: for the cyclic Volterra operator with a = b = c = 1, matrix A = [[0,1,-1],[-1,0,1],[1,-1,0]], whose leading 2x2 minor is 1 so the operator is transversal and whose fixed-point set - the three vertices and the centre - is finite, the itinerary of every non-fixed interior point is periodic, 1 -> 3 -> 2 -> 1 -> ..., with sojourns 12, 51, 1073, ... growing geometrically by the heteroclinic-cycle mechanism of Ganikhodzhaev and Zanin (2004). (ii) NO in general: at m = 4, Ganikhodjaev and Zanin (arXiv:1205.3841, Theorem 5) show the trajectory moves along the routes 1-4-3-2-1, 1-4-2-1 or 1-4-3-1, and a simulated cyclic-type m = 4 map produces the MIXED itinerary 1,4,3,2,1,4,2,1 - so itineraries need not be periodic. THE SHARP OPEN QUESTION, which is what the source presumably meant: is every itinerary eventually periodic, or which matrices A force it? The 2012 route analysis is the starting point. A periodic ITINERARY is a symbol sequence, not a periodic ORBIT: periodic orbits are typically absent while periodic itineraries need not be.","status":"unverified"}

# Target 1: exact normal stability of the factored GD stationary curve

Version 1, proof unaudited. This is a linearized stability classification;
it does not claim a nonlinear flip bifurcation or a full-space GD basin theorem.

Assume precisely the n-example factored model of claim 010:
0<a_i<b_i, b_i,kappa_i>0, logistic average loss of
v h_i(kq), h_i(s)=a_i+b_i tanh(kappa_i s), and simultaneous Euclidean GD
with any fixed eta>0. Let p_bar<0 be the unique mean root and define

 A=mean_i h_i(p_bar)^2/4>=0,
 B=mean_i h_i'(p_bar)/2>0.

All finite stationary points, equivalently all GD fixed points, form the
curve E={v=0,kq=p_bar}. At such a point write S=k^2+q^2>=2|p_bar|.
The GD Jacobian has tangent multiplier 1 and normal multipliers

 mu_-=1-eta lambda_-, mu_+=1-eta lambda_+,
 lambda_+/-=(A +/- sqrt(A^2+4B^2 S))/2.

Here lambda_-<0<lambda_+, hence mu_->1 everywhere: no point of E is
linearly attracting in all normal directions. The other normal direction is

* strictly attracting in the linearization when eta lambda_+<2;
* neutral with multiplier -1 when eta lambda_+=2;
* strictly repelling with multiplier less than -1 when eta lambda_+>2.

Let
 J_eta=(4/eta^2-2A/eta)/B^2.

The first case is EXACTLY S<J_eta, the middle case exactly S=J_eta,
and the last exactly S>J_eta. Equivalently, with C=k^2-q^2,
S=sqrt(C^2+4p_bar^2): there is an attracting normal direction only if
J_eta>2|p_bar|, and then precisely at

 |C|<sqrt(J_eta^2-4p_bar^2).

Equality gives neutral normal points when J_eta>=2|p_bar|. If J_eta
is smaller than 2|p_bar|, every point is repelling in both normal directions.
In particular, for EVERY eta>0, sufficiently unbalanced factorizations on
E are normally repelling in both directions. There is no positive constant
step that preserves the flow's one attracting normal direction uniformly
along the entire stationary curve. This does NOT imply an open basin of
cycles or disprove a full-space almost-everywhere GD endpoint theorem.

## Proof

The fixed-point condition is gradient L=0, classified in proof 008.
Its loss Hessian at E is
 [[A,-Bq,-Bk],[-Bq,0,0],[-Bk,0,0]].
The tangent vector (0,k,-q) is in its kernel. In the orthonormal basis
e_v=(1,0,0), e_s=(0,q,k)/sqrt(S) of the normal plane, the Hessian is
 [[A,-B sqrt(S)],[-B sqrt(S),0]].
The quadratic characteristic polynomial is lambda^2-A lambda-B^2 S,
which yields lambda_+/- and their signs. The GD Jacobian is I-eta Hessian,
proving the multipliers and their linear classifications.

For equivalence with J_eta, consider the polynomial
f(z)=z^2-Az-B^2 S, whose positive zero is lambda_+ and negative zero
lambda_-. Since 2/eta>0, lambda_+<2/eta is equivalent to
f(2/eta)>0, or S<J_eta; equality and the reverse inequality follow likewise.
This avoids squaring a potentially negative expression 4/eta-A.
Finally S^2=C^2+4p_bar^2 by algebra, and S is unbounded along E by
taking k->infinity, q=p_bar/k. All asserted threshold statements follow.

## Scope of the obstruction

The obstruction is to a PARTICULAR transfer from flow to GD: retaining
one attracting normal direction uniformly on every imbalance leaf at fixed
step. It is not an obstruction to every possible discrete-time proof.
The imbalance leaves themselves are not invariant under GD:
C_+=(1-eta^2 v^2 G^2)C. Both facts must be accounted for in further work.
Normal multipliers on the unit circle require separate nonlinear analysis;
no attracting two-cycle is claimed. Scalar genuine self-attention embeddings
of this family are supplied in claim 008.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149322+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, Schauder and L^p theory","id":"claim_7bb2c58aa2918e859c731bf67503266f6c9b7d91791ab1a5552f2ca3db2a40ef","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: the Hoelder exponent satisfies 0 < alpha < 1 strictly, and the Lebesgue exponent satisfies 1 < p < infinity strictly. The reason is that the second derivatives of the Newtonian potential are given by a singular integral operator, which is bounded on C^{0,alpha} and on L^p only in the open ranges. Failure at alpha = 0 (continuous right-hand side does not give a C^2 solution): in the plane put u(x) = (x_1^2 - x_2^2) (log(1/r))^{1/2} for 0 < r = |x| < 1/2, u(0) = 0. A computation with u = p g, p = r^2 cos(2 theta) harmonic and g = (log(1/r))^{1/2}, using Laplacian(p g) = 4 p g'/r + p (g'' + g'/r), gives Laplacian u = -cos(2 theta) ( 2 (log(1/r))^{-1/2} + (1/4)(log(1/r))^{-3/2} ), which extends continuously by 0 at the origin, while D_{11}u = 2(log(1/r))^{1/2} + o(1) blows up. Since u is C^1 and C^infinity off the origin, it solves Laplacian u = f distributionally on the ball with f continuous; no C^2 solution of Laplacian v = f exists near 0, because v - u would be harmonic hence smooth. (Consistently, this f is continuous but not Dini continuous, and Dini continuity is the correct substitute hypothesis.) Failure at alpha = 1: with q = x_1^3 - 3 x_1 x_2^2 and g = log(1/r), the function u = q g has Laplacian u = -6 q/r^2 = -6 r cos(3 theta), which is Lipschitz, while D_{111}u = 6 log(1/r) + O(1) is unbounded, so u is not in C^{2,1}. Failure at p = infinity: u = (x_1^2 - x_2^2) log(1/r) has Laplacian u = -4 cos(2 theta) in L^infinity while D_{11}u = 2 log(1/r) + O(1) is not bounded, so Laplacian u in L^infinity does not give u in W^{2,infinity} = C^{1,1}; the correct endpoint statement is Laplacian u in L^infinity implies D^2 u in BMO. Failure at p = 1: let f_k = rho_{1/k} be standard mollifiers and u_k = Gamma convolved with f_k, so Laplacian u_k = f_k with ||f_k||_{L^1} = 1 and ||u_k||_{L^1(B_2)} bounded; on B_1 minus the origin D_{12}u_k converges pointwise to D_{12}Gamma, whose size is comparable to |x|^{-n} and hence not integrable near 0, so by Fatou ||D^2 u_k||_{L^1(B_1)} tends to infinity. No estimate of the form ||D^2u||_{L^1} <= C(||Laplacian u||_{L^1} + ||u||_{L^1}) can hold; the correct endpoint statements are weak-L^1 bounds and the Hardy space result Laplacian u in H^1 implies D^2u in L^1. Practical consequence: from f merely continuous (or bounded) one gets u in W^{2,p}_loc for every finite p and u in C^{1,alpha}_loc for every alpha < 1, but not, in general, u in C^2 - the first example above is exactly the obstruction (for particular right-hand sides, a smooth f say, the solution is of course C^2).","status":"unverified"}

(Stampacchia, Ann. Inst. Fourier 1965.) (I) $L^\\infty$ estimate. If $f \\in L^m(\\Omega)$ with $m > N/2$ (so $f \\in H^{-1}$ and the weak solution $u \\in H_0^1(\\Omega)$ exists and is unique), then $u \\in L^\\infty(\\Omega)$ and $\\|u\\|_{L^\\infty} \\leq C\\,\\|f\\|_{L^m}$ with $C = C(N, \\lambda, m, |\\Omega|)$. (II) $L^1$ and measure data. If $f \\in L^1(\\Omega)$ (or more generally $f = \\mu$ is a bounded Radon measure on $\\Omega$), there exists a unique DUALITY solution: a function $u \\in L^1(\\Omega)$ with $\\int_\\Omega u\\,g\\,dx = \\int_\\Omega w_g\\,d\\mu$ for every $g \\in L^\\infty(\\Omega)$, where $w_g \\in H_0^1(\\Omega) \\cap L^\\infty(\\Omega)$ is the weak solution of the adjoint problem $-\\operatorname{div}(A^{T}\\nabla w_g) = g$ (bounded by part (I), which is all that is needed to pair with $f \\in L^1$); for MEASURE data one needs $w_g$ continuous on $\\overline\\Omega$ so that $\\int w_g\\,d\\mu$ makes sense - interior continuity is De Giorgi-Nash-Moser, continuity up to the boundary requires a mild regularity of $\\partial\\Omega$ (e.g. Lipschitz, or an exterior cone condition), which is then an extra hypothesis in the measure case. This $u$ satisfies: $u \\in W_0^{1,q}(\\Omega)$ for EVERY $q < N/(N-1)$ with $\\|u\\|_{W_0^{1,q}} \\leq C(N,\\lambda,\\Lambda,q,\\Omega)\\,\\|\\mu\\|_{\\mathcal{M}}$ ($= \\|f\\|_{L^1}$ for $L^1$ data); $|\\nabla u|$ lies in the Marcinkiewicz (weak-$L$) space $M^{N/(N-1)}(\\Omega)$ and, for $N \\geq 3$, $u \\in M^{N/(N-2)}(\\Omega)$; $u$ is the strong $W_0^{1,q}$ limit of the weak solutions $u_n$ with smooth data $f_n \\to f$ in $L^1$ (or $f_n \\to \\mu$ weakly-* with $\\|f_n\\|_1$ bounded); $u$ solves the equation in the sense of distributions, $\\int A\\nabla u\\cdot\\nabla\\varphi = \\int \\varphi\\,d\\mu$ for $\\varphi \\in C_c^\\infty(\\Omega)$; and $T_k(u) \\in H_0^1(\\Omega)$ for every $k$ with $\\lambda\\int|\\nabla T_k(u)|^2 \\leq k\\|\\mu\\|$. Sharp edges: (a) $q = N/(N-1)$ is excluded and cannot be reached - for $\\mu = \\delta_0$ and $A = I$ the Green function has $|\\nabla u| \\sim |x|^{1-N}$, which is in $L^q$ near 0 iff $q < N/(N-1)$; (b) uniqueness holds among DUALITY solutions (equivalently among limits of approximations, or entropy/renormalized solutions), NOT among all distributional solutions in $W^{1,q}$, $q < N/(N-1)$: for merely measurable uniformly elliptic $A$ Serrin (1964) constructed, for any $1 < q < 2$, a nonzero $u \\in W^{1,q}(B)$ on a ball $B$ with $\\operatorname{div}(A\\nabla u) = 0$ distributionally and $u \\notin H^1_{loc}$ (a 'pathological solution'), so a distributional $W^{1,q}$ solution is not determined by its data without a selection principle such as duality, approximation, or the entropy/renormalized formulation; (c) with $L^1$ data the solution is in general NOT in $H_0^1$ (its energy is infinite), so the Lax-Milgram framework does not apply directly - the estimates are obtained on approximations via the truncation method and passed to the limit.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:53:10.207646+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7bbcc3055ed966d80d6ae6e65031be16b5d3b953e5585a069d7d245f216acd91","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defi Def:W-cont-map of arXiv:2608.29013, 'Weighted Homology and Cohomology of Weighted Polyhedra'] Suppose $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are
   weighted polyhedra of the same type. 
   A \emph{W-continuous map} from $(X,\lambda)$ to 
   $(X',\lambda')$ is a continuous map $f: X\rightarrow X'$   which satisfies: for all $x\in X$,
   $$ \begin{cases}
   \lambda'(f(x)) \mid \lambda(x),  &  \text{if  $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are of ascending type}; \\
   \lambda(x) \mid \lambda'(f(x)),  &  \text{if  $(X,\lambda)$ and $(X',\lambda')$ are of descending type}.
 \end{cases}  
   $$  
    We also denote such a map by $f: (X,\lambda)\rightarrow (X',\lambda')$ to indicate its W-continuity
    since the definition of $f$ depends on the type of the weighted polyhedra involved.
   Moreover, $f$ is called \emph{weight-preserving} if 
$\lambda'(f(x))=\lambda(x)$ for all $x\in X$.\vskip 0.1cm

We say that $(X,\lambda)$ is \emph{isomorphic} to $(X',\lambda')$ if there exists a weight-preserving homeomorphism from $(X,\lambda)$ to $(X',\lambda')$.","status":"unverified"}

    We say that $\mu$ satisfies the \emph{small-ball condition with parameter $s$}, if there exist constants $c,r_0>0$ (depending on $s$) such that
    \begin{equation}
      \mu^\ast \bigl(\ball(x,r)\bigr)
      \leq \exp\bigl( -c \cdot (1/r)^s \bigr)
      \qquad \forall \, x\in \XX \text{ and } 0 < r < r_0
      .
      
    \end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:43:45.382133+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c11e3790072a76151a38dbe6a274df3e9e9d07e8932f362a2ab6c492e38a8b6","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 47 of arXiv:2609.04033, 'From configuration spaces to graph complexes via $\mathbf{FA}$-modules'] There exists an isomorphism of graded $S_n$-modules:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:28:33.869400+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c307c4330f1aae07b7e103c0ede79ee58bde7eb83e03928171802183d10dcc6","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:saturated-properties of arXiv:2504.19367, 'Reduced Random Walks in the Hyperbolic Plane\textinterrobang'] Let $a \leq b \leq c$ be real numbers, let $T \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, and let $f, g \colon T \to \mathbb{R}$ be functions.     \begin{lemenum}
        \item  If $\left\lvertf(b) - f(a)\right\rvert < \epsilon$, then $f$ is $\epsilon$-saturated on $[a, b]$.

        \item  If $f$ is $\epsilon$-saturated on $[a, b]$, then $f + C$ is also $\epsilon$-saturated on $[a, b]$.

        \item  Let $U \subseteq \mathbb{R}$, and let $h \colon U \to T$ be a monotone (increasing or decreasing) function. If $f \circ h$ is $\epsilon$-saturated on $[a, b]$, then $f$ is $\epsilon$-saturated on $[h(a), h(b)]$.

    To see that the internal CRN is not explosive, let $g(e,s)=e+\ln(s+1)$. Then
    \begin{align*}
    \mathcal A g(e,s)
    &=e(g(e+1,s)-g(e,s))+es(g(e,s+1)-g(e,s))\\
    &=e+es\ln\left(\frac{s+2}{s+1}\right) =e+es\ln\left(1+\frac1{s+1}\right)\\
    &\le e+es\frac1{s+1} \le e+e \le 2g(e,s).
    \end{align*}
    So the claim follows from Theorem (thm:lyapunov-nonexplosivity of the paper).
    
    To see that $g(e,s)=e+\log(s+1)$ cannot be replaced with a linear Lyapunov function above, fix $c_1,c_2>0$ and $c_3,c_4\ge0$, and let $f(e,s)=c_1e+c_2s$. Notice that
    \[
    \mathcal A f(e,s)=c_1e+c_2es.
    \]
    If $s$ is chosen such that $h(s):=c_2s^2+c_1s-c_3c_1s-c_3c_2s-c_4>0$ and we set $e=s$, then $\mathcal A f(e,s)>c_3 f(e,s)+c_4$. But $c_2>0$, so $h$ is a quadratic function with positive leading term and hence we can always pick such an $s$.

    Lastly, we have to show that $N$ is not explosive. For $n\in\mathcal N$, let
    \begin{align*}
        C(n)&=\sum_{x\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} n_x, \qquad\qquad S(n)=\!\sum_{(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} sn_{(e,s)}, \qquad\qquad
        E(n)=\!\sum_{(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} en_{(e,s)}
    \end{align*}
    denote the total number of compartments, $S$ molecules, and enzymes, respectively, when in state $n$. Consider the function $V(n)=E(n)+\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)$. Then if $\mathcal L$ denotes the generator of $N$, we have
    \begin{align*}
        \mathcal LV(n)
        &=\sum_{x=(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2}\Bigg[
        n_xe\big(E(n)+1-E(n)\big)
        +n_xes\big(\log(S(n)+1+C(n)+1)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\\
        &\quad\quad
        +sn_x\left(\sum_{y\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2} \psi(x,y)\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+1+1)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\right)\Bigg]\\
        &=E(n)+\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+2)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\sum_{x=(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2}
        n_x(es+s)\\
        &\le E(n)+\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+2)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\sum_{x=(e,s)\in\mathbb Z_{\ge0}^2}
        n_x(E(n)s+s)\\
        &=E(n)+\big(E(n)S(n)+S(n)\big)\big(\log(S(n)+C(n)+2)-\log(S(n)+C(n)+1)\big)\\
        &\le E(n)+\big(E(n)S(n)+S(n)\big)\frac1{S(n)+C(n)+1}\\
        &\le E(n)+E(n)+1\\
        &\le 2V(n)+1.
    \end{align*}
    So the remaining claim follows, as before, from Theorem (thm:lyapunov-nonexplosivity of the paper).
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

# Balanced opposite-head two-cycles: complete implicit parametrization

T328-W698-017 v1, Target 1, proof (unaudited).

Consider L(v,k,q)=log(1+exp(-v h(kq))), h(s)=a+b*tanh(kappa*s),
0<a<b, kappa>0 and simultaneous Euclidean GD with fixed eta>0.
For this scalar signed link, every balanced period-two orbit whose heads have
opposite signs is covered by the following construction, up to interchanging
the two phases and simultaneously negating both factors. The construction
parametrizes cycles across the data/step parameters; for prescribed a,b,kappa,
eta these parameter equalities are necessary and sufficient, not a claim that
every prescribed model has such a cycle.

## Construction from four positive parameters

Choose 0<r<1 and T,y0,kappa>0. Define

    A=tanh T, B=tanh(r^2*T),
    D=cosh(T)^2/cosh(r^2*T)^2,
    sig(y)=1/(1+exp(-y)), f(y)=y*sig(y)^2.

There is a unique y1>0 solving

    f(y1)=f(y0)/(r*D).

Indeed f'(y)=sig(y)^2*[1+2y*(1-sig(y))]>0 on y>0,
and f increases continuously from 0 to infinity. Put

    g0=sig(y0), g1=sig(y1), c=g0/g1,
    t=y1/(y0*c),
    v0=sqrt((1-r)*(A-B)/((1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2)),
    H0=y0/v0, H1=c*H0,
    b=H0*(1+c)/(A-B), a=b*A-H0,
    eta=v0*(1+t)/(g0*H0), w=sqrt(T/kappa).

All denominators are strictly positive. Also a/b=(c*A+B)/(1+c) lies
strictly between B and A, hence 0<a<b. These parameters give the exact
period-two orbit

    (v0,w,-w) <-> (-t*v0,r*w,-r*w).

The two signed margins are -y0 and -y1. In particular the logistic factors
are exactly g0 and g1, not factors obtained from a limiting approximation.

## Verification

h(-w^2)=-H0 and h(-r^2*w^2)=H1. Thus g0*H0=g1*H1 and
the two head increments are respectively -v0*(1+t) and v0*(1+t).
Let d0=b*kappa*sech(T)^2, d1=b*kappa*sech(r^2*T)^2=D*d0.
The first factor coefficient is

    delta0=eta*v0*g0*d0
          =v0^2*(1+t)*(1+c)*kappa*sech(T)^2/(A-B)=1-r.

For the second coefficient, the scalar equation gives

    t*(g1/g0)*D = y1*g1^2*D/(y0*g0^2)=1/r.

Consequently delta1=eta*(-t*v0)*g1*d1=-(1-r)/r=1-1/r.
On k=-q the factor multipliers 1-delta0=r and 1-delta1=1/r
return the factors exactly. The head changes sign, so the orbit is nonfixed.

## Completeness within the stated class

Balance means k^2=q^2. If k=q, the product is nonnegative, h(kq)>0,
and the head strictly increases at every finite point, so there is no finite
cycle. If k=q=0 the same argument applies. Thus a balanced cycle must lie
on k=-q with nonzero k. Interchange phases so v0>0>v1 and simultaneously
negate both factors so k0=w>0. Since delta_j=eta*v_j*g_j*h'_j,
delta0>0>delta1. The returning-factor equation is

    (1-delta0)*(1-delta1)=1.

The second factor is >1; therefore 0<1-delta0<1. Write this number r.
It follows that k1=r*w and delta1=1-1/r. In particular no factor sign flip
is possible for an opposite-head balanced two-cycle in this class.
The head update v1-v0<0 forces h0<0, and the reverse update forces h1>0.
Set H0=-h0, H1=h1, t=-v1/v0, T=kappa*w^2,
y0=v0*H0, y1=t*v0*H1. These are positive. The equal and opposite
head increments imply H1/H0=g0/g1=c, whence t=y1/(y0*c).
Dividing the two factor coefficients gives r*D*f(y1)=f(y0).
The identities h1-h0=b*(A-B), delta0=1-r and the head increment then
recover precisely the formulas for b,a,v0,eta above. This proves completeness.

## Full Jacobian test and its present limit

The normal two-step multiplier is exactly

    mu_U=(1+delta0)*(1+delta1)=(2-r)*(2-1/r)=5-2r-2/r.

It satisfies |mu_U|<1 precisely for (3-sqrt(5))/2<r<1,
equals -1 at the left endpoint, and is <-1 below it. It is zero at r=1/2.
The other two multipliers are exactly the eigenvalues of J1*J0, using
the general balanced Jacobian given in proofs/014_opposite_head_cycles.md.
This is an exact formula for the full spectrum, but no uniform inequality
for that balanced block has been proved for unequal head magnitudes.

The reproducible script scripts/asymmetric_cycles.py sampled 576 choices:
r in {.1,.2,.35,.4,.5,.65,.8,.9,.98}, T in {.1,.3,.6,.9,1.3,2,3,5},
y0 in {.01,.1,.4,1,2,4,8,16}, with kappa=1. It solved the monotone
equation by floating-point bisection and differentiated the full 3D loss.
It found zero attracting candidates; the smallest observed full spectral
radius was approximately 8.9666956. The largest relative cycle residual was
approximately 2.56e-13. These are numerical evidence, not rigorous bounds,
and cannot establish instability throughout the parametrization.

Claim 016 proves full instability and the complete second-multiplier phase
diagram on the equal-head-magnitude subfamily r=1/2,
cosh(T)^2=2cosh(T/4)^2. The SINGLE remaining hard step for upgrading
the wider numerical finding to a theorem is a rigorous spectral-radius
inequality for J1*J0 throughout (r,T,y0)>0 with 0<r<1. This proof
does not claim that step or almost-everywhere factored-GD convergence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:19:47.272105+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c65d5f6b42d957359a385c83fae17c845d7b1786630ec0d59a0fd6787e8a37d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:pred_proj of arXiv:2601.09976, 'Stochastic Calculus as Operator Factorization:\\ An Operator--Covariant Derivative and Uni'] Assume that $\mathcal{H}_X$ consists of jointly measurable processes and that the predictable processes form a closed subspace of~$\mathcal{H}_X$. The \emph{predictable projection} $\Pi_X \colon \mathcal{H}_X \to \mathcal{H}_X$ is the orthogonal projection onto this subspace.

The closedness assumption is not automatic for an arbitrary energy space; it must be verified. In all examples of this paper, the predictable subspace is either all of~$\mathcal{H}_X$ (for It\^o integrals with respect to martingales and compensated Poisson processes, where $\mathcal{H}_X$ consists entirely of predictable processes) or is closed by standard results on conditional expectation.

For the integral-form energy spaces used throughout this paper---specifically, those where $u_t \in L^2(\Omega)$ for each~$t$ and the $\mathcal{H}_X$ inner product takes the form $\langle u, v \rangle_{\mathcal{H}_X} = \mathbb{E}[\int_0^T u_t v_t\, d\mu_t]$ for some positive measure $\mu$ on $[0,T]$ (possibly random, as with $d\langle X\rangle_t$)---the predictable projection admits the pointwise representation
\[
(\Pi_X u)_t = \mathbb{E}[u_t \mid \mathcal{F}_{t-}] \quad \text{for } t \in (0,T], \qquad (\Pi_X u)_0 = \mathbb{E}[u_0 \mid \mathcal{F}_0],
\]
where $\mathcal{F}_{t-}$ is the left-limit $\sigma$-algebra defined in Section~(sec:setup of the paper). This is the standard predictable projection of optional processes; see, e.g., [Revuz1999].","status":"unverified"}

Method: Analyse M(1,1) on Z^2 through the range of the first-coordinate walk. Result: In M(1,1) the first coordinate moves only at first visits and the second at later visits; the set of visited vertices is the range, and the first-coordinate process is a simple random walk on Z run at the rate of new visits. Recurrence of M(1,1) would follow if the walk returns to the origin infinitely often; since the second coordinate performs a simple random walk on the column above the current first coordinate whenever the vertex was visited before, the walk behaves in each column like a 1D random walk (recurrent) until it hits an unvisited vertex, at which time the first coordinate steps. The number of new visits up to time n is the range R_n; the first coordinate after n steps is a simple random walk at time R_n, so |X^1_n| is of order sqrt(R_n), and R_n <= n, so |X^1_n| is typically at most of order sqrt n - not deterministically: n first-visit moves to the right, which have probability 2^-n, give X^1_n = n; a return to the origin requires both coordinates to vanish. A heuristic: if R_n ≍ n/log n as for planar simple random walk then the first coordinate is diffusive at the slower clock, and the walk is 'more recurrent' than planar simple random walk, supporting the conjecture; but the range of M(1,1) is not that of simple random walk because the exploration is column-wise. A rigorous partial fact: M(1,1) is recurrent if and only if the first coordinate returns to 0 infinitely often at times when the second coordinate is 0; since within a column the second coordinate is a recurrent 1D walk that keeps returning to 0 until it finds a new vertex, and new vertices in a column are found at the ends of the visited interval, the question is whether the first-coordinate walk (which is a simple random walk in the clock of new visits) visits 0 infinitely often, which it does a.s. (1D recurrence), and whether at those visits the second coordinate is 0 - not automatic. So recurrence of M(1,1) reduces to: at the (infinitely many) times the first coordinate is 0, the second coordinate, which then performs a 1D walk in the column of 0 with the visited interval of that column, returns to height 0 before finding a new vertex - which has probability bounded below by a constant each time if the visited interval around height 0 in column 0 has length bounded... the visited interval in column 0 grows, and the probability of returning to 0 from the boundary of an interval of length L before exiting is of order 1/L... summing over the visits to column 0 gives a divergent series only if the interval lengths grow slowly enough. This is the crux and I did not settle it; the reduction is recorded. Key identity: M(1,1) recurrent iff, at the infinitely many returns of the first coordinate to 0, the second coordinate returns to 0 in column 0 before finding a new vertex; the return probability is of order 1/(visited interval length). Obstruction: Growth rate of the visited interval in column 0 not controlled.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:52:00.177355+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_7c77d10410d2d17d2b29a13890e9d2446c665544a522565398fd2ddbdfe6823f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Little Picard theorem: if f : C -> C is entire and non-constant, then the image of f is either all of C or C minus a single point, i.e. f omits at most one complex value. If moreover f is transcendental (not a polynomial), then f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely often. Great Picard theorem: if f is holomorphic on a punctured neighborhood of z_0 and z_0 is an essential singularity, then on every such punctured neighborhood f takes every complex value, with at most one exception, infinitely many times. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:12:13.389794+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c782ce712bbbe740f1b4b1368e7d7b76443313549230642b4440e243c95cbbd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 80 of arXiv:2608.28200, '\textbf On the Formality of Configuration Spaces of $\aka$'] A diagram consists of the data $\Gamma=(A_\Gamma,I_\Gamma,E_\Gamma,s_\Gamma,t_\Gamma, W^V_{\Gamma},W^E_{\Gamma})$, where
\begin{itemize}
\item $A_\Gamma$ is a finite set of external vertices.
\item $I_\Gamma$ is a linearly ordered finite set of internal vertices, disjoint from $A_\Gamma$.

Denote by $V_\Gamma:= A_\Gamma \sqcup  I_\Gamma$ the set of all vertices.
\item $E_\Gamma$ is a linearly ordered finite set of edges.  
\item $s_\Gamma,t_\Gamma:E_\Gamma \to V_\Gamma$ are the source and the target. Both of them are endpoints of edges. 
\item $W^V_\Gamma:V_\Gamma \to \C[\ZZi ]$ is the weight of vertices.
\item $W^E_\Gamma:E_\Gamma \to \C[\partial_{1},\cdots,\partial_{n}]$ is the weight of edges. 
\end{itemize}  
We adopt the following terminology and notation:
\begin{itemize}
\item Denote the set of endpoints of an edge $e$ by $\partial e$.
\item We extend the linear order of $I_\Gamma$ to a partial order on $V_\Gamma$ by letting $a<i$ when $a\in A_\Gamma$ and $i\in I_\Gamma$. 
\item Two distinct vertices are said to be adjacent if they are the endpoints of an edge.
\item We say that the edge $e$ is oriented from $s_\Gamma(e)$ to $t_\Gamma(e)$.
\item We divide the set of edges into the following four families:
\begin{itemize}
    \item a loop is an edge whose endpoints are identical;
    \item a chord is an edge between two distinct external vertices;
    \item a dead end is an edge that is not a loop and such that at least one of its endpoints is internal and has only one adjacent vertex;
    \item a contractible edge is an edge that is neither a chord, nor a loop, nor a dead end.
\end{itemize}

\item The {valence} of a vertex is the number of edges for which the vertex is
an endpoint, with loops adding two to the valence.
\item An edge $e$ is {simple} if there exists no other edge with the same set of endpoints.
\item {Double edges} are distinct edges with the same set of endpoints. 
\item Two vertices $v$ and $w$ are {connected} if there exists a path of edges joining them (ignoring orientations). 
\item Given a finite set $A$, a  {diagram on $A$} is a diagram $\Gamma$ such that $A_\Gamma=A$.
\item A diagram on $A$ is a {unit} if it has no internal vertices or edges.  We denote a unit by $\boldsymbol{1}$. 
\item Two diagrams  $\Gamma$ and  $\Gamma'$ are {isomorphic} if $E_\Gamma=E_{\Gamma'}$ and there exist two order-preserving bijections $\phi_E\colon E_\Gamma\cong E_{\Gamma'}$ and $\phi_I\colon I_\Gamma\cong I_{\Gamma'}$. 
\item We will abuse notation by denoting a diagram and its isomorphism class by the same letter $\Gamma$.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:12:09.028118+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7c9b14f84997d87fdcec1796690723a0d665fc089c98c7d09c51fa737e0939fd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary cor:semilinear-additive of arXiv:2608.21805, 'Logarithmic derivatives of variational and singular stochastic partial differential equati'] Consider semilinear SPDEs with additive noise,
\[
  \mathrm{d}X(t) = [AX(t) + F(X(t))]\,\mathrm{d}t + Q^{1/2}\,\mathrm{d}W(t),
\]
where $A$ generates an analytic semigroup on $H$, $Q^{1/2} \in L_2(U,H)$, and $F: V \to V^*$ is twice continuously Fr\'echet differentiable with $F'_u, F''_{uu}$ satisfying the growth and integrability conditions of Assumptions \textup{(D1)--(D3)} (so that $\mathcal{A}(t,u) := -[Au + F(u)]$ fits the abstract framework of Assumptions (ass:LR of the paper)--(ass:diff2 of the paper)). Assume that the hypotheses of Theorem~(thm:main of the paper), Part~II, hold for the given deterministic direction $h \in H$, namely the structural Assumptions~(ass:SC of the paper) and~(ass:SC-raised of the paper), all three clauses of Assumption~(ass:nondeg of the paper) (the range and moment conditions \textup{(i)}--\textup{(ii)} at the chosen H\"older-triangle pair $(q, p^*)$, and the Cameron--Martin compatibility \textup{(iii)}), and the fixed-Tikhonov substitution regularity~(hyp:iii-F-prime of the paper).
Then $\mathcal{B}'_u = 0$, $\mathcal{B}''_{uu} = 0$, the Malliavin--second variation equation (equation eq:second-var of the paper) has no stochastic integral term, the correction terms involve only $F''_{uu}$ (not $\mathcal{B}''_{uu}$), and the formula reads
\[
\begin{aligned}
  \delta_U(v_h) &= \bigl[\delta_U\bigl(r \mapsto \Phi_r^{*}z\bigr)\bigr]_{z = \gamma_t^{\dagger}h}\\
  &\quad + \lim_{\varepsilon \downarrow 0}\int_0^t \operatorname{Tr}_U\bigl[\Phi_r^{*}\,(\gamma_t+\varepsilon I)^{-1}\,[\mathcal{D}_r\gamma_t]\,(\gamma_t+\varepsilon I)^{-1}h\bigr]\,\mathrm{d}r,
\end{aligned}
\]
with $\Phi_r = \mathcal{D}_r X(t)$. The first line must be read as ``first take the frozen-$z$ divergence, then substitute $z = \gamma_t^{\dagger}h$''; it is not the composed divergence $\delta_U(r \mapsto \Phi_r^{*}\gamma_t^{\dagger}h)$, which already absorbs the trace correction (Lemma~(lemma:HS-kernel of the paper)(iv)). The frozen-$z$ divergence is genuinely anticipating unless $F = 0$, in which case it reduces to an It\^o integral. If the random evolution family generated by $A + F'(X(\cdot))$ admits an a.s.\ bounded realisation $Y(t,r) \in L(H)$, an additional structural input, not a consequence of analyticity of $S(t)$ alone, then $\Phi_r^{*} = (Q^{1/2})^{*}Y(t,r)^{*}$ and the frozen-$z$ field may be written in that factored form; otherwise the factorisation is shorthand for the Hilbert--Schmidt kernel $\Phi_r$.

\medskip\noindent The Cameron--Martin hypothesis carries conditional content. Clause~\textup{(iii)} of Assumption~(ass:nondeg of the paper) is a genuine joint convergence-and-integrability condition on the quadruple $(\gamma_t, \mathcal{D}_r\gamma_t, \Phi_r, h)$ and is not an automatic consequence of $A$ being analytic ``via parabolic regularisation''. Even in the additive case $\mathcal{B} = Q^{1/2}$ state-independent, the first variation $Y(t,r)$ is random whenever the drift is nonlinear, hence $\mathcal{D}_r\gamma_t \neq 0$ in general, and the trace integrand $\mathcal{I}^{(\varepsilon)}_r$ does not vanish identically. Its verification is therefore a real task. It can be carried out, in principle, via parabolic maximal-regularity bounds on the linearised semigroup $\{S_F(t,r)\}$ generated by $A + F'(X(\cdot))$ at the relevant operating point $(q, p^*)$ on the H\"older triangle, but it requires explicit input on the spectral structure of $\gamma_t$ relative to $h$. We record it as an explicit hypothesis to make this dependence transparent. The fully linear case ($F = 0$, $A$ linear with $\mathcal{B}$ deterministic) is the only subcase in which it is automatic, with $\mathcal{I}^{(0)} \equiv 0$ and $\Psi \equiv 0$ (cf.\ Remark~(rem:CM-compat-role of the paper)).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.737095+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7cb88d363523b9a15633e50763e3f5ce3f4824173bbc065e9cddf6f19ac8a5e5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2506.10476, 'Construction of ergodic \textsc{idla} forests in $\mathbb{Z}^d$'] Let $d \geq 2$. The infinite-volume \textsc{idla} forests $\fdag{\infty}$ and $(\fdag{n})_{n\geq 0}$ satisfy the following properties: 
\begin{enumerate}
	\item Almost surely, the set of vertices of $\fdag{\infty}$ satisfies $V(\fdag{\infty}) = \mathbb{Z}^d$.
	\item The distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are invariant w.r.t. translations $T_k,\ k \in \mathcal{H}$.
	\item The distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are $\alpha$-mixing, that is for all $n\geq 0$, for all events $\mathcal{A},\ \mathcal{B}$, 
	\[
	\lim_{|k| \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{A},\ T_k\fdag{n} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{A} \right) \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{n} \in \mathcal{B} \right)
	\] 
	and
	\[
	\lim_{|k| \to \infty}\mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{A},\ T_k\fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{B}\right) = \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{A} \right) \mathbb{P}\left( \fdag{\infty} \in \mathcal{B} \right).
	\] 
	Consequently, the distributions of $\left(\fdag{n}\right)_{n \geq 0}$ and $\fdag{\infty}$ are ergodic, w.r.t. translations $T_k,\ k \in \mathcal{H}$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:57:20.684129+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7cbb18d9136f627d578411da8c72e356546d7b2add59f2f9b1d1d25bfeace4bd","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary coro:diffusregu of arXiv:2411.10235, '\textbf{Smooth transport map via diffusion process}'] Let $p : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be a probability density function of the form

p(x) = \exp\left( -\frac{\|x\|^2}{2} + a(x) \right),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.224684+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7cbb3f38cc9008fe5190d9cf358dd75d03cff1d730d6ac392c830054f5a49e49","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Asymptotics via Taylor Expansion) of arXiv:2608.14143, 'Mod-$\phi$ convergence for random variables with cyclotomic generating functions'] Let $s_N \in \N$ be a sequence of natural numbers and, for each $N\in\N$, let $(a_{N,j})_{j=1}^N$ be a sequence of natural numbers. Let $h(w, z) := \log\bigl(\frac{1-e^{zw}}{-zw}\bigr)$ for $w \neq 0$ and $h(0, z):=0$. For each $N \in \N$, set $\delta_{N,j} := a_{N,j}/s_N$. Assume that $\max_{1\le j \le N} \delta_{N,j} \to 0$ as $N\to\infty$ and that the limit
\[
\Sigma := \lim_{N\to\infty} \sum_{j=1}^N \delta_{N,j}
\]
exists in $\R$. Then, for every compact set $K\subset\C$, the sum $S_N^a(z) = \sum_{j=1}^N h(a_{N,j}/s_N, z)$ admits the asymptotic expansion
\[
S_N^a(z) = \frac{z}{2}\,\Sigma + o(1),
\]
uniformly for $z\in K$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:11:09.318259+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7cbdacd25b676b140f82796e58a9af90780315b8f74861bc26e7e26ac78c989a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma le:bounds-W-l-one-step of arXiv:2411.06195, 'Restrictions of some reinforced processes to subgraphs'] \mbox{}\\
  Consider the setup of Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper). 
  For $l\in\{1,\ldots,r\}$, $\bar e\in E_{l-1}$, and $e'\in E_l$, 
  we have
  \begin{align}
    
    &{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le 2^{-\alpha}{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,1],\\
    
&{\mathbb E}[(W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e})^\alpha]\le C_\alpha {\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]^2
      \quad\text{for }\alpha\in[0,\tfrac12),\\
    
    &{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l-1)}_{\bar e}]\le\min\{{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2,2{\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]+{c_2}\}
  \end{align}
  with the constants $C_\alpha$ and ${c_2}$ from Theorem (thm:from-r-to-l of the paper).
  For $\alpha\in[0,\frac12)$,
  the bound  in (equation eq:bound-exp-w-l-alpha of the paper) is stronger than
  the bound in (equation eq:bound2-exp-w-l-alpha of the paper) if and only if
  ${\mathbb E}[(W^{(l)}_{e'})^\alpha]>2^{-\alpha}C_\alpha^{-1}$.
  Similarly, the minimum in bound (equation eq:bound2-exp-w-l-log of the paper) equals
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]-\log 2$ if and only if
  ${\mathbb E}[\log W^{(l)}_{e'}]\ge -\log 2-{c_2}$.
  Note that the expectations do not depend on the choice of $\bar e$ and
  $e'$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

\delta_{\msp} (X) \ge
\min \left\{ 4 l_Y, \ \frac{1}{S (V_{\bullet, \bullet}^Y; \Gamma)}, \ \frac{1}{r_{\msp} S (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}; \msp)} \right\},

where

\begin{split}

S (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}; \msp) &= \frac{3}{(A^3)} \int_0^{l_Y} \left( \int_0^{\frac{\nu-\mu}{\nu} t (u)} ((\nu+\lambda) t(u) - \lambda v)^2 d v  \right. \\
& \left. \hspace{2cm} + \int_{\frac{\nu-\mu}{\nu} t (u)}^{t(u)} \left( \frac{\nu^2 + \lambda \mu}{\mu} \right)^2 (t(u) - v)^2 d v \right) d u + F_{\msp} (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}),
\end{split}
\]
with $t (u) = (1 - l_Y u)/l_H$ and
\[
F_{\msp} (W_{\bullet, \bullet, \bullet}^{Y, \Gamma}) = \frac{1}{4 l_Y l_H^3 (A^3)} \cdot \frac{\mu(\nu^2 + \lambda \mu)}{\nu^2} \cdot \ord_{\msp} (\Delta|_{\Gamma}).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.179126+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ceb1b95c0e64951a2d9f8f4b1393598463871053d23b3f68d1d750a84d515da","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 90 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recalling \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym} and Definitions \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}--\ref{d:measure.classes.sym}, we have
	\[\sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha) \subseteq \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)\,.\]

\begin{proof}
Consider any $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, as defined by \eqref{e:sM.Lip.sym}. 
    By Lemma~\ref{l:control.problems.Lip.to.Lip.sym}, we can find $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha)$ with $\sym(\tilde\mu) = \mu$.
It was shown in the \hyperlink{p:thm.control.problems.main}{proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:control.problems.main}} that $\sM^{\Lip}(\alpha) = \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$, so $\tilde\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0)$.
Therefore, for any $\epsilon>0$ we can find $L>0$ and controls 
    \beq
        
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)
    \eeq
such that (recalling that $\sym$ is a contraction) we have
    \[
        \bbW_2\Big(\mu, \mu^{\sym}(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
        \le\bbW_2\Big(\tilde \mu, \mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta)\Big)
         \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
We see from Definitions~\ref{d:SDE.classification} and \ref{d:SDE.classification.sym}
that the sets of controls $\Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ and $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$ are in fact identical, so the controls \eqref{e:Lip.general.in.IAMP.sym.controls} belong to $\Adm^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)$, and 
    \[
        \mu \in \cB_\epsilon\Big(\cM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)\,.
    \]
    Since for all $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $L > 0$ so that this holds, we conclude $\mu \in \sM^{\IAMP,\sym}(\alpha,0)$.
    As this holds for all $\mu \in \sM^{\Lip,\sym}(\alpha)$, the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:44:27.937186+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d06f2588198b7a283af6e35cebd7d4f7b5b0ae96f3fb80a6f6cf11478014dd9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 6 (Aldous meeting-time comparison) of arXiv:2607.13183, '2607.13183'] Let $(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a finite irreducible reversible continuous-time chain
with stationary law $\pi$, and write $P^t$ for its transition semigroup. Let
$\tau_{\rm meet}$ be the first time two independent copies of the chain occupy
the same state. Put
\begin{equation}
        t^*_{\rm mix}:=\inf\left\{t\ge0:
        \max_x\|P^t(x,\cdot)-\pi\|_{\TV}\le \frac1{2e}\right\},
\end{equation}
and let
\[
        T_M:=\max_{x,y}\E_{x,y}\tau_{\rm meet} .
\]
If $H_i$ denotes the hitting time of state $i$ by one copy of the chain, then
there is a universal constant $K_A<\infty$ such that
\begin{equation}
        T_M
        \le
        K_A\left(\sum_i
        \frac{\pi_i}{t^*_{\rm mix}\vee \E_\pi H_i}\right)^{-1} .
\end{equation}
It follows that, for continuous-time simple random walk with jump rate $1$ on a
finite connected multigraph $G$,
\begin{equation}
        t_{\rm meet}(G)
        \le K'_A\bigl(\tmix(G)+\Kemeny(G)\bigr)
\end{equation}
for another universal constant $K'_A$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.397522+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d082e1ff5dfa02353b95271840642f42769211252aa982bdacfb6e076fbf239","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 2. prop: atom convergence from simple measure convergence of arXiv:2412.08236, 'Aging and sub-aging for Bouchaud trap models on resistance metric spaces'] Let $\nu, \nu_{1}, \nu_{2}, \cdots$ be simple measures on $S$.

A bounded operator T on H is trace class (nuclear) if it is compact and ||T||_1 := sum_n s_n(T) < infinity. Equivalently: sum_i <|T| e_i, e_i> < infinity for some (hence every) orthonormal basis (e_i), where |T| = (T*T)^{1/2}, and this sum then equals ||T||_1; equivalently, T = AB with A and B Hilbert-Schmidt operators. The trace of a trace-class T is tr T = sum_i <T e_i, e_i>; this series converges absolutely for every orthonormal basis and its sum does not depend on the basis. The trace-class operators S_1(H) form a two-sided ideal of B(H) and a Banach space under ||.||_1, with ||T|| <= ||T||_2 <= ||T||_1; finite-rank operators are ||.||_1-dense in S_1(H); under the pairing (T, B) -> tr(TB), S_1(H) is isometrically the dual of the compact operators K(H) and the predual of B(H). For a positive operator T >= 0 the sum sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in [0, infinity] is basis-independent and is finite exactly when T is trace class; for operators that are not positive, convergence (even absolute convergence) of sum_i <T e_i, e_i> in one basis does not imply trace class.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.970559+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d866816abb2b2313aa7d616a31898808b56fba17a93a631553e530e89563a86","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 3 (Anti-diagonal equilibria and stability) of arXiv:2607.22438, 'A deterministic scalar reduction for the phase transition in two interacting urns'] Let \(\alpha>1\). The point \(\left(\frac12,\frac12\right)\) is an equilibrium for every
\(p\in[0,1]\). 
If $0\le p<\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}$,
then there is a unique \(u_{\alpha,p}\in[0,1/2)\) satisfying
\begin{equation}
 u=(1-p)h(u)+\frac p2 .
\end{equation}
The corresponding off-center anti-diagonal
equilibria are exactly
\[
 (u_{\alpha,p},1-u_{\alpha,p})\text{ and }
 (1-u_{\alpha,p},u_{\alpha,p}).
\]
If $ p\ge \frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}$,
there is no off-center equilibrium on the anti-diagonal.

Furthermore, there exists a unique number
\[
 p_{\mathrm{ad},*}=p_{\mathrm{ad},*}(\alpha)
 \in\left(0,\frac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}\right)
\]
such that, for \(0\le p<(\alpha-1)/\alpha\),
\[
 \lambda_+(u_{\alpha,p},1-u_{\alpha,p})
 \begin{cases}
 <0, & \text{if }0\le p<p_{\mathrm{ad},*},\\
 =0, & \text{if }p=p_{\mathrm{ad},*},\\
 >0, & \text{if }p_{\mathrm{ad},*}<p<\dfrac{\alpha-1}{\alpha}.
 \end{cases}
\]
Consequently, the off-center anti-diagonal equilibria are asymptotically stable for
\(0\le p<p_{\mathrm{ad},*}\) and unstable for
\(p_{\mathrm{ad},*}<p<(\alpha-1)/\alpha\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:09.929240+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d88710f02a1dc23e546b9bdf585d75162664cfaeb315221e3fbd0d2a8d1f1fb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 27 (\cite{BJMP1}, Lemma 3.4) of arXiv:2603.27940, '\Large \bf Stability of supermartingale optimal transport problems'] Let $r\ge1$. Let $\mu,\mu^k\in\mathcal M_r(X)$ and $\nu,\nu^k\in\mathcal M_r(Y)$ have equal masses, and assume that
\[
\pi^k\in\Pi(\mu^k,\nu^k)\ \xrightarrow{AW_1}\ \pi\in\Pi(\mu,\nu).
\]
Let $A\subset X$ be measurable and let $B\supset A$ be open.

\vspace{1mm}

\noindent \rm(i)\,
Let $\gamma^k\in\Pi(\mu^k,\mu)$ be an optimizer in \eqref{eq:AW_def} for $\AW(\pi^k,\pi)$ and set
\[
\tilde\mu^k:=\gamma^k(\cdot\times A),
\qquad
\varepsilon_k:=1-\frac{\tilde\mu^k(X)}{\mu(A)}.
\]
Then $\tilde\mu^k\le \mu^k|_B$ and $\varepsilon_k\ge0$. Moreover, defining
\[
\tilde\pi^k:=\tilde\mu^k\times \pi_x^k,
\]
one has
\[
AW_1\!\big(\tilde\pi^k,\ (1-\varepsilon_k)\,\pi|_{A\times Y}\big)+\varepsilon_k\longrightarrow0.
\]
\noindent \rm(ii)\,
Suppose that $\nu$ is concentrated on some $C\subset Y$.
Let $\tilde\nu^k$ and $\tilde\nu$ be the second marginals of $\tilde\pi^k$ and $\pi|_{A\times Y}$, respectively, and define
\[
\hat\mu^k=\frac{\tilde\nu^k(C)}{\tilde\mu^k(X)}\,\tilde\mu^k,
\qquad
\varepsilon_k':=1-\frac{\tilde\nu^k(C)}{\mu(A)}.
\]
Then there exist $\hat\nu^k\le\nu^k$ and $\hat\pi^k=\hat\mu^k\times\hat\pi_x^k\in\Pi(\hat\mu^k,\hat\nu^k)$
concentrated on $B\times C$ such that
\[
AW_1^r \!\big(\hat\pi^k,\ (1-\varepsilon_k')\,\pi|_{A\times Y}\big)
+\int_X W_r^r(\hat\pi_x^k,\pi_x^k)\,\hat\mu^k(dx)
+\varepsilon_k'\longrightarrow0.
\]
In particular, $1-\varepsilon_k'\le 1-\varepsilon_k$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Counterexample: F(p,z,x) = p_1 (equation u_x = 0), Γ = {y=0}","Noncharacteristic condition: D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0","Compatibility (admissibility): F(p0,z0,x0) = 0 and p0 agrees with the tangential gradient of g on Γ","Even when the conditions hold, the conclusion is only local in a neighbourhood of the point"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418512+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: first-order equations, method of characteristics","id":"claim_7d8c544f22ddfa6bc426587ded0c72b9450163a966ed4890aa02b90253645958","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: local solvability of F(Du,u,x) = 0 with u = g on Γ requires D_pF(p0,z0,x0)·ν(x0) ≠ 0, i.e. the characteristic direction must be transversal to the data surface; and the initial triple must be admissible (the tangential derivatives of g must match p0). If the surface is characteristic, existence can fail outright and uniqueness can fail catastrophically. Counterexample: the equation u_x = 0 in R^2 (F(p,z,x) = p_1, so D_pF = (1,0)) with data on Γ = { y = 0 }, whose normal is ν = (0,1): D_pF·ν = 0, so Γ is characteristic — indeed the characteristics are the horizontal lines y = const, which lie IN Γ. Every C^1 solution satisfies u(x,y) = u(0,y), so u(·,0) must be constant: if g is not constant there is NO solution in any neighbourhood of a point of Γ; if g ≡ c there are infinitely many solutions u(x,y) = h(y) with h ∈ C^1 arbitrary and h(0) = c. The same pathology occurs for u_t + u_x = 0 with data prescribed on the characteristic line { x = t }. Auditor's check: before invoking local existence by characteristics, compute D_pF·ν at the point in question; for quasilinear equations a(x,u)·Du = b this is a(x0,g(x0))·ν(x0) ≠ 0, and for the Cauchy problem u_t + H(x,Du) = 0 on { t = 0 } it is automatic (the coefficient of u_t is 1).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:52:08.664699+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d8db8fd4c67bde605a9b558b98bcad5b75ed77bb6f06554007dda7f09dc8a1c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Main theorem) of arXiv:2608.30027, 'Under Ricci flow, a 3-torus goes flat'] Let \(M\) be a closed connected three-manifold which admits a locally
homogeneous metric modeled on one of \(\RR^3\), \(\Nil\), or \(\Sol\), and let
\(g(t)\), \(0\leq t<\infty\), be any immortal Ricci flow on \(M\).  In all
three cases, for every basepoint \(\widetilde m\in\widetilde M\) in the
universal cover, the lifted blowdown flows
\((\widetilde M,\widetilde m,s^{-1}\widetilde g(s\tau))\), \(\tau>0\),
converge as \(s\to\infty\) in the pointed Cheeger--Hamilton sense to a
homogeneous expanding Ricci soliton solution.  The compact
and lifted limits are as follows.
\begin{enumerate}
\item If \(M\) has type \(\RR^3\), then, for every \(m\geq0\), \(g(t)\)
converges exponentially fast in the \(C^m\)-norm of any fixed smooth
background metric, as \(t\to\infty\), to a flat metric on \(M\).
The Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.
The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the flat expanding soliton solution
\[
        (\RR^3,0,g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)),
        \qquad
        g_{\mathrm{Euc}}(\tau)=dx^2+dy^2+dz^2,
        \quad \tau>0.
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Nil\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a point.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Nil
expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,
        \frac{1}{3\tau^{1/3}}
        \left(dx+\frac12 y\,dz-\frac12 z\,dy\right)^2
        +\tau^{1/3}(dy^2+dz^2)
        \right).
\]
\item If \(M\) has type \(\Sol\), then the Gromov--Hausdorff limit of
\((M,t^{-1}g(t))\), as \(t\to\infty\), is a metric circle or a compact
interval of positive length.  The limit of the lifted blowdown flows is the Sol expanding soliton solution
\[
        \left(\RR^3,0,e^{-2z}dx^2+e^{2z}dy^2+4\tau\,dz^2\right).
\]
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:10:07.424632+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7d922fc74e165300d4137e2753b638ed7631e6a80e9f43ecedeb9ceeee2e31a4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem eq:bounded-block-max of arXiv:2607.27613, 'Regularized Bulk Universality versus Bounded-Disorder Nonuniversality\\for Annealed Comple'] \label[theorem]{thm:bounded-block-counterexample}
Fix \(p\ge3\) and an integer \(r\ge2\).  There is a symmetric,
compactly supported probability law \(\mu\) with a \(C^\infty\) density
such that
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),leftmargin=2em]
\item \(\mu\) matches the standard Gaussian moments through order \(r\)
(hence is centered and has variance one);
\item for i.i.d.\ ordered-tensor entries with common law \(\mu\), there
is a compact interval \(B\subset(0,\infty)\) for which
\begin{align}
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^J(B)
 &>\limsup_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_{N,\max}^G(B),\\
 \liminf_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E_\mu\operatorname{Crt}_N^J(B)
 &>\lim_{N\to\infty}\frac1N\log
 \mathbb E\operatorname{Crt}_N^G(B).
\end{align}
The reflected local-minimum inequality holds on \(-B\).
\end{enumerate}
In particular, for every fixed \(\varepsilon\in[0,1/2)\),
\begin{equation}
 \max_{I\in[N]^p}|J_I|\le N^{1/2-\varepsilon}
 \qquad\text{almost surely for all sufficiently large \(N\)}.
\end{equation}
Thus an \(N^{1/2-\varepsilon}\) entrywise cutoff, or even an
 \(N\)-independent entry bound, does not restore universality of the
 unregularized annealed count.  The obstruction in this theorem is a
 coherent block involving on the order of \(N^{1/p}\) coordinates,
 rather than a single quadratic-scale entry. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.017841+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7db70972f46c1e25f2c6a8813bfb452696404edce87a690c2287086c6d2f16f1","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 11 (Finite-intensity two-level reductions) of arXiv:2608.15137, '2608.15137'] Let a determinantal point process be defined on the disjoint union of two sigma-finite measure spaces $(E_s,\nu_s)$ and $(E_t,\nu_t)$, with kernel blocks $K_{uv}$. Let $A_s\subseteq E_s$ and $A_t\subseteq E_t$ be measurable, put
\[
 N_u=\#(\text{points in }A_u),
 \qquad
 \mu_u=\int_{A_u}K_{uu}(x,x)\,\nu_u(\dd x),
\]
and assume that $\mu_s,\mu_t<\infty$. Suppose the equal-level restricted kernels have Hermitian representatives and that
\[
 C_{st}
 =
 \int_{A_s\times A_t}
 K_{st}(x,y)K_{ts}(y,x)
 \,\nu_s(\dd x)\nu_t(\dd y)
\]
converges absolutely. Then
\[
 \E[N_sN_t]=\mu_s\mu_t-C_{st}
\]
and
\[
 \mu_u-\frac{\mu_u^2}{2}
 \leq
 \Prob(N_u>0)
 \leq
 \mu_u.
\]
Consequently, if $0\leq\mu_s,\mu_t\leq1$, $c\geq0$, and
\[
 \abs{C_{st}}\leq c\mu_s\mu_t,
\]
then
\[
 \Prob(N_s>0,N_t>0)
 \leq
 4(1+c)\Prob(N_s>0)\Prob(N_t>0).
\]

For measurable $B_s\subseteq E_s$ and $B_t\subseteq E_t$, put
\[
 H_u=L^2(B_u,\nu_u)
\]
and suppose the restricted block kernel
\[
 \mathcal K_B=
 \begin{bmatrix}
 K_{ss}&K_{st}\\
 K_{ts}&K_{tt}
 \end{bmatrix}
\]
is trace class on $H_s\oplus H_t$. Put
\[
 A=I-K_{ss},
 \qquad
 D=I-K_{tt},
\]
and suppose that $A$ and $D$ are boundedly invertible. Let $G_u$ be the event that $B_u$ contains no process point, and define
\[
 R=D^{-1}K_{ts}A^{-1}K_{st}.
\]
Then $R$ is trace class and
\[
 \Prob(G_s\cap G_t)
 =
 \Prob(G_s)\Prob(G_t)\det(I-R),
\]
so
\[
 \Prob(G_s\cap G_t)
 \leq
 \ee^{\norm{R}_1}
 \Prob(G_s)\Prob(G_t).
\]
The same conclusions hold almost surely for conditional determinantal laws. In particular, they apply to the conditional kernel in Theorem~\ref{thm:conditional-growth-kernel} for almost every starting spectrum whenever the stated fiberwise hypotheses hold.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.352496+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7dc8d5560e962181bc027758d37b6bf2ab9eb94d14f988ed537bf73a53b9c014","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:TASEPcp of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] For each $\alpha>0$ and $d\in \mathbb{N}$, we defined the \textbf{$d$-coupling} of half-space TASEPs with boundary parameter $\alpha$, as follows.

        Take the Poisson process $\Pi$, and view this as a collection of Poisson clocks on $\Lambda_d$. These clocks generate half-space TASEPs as follows.
        Let $\pi:\{(x,a)\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}\times \mathbb{Z}, x+a\in 2\mathbb{Z}\} \to \Lambda_d$ be the projection map.
        Recall that we can define half-space TASEP as a Markov process $(h_t: t\ge 0)$ on the state space $\SRW_+$ (from (equation eq:defSRW+ of the paper)). 
        We flip $h_t(i) \mapsto h_t(i) + 2$ according to the Poisson clock at the vertex $\pi(i, h_t(i))$. In words, there is a flip $h_{t}(i)= h_{t-}(i)+2$ if and only if the Poisson clock at $\pi(i, h_t(i))$ rings at times $t$, and $h_t(j)=h_{t-}(i)+1$ for $j\in \{i-1, i+1\}\cap \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$.

        By using the same set of Poisson clocks, we get a coupling of half-space TASEPs with boundary parameter $\alpha$, started from all initial configurations and all times.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:20.880849+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7dcb93c91b72dbbc704681fcb49b1f1be63d1effc3db4273f0d92be16d174472","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 17 of arXiv:2506.11707, 'Fluctuations of two-dimensional determinantal processes associated with Berezin--Toeplitz '] Let $\delta>0$ and, for $j\in\{1,2\}$, let $\chi_j : \C \to[0,1]$ be smooth functions such that 
\[
\1\{V\le \mu-\delta\} \le \chi_2 \le \1\{V\le \mu-\tfrac12\delta\}
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
\1\{|V- \mu| \le 2\delta\}\le  \chi_1 \le \1\{|V- \mu| \le 3\delta\}.
\]
Let $f : \C \to \R$ be a smooth bounded function, and let ${\rm f}_j:= f \chi_j$ for $j\in\{1,2,3\}$ where \[\chi_3 :=(\chi_1+\chi_2-1)\1\{V<\mu\}.\] 
Then, for every $\alpha>0$,
\[\begin{aligned}
\Upsilon(f;\Pi_N) = \Upsilon({\rm f}_1;\Pi_N)+ \Upsilon({\rm f}_2;\Pi_N) - \Upsilon({\rm f}_3;\Pi_N) + \O(e^{-\alpha \sqrt{N}}). 
\end{aligned}\]
By construction, ${\rm f}_1 ,{\rm f}_3$ are smooth, supported in the bulk $\{V\le \mu-\tfrac12\delta\} $, and ${\rm f}_2$ is smooth, supported in a neighborhood of the boundary $\{|V- \mu| \le 3\delta\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.359585+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7ddab1f634adb859e3a1d50f98edd295da2873929e40f587a149519dcccc4d43","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 247 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Assume that $L\ge1$ and that condition \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound} holds. Let $\vX\equiv \vX^N$ be the process defined by \eqref{e:X.decomp}
 and \eqref{e:Delta.X.Ising}, and assume that condition~\eqref{e:w2.coupling.assumption} holds. Then the process $\vX^\trstar$ of Definition~\ref{d:trunc} satisfies
	\[
	\E'\Big[\|\vX(1)-\vX^\trstar(1)\|^2\Big]
	\le O(\epsilon) + o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
uniformly in $N$.

\begin{proof} 
For $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$ we have $X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1,a)=X^\sigma(\tau(a),a)$, with $\tau$ the stopping time defined by \eqref{e:trstar.stopping.time}. It follows that, for $\sigma\in\{\RomI,\RomII,\RomIII\}$, we have
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\sigma(1)-X^{\trstar,\sigma}(1))^2\Big]
	\le O(1)
	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\sigma(q_d)^2;\tau<1\bigg] 
	\le O(\epsilon) +o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
where the last bound is by Proposition~\ref{p:max.X.process.on.trstar.stopped.event}. Similarly,
	\[
	\E'\Big[( X^\Ising(1)-X^{\trstar,\Ising}(1))^2\Big]
	\le O(1)
	\E'\bigg[
	\max_{0\le d\le \dmax}
	X^\Ising(q_d)^2;\tau^\Ising<1\bigg] 
	\le o_{\trK}(1)\,,
	\]
again by Proposition~\ref{p:max.X.process.on.trstar.stopped.event}. The conclusion follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:28:31.997839+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7dec0591ddeecea8508078a8cd6033224d69ff624d662c3d20b1d5aeb7db04f1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Def 14 of arXiv:2512.02322, 'Ursell functions in lattice gauge theory'] Assume that $B_N$ is large enough, such that all oriented surfaces and loops in this definition are well-defined.
Let $x \in \Z^m$ and $L_1,L_2 \in \N$. Define the discrete rectangle
\[
R := \{x +a \tilde{e}_1+b \tilde{e}_2: 0 \leq a \leq L_1, 0 \leq b \leq L_2\}.
\]
Define the 2-chain $q_1 \in C_2(B_N,\Z)$ as the formal sum of all positively oriented plaquettes $p \in C_2(B_N)^+$ whose four boundary edges lie in the rectangle $R$. \newline 
Then, define the translation operator $\tau$ by
\[
\tau : C_2(B_N,\Z) \to C_2(B_N,\Z), ~ (\tau\chi)[p] := \chi[p-d\tilde{e}_3].
\]
Now we define recursively the two chains $q_i$ for $i \in \{2,...,n\}$, by
\[
q_i := \tau q_{i-1}.
\]
In words, every $q_i$ is the translation of the positively oriented plaquettes of $q_{i-1}$ by $d\tilde{e}_3$. \newline  
Finally, for $i \in [n]$, define
\[
\gamma_i := \partial q_i.
\]
Note that by construction $\partial \gamma_i =0$ so that $(\gamma_i)_{i \in [n]}$ are well defined Wilson loops, and $(q_i)_{i \in [n]}$ well defined oriented surfaces.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:49:05.348709+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7def1206eddf00c91658d97780b1ffab0fee35eaf0bb4911c71e3ea1841c7d20","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defn:no-underrun of arXiv:2601.07045, 'From Continuous to Discrete: \\ a No-U-Turn Sampler for Permutations'] Let $\mathcal{O} = (\sigma \circ \rho^k)_{k = a}^{b}$ be an orbit indexed by
consecutive integers from $a$ to $b$, and let $\varepsilon \in (0,1)$.
We say that $\mathcal{O}$ satisfies the \emph{no--underrun condition},
denoted $\textsc{Stop}(\mathcal{O},\varepsilon,w)$, if
\[
\max \!\left\{ w(\sigma \circ \rho^{a}),\, w(\sigma \circ \rho^{b}) \right\}
\;\le\;
\varepsilon \sum_{\tau \in \mathcal{O}} w(\tau).
\]
Equivalently, the combined weight at the two boundary points of the orbit
accounts for at most an $\varepsilon$ fraction of the total weight accumulated
along $\mathcal{O}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.372086+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e0786242cae037154dde86085a7965ebe039fcbada5c7994298c08bdcafb103","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The orthogonal polynomials for $L^2[-1,1]$, with measure

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:07:17.249588+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e083884be832f46cce336a829a5c3bbb9a3bd4adca8daaa024694c1282c7fdc","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:backoff of arXiv:2602.21315, 'The Instability of all Backoff Protocols\thanks{For the purpose of Open Access, the author'] Fix a send sequence
$\newsym{p}{send sequence, Def~(def:backoff of the paper)}{\overline{p} = (p_0,p_1,p_2,\ldots)}$  and a birth rate 
$\newsym{lambda}{birth rate, Def~(def:backoff of the paper)}{\lambda}>0$. Each~$p_k$   is  a real number in~$(0,1]$.   $W_k$   denotes~$1/p_k$.
The \emph{backoff process} $X$
with send sequence~$\overline{p}$ and birth rate~$\lambda$ is defined as follows.
For each $i\geq 0$ and $t\geq 1$, 
$\mathbf{b}^X_i(t)$~is the set of balls that  collide exactly $i$ times during steps $1,\ldots,t$. 
The process starts from the empty state, so  
for each~$i\geq 0$, 
$\mathbf{b}^X_i(0) = \emptyset$.
For each $t\geq 1$, $\mathbf{n}^X(t)$ is the set of balls that are born at time~$t$. Its size is given by $n^X(t)$,  which 
is a Poisson random variable with mean~$\lambda$.
After the births, but just
before the sends at step~$t$, the bin populations are defined as follows.
$\mathbf{B}^X_0(t) = \mathbf{n}^X(t) \cup \mathbf{b}^X_0(t-1)$. For every $i\geq 1$, $\mathbf{B}^X_i(t) = \mathbf{b}^X_i(t-1)$.  
For every $i\geq 0$, the set of balls that send from bin~$i$ at time~$t$,  {$\mathbf{s}^X_i(t)$}, is
formed by including each ball from $\mathbf{B}^X_i(t)$ independently with probability~$p_i$.  The
set of balls that escape from bin~$i$ at time~$t$,  $\mathbf{e}^X_i(t)$, is equal to $\mathbf{s}^X_i(t)$ if 
$|\mathbf{s}_i^X(t)| = |\cup_{k\geq 0} \mathbf{s}_k^X(t)| = 1$. Otherwise,
$\mathbf{e}^X_i(t) =  \emptyset$.
Finally, $\mathbf{b}_0^X(t) = \mathbf{B}_0^X(t) \setminus \mathbf{s}_0^X(t)$ and for all  $i\geq 1$,
$\mathbf{b}_i^X(t) = (\mathbf{B}_i^X(t) \setminus \mathbf{s}_i^X(t)) \cup (\mathbf{s}^X_{i-1}(t) \setminus \mathbf{e}^X_{i-1}(t))$.
For every variable $\mathbf{b}^X_i(t)$, $\mathbf{B}^X_i(t)$, $\mathbf{s}^X_i(t)$, and $\mathbf{e}^X_i(t)$, the roman (non-bold-face) version represents its size, so, for example, $b^X_i(t) = |\mathbf{b}^X_i(t)|$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.249075+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e13b077aa89eda54fcf1c704e86f63b8accf04342b781a5408ddd8bcf5d5e84","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 25 (General Poisson approximation of large gaps) of arXiv:2605.22146, 'Poisson approximation of the largest gaps between zeros of a stationary Gaussian process'] Suppose a stationary point process $\mathcal{Z}$ on $\R$ satisfies the following properties, with $G$, $\mathcal{G}_I$, $\rho_{r,s}^k$, and $\phi_r$ defined as above:
\begin{enumerate}

\item (Regularity) $G$ is twice differentiable, convex, and
\[ \log (-G'(r)) \sim \log G(r) \qquad \text{and} \qquad  \log G''(r) \le \log G(r)(1+o(1)) .\]
\item (Splitting) For every $k, \delta > 0$ there exists $\delta' > 0$ such that, for every $r =R^{o(1)}$ and  $s = R^{\delta+o(1)}$,
\[ \rho^k_{r,s} \le R^{-\delta' + o(1) } . \]
\item (Clustered decoupling) For every $k, \delta > 0$ there exists $c > 0$ such that, for every $r =R^{o(1)}$, $s = R^{\delta+o(1)}$, and $\bar{r} \le s /  c$, and every  $(\mathcal{C}_{\ell})_{\ell \ge 1} \in \bar{\mathcal{Q}}^k_{r,\bar r,s}$,
\[  \P \big[ \cap_i \mathcal{G}_{I_i} \big]  \le R^{o(1)} \Big(  \prod_{\ell \ge 1} \P \big[ \cap_{I_i \in \mathcal{C}_\ell}  \mathcal{G}_{I_i} \big]  \Big)^{1 + o(1)} + R^{-k} \Big) .\]
\item (Absence of clustering) There exists $\eta > 0$ such that 
\[ \phi_r \le G(r)^{1+\eta + o(1)} .\]

Then the largest gaps of $\mathcal{Z}$ obey a Poisson approximation in the sense of Definition \ref{d:pa}. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:45:17.650411+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e23472a7ad06f3f04e4aad3ed47b142a5b5269484d50a4bcd0073be2899e5ce","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition defin:pivs of arXiv:2604.08462, 'Convergence of $k$-point functions in\\\\ high dimensional percolation'] Let $\\mathcal{P}(u,v)$ denote the set of open pivotals for the event $\\{ u \\leftrightarrow v \\}$: open edges through which every open connection from $u$ to $v$ must pass.  We consider these as directed edges in the natural way: if $\\{x, y\\}$ is an undirected edge traversed by every open path from $u$ to $v$, then either all these paths traverse $\\{x,y\\}$ from $x$ to $y$ (in which case $(x,y) \\in \\mathcal{P}(u,v)$) or all these paths traverse $\\{x,y\\}$ from $y$ to $x$ (in which case $(y,x) \\in \\mathcal{P}(u,v)$). Similarly, these pivotals can be naturally ordered in terms of ``distance'' to $u$: if $\\gamma_1, \\gamma_2$ are any (ordered) open paths from $u$ to $v$, the elements of $\\mathcal{P}(u, v)$ appear in the same relative order along $\\gamma_1$ as along $\\gamma_2$. We use this ordering implicitly several times in what follows, saying ``closer to'' or ``further from'' $u$ to mean with respect to this order and not with respect to (e.g.) the Euclidean distance. We extend this notion for pivotals from $u$ to a set $A$ of vertices in the natural way.\n        \n        Given a vertex set $A$, we define $\\underline{\\mathcal{P}}(u, A)$ to be the common open pivotal which is closest to $u$ for all the connections of the form $u \\leftrightarrow x$, $x \\in A$. We define $\\overline{\\mathcal{P}}(u, A)$ to be the common pivotal furthest from $u$. In case there are no common pivotals, we write $\\underline{\\mathcal{P}}(u, A) = \\overline{\\mathcal{P}}(u, A) = \\varnothing$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:40:21.314327+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e243edfd0aba91166d5a9c72a1e5f55dfd4cc77ec70ae143cc0d48fb28bb438","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 9 of arXiv:2604.08623, 'Central limit theorem for the Allen-Cahn equation with supercritical random initial condit'] Let $d\\geq 3$ and defining $u_\\eps$ as in \\eqref{eq:rescaled_u}, we have that \n  $$\\left(\\<u_\\eps(t_1, \\cdot), \\phi_1\\>, \\dots, \\<u_\\eps(t_n, \\cdot), \\phi_n\\>\\right) \\underset{\\eps \\to 0}{\\implies} \\left(\\<\\sigma_\\lambda p_{t_1} * \\tilde{\\xi}, \\phi_1\\>, \\dots, \\<\\sigma_\\lambda p_{t_n} * \\tilde{\\xi}, \\phi_n\\>\\right)$$\n  for any \\(\\phi_1, \\dots, \\phi_n \\in \\mathcal{S}\\) and \\(t_1, \\dots, t_n > 0\\) where $\\tilde{\\xi}$ is a spatial white noise and $\\sigma_\\lambda$ is a positive constant.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:54:18.302319+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e31600f9d01adbc27be70f4366d322c49e3e0208945ef424711bec597ce2ad9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop nonlinear-regression-regularity of arXiv:2608.30382, 'Convergence rates for the RMSprop optimizer with full control of the hyperparameters'] Let $\mathcal V\subseteq{\mathbb R}^d$ be nonempty and compact,
let $ r \in ( 0, \nicefrac{ 1 }{ 2 } ) $, $ \delta \in (0, \infty ) $,
and suppose that there exist nonempty compact sets
$ K_Z \subseteq \mathcal Z $ and $ K_Y\subseteq {\mathbb R}^m $ and a constant
$ B \in (0,\infty) $ with the following properties:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*)]

\item
The random variables are compactly supported in the sense that
\begin{align}\begin{split} 
  {\mathbb P}\bigl( Z \in K_Z , \, Y \in K_Y \bigr) = 1 .
 \end{split}\end{align}

\item
For $ {\mathbb P}_Z $-almost every $ z \in K_Z $, the conditional law of $ Y $
given $ Z = z $ has a Lebesgue density~$ p_z $ satisfying
\bas{

  \| p_z \|_{ L^\infty } \le B .
}

\item
The map $ ( \theta, z ) \mapsto \Gamma^{ \theta }( z ) $ and, for every
$ i \in \{ 1, \dots, d \} $,
the map
$
  ( \theta, z ) \mapsto\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}( z )
$
are continuous on $ \mathcal V \times K_Z $.

\item
The coordinate derivatives satisfy the uniform moment lower bound
\bas{

D_r
=
\inf_{ \substack{ \theta \in \mathcal V } }
\inf_{
  1 \le i \le d
}
{\mathbb E}\biggl[
\Bigl|
\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}(Z)
\Bigr|^{r}
\biggr]
\ge \delta.
}
\end{enumerate}
Choose $R\in(0,\infty)$ such that $K_Y\subseteq B(0,R)$, let
$\omega_{m-1}$ denote the volume of the unit ball in ${\mathbb R}^{m-1}$, use the
convention $\omega_0=1$, and set
\bas{
\mu_r
&=\frac{\delta^{1/r}}{2B\omega_{m-1}R^{m-1}}
\left(\frac{1-2r}{1-r}\right)^{(1-r)/r},\\
C_X
&=\max_{\substack{\theta\in\mathcal V,\ z\in K_Z,\ y\in K_Y\\1\le i\le d}}
\left|
\left\langle
\frac{\partial\Gamma^\theta}{\partial\theta_i}(z),
\Gamma^\theta(z)-y
\right\rangle
\right|.
}
Then $\mu_r,C_X\in(0,\infty)$. The innovation $(X,U)$ defined in
(equation eq:nonlinear-regression-loss-innovation of the paper) is $(c_r,q_r)$-regular on
$\mathcal V$ with
\bas{
c_r
=\frac{(1-e^{-1})\mu_r^3}{8C_X},
\qquad
q_r=\frac{(1-e^{-1})\mu_r}{2C_X}.
}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.192777+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_7e3f5b15ad9523f72f759ea3fac17287c810ffbd8ec64dd852c688f140f1c64e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Fix two distinct coordinates $u\neq v$ and times $k_u,k_v\in\mathbb{N}$.
Let $M^{[u]}(k_u)=\mathbb{E}[N^{[u]}(k_u)]$ and $M^{[v]}(k_v)=\mathbb{E}[N^{[v]}(k_v)]$.
Let $M^{[u,v]}:\mathbb{N}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ denote the \emph{bivariate} renewal function of
the projected increment vector $(X^{[u]},X^{[v]})$, i.e.
$M^{[u,v]}(k_u,k_v)=\mathbb{E}[N^{[u,v]}(k_u,k_v)]$ with
$N^{[u,v]}(k_u,k_v)=\sup\{n:(S_n^{[u]},S_n^{[v]})\le_2(k_u,k_v)\}$.

Define the univariate renewal kernels
$\psi_u:=(\ez-f^{[u]})^{(-1)}$ and $\psi_v:=(\ez-f^{[v]})^{(-1)}$ on $\mathbb{N}$, and
define $\widetilde{\psi}_{u,v}:\mathbb{N}^2\to\mathbb{R}$ by

\begin{equation}
\widetilde{\psi}_{u,v}(r_u,r_v)
=
\left\{
\begin{array}{ll}
\psi_u(r_u), & \text{if } r_u>0 \text{ and } r_v=0,\\[0.2em]
\psi_v(r_v), & \text{if } r_v>0 \text{ and } r_u=0,\\[0.2em]
\psi_u(0)+\psi_v(0)-1, & \text{if } r_u=r_v=0,\\[0.2em]
0, & \text{otherwise.}
\end{array}
\right.
\end{equation}

Then

\begin{equation}
\mathbb{E}\!\left[N^{[u]}(k_u)\,N^{[v]}(k_v)\right]
=
\big[M^{[u,v]}*\widetilde{\psi}_{u,v}\big](k_u,k_v),
\end{equation}

and consequently

\begin{equation}
\mathrm{Cov}\!\left(N^{[u]}(k_u),\,N^{[v]}(k_v)\right)
=
\big[M^{[u,v]}*\widetilde{\psi}_{u,v}\big](k_u,k_v)
-
M^{[u]}(k_u)\,M^{[v]}(k_v).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}
