{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:11.416344+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8a3059a884f047bad8c528bd7c7635653ba53feb6b0aeed02eeb509d58900274","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Fourier, energy and correlation dimensions) of arXiv:2606.08703, '2606.08703'] Let \(\nu\) be a nonzero finite Borel measure on \(\R^m\).  The Fourier
dimension of \(\nu\) is
\begin{equation}
\dimF(\nu)
=
\sup\bigl\{0\le s\le m:
|\wh\nu(\xi)|=O(|\xi|^{-s/2}) \text{ as } |\xi|\to\infty
\bigr\}.
\end{equation}
The energy dimension of \(\nu\) is
\[
\dimE(\nu)=
\sup\biggl\{0<s<m:
\iint |x-y|^{-s}\,d\nu(x)d\nu(y)<\infty
\biggr\}.
\]

For the dyadic interval grid on \([0,1]\), let \(\mathcal D_n\) denote the
family of dyadic intervals of length \(2^{-n}\).  The corresponding correlation
dimension is
\begin{equation}
        \dimtwo(\nu)
        =
        \liminf_{n\to\infty}
        \frac{-\log_2\sum_{I\in\mathcal D_n}\nu(I)^2}{n}.
\end{equation}
For the \(b\)-adic cube grid on \([0,1]^d\), let
\(\mathcal D_n^{b,d}\) denote the family of \(b\)-adic cubes of side length
\(b^{-n}\).  The corresponding correlation dimension is
\begin{equation}
        \dimtwo(\nu)
        =
        \liminf_{n\to\infty}
        \frac{-\log_2\sum_{Q\in\mathcal D_n^{b,d}}\nu(Q)^2}
        {n\log_2 b}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:48:00.295175+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8a32ae55a02721d7cfbd0f8bf641dbcb0d1973a40bb06e32be1307d96d4dbd3f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition $\gamma$-Fat-Shattering Dimension of arXiv:2609.03129, 'A Closed-Form Formula for Consistent Lipschitz Regression on Metric Spaces with Sparse Neu'] Let $X$ be a set, let $\mathcal{F}\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{X}$, and fix $\gamma>0$. A finite set $\{x_1,\ldots,x_m\}\subseteq X$ is said to be $\gamma$-\emph{fat shattered} by $\mathcal{F}$ if there are $t_1,\ldots,t_m\in\mathbb{R}$ such that: for every $\sigma=(\sigma_1,\ldots,\sigma_m)\in\{-1,1\}^m$, there is an  $f_\sigma\in\mathcal{F}$ satisfying
\[
    \sigma_j(f_\sigma(x_j)-t_j)\ge\gamma
\]
for every $j\in[m]_+$. The $\gamma$-fat-shattering dimension $ \operatorname{fat}_{\gamma}$ of $\mathcal{F}$ is the largest such $m$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:38:04.516148+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8a333dfb7bc31da47b276764d03e992ea42844225e2a7cf5d67eacccb4df249c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eq:rho_definition of arXiv:2607.18011, 'From local giants to locality in long-range percolation'] \thlabel{def:berger_good}
    For $i \geq 1$, for $s$ as in \thref{def:renormalisation_scheme}, and for $c_{\mathrm{vor}}{}$ as in \thref{prop:tile_and_cell_volume_bounds}, let
    
    \begin{equation}
    
        \rho_0 
        = 
        \theta 
        c_G
        /
        2^{2d + 1},
        \quad
        \rho_i 
        =
        1
        /
        \left(
            c_{\mathrm{vor}}{} 
            (i+s)^{2d}
        \right).
    \end{equation}
    
    Let $((\Tile{i}{j})_{j \geq 0})_{i \geq 0}$ be the renormalisation scheme in \thref{def:renormalisation_scheme}, and consider the associated sequence of cells $((\Cell{i}{j})_{j \geq 0})_{i \geq 0}$. 
    
    We say that a level-$0$ cell $\Cell{0}{j}$ is \textbf{good} if it contains a cluster $\goodcluster{0}{j}$ satisfying
    
    \begin{equation}
        
        \# (\goodcluster{0}{j} \cap B(\netvertex{0}{j},r_0/4))
        \geq 
        \rho_0
        r_0^d. 
    \end{equation}
    
    We call the cluster $\goodcluster{0}{j}$ the \textbf{good cluster} and we call the set $\goodsize{0}{j} = \goodcluster{0}{j} \cap B(\netvertex{0}{j},r_0/4)$ the \textbf{semi-cluster}.

    We call the cluster $\goodcluster{i}{j}$ the \textbf{good cluster} and we call the set $\goodsize{i}{j} = \goodcluster{i}{j} \cap \Tile{i}{j}$ the \textbf{semi-cluster}.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:01:22.595490+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8a3e5360762bb0ee9a862122e6fe1efb99314b6bccf140920d1f2d159e93d22e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma LOP of arXiv:2605.16963, 'Stochastic Euler Equations with Pseudo-differential Noise: Continuous and Discontinuous Pe'] Let $r,r_{1},r_{2}\in \mathbb R$, $\mathscr{p}\in \mathbf S^{r}$,
		$\mathscr{p}_{1}\in \mathbf S^{r_{1}},\mathscr{p}_{2}\in \mathbf S^{r_{2}}$,
		and let ${\mathrm{OP}}$ be given in (equation OP define of the paper). The following results hold:
		
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{\textbf {(\arabic{enumi})}},leftmargin=0.79cm]\setlength\itemsep{0.2em} 
			\item
			
			\textup{\textbf{(Continuity of ${\normalfont{\mathrm{OP}}}$)}} For any $q,s\in \mathbb R$,
			${\mathrm{OP}}: \mathbf S^{s}\to {\rm OP}\mathbf S^s$ is one-to-one  and ${\mathrm{OP}}: \mathbf S^{s}\to \mathscr L(H^{q+s};H^{q})$ is bounded. More precisely, there

			\end{align*}
			where $|\cdot|^{\widetilde \beta ,\widetilde \alpha ; s}$ is the seminorm given in (equation OPS+seminorms of the paper).
			
			\item
			\textup{\textbf{(Adjoint)}} There is a symbol $\widetilde{\mathscr{p}}\in \mathbf S^{r}$ such that
			$$\big({\mathrm{OP}}(\mathscr{p})\big)^{*}={\mathrm{OP}}(\widetilde{\mathscr{p}}),\quad 
			\widetilde{\mathscr{p}}\equiv \mathscr{p}\ \text{mod}\ \mathbf S^{r-1},$$
			and

				\mathbf S^{r}\ni \mathscr{p}\mapsto \widetilde{\mathscr{p}}\in
				\mathbf S^{r}  \ \text{is continuous}.

			\item

				\mathscr{p}_{2})\mapsto \mathscr{p}_{1}\# \mathscr{p}_{2}\in
				\mathbf S^{r_{1}+r_{2}}\ \text{is bi-linear continuous},
			\end{equation*}
			
			
			\item 
			\textup{\textbf{(Commutator)}} If
			$\mathscr{p}_{1}\in \mathbf S^{r_{1}}$ and
			$\mathscr{p}_{2}\in \mathbf S^{r_{2}}$ are commuting matrices, then
			\begin{equation*}
				\big[{\mathrm{OP}}(\mathscr{p}_{1}),{\mathrm{OP}}(\mathscr{p}_{2})\big]\in {
					\mathrm{OP}}\mathbf S^{r_{1}+r_{2}-1}.
			\end{equation*}
		\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:01:48.617577+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8a5eca7f6dc7684ff8d37f31926d48133ee21f201d3c33fb75f893f22465d5df","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma l:subgaus.with.constant of arXiv:2607.02013, 'Resolution of the Detection Threshold Conjecture for Random Geometric Graphs in the $d>n$ '] Suppose $X$ is a real-valued random variable, mean zero, such that
    \[
    \mathbb E[e^{tX}] \le c \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{vt^2}{2}\bigg)
    \]
for all $t\in\mathbb{R}$, with $c\ge1$ a constant. Then $X$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $v' \le 2cev$.
    
    
    
    

\begin{proof}
First note that for large $t$ a subgaussian bound holds, since
    \[
    \mathbb E[e^{tX}]
    \le \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{vt^2}{2} + \log c\bigg)
    \le \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg((1+M)\frac{vt^2}{2}\bigg)
    \]
as long as $|t|\ge h$, where $M>0$ is a parameter to be determined, and 
    \[h \equiv \bigg(\frac{2 \log c}{Mv}\bigg)^{1/2}\,.
    \]
We then consider $|t| \le h$.
For $a,y\in\mathbb{R}$ with $|a|\le1$, we can bound
    \[e^{ay}
    -1-ay
    \le a^2 \sum_{k\ge2}
    \frac{|y|^k}{k!}
    \le a^2 e^{|y|}
    \le a^2 (e^y + e^{-y})\,.
    \]
Since $\mathbb E [X]=0$, it follows that, for all $|t| \le h$,
    \[
    \mathbb E[e^{tX}]
    \le 1 + \frac{t^2}{h^2}\mathbb E[e^{hX} + e^{-hX}]
    \le
    1 + \frac{2}{h^2}
        { c} t^2 \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{vh^2}{2}\bigg)
    = 1 + v t^2 \frac{M  c}{\log c}
    \mathop{\rm exp}\bigg(\frac{\log c}{M}\bigg)\,.
    \]
Taking $M=\log c$ gives
    \[
    \mathbb E[e^{tX}]
    \le 1 + {c} e vt^2 
    \le \mathop{\rm exp}({c} evt^2)
    \]
for all $|t| \le h$. Combining with the above bound for $|t| \ge h$ shows that $X$ is subgaussian with variance proxy
    \[v' \le 
    \max\{1+\log c, 2ce\} v = 2ce v\,,
    \]
proving the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["g a norm on R^2, even in the transversal coordinate","axis-aligned span"],"created_at":"2026-08-10T03:48:49.000000+00:00","domain":"convex geometry / first-passage percolation limit shapes","id":"claim_8a7b59a8053743091e4ad8ab9f95efc7b0a8f53dbde795774d159a9d7518d243","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let g be a norm on R^2 even in the first coordinate (every lattice-symmetric FPP limit-shape norm qualifies). Fix a transversal offset h and span length r, and for a dogleg from (0,0) through v = (h, j) to (0, r) consider F(j) := g((h, j)) + g((h, r-j)) (the second leg g((0,r) - v) = g((-h, r-j)) equals g((h, r-j)) by evenness). F is convex in j (a sum of compositions of g with affine maps) and satisfies F(r - j) = F(j), so it is symmetric about j = r/2 and therefore minimized there: F(j) >= F(r/2) for EVERY real j, including j < 0 and j > r. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.023106+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8a80380bfa0c1c1abfc1dc935b76c988a95843ff5816961269dffa9472a1429b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 14 of arXiv:2608.15379, 'Stochastic Jacobi fields along discontinuous martingales on Riemannian submanifolds'] Let $(\cE,\cF)$ be a regular Dirichlet form on $L^2(E;\bdm)$ satisfying \thetag{C} for some vector field $\cH \in \mathfrak{X}(E)$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663849+00:00","domain":"geometric topology","id":"claim_8a919fd46e21536498d55106d7726f8d70f6a43dc0b789ccc7c60448c0b447ba","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The Poincare conjecture states that every closed (compact, boundaryless) simply connected 3-dimensional topological manifold is homeomorphic to the 3-sphere S^3; equivalently, S^3 is the only closed 3-manifold, up to homeomorphism, with trivial fundamental group. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:14:46.481500+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8aa0cc22f8094a0904f2148924579f72f0ce60953c20abf2900754d318ed7822","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The measurable functions have the following properties:

\item $f:X\to\mathbb C$ is measurable precisely when $Re(f),Im(f):X\to\mathbb R$ are measurable. In this case, the function $|f|:X\to\mathbb R$ is measurable too.

\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:23:03.034095+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8abb922e70d75ba0c9a6df4dff99c352bf8e4ffe5b48d9a2b91fc884e126f723","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 16 of arXiv:2605.03057, 'Uniform-in-time quantitative fluctuations of large scale interacting particle systems'] Fix $T>0$ and let $\eta_t$ be a random finite signed measure on $\R^d$ for each $t\in[0,T]$.
Assume that for every fixed test function $f\in C_b^2(\R^d)$, the real
process
\begin{equation*}
t\mapsto \langle \eta_t,f\rangle
\end{equation*}
is a continuous semimartingale admitting a decomposition
\begin{equation}

\langle \eta_t,f\rangle
=
\langle \eta_0,f\rangle + \int_0^t \langle \eta_s, \mathcal G_s f\rangle ds + M_t(f),
\end{equation}
where $(\mathcal G_s)_{s\in[0,T]}$ is a (possibly random, but progressively measurable) family of linear operators on $C_b^2(\R^d)$
and $M_t(f)$ is a continuous martingale.
\\~\\
Let $\psi \colon [0,T]\times\R^d\to\R$ be deterministic with $\psi\in
C^1\left([0,T];C_b^2(\R^d)\right)$, i.e., $t\mapsto
\psi_t=\psi(t,\cdot)$  is $C^1$ into $C_b^2$. Then, $\langle \eta_t,\psi_t\rangle$ is a continuous semimartingale and satisfies
\begin{equation}

d\langle \eta_t,\psi_t\rangle
=
\langle \eta_t,\partial_t\psi_t\rangle dt
+\langle \eta_t,\mathcal G_t\psi_t\rangle dt
+dM_t(\psi_t).
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f ∈ C^2 with f'' > 0 everywhere (genuine nonlinearity); for nonconvex f the Riemann solution is a composite of shocks and rarefactions given by the convex/concave hull construction","initial datum exactly the two-state Riemann datum","entropy (Kruzhkov / Oleinik) admissibility is what excludes the nonphysical expansion shock when u_l < u_r"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T10:04:12.418000+00:00","domain":"partial differential equations: hyperbolic conservation laws","id":"claim_8ac03e996b3b87a605fc6323901992a6fdd8ce364550e7a1265b2c2093413b70","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f ∈ C^2(R) with f''(s) > 0 for all s, and let u_l, u_r ∈ R with initial datum u0(x) = u_l for x < 0 and u0(x) = u_r for x > 0. The unique Kruzhkov entropy solution of u_t + f(u)_x = 0 is: (a) if u_l > u_r (shock): u(x,t) = u_l for x < σ t and u(x,t) = u_r for x > σ t, with σ = ( f(u_l) - f(u_r) ) / ( u_l - u_r ); this jump satisfies the Lax inequalities f'(u_l) > σ > f'(u_r); (b) if u_l < u_r (rarefaction wave): u(x,t) = u_l for x ≤ f'(u_l) t, u(x,t) = (f')^{-1}( x/t ) for f'(u_l) t ≤ x ≤ f'(u_r) t, u(x,t) = u_r for x ≥ f'(u_r) t; this function is continuous on t > 0 and Lipschitz away from t = 0. (c) if u_l = u_r the solution is constant. For Burgers' equation f(u) = u^2/2 these read: shock speed (u_l+u_r)/2 when u_l > u_r, and the rarefaction u = x/t between the lines x = u_l t and x = u_r t when u_l < u_r. Both solutions are self-similar: u(x,t) = U(x/t).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:14:46.370944+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ac21cfc89cca779a6e363571f938e1b2d69ab36b66bdb69419ac40188a98c27","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] When playing with a biased coin, your winning law is
$$b_p=(1-p)\delta_0+p\delta_1$$
called Bernoulli law of parameter $p\in[0,1]$. When playing $n$ times, your winning law is
$$b_{np}=\sum_{s=0}^n\binom{n}{s}p^s(1-p)^{n-s}\delta_s$$
called binomial law of parameter $p\in[0,1]$. We have the formula $b_{np}=b_p^{*n}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f continuous (or merely integrable) on the circle","symmetric partial sums S_N of the Fourier series"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:39.264258+00:00","domain":"Fourier series, common errors","id":"claim_8ac39be5488e62ef2062744a8805090f4ff3f7a198a608caf56cfdc735eca673","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: a local regularity condition (Dini, Holder, bounded variation), not mere continuity. The evaluation functionals $f\\mapsto S_Nf(0)$ on $C(\\mathbb T)$ have norms equal to the Lebesgue constants $\\|D_N\\|_{L^1}=\\frac4{\\pi^2}\\log N+O(1)\\to\\infty$, so by Banach-Steinhaus the set of continuous $f$ with $\\sup_N|S_Nf(0)|=\\infty$ is a dense $G_\\delta$ in $C(\\mathbb T)$; du Bois-Reymond (1873) gave the first explicit example. Kahane-Katznelson: for every set $E\\subset\\mathbb T$ of measure zero there is a continuous $f$ whose Fourier series diverges at every point of $E$. Kolmogorov (1926): there is $f\\in L^1(\\mathbb T)$ whose Fourier series diverges at every point. What is true: Carleson (1966) - $f\\in L^2(\\mathbb T)$ implies $S_Nf\\to f$ a.e.; Hunt - the same for $L^p$, $p>1$; Riesz - $S_Nf\\to f$ in $L^p$ for $1<p<\\infty$, but this fails in $L^1$ and in the uniform norm; Fejer - $\\sigma_Nf\\to f$ uniformly for continuous $f$. Also note convergence in norm does not repair the pointwise picture near a jump: for a function with a jump $J$, the partial sums overshoot by $\\big(\\frac1\\pi\\int_0^\\pi\\frac{\\sin t}{t}dt-\\frac12\\big)J\\approx0.0895\\,J$ on each side (Gibbs phenomenon), so $\\|S_Nf-f\\|_\\infty$ does not tend to 0 even though $\\|S_Nf-f\\|_2\\to0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:12:19.464282+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ad4850031c2ab1371de9a748b4112ddc273de39142211075fea80bfc430bccc","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 14 (Explicit log-annular mollifier) of arXiv:2608.17540, 'Pathwise stability for one-dimensional SDEs driven by Brownian motion and a symmetric stab'] Let $\varphi\in C_c^\infty((0,1))$ satisfy
\[
  \varphi\ge0,\qquad \int_0^1\varphi(r)\dd r=1.
\]
For $\delta\ge2$, $\eps\in(0,1)$, put $L_\delta:=\log\delta$. For $y\ne0$, define
\[
  r_{\delta,\eps}(y):=\frac{\log(\eps/|y|)}{L_\delta}
\]
and
\begin{equation}
  \psi_{\delta,\eps}(y)
  :=\frac{1}{2L_\delta |y|}\,\varphi\!\left(r_{\delta,\eps}(y)\right),
  \qquad y\ne0,
\end{equation}
while setting $\psi_{\delta,\eps}(0)=0$. Then
\[
  \psi_{\delta,\eps}\in C_c^\infty(\R),\qquad
  \psi_{\delta,\eps}\ge0,
  \qquad
  \int_\R\psi_{\delta,\eps}(y)\dd y=1,
\]
and
\[
  \supp\psi_{\delta,\eps}\subset\{y:\eps/\delta<|y|<\eps\}.
\]
Moreover, there exists a constant $C_\varphi>0$, independent of $\delta$ and $\eps$, such that
\begin{align}
  \|\psi_{\delta,\eps}\|_\infty
  &\le C_\varphi\frac{\delta}{\eps\log\delta}, \\
  \|\psi_{\delta,\eps}'\|_\infty
  &\le C_\varphi\frac{\delta^2}{\eps^2\log\delta}, \\
  \|\psi_{\delta,\eps}''\|_\infty
  &\le C_\varphi\frac{\delta^3}{\eps^3\log\delta}. 
\end{align}
Finally,
\begin{equation}
  0\le \psi_{\delta,\eps}(y)
  \le \frac{C_\varphi}{|y|\log\delta},
  \qquad \eps/\delta<|y|<\eps.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:30:14.226044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ae7fa145fa7e5e8ae2e24df8d2494db2f5f66e8d3d8af08f98ec1c5aa5538c6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop Prop_finite N formula of arXiv:2608.23156, 'Disc counting statistics of the real Ginibre ensemble'] Let $N=2n$ be a positive even integer and let $R\in[0,\infty]$. For $t,u \in \mathbb{R}$, define 
\begin{align}

    &:=

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:54:15.623160+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8af7988f9b95d08cc68c88060a9758acd06958731f34c35d3b9612919d75aece","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 71 (Universal and minimax spectral depth) of arXiv:2608.08756, 'Infinite-Dimensional L\'evy Area and Spectral Ancestry'] Fix the stable natural exact-layer family
\[
 G^{\mathrm{Schur}}_{\lambda,n,r}(-):
 H\longmapsto
 {\mathbf S}_{\lambda}H_{\mathbb C}\otimes
 \operatorname{gr}^{\mathrm{anc}}_rM_{\lambda,n},
 \qquad r\geq1,
\]
assume that its stable multiplicity space is nonzero, and fix the
adapted projector \(P_{\lambda,r}\).  This is a polynomial-functor
type: evaluating it on a particular Hilbert space is not part of the
spectral-depth datum.  Its ancestry depth is
\(d_{\mathrm{anc}}(G^{\mathrm{Schur}}_{\lambda,n,r})=r\).  Its
universal critical spectral depth
\(d_{\mathrm{sp}}^{(\beta)}(G^{\mathrm{Schur}}_{\lambda,n,r})\) is the
least \(q\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\) for which a constant
\(C_{G,P,\beta}\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \|P_{\lambda,r}L_n(s,t)\|_{\mathfrak W_{\mathrm{mf}}^{[q]}(n)}
 \leq C_{G,P,\beta}\omega(s,t)^{n\beta}
 
\end{equation}
for every \(T\), every member of
\(\mathfrak C_{\beta}^{\mathrm{crit}}(T)\), and every \(s<t\).
The constant is uniform over the natural family, in particular
independent of the ambient Hilbert-space dimension.

An integer grade \(q\in\mathbb N_{\geq1}\) is called minimax sharp if
there are \(T_G,N_G,c_G,p_G>0\) and one fixed nontrivial cut
\(S_G\subset[n]\), chosen for the natural family before the spectral
window, with the following property.  For every \(L\geq N_G\) there is
a finite-dimensional random realization and an event \(G_L\) of
probability at least \(p_G\) on
which the realization belongs to
\(\mathfrak C_{\beta}^{\mathrm{crit}}(T_G)\) and
\begin{equation}
 s_N\!\left(
 \operatorname{Mat}_{S_G}
 (P_{\lambda,r}L_n(0,T_G))
 \right)
 \geq c_G\phi_q(N),
 \qquad N_G\leq N\leq L.
 
\end{equation}
All constants and algebraic data are independent of the ambient
dimension; only the finite block dimensions may depend on \(L\).  In particular,
minimax sharpness is not the assertion that every realization, or every
flattening of one realization, is extremal.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:18:27.580890+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b0a3710c6a46c0351b307840543431e0215611178908f4747d58d6f99ba3029","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 24 (Echo decay beats volume growth: unconditional front decoupling) of arXiv:2608.15987, 'Threshold cascades of interacting diffusions on unimodular random trees: a conditional bra'] Assume bounded degrees, the saturated regime with margin $\delta$, the dissipative condition $\kappa<1$ of \eqref{eq:kappa}, and $\kappa\,\rho(M)<1$. Then Hypothesis~\ref{hyp:red} holds: there is a constant $C=C(\kappa,\alpha_{\min},\mu_0,\Delta_{\max})$ such that for the cascade on $G_n$,
\[

\]
with $\eta_n\to0$ as $G_n\xrightarrow{\mathrm{BS}}T$, in the subcritical regime $\rho(M)<1$. Consequently all results of Sections \ref{sec:spectral}--\ref{sec:stab} hold unconditionally, as statements about the SDE, on the open parameter region

in the iterated limit $n\to\infty$ then $\delta\to\infty$. At criticality the bound degrades: conditionally on $\{|S|=n\}$ the total-variation error is $\le C\,n\,\varepsilon(\delta)/(1-\kappa)$, so the critical limit theorems (Theorems \ref{thm:32} and \ref{thm:crt}) hold unconditionally along any joint limit $\delta_n\to\infty$ with $n\,\varepsilon(\delta_n)\to0$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:26:20.678541+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b1f2e918c5ab866982a07ebe1705a5f626a84fdfc529753fb83739db55f1ff9","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:walkbridge of arXiv:2411.12149, 'Airy limit for $\beta$-additions through Dunkl operators'] For $H_{1},H_{2}\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}$, $L\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$, $N\in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 1}$, $\mathcal{\tilde{W}}(H_{1},H_{2},L;N)$ is the set of walk bridges of length $L$  from $H_{1}$ to $H_{2}$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:35:56.896453+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b24d3f33f1dffa94f9f40feaf5d6b4041c1ae247442873b83561cf9a8526de9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem lem_app of arXiv:2603.29711, 'Strong Feller property, irreducibility,\\ and uniqueness of the invariant measure\\ for st'] The following properties hold.
        \begin{itemize}
\item[(i)]

For every $\varsigma\geq1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ 
it holds
that $m_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}\in C^{\infty}_c(\mathbb R)$ and 
\[
  \norm{m_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}}_{L^\infty\left(\mathbb R\right)}
  \leq
\norm{m_\varsigma}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}+1,
\qquad
\norm{m'_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}\leq
\norm{m'_\varsigma}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}.
\]
\item[(ii)]

For every $\varsigma\geq1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$ 
it holds
that 
\[
  \frac{1}{m_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}(r)}\le \frac{1}{\varepsilon^\varsigma} \quad \forall\, r \in \mathbb{R}.
\]
\item [(iii)]
 
For every $\varsigma\geq1$ and $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$
it holds that $\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}\in C^2(\mathbb R)$
is strictly convex, 
$\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}'$ is monotone increasing and $\frac{1}{\varepsilon^\varsigma}$-Lipschitz continuous,
with $\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}'(0)=0$, 
$m_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}''\equiv1$,
and 
\[
  \frac1{\norm{m_\varsigma}_{L^\infty(\mathbb R)}+1}\leq\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}''(r)\leq \frac1{\varepsilon^\varsigma}
  \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\]
\item [(iv)]

For every $\varsigma>1$, there exist $C_\varsigma, c_\varsigma>0$
such that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
it holds that 
\[
c_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma-1, \varepsilon}''(r)\leq 
|\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'(r)| 
\le C_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma-1, \varepsilon}''(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\]
\item [(v)]

For every $\varsigma\geq1$, there exist $C_\varsigma, c_\varsigma>0$
such that, for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$,
it holds that 
\begin{alignat*}{2}
c_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r) &\leq 
|\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'(r)| &&\le C_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R,\\
c_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+2, \varepsilon}(r) &\leq 
\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}''(r) &&\le C_\varsigma\Psi_{\varsigma+2, \varepsilon}(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R,\\
c_\varsigma\Psi''_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r) &\leq 
|\Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'''(r)| &&\le 
C_\varsigma\Psi''_{\varsigma+1, \varepsilon}(r)
\quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\end{alignat*}
\item [(viii)]

For every $\varsigma, \zeta \ge 1$, $\varsigma\le\zeta$,
there exists $C_{\varsigma,\zeta}>0$ such that,
for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, it holds that
\[
\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}(r)\leq C_{\varsigma,\zeta}
\Psi_\zeta(r) \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R, \qquad
\Psi_{\varsigma,\varepsilon}''(r)\leq C_{\varsigma,\zeta}
\Psi_\zeta''(r) \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
\]
\item [(ix)]

For every $\varsigma, \zeta \geq 1$ with $\varsigma+\zeta>2$,
there is $K_{\varsigma,\zeta}>0$ such that,
for every $\varepsilon\in(0,1)$, it holds 
    \[
    \Psi_{\varsigma, \varepsilon}'(r)
    \Psi_{\zeta, \varepsilon}'(r)
    \geq K_{\varsigma,\zeta}
    \Psi_{\varsigma+\zeta-2, \varepsilon}''(r) - K_{\varsigma,\zeta}^{-1} \quad\forall\,r\in\mathbb R.
    \]
   \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:13:21.345756+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b483ecada9d03b43ace050f76a7e78c5bdc30d005a7823e5d684517aa060ba5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 1 (Truncated Poisson for $Q+C\le k$) of arXiv:2609.01559, 'Erlang Loss Model with Energy Constrained Servers'] Let $Q \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu} \right)$, $C \sim \mathrm{Poisson}\left( \frac{\lambda p}{\gamma}\right)$, independent.  
Define the truncated state space
\[
\mathcal{S}_k := \{ (Q,C) \in \mathbb{Z}_{\ge 0}^2 : Q + C \le k \}.
\]

The truncated joint distribution is
\begin{align}
\mathbb{P}_{\rm trunc}(Q=x,C=y) 
= \frac{ \frac{\rho_Q^x}{x!} \frac{\rho_C^y}{y!} }{ Z_k}, \quad (x,y) \in \mathcal{S}_k,
\end{align}

where the normalization constant $Z_k$ is given by
\[
Z_k := \sum_{i=0}^{k}\sum_{j=0}^{k-i} \frac{\left(\frac{\lambda}{\mu} \right)^i}{i!} \frac{\left( \frac{\lambda p}{\gamma}\right)^j}{j!} = e^{\frac{\lambda}{\mu} + \frac{\lambda p}{\gamma}} \frac{\Gamma \left( k+1, \frac{\lambda}{\mu} + \frac{\lambda p}{\gamma} \right)}{\Gamma(k+1)}
\]
and where the incomplete gamma function is given by
\[ \Gamma \left( k, x \right)  = \int_{x}^{\infty} t^{k-1} e^{-t}  dt.\]
\begin{proof}
First rewrite the double sum using $n=i+j$:
\begin{align}
Z_k 
&= \sum_{n=0}^{k} \sum_{i=0}^{n} \frac{\rho_1^i}{i!} \frac{\rho_2^{\,n-i}}{(n-i)!}.
\end{align}

Use the identity
\[
\frac{1}{i!(n-i)!} = \frac{1}{n!} \binom{n}{i},
\]
and represent the binomial coefficient using the Beta identity
\[
\binom{n}{i} 
= \frac{1}{B(i+1,n-i+1)} 
\int_0^1 x^i (1-x)^{n-i} \, dx,
\]
where $B(a,b) = \int_0^1 x^{a-1}(1-x)^{b-1} dx$ is the Beta function.

Thus,
\begin{align}
\frac{\rho_1^i}{i!} \frac{\rho_2^{\,n-i}}{(n-i)!}
&= \frac{1}{n!} \binom{n}{i} \rho_1^i \rho_2^{\,n-i} \\
&= \frac{1}{n!} \int_0^1 \binom{n}{i} x^i (1-x)^{n-i} \rho_1^i \rho_2^{\,n-i} \, dx.
\end{align}

Summing over $i=0,\dots,n$ and interchanging sum and integral,
\begin{align}
\sum_{i=0}^{n} \frac{\rho_1^i}{i!} \frac{\rho_2^{\,n-i}}{(n-i)!}
&= \frac{1}{n!} \int_0^1 \sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} (\rho_1 x)^i (\rho_2 (1-x))^{n-i} \, dx.
\end{align}

The inner sum is a binomial expansion:
\[
\sum_{i=0}^{n} \binom{n}{i} (\rho_1 x)^i (\rho_2 (1-x))^{n-i}
= \big( \rho_1 x + \rho_2 (1-x) \big)^n.
\]

Hence,
\begin{align}
\sum_{i=0}^{n} \frac{\rho_1^i}{i!} \frac{\rho_2^{\,n-i}}{(n-i)!}
&= \frac{1}{n!} \int_0^1 \big( \rho_1 x + \rho_2 (1-x) \big)^n \, dx.
\end{align}

Now observe that
\[
\rho_1 x + \rho_2 (1-x) = \rho_2 + (\rho_1 - \rho_2)x,
\]
so the integral evaluates to
\[
\int_0^1 (\rho_1 x + \rho_2 (1-x))^n dx = \frac{(\rho_1+\rho_2)^n}{n+1}.
\]

Thus,
\begin{align}
\sum_{i=0}^{n} \frac{\rho_1^i}{i!} \frac{\rho_2^{\,n-i}}{(n-i)!}
= \frac{(\rho_1+\rho_2)^n}{n!}.
\end{align}

Therefore,
\begin{align}
Z_k = \sum_{n=0}^{k} \frac{(\rho_1+\rho_2)^n}{n!}.
\end{align}

Finally, using the incomplete gamma function identity for the truncated exponential sum,
\[
\sum_{n=0}^{k} \frac{x^n}{n!} = e^{x} \frac{\Gamma(k+1,x)}{\Gamma(k+1)},
\]
we obtain
\[
Z_k = e^{\rho_1+\rho_2} \frac{\Gamma(k+1,\rho_1+\rho_2)}{\Gamma(k+1)}.
\]

Substituting $\rho_1 = \frac{\lambda}{\mu}$ and $\rho_2 = \frac{\lambda p}{\gamma}$ gives the result.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

			\frac{(n-1)!n!}{(n-1-j)!(n+j)!} 
			\bigg(1-\frac{j(j+1)}{n(n+1)}\bigg)^m

     \begin{equation}

    	 \Delta _ F ( t )

    			\sum_{ j = 1 }^\infty 
					( -1 )^{ j - 1 } ( 2j + 1 ) 
    				e^{ -t j ( j + 1 ) }
    		,
				\qquad
				t > 0
			.
         \end{equation}
    
    \noindent
    Moreover, $  \Delta _ F  $ exhibits the following properties:
    \begin{enumerate}[ label = (\roman*)]

    $

				\right)^{ 3/2 }
				\big( 1 -  \Delta _ F \big( \frac{ \pi^2 }{ t } \big) \big)
	$
	for $ t > 0 $,

  \item 
    $  \Delta _ F ( t ) \sim 3 e^{ - 2 t } $ as $ t \to \infty $,
    
    \item 
	$
		1 -  \Delta _ F ( t )

    as $ t \to 0 $,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:13:22.515960+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b7e9dd55f685d115b40d088d51ca9ec5c42743c910fdba6ad6c3798efdd0fae","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Loewner coordinate change in H of arXiv:2505.16093, 'Multiple chordal SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Moser system'] Let $\gamma = \gamma(t)$ be a continuous, non-self-crossing curve in the closed upper half-plane $\overline{\mathbb{H}}$, with $\gamma(0) = x \in \mathbb{R}$ and $\gamma((0, t]) \subset \mathbb{H}$. Assume that $\gamma$ is generated by the Loewner chain
\[
\partial_t g_t(z) = \frac{2}{g_t(z) - W_t}, \quad \dot{W}_t = b(W_t, g_t(z_1), \ldots, g_t(z_m)), \quad g_0(z) = z, \quad W_0 = x,
\]
for some function $b : \mathbb{R} \times \mathbb{C}^m \to \mathbb{R}$. To simplify notation, we write $\dot{W}_t = b(W_t)$, with the understanding that $b$ may depend implicitly on the evolution of marked points $g_t(z_j)$.

Let $\Psi : \mathcal{N} \to \mathbb{H}$ be a conformal map defined on a neighborhood $\mathcal{N}$ of $x$, such that $\gamma([0,T]) \subset \mathcal{N}$ for some $T > 0$, and $\Psi$ maps $\partial \mathcal{N} \cap \mathbb{R}$ into $\mathbb{R}$. Define the image curve $\widetilde{\gamma}(t) := \Psi \circ \gamma(t)$.

Let $\widetilde{g}_t$ be the conformal map from $\mathbb{H} \setminus \widetilde{\gamma}([0,t])$ onto $\mathbb{H}$ normalized at infinity by $\widetilde{g}_t(z) = z + o(1)$ as $z \to \infty$. Define
\[
\Psi_t := \widetilde{g}_t \circ \Psi \circ g_t^{-1}.
\]
Then the Loewner chain $\widetilde{g}_t$ satisfies
\[
\partial_t \widetilde{g}_t(z) = \frac{2 \Psi_t'(W_t)^2}{\widetilde{g}_t(z) - \widetilde{W}_t}, \quad \widetilde{g}_0(z) = z, \quad \widetilde{W}_0 = \Psi(x),
\]
where the new driving function is given by
\[
\widetilde{W}_t = \widetilde{g}_t \circ \Psi \circ \gamma(t) = \Psi_t(W_t).
\]

The image curve $\widetilde{\gamma}$ is parameterized such that its half-plane capacity satisfies
\[
\operatorname{hcap}(\widetilde{\gamma}[0, t]) = 2 \sigma(t), \quad \text{where} \quad \sigma(t) := \int_0^t \Psi_s'(W_s)^2 \, ds.
\]

Moreover, assuming the evolution of $W_t$ is sufficiently smooth, the driving function $\widetilde{W}_t$ evolves according to
\begin{equation}
\dot{\widetilde{W}}_t = \partial_t \Psi_t(W_t) + \Psi_t'(W_t) \dot{W}_t = -3 \Psi_t''(W_t) + \Psi_t'(W_t) b(W_t),
\end{equation}
where the identity $\partial_t \Psi_t(W_t) = -3 \Psi_t''(W_t)$ follows from Equation (4.35) in [Lawler:book].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T15:09:56.128489+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b8d6dc7448442919ddc83d65ba2832e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X have independent coordinates with densities at most 1, and let u, v be orthonormal with u_i^2 + v_i^2 <= 1/2 for every coordinate. Then the density of <u, X> + c <v, X>^2 is at most 8 |c|^{-1/2} for every real c != 0 and all laws. Proof: the Fresnel identity in V (with Gaussian damping) gives |E e^{i eta (U + cV^2)}| <= (4 pi |eta c|)^{-1/2} g(eta) with g(eta) = int |prod_i psi_i(eta u_i + xi v_i)| d xi; Hoelder along the line with p_i = 1/v_i^2 >= 2 and int |psi|^p <= 4 pi p^{-1/2} give g(eta) <= 4 pi for EVERY eta, and the two-dimensional Brascamp-Lieb bound gives int g <= (4 pi)^2; split the frequency integral at |eta| = pi. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:06:07.083786+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8b9f295ae87a6b776f3fe2c8a4f8e7483b7b2e13fa00781b100a1b0f50b06e34","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defini 10 of arXiv:2608.27934, 'An example of biquandle and an invariant of long virtual knots defined through it'] (Pointed Gauss diagram)\\
Take a counterclockwise oriented circle $S^{1}$ with one specified point $p$ on it. 
For a long virtual knot diagram $D$, fix an orientation preserving immersion $\phi$ from $S^{1}\setminus \{p\}$ to the image of $D$. 
For each classical crossing $c$ of $D$, the preimage $\phi^{-1}(c)$ of $c$ consists of two points of $S^{1}\setminus \{p\}$. 
Let $c_{O}$ and $c_{U}$ be the points of $\phi^{-1}(c)$ corresponding to for the points being on  the overarc and the under arc, respectively. 
Connect $c_{O}$ and $c_{U}$ by a dashed arrow oriented from $c_{O}$ to $c_{U}$ for each classical crossing of $D$. 
Assign this dashed arrow the symbol $+$ or $-$ according to the sign of the crossing $c$. 
The obtained pointed circle with dashed arrows is called {\it the pointed Gauss diagram of} $D$, denoted by $G(D)$. 
An example of a pointed Gauss diagram of a long virtual knot is presented in Figure~\ref{gaussdiagram_k3(4)}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:50:44.874528+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ba9b6424051bc56095131f436eb9f5032e27c5440b559aff5051fa0bf5907c0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 43 (Finite Peter--Weyl block family) of arXiv:2607.16724, 'Algebraic Transfer for Operator-Valued Gaussian Chaoses: Oriented Schatten Profiles and Si'] Let $J_v$ be a finite ordered leg set.  For every $h\in J_v$, fix a
countable label set $\mathscr L_{v,h}$, finite-dimensional Hilbert spaces
$Z_{v,h}(\lambda)$ for $\lambda\in\mathscr L_{v,h}$, and a sign
$\sigma_{v,h}\in\{+,-\}$.  Put
\[
 E_{v,h}(\lambda)
 :=
 \begin{cases}
  Z_{v,h}(\lambda),&\sigma_{v,h}=+,\\
  \conj{Z_{v,h}(\lambda)},&\sigma_{v,h}=-.
 \end{cases}
\]
A finite Peter--Weyl block family at $v$ is a specified tensor
\begin{equation}

 \mathbf v_{\boldsymbol\lambda_v}
 \in\bigotimes_{h\in J_v}E_{v,h}(\lambda_h)
\end{equation}
for every
$\boldsymbol\lambda_v\in\prod_{h\in J_v}\mathscr L_{v,h}$; zero tensors
are allowed.  All tensor products over subsets of $J_v$ use the inherited
order.  For $I\subset J_v$, let
\[
 \Flat_I^{\mathrm{str}}(\mathbf v_{\boldsymbol\lambda_v}):
 \conj{\bigotimes_{h\in I}E_{v,h}(\lambda_h)}
 \longrightarrow
 \bigotimes_{h\in J_v\setminus I}E_{v,h}(\lambda_h)
\]
be the canonical Hilbert-space linearization and define
\begin{equation}

 \mathfrak f_{v,r,I}(\boldsymbol\lambda_v)
 :=
 \norm{\Flat_I^{\mathrm{str}}
        (\mathbf v_{\boldsymbol\lambda_v})}_{\Sch_r}.
\end{equation}
Singleton label sets encode fixed auxiliary legs.  A dyadic Peter--Weyl leg
has label set $\Dya$ and space $H_L$; conjugating the leg changes its sign.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.742750+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8bbd03f4f9ca2c8349245fff9915ecb87b254c1a254eb110b0bbb06808462659","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 39 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] Let $\nu$ be a supercritical offspring distribution whose mean is denoted by $\ttm_\nu$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:23:27.786659+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8bbd14c695f07547067a7b63859fcce832b3771001f74a10d8af606d3d832733","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:main of arXiv:2606.09022, 'Steady-State Approximation Error of Heterogeneous Mean-Field Models'] Consider the heterogeneous \(M\)-agent system introduced in the previous section and the corresponding quenched and annealed mean-field models. Assume that A1-A3 and the following additional conditions hold.

\begin{itemize}
\item
\textbf{A4 - Occupancy stability.}
There exists a constant \(C_0>0\), independent of \(M\), \(\nu_M\), and \(\hat w\), such that
\[
\int_0^\infty
\|x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)-x_{\nu_M}^*\|^2\,dt
\le C_0,
\] where $x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)=\frac1M \sum_m w_{\nu_M,m}(t;\hat w)$. 

\item
\textbf{A5 - Occupancy robustness.}
Let \(\Delta\) denote the change in the full state vector  $w$ resulting from a single transition of the CTMC.
There exists a constant \(C_1>0\), independent of \(M\), \(\nu_M\), \(\hat w\), and \(\Delta\), such that
\[
\int_0^\infty
\left\|
\nabla_{\hat w}x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)[\Delta]
\right\|^2dt
\le
\frac{C_1}{M^2},
\]
and
\[
\int_0^\infty
\left\|
\nabla_{\hat w}^2x_{\nu_M}(t;\hat w)[\Delta,\Delta]
\right\|dt
\le
\frac{C_1}{M^2}.
\]
\end{itemize}

Then the steady-state approximation error with respect to the quenched mean-field equilibrium satisfies
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
\left\|
X_{\nu_M}(\infty)-x_{\nu_M}^*
\right\|^2
\,\middle|\,\nu_M
\right]
=
O\left(\frac1M\right).
\]

Furthermore, if the following condition also holds:
\begin{itemize}
\item
\textbf{A6 - Equilibrium regularity.}
There exists a distance measure \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\) on probability measures over \(\Theta\) such that
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
\|\nu_M-\nu\|_{\mathcal D}^2
\right]
=
O\left(\frac1M\right),
\]
and the equilibrium map is Lipschitz continuous with respect to \(\|\cdot\|_{\mathcal D}\), i.e.,
\[
\|x_{\nu_M}^*-x^*\|
\le
L\|\nu_M-\nu\|_{\mathcal D},
\]
\end{itemize}
then the steady-state approximation error with respect to the annealed mean-field equilibrium satisfies
\[
\mathbb E
\left[
\left\|
X_{\nu_M}(\infty) - x^*
\right\|^2
\right]
=
O\left(\frac1M\right).
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:59:58.454291+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8bc55498a07176d347866dcaac9c2ea831fc29d9b70559122a7d97832d052db4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Df inf_tube of arXiv:2605.14910, 'Sharp Phase Transition for the Formation of Infinite Tubes'] Let $X\subset\mathbb{R}^d$.
  A continuous map $\gamma\colon\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times[0,\infty)\to X$ is called an \emph{infinite $k$-tube} in $X$ if the following conditions hold:
  \begin{itemize}
    \item (\emph{Local self-avoidance}).
    For every $t\in[0,\infty)$, there exists a neighborhood $U\subset[0,\infty)$ of $t$ such that the restriction $\gamma|_{\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times U}$ is injective.
    \item (\emph{Finite width}).
    The \emph{width}
    \[
    \width(\gamma):=\sup_{t\in[0,\infty)}\diam\gamma(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times\{t\})<\infty.
    \]
    \item (\emph{Escape to infinity}).
    It holds that
    \[
    \lim_{t\to\infty}d_\infty(o,\gamma(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times\{t\}))=\infty,
    \]
    where $d_\infty(o,S):=\inf_{x\in S}\|x\|_\infty$ denotes the $\ell^\infty$-distance from the origin $o\in\mathbb{R}^d$ to $S$.
  \end{itemize}
  If $\gamma$ itself is injective, then $\gamma$ is said to be \emph{self-avoiding}.
  The topological $(k-1)$-sphere $S=\gamma(\mathbb{S}^{k-1}\times\{0\})$ is called the \emph{initial sphere} of $\gamma$ (the \emph{initial loop} of $\gamma$ when $k=2$).
  In this case, we further say that $S$ is \emph{joined to infinity} in $X$, and denote this by $S\overset X{\approx}\infty$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["a product probability measure on independent, not necessarily identically distributed coordinates","the function or event of interest admits a certifiable Lipschitz-type structure with bounded, possibly nonuniform, weights","measurability of the relevant sets","typically only median concentration is obtained directly; mean concentration needs a separate argument"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.985402+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8bc6218023d8f024ef67f80f2057021b0e367a5c321ceeb28f5937f91f9987b7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). On a product probability space (Omega_1 x ... x Omega_n, mu), define the convex distance d_T(x,A) = sup_{alpha>=0, |alpha|=1} inf_{y in A} sum_i alpha_i 1_{x_i != y_i}, a weighted Hamming-type distance from x to a set A, maximized over convex combinations of nonnegative unit-norm weight vectors. Talagrand's inequality states integral exp(d_T(x,A)^2/4) dmu(x) <= 1/mu(A), which implies mu(A) mu({x : d_T(x,A) >= t}) <= exp(-t^2/4), a strong concentration of any set A around itself in convex distance. Applied to a function f that is certifiable, meaning any difference f(x) - f(y) can be witnessed by a bounded number of coordinates with bounded weight, this yields subgaussian concentration of f around its median without requiring f to be linear or even close to it, making the method far more flexible than Azuma-Hoeffding for combinatorial optimization functionals such as the longest increasing subsequence, bin-packing cost, or chromatic number. It does not directly give concentration around the mean, only the median, so a separate median-to-mean gap argument is needed, and it requires exhibiting an explicit certificate structure for f, which can be technically demanding to construct. Typical failure: Applying Talagrand concentration by treating f as ordinary Hamming-Lipschitz (uniform weight 1 per coordinate change) when the natural certificate for f actually requires nonuniform or superlinear weighting, since changing one coordinate can move f by an amount depending on many other coordinates; using the wrong or absent certificate yields either the wrong concentration scale or, more commonly, no valid proof at all, since the convex-distance formulation is easy to state and easy to misapply. Canonical reference: Talagrand, 1995, Publications Mathematiques de l'IHES; Steele, Probability Theory and Combinatorial Optimization, 1997, SIAM.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.358607+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c10ca19cfaf34c6093c5205c472af236903ea169d1f622896435f13c67fe984","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:v not orthogonal to reactions of arXiv:2507.09421, 'Stability of randomly switching stochastic reaction networks with asymptotically linear tr'] In the setting of Theorem (thm:fast-switching-transience of the paper), suppose we are given a finite collection $\Xi\subset\mathbb R^d$ with the property that for all $\xi\in\Xi$ we have $\operatorname{supp}(v)\cap\operatorname{supp}(\xi)\ne\varnothing$. Then without loss of generality we may assume that $v\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$.

Explicitly, the claim is that in the setting of Theorem (thm:fast-switching-transience of the paper) there exists a vector $v^\varepsilon$ such that:
\begin{itemize}
    \item $v^\varepsilon\in\mathbb R^d_{\ge0}$.
    
    \item $(v^\varepsilon M)_m>0$ for each $m$ such that $v^\varepsilon_m>0$.

    \item $\operatorname{supp}(v^\varepsilon)=\operatorname{supp}(v)$ (and hence in particular $\operatorname{supp}(v^\varepsilon)\cap\operatorname{supp}(x)=\operatorname{supp}(v)\cap\operatorname{supp}(x)$ for all $x\in\mathbb Z^d_{\ge0}$).

    \item $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$.
\end{itemize}
\begin{proof}
Let $v\in\mathbb R^d_{\ge0}$ be the vector given by the statement of the theorem, and consider the subspace $A$ of $\mathbb R^d$ defined by
\[
    A:=\{z\in\mathbb R^d:\operatorname{supp}(z)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(v)\}=\operatorname{span}\{e^m:v_m>0\},
\]
where $e^m$ is the unit vector in direction $m$. For each $\xi\in\Xi$, the space $\{z\in A:z\cdot\xi=0\}$ is a subspace of $A$ of dimension at most one less than that of $A$. Since the union of finitely many lower-dimensional sets is not the whole space, there exists some $z\in\mathbb R^d$ such that $z\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$ and also $\operatorname{supp}(z)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(v)$.

Let $z$ be such. For $\varepsilon>0$, consider the vector $v^\varepsilon:=v+\varepsilon z$. Notice that as long as $\varepsilon$ is small enough, $v^\varepsilon$ will be a non-negative vector with $\operatorname{supp}(v^\varepsilon)=\operatorname{supp}(v)$ (here it is important that $v$ is non-negative and $\operatorname{supp}(z)\subseteq\operatorname{supp}(v)$). Furthermore, notice that
\begin{align*}
    (v^\varepsilon M)_m
    &=(vM)_m+\varepsilon (zM)_m.
\end{align*}
From this it follows that if $\varepsilon$ is small enough, $(v^\varepsilon M)_m$ will be positive whenever $(vM)_m$ is.

Lastly, we claim that $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi\ne0$ for all $\xi\in\Xi$ as long as $\varepsilon$ is small enough. Toward this end, notice that $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi=v\cdot\xi+\varepsilon z\cdot\xi$; since $z\cdot\xi\ne0$ this quantity is a linear function of $\varepsilon$ (with non-zero slope). It follows that for each $\xi$ there is exactly one value of $\varepsilon$ for which $v^\varepsilon\cdot\xi=0$. The desired result follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:00:30.494359+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c171c1cb2a90b9c8f1bf1c5d36e7a9989ee7a55e05871a8371a429912b9445b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 22 (Weyl integration formula for Hermitian matrices; see {\cite[Sec.~3.1) of arXiv:2607.04138, 'Hives from deformed GUE minor processes'] {Mehta}}]\lab{lem:Weyl}
Let $ \Herm_n$ denote the real vector space of $n\times n$
complex Hermitian matrices, equipped with Lebesgue measure
\[
  dH
  = \prod_{i=1}^n dH_{ii}
    \prod_{1\leq i<j\leq n}
    d(\operatorname{Re}H_{ij})\,d(\operatorname{Im}H_{ij}).
\]
Let $dU$ be normalized Haar probability measure on $\mathrm U(n)$.
We equip \(\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one\) with the induced \(n\)-dimensional
Lebesgue measure \(d\lambda\).
Then, for every nonnegative measurable function
$F\colon\mathcal H_n\to[0,\infty]$ (and hence for every integrable
function $F$),
\[
	  \int_{\Herm_n} F(H)\,dH
	  =
	  \frac{\pi^{n(n-1)/2}}{V_n(\tau_n)}
	  \int_{\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one}\int_{\mathrm U(n)}
	  F\!\left(U\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)U^*\right)
	  V_n(\lambda)^2\,dU\,d\lambda,
	\]
	where \(V_n\) is the sorted Vandermonde defined above.  Since
	\(\lambda\in\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one\), this is simply
	\(\prod_{1\leq i<j\leq n}(\lambda_i-\lambda_j)\).

In particular, if $F$ is invariant under unitary conjugation, then
\[
	  \int_{\Herm_n} F(H)\,dH
	  =
	  \frac{\pi^{n(n-1)/2}}{V_n(\tau_n)}
	  \int_{\Spec_n+\mathbb R\one}
	  F\!\left(\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\ldots,\lambda_n)\right)
	  V_n(\lambda)^2\,d\lambda.
	\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:25:35.766172+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c2b5d037f8349d033b3eee2f2108c15c6e0d90ed895e0fcd10257efc00ecfc0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem.variance of arXiv:2603.11043, 'An asymptotically optimal bound for the concentration function of a sum of independent int'] Let $Y_\alpha \sim \nu_{\alpha}$. Then
    \[
       {\mathrm{Var}}\, Y_\alpha 
= \frac 1 {12} \left(-3 \alpha^2 k^2 (k+1)^2 + 2\alpha k (k+1) (2k+1) \right), \quad  k = \lfloor \alpha^{-1} \rfloor.

    In particular, if $\alpha = \frac 1 k$ for a positive integer $k$ then

         {\mathrm{Var}}\, Y_\alpha = \frac {k^2 - 1} {12}.

 - \frac 1 6  k (k^2-1) =

     = \partial_- f(\frac 1 {k-1}),

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:27:36.727548+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c4b469bcbc34fb0b8600f6f014413475ab48ba3a9b51afd98c990fb2cde1786","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2511.14740, 'Marking and re-marking'] Let $n \in \mathbb N$ and $p \in [0,1]$. A one-dimensional random variable $Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N$ with probability mass function
\[ p(y) = \binom{n}{y} p^{y} (1-p)^{n-y}  \]
is said to be a \emph{binomial distribution} with parameters $n$ and $p$. We write $Y \sim \Bin(n, p)$.

Let $n \in \mathbb N$ and $\mathbf p \in [0,1]^c$ with $|\mathbf p| \leq 1$. A $c$-dimensional random variable $\mathbf Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N^c$ with probability mass function
\[ p(\mathbf y) = \binom{n}{\mathbf y} \prod_{i=1}^c p_i^{y_i} \, \big(1 - |\mathbf p|\big)^{n-| \mathbf y|}  \]
is said to be a \emph{multinomial distribution} with parameters $n$ and $\mathbf p$. We write $\mathbf Y \sim \Multi(n, \mathbf p)$.

Let $X$ be a random variable taking values in $\mathbb N$ and $a \in [0,1]$. Consider the one-dimensional random variable $Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N$ whose conditional distribution given $X$ is $\Bin(X,a)$, so its probability mass function is
\[ p(y) = \mathbb E \left(\binom{X}{y} a^{y} (1-a)^{X-y}\right) . \]
We call $Y$ the \emph{binomial thinning} (or just \emph{thinning}) of $X$ with parameter $a$, and write $Y = a \circ X$.

Let $X$ be a random variable taking values in $\mathbb N$ and $\mathbf a \in [0,1]^c$ with $|\mathbf a| \leq 1$.  Consider the $c$-dimensional random variable $\mathbf Y$ taking values in $\mathbb N^c$ whose conditional distribution given $X$ is $\Multi(X,\mathbf a)$, so its probability mass function is
\[ p(\mathbf y) = \mathbb E \left(\binom{X}{\mathbf y} \prod_{i=1}^c a_i^{y_i} \, \big(1 - |\mathbf a|\big)^{X-| \mathbf y|} \right) . \]
We call $\mathbf Y$ the \emph{multinomial marking} (or just \emph{marking}) of $X$ with parameters $\mathbf a = (a_i)$, and write $\mathbf Y = \mathbf a \circ X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:35:04.199863+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c4ba0eee6efbf055a309d070aa348b3fda783fd15772e833734cfe64187b73e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 23 (Finite-scale flexibility) of arXiv:2608.03497, 'Connective Constants on Nested Fractal Graphs'] For \(r\ge1\), let
\[
  \cS_r=\{\sigma\in\cS:\cC_r(\sigma)\ne\varnothing\}.
\]
Given an integer \(h\ge1\), the graph is
\emph{\(h\)-flexible at scale \(r\)} if, for every
\(\sigma\in\cS_r\), there are forests
\[
  \Gamma_\sigma^-,\Gamma_\sigma^+\in\cC_r(\sigma)
  \quad\text{such that}\quad
  \#E(\Gamma_\sigma^+)=\#E(\Gamma_\sigma^-)+h.
\]
Thus every realizable way of connecting the boundary of an \(r\)-cell
has two internal realizations whose lengths differ by exactly \(h\).
The graph is \emph{\(h\)-flexible} if it is \(h\)-flexible at some
finite scale; such an \(h\) is called a \emph{flexibility step}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Orientation-preserving, irrational rotation number, and log f' of bounded variation (C^2 suffices, C^1 does not).","The conjugacy produced is a homeomorphism;","its smoothness requires Diophantine conditions on alpha and much more regularity (Herman-Yoccoz theory)."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:04:29.025227+00:00","domain":"dynamical systems, circle diffeomorphisms","id":"claim_8c52739a81eba24dccec57aa97bd0aa341782637f37c8ae8fba3edff78cde085","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f be an orientation-preserving C^1 diffeomorphism of the circle with irrational rotation number alpha, and suppose log f' has BOUNDED VARIATION (in particular this holds if f is C^2). The engine is Denjoy's inequality: for every n the distortion is controlled, exp(-V) <= (f^n)'(x) / (f^n)'(y) <= exp(V) where V is the total variation of log f', valid whenever the intermediate iterates of the interval between x and y are disjoint - which the combinatorics of closest returns to an irrational rotation number supplies. Regularity is sharp: Denjoy also constructed C^1 examples with irrational rotation number and a wandering interval, so the bounded-variation hypothesis cannot be dropped.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.719986+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c57fe8282e704cb829c7fa2fe5a1d916bd2cd052c5218882dccdb058c2f91f1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:relations of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] A binary relation $R$ is said to be
  \emph{serial} if $\forall x\, \exists y\, (x R y)$,
  \emph{reflexive} if $\forall x\, (x R x)$,
  \emph{symmetric} if $\forall x,y\, (x R y \mathrel{\Rightarrow} y R x)$,
  \emph{transitive} if $\forall x,y,z\, (x R y \mathrel{\text{\&}} y R z \mathrel{\Rightarrow} x R z)$,

  We also say $R$ is \emph{preordered} if $R$ is both reflexive and transitive.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["each F_n nondecreasing, right-continuous, with values in [0,1]","no tightness is assumed, and without it the limit can be defective"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T12:13:53+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c5cd17030a65ecdbe60f4f7255a5f34afa5ee5bff2e761be63adba0ecc0f134","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (F_n) be a sequence of distribution functions on R, that is nondecreasing right-continuous functions with values in [0,1]. Then there exist a subsequence (F_{n_k}) and a nondecreasing right-continuous F : R -> [0,1] such that F_{n_k}(x) -> F(x) at every continuity point x of F. The limit F need NOT be a distribution function: mass can escape to plus or minus infinity, and with F_n the distribution function of the point mass at n one gets F identically 0. This is exactly the gap that tightness closes: when every F_n is a proper distribution function (F_n(x) -> 0 as x -> -infinity and F_n(x) -> 1 as x -> +infinity), the family is tight, meaning sup_n (1 - F_n(M) + F_n(-M)) -> 0 as M -> infinity, if and only if every such subsequential limit is a proper distribution function, which is Prokhorov's theorem on R (without properness the 'if' fails: a single improper F_1 makes the family non-tight while every subsequential limit can be proper). For the selection itself nothing is assumed about the F_n beyond monotonicity, right-continuity and the range [0,1] - no continuity, no tightness, no common support. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 3.2.6]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:24:10.199519+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8c9787e5c6151670188ab04eaf614efb64d6e2d7d53c671ed14b6afada7da96d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 9 (Random environment: simple sufficient conditions) of arXiv:2605.04048, 'Catastrophe--dispersion models in random and varying environments across generations'] Consider the Poissonian growth with binomial survival of Example~\ref{ex:poisson-binomial}. {"assumptions":["the series is real-valued and conditionally convergent","for the affine-subspace conclusion: finite-dimensional target R^d and a convergent (not necessarily conditionally convergent) series"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752356+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_8cac9c7bdc207f01ab297921ae09bfe7234b1fd5d6dee6f7121badbca7085a69","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let sum_n a_n be a series of REAL numbers that converges but not absolutely (a conditionally convergent series). Then for every alpha in the extended reals [-infinity, +infinity] there is a permutation sigma of the indices with sum_n a_{sigma(n)} = alpha, and there are permutations for which the partial sums have any prescribed pair liminf <= limsup in the extended reals. Consequently a real series is unconditionally convergent (every rearrangement converges to the same sum) if and only if it is absolutely convergent. In R^d with d >= 2 the analogous statement is FALSE and is replaced by the Levy-Steinitz theorem: the set of sums achievable by rearranging a convergent series in R^d is an AFFINE SUBSPACE of R^d, that is a translate of a linear subspace, so it can be a single point, a line, a plane, or all of R^d, but never for instance a disc or two isolated points. In infinite-dimensional Banach spaces unconditional and absolute convergence differ (Dvoretzky-Rogers), so the equivalence in the first sentence is a strictly finite-dimensional phenomenon. [Riemann (1854); Levy (1905) and Steinitz (1913); Dvoretzky and Rogers (1950)]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:43:53.598179+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8cdd29cf06209908042e2a4128a0f26d1dd7e749285c322fe58dc2bf9986cc8e","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem: IIfor d of arXiv:2512.12902, 'Non-equilibrium fluctuations for the \\stirring process with births and deaths'] Let  $K\geq 2$ be a fixed integer, $0\leq t^*<t\leq T$ and $\zeta>0$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T08:46:06.530785+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_8ce9d8dfa1be2b877f4ce98ce70b432c3025bc0db33c8705aa274cf7bb3cee4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a square-integrable function of independent coordinates and X^L its value after an independent resampling of a block L, and suppose the pair (X, X^L) is exchangeable (automatic for independent block resampling). Consequences: Cov(X, X^L) <= Var(X) always; summing over a partition of blocks turns Efron-Stein into the exact statement Sum_L E[((X^L - X)^+)^2] = Sum_L (Var(X) - Cov(X, X^L)), so bounding the positive-part functionals a resampling engine consumes is EXACTLY the problem of lower-bounding the block covariances. {"assumptions":["A in C4(R^d,R^{q x q}), H=A^T A, 0<mI<=H<=MI globally","sup_u sum_i operator_norm(partial_i A)^2<=D^2","jth Frechet derivative H has multilinear operator bound B_j for j=1..4","iid centrally symmetric labels independent of the past, EzzT=I_q, E|z|6 finite","deterministic u0, v0=0, sigma>=0, eta<=min(1,1/M)","bounded C3 observable F with bounded derivatives"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T19:48:52.751151+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_8d156243bb4b38cd384035c284eb21cb9225cfd962d41818e04245168d977da0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited), w730-T355-C003 version 2. Not independently checked. Let d,q>=1 be finite integers. Let u in R^d, v,z in R^q, and
A in C^4(R^d,R^{q x q}). Put H=A^T A and assume globally

    0<m I<=H(u)<=M I,
    (sum_{i=1}^d ||partial_i A(u)||^2)^(1/2)<=D,
    ||D^j H(u)[e_1,...,e_j]||<=B_j product_l |e_l|, j=1,...,4.

All vector norms are Euclidean; matrix norms are operator norms. The bounds
on the derivatives of H are multilinear operator bounds, not coordinatewise
bounds. No common eigenbasis or commutation assumption is made. Let sigma>=0,
0<eta<=min(1,1/M). Let z_k be iid, independent of the past, centrally
symmetric with E z_k z_k^T=I_q, and mu_6=E|z_k|^6<infinity;
mu_4=E|z_k|^4. Start at deterministic u_0 and v_0=0. The full-gradient
label-noise recursion for residual A(u)v is

    u' = u + h,
    h_i = -eta v^T (partial_i H)v/2
          -eta sigma z^T (partial_i A)v, i=1,...,d,
    v'=(I-eta H)v-eta sigma A^T z.

Define the global ODE

    U'=b(U), b=-(sigma^2/4) grad tr H, U(0)=u_0.

For bounded C^3 observables F with bounded derivatives put f(u)=F(u,0),
F_j=sup ||D^j f||, j=1,2,3, and F_vv=sup ||D_v^2 F||.
For T>=0 define the following finite nonnegative constants:

    c2=sigma^2 q M/m,
    c4=[sigma^2 M(2q+4)c2+sigma^4 M^2 mu_4]/m,
    c6=[sigma^2 M(3q+12)c4+15 sigma^4 M^2 mu_4 c2
        +sigma^6 M^3 mu_6]/m,
    J2=B_1^2 c4/4+sigma^2 D^2 c2,
    Jcv=B_1^2 c6/4+B_1^2 sigma^2 M q c4/4
         +sigma^2 D^2 q c4+sigma^4 D^2 M mu_4 c2,
    beta_j=sigma^2 q B_{j+1}/4, j=0,1,2,3,
    G1=F_1 exp(beta_1 T),

    C2=(G3 S0+2G2 S1+G1 S2)/2, Ct=Gtu S0/2,
    Qg=G2 J2/2+Gtu sqrt(J2)+Gtt/2,
    Qc_d=C0 M^2 c2+C1 B_1(c4+sigma^2 q M c2)/2
         +2 sigma^2 C1 sqrt(d M) D c2+2 C2 Jcv+Ct c2,
    C_d(T)=(C0+F_vv/2)c2+T(Qg+Qc_d).

Then

    sup_{0<=k<=T/eta^2}
      |E F(u_k,v_k)-F(U(k eta^2),0)| <= C_d(T) eta.       (1)

The supremum is over integer k. Thus a=1, with an explicit constant for

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:16:49.564045+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8d2e8f2054037a3aa67dfe4d17486e3a47ccd5a351b6caf3fa68bd2949d01ced","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 9 (Majorization) of arXiv:2608.25188, 'Transforms for LLM Quantization:\\\\ The Great Inversion and Format Co-Design'] For $a,b\\in\\R^d_{\\ge0}$ with equal sums, $a$ \\emph{majorizes} $b$ ($a\\succeq b$) if $\\sum_{i=1}^k a_{[i]}\\ge\\sum_{i=1}^k b_{[i]}$ for all $k$, where $x_{[1]}\\ge\\cdots\\ge x_{[d]}$ are the sorted entries. Intuitively $a$ is ``more concentrated'' than $b$.\\footnote{A terminology caution held throughout the survey: we use \\emph{concentration} in the transform-coding sense: energy packed onto few coordinates. Part of the quantization literature uses the word in the \\emph{opposite} sense, for low distributional spread, so that a Hadamard, which we call \\emph{flattening}, \\emph{increases} their ``concentration'' \\citep{federici2026dissecting}. The two senses are inverses; we always mean the former.} A function $f$ is \\emph{Schur-convex} if $a\\succeq b\\Rightarrow f(a)\\ge f(b)$, and \\emph{Schur-concave} if the inequality reverses. Fixing the partition of the coordinates into scale groups, we write $a\\succeq_G b$ ($a$ majorizes $b$ \\emph{within groups}) when the two agree on every group's sum and the restriction of $a$ to each group majorizes the restriction of $b$. A block-diagonal doubly stochastic map is doubly stochastic, so $a\\succeq_G b$ implies $a\\succeq b$, and every Schur-concave function is therefore monotone along $\\succeq_G$ as well. The converse fails, and that failure is what matters below: a sum of per-group maxima depends on the grouping, so it is not a functional of $\\succeq$ at all, and the opposition of \\Cref{prop:schur} is stated along $\\succeq_G$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:09:23.952052+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8d61a19c09808375319226a95facbdaaacc78e30cd4f8e4b4fec28abab6d3024","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2607.21759, 'Marchenko--Pastur law for tensor powers of exchangeable unconditional vectors'] For each $n$ and corresponding $d$, set $p = \binom{n}{d}$ and consider i.i.d.\ samples \[\mathbf x_p^{(1)},\dotsc,\mathbf x_p^{(m)} \sim \PrincipalT(n,d,\nu).\] Let $K = K_p = \frac{1}{m}\sum_{k=1}^m \mathbf x_p^{(k)}{\mathbf x_p^{(k)}}^\trp$ be the sample covariance matrix, and assume $\binom{n}{d} / m \to c$.     For all $n$, let $\mathbf X^{(n)} = \mathbf X = (X_1,\dotsc,X_n)$ have independent components with zero mean, unit variance, and $\sup_n \max_{1\leq \alpha\leq n} \E X_\alpha^4 < \infty$. If $d = o(\sqrt n)$, then $\ESD(K) \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}$ with probability $1$.

    Furthermore, for base vectors with i.i.d.\ components, we have the following complete characterization:

Then $\ESD(K) \wkconv \mu_{\MP(c)}$ with probability $1$ if and only if $d = o(\sqrt n)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.822501+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8d6d08c01482d10b9263acf3595d452a27dd6d39dafe3bb89a9e0773ba768ac8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:rank-diversity-frequency of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] Fix $k\geq3$. For every $0\leq r\leq k-2$,
\begin{equation}
 \tau_{k,r}(h)
 =\Theta_{k,r}\!\left(h^{(k-1)r}\right)
 \qquad(h\to\infty).
\end{equation}
For $r=0$ one has, more precisely, $\tau_{k,0}(h)=1$ for every $h$.
More locally, let $U$ be any nonempty relatively compact open subset of
$\Delta_{k-1}^{\circ}$. There is a constant $c_{k,U}>0$ such that, for all
sufficiently large $h$, at least
\[
 c_{k,U} h^{(k-1)(k-2)}
\]
maximal-rank types have a representative
$A=\{0=a_1<a_2<\cdots<a_k\}$ for which
\[
 \frac{(a_2-a_1,\ldots,a_k-a_{k-1})}{a_k-a_1}\in U,
 \qquad a_k\leq h^{k-2}.
\]

For each fixed $h$ and each $\mathsf T\in\mathfrak T_{h,k}$ of rank $r$,
the exact frequency law is
\begin{equation}
 F^{(k)}_{h,\mathsf T}(q)
 =c_{h,k,\mathsf T}q^{k-r}
  +O_{h,k,\mathsf T}(q^{k-r-1}),
 \qquad c_{h,k,\mathsf T}\in\mathbb Q_{>0},
\end{equation}
and this function is a quasipolynomial in $q-1$ for every positive integer
$q$. Consequently, whenever $\tau_{k,r}(h)>0$,
$G^{(k)}_{h,r}(q)$ is an exact quasipolynomial in $q-1$ of degree $k-r$,
with
\begin{equation}
 G^{(k)}_{h,r}(q)
 =C_{h,k,r}q^{k-r}+O_{h,k,r}(q^{k-r-1}),\qquad
 C_{h,k,r}=\sum_{\substack{\mathsf T\in\mathfrak T_{h,k}\\

                    c_{h,k,\mathsf T}\in\mathbb Q_{>0}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:50:26.916153+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8d74530410125d1d8919b743d041dc3ac5ec86c33190bcd8b24a7cd00bbe05d8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:DL_SIG_cons_intro of arXiv:2505.09604, 'Exceptional force, uncountably many solutions in the KPZ fixed point'] [Busa-Sepp-Sore-22a]

    \item

    \begin{enumerate} [label=\rm(\alph{*}), ref=\rm(\alph{*})]

        \item  For all  $ s < u \le t$,
    \begin{equation} 
    \mathcal{L}(g(s),s;g(u),u) = W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(g(s),s;g(u),u).
    \end{equation}
    \item  For all  $ s < u$ in $(-\infty,s]$, $g(u)$ maximizes $z \mapsto W^{\xi {\scaleobj{0.8}{\boxempty}}}(0,s;z,s) + \mathcal{L}(z,s;g(u),u) $ over $z \in \mathbb{R}$.

    \item

Let $\mathbf{p} := (p_{i})_{i \geq 0}$ be a probability distribution on
$\mathbb{N}_0$ such that $p_{0} >0$ and $p_{i} >0$ for at least one $i \geq 2$. Let
$\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{p},n}$ be a Galton--Watson tree 
with offspring distribution $\mathbf{p}$ conditioned to have
size $n \in \mathbb{N}$
(we only consider $n$ along values for which the conditioning is well
defined). 
Furthermore, suppose that $\mathbf{p}$ is nonlattice, 
the mean $\sum_{i  \geq 0} i p_{i} = 1$, and the variance
$\sigma^{2}_{\mathbf{p}} := \sum_{i \geq  0}(i-1)^{2}p_{i} <\infty$. 
Let $m_n$ be integers with $1\leqslant m_n \leqslant
n$ 
such that $m_n \sim a n^{2/3}$ as $n \rightarrow \infty$,
for some constant $a>0$.  
Then, as $n \rightarrow \infty$,
\begin{align} 
N_{m_n}(\mathcal{T}_{\mathbf{p},n}) \overset{\mathrm{d}}{\longrightarrow}\operatorname{Po}\bigl((2\pi\sigma_\mathbf{p}^2 a^3)^{-1/2}\bigr)
.\end{align}","status":"unverified"}

Let Theta_star and Y take values in standard Borel spaces with their actual joint probability law, and let pi_y be a regular conditional law of Theta_star given Y=y. On an extension of this probability space, draw replicas Theta_1,...,Theta_{k+1}, for integer k>=0, conditionally iid from pi_Y and conditionally independent of Theta_star given Y. Let eta be a smooth cutoff equal to 1 near the vertex and supported in {r < 1/2}, and set u = eta v. Then u is in H^1_0(Omega) (grad v is comparable to r^{pi/beta - 1}, which is square integrable in the plane for every beta, since pi/beta > 0) and f = -Laplacian u = -(2 grad v . grad eta + v Laplacian eta) is smooth and bounded (it is supported in an annulus away from the vertex). But near the vertex |D^2 u| is comparable to r^{pi/beta - 2}, and integral of r^{2(pi/beta - 2)} r dr diverges precisely when pi/beta <= 1, i.e. when beta >= pi. So u is not in H^2(Omega) although the data are smooth: the singularity is created by the geometry, not by the coefficients or the right-hand side. Remarks an auditor should keep in mind: interior H^2 regularity is untouched (it needs only Lipschitz coefficients and no boundary hypothesis); on a convex domain, even a convex polygon, the H^2 estimate does hold (Kadlec/Grisvard), which is why finite-element arguments often assume convexity; on a general polygon the solution splits into an H^2 part plus explicit corner singularities r^{k pi/beta} sin(k pi theta/beta); and the analogous failure occurs for the W^{2,p} estimate, so a C^{1,1} (or convexity) hypothesis cannot be quietly weakened to Lipschitz.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:30:50.707605+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ddb9471a4c28bb5bd969dfe974d04093a85cea7c4f17f4bc8369498cb5f46e4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2609.00481, 'The frameset of the second-order B-spline along $ab=1/q$'] The \emph{Zak transform} of $f\in L^2(\mathbb R)$ with parameter $\lambda>0$ is
\[
    (Z_\lambda f)(x,\gamma) = \sqrt\lambda \sum_{k\in\mathbb Z} f(\lambda(x-k))\, e^{2\pi ik\gamma}, \qquad \text{a.e. } (x,\gamma)\in\mathbb R^2,
\]
with convergence in $L^2_{loc}(\mathbb R^2)$. This normalization makes $Z_\lambda$ a unitary map of $L^2(\mathbb R)$ onto $L^2([0,1)^2)$, satisfying

    Z_\lambda f(x+1,\gamma) = e^{2\pi i\gamma}Z_\lambda f(x,\gamma), \qquad Z_\lambda f(x,\gamma+1) = Z_\lambda f(x,\gamma),

so that $[0,1)^2$ is a fundamental domain for $|Z_\lambda f|$, independent of $\lambda$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479922+00:00","domain":"commutative algebra","id":"claim_8de0f9044164fe2b452d0173a984390480cda436dec0025cb6e5cbbb40cebac3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A commutative ring R is Noetherian if every ideal is finitely generated; equivalently every ascending chain of ideals I_1 <= I_2 <= ... stabilises, equivalently every nonempty set of ideals has a maximal element. Facts: fields, Z, and principal ideal domains are Noetherian; quotients and localisations of Noetherian rings are Noetherian; the Hilbert basis theorem says R[x] is Noetherian when R is, hence every finitely generated algebra over a field or over Z is Noetherian; a Noetherian ring has finitely many minimal primes and every ideal has a primary decomposition (Lasker-Noether); the power series ring R[[x]] over a Noetherian ring is Noetherian; a subring of a Noetherian ring need not be (the ring of all algebraic integers is not Noetherian). The KRULL DIMENSION dim R is the supremum of the lengths n of chains of prime ideals P_0 < P_1 < ... < P_n. Facts: a field has dimension 0, and a Noetherian ring has dimension 0 exactly when it is Artinian (Akizuki); Z and every principal ideal domain that is not a field have dimension 1, as does every Dedekind domain; dim k[x_1, ..., x_n] = n for a field k (Krull's principal ideal theorem and Noether normalisation), and more generally dim R[x] = dim R + 1 for Noetherian R; the dimension of a finitely generated k-algebra that is a domain equals the transcendence degree of its field of fractions over k; Krull's height theorem: in a Noetherian ring a minimal prime over an ideal generated by n elements has height at most n; a Noetherian LOCAL ring (R, m) has finite dimension, equal to the least number of generators of an m-primary ideal, and dim R <= dim_k (m / m^2) with equality exactly for regular local rings. Non-Noetherian rings can have infinite dimension, and there are Noetherian rings of infinite dimension (Nagata's example), though every Noetherian local ring has finite dimension.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663755+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory","id":"claim_8de81c29a1406da7f47b7819df7f69538247ac004b47bf6b106fafdadffdc25b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, F, mu) be a measure space with mu(X) < infinity and let T: X -> X be measurable and measure-preserving, meaning mu(T^{-1}A) = mu(A) for every measurable A. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.646190+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e02d77eef81496282b33f698170286728358ac2c45cb207a478f652ea015f05","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 25 (Uniform moments for tRLMC) of arXiv:2605.24937, '2605.24937'] Assume \hyperref[ass:PJG]{\textup{(A1)}}, \hyperref[ass:PLC]{\textup{(A2)}}, and
\hyperref[ass:D]{\textup{(A4)}}. Let \((\bar Y_n)_{n\ge0}\) denote the tamed randomized
Langevin Monte Carlo scheme \eqref{eq:tamed-rLMC}, initialized at
\(\bar Y_0=x_0\in\R^d\). Then the following statements hold.

\begin{enumerate}
\item
There exist constants \(\lambda_{2,\max}^{tRLMC}>0\), \(\mu>0\), and \(M_2>0\),
depending only on \(a,b,L,L_0,\beta\), such that for every
\(\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{2,\max}^{tRLMC}]\),
\[
\E\|\bar Y_n\|^2
\le
e^{-\mu n\lambda}\,\E\|x_0\|^2 + M_2\,d,
\qquad n\in\mathbb N_0.
\]

\item
For every \(p\in[2,4\ell]\cap\mathbb N\), there exist constants
\(\lambda_{p,\max}^{tRLMC}>0\), \(c_p>0\), and \(\widetilde C_p>0\), depending only on
\(p,a,b,L,L_0,\beta\), such that for every
\(\lambda\in(0,\lambda_{p,\max}^{tRLMC}]\),
\[
\E\|\bar Y_n\|^{2p}
\le
(1-c_p\lambda)^n\,\E\|x_0\|^{2p}
+
\widetilde C_p(1+d^p),
\qquad n\in\mathbb N_0.
\]
In particular,
\[
\sup_{n\ge0}\E\|\bar Y_n\|^{2p}<\infty.
\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.772669+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e04743f9a88d6aa488e2d416543e23d7e20b7f3220e3652a24dbd2ad971681f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.00295, 'Quadratic Perturbations of Markov Systems'] A {\\it probability vector} is a vector $v=(v^{(i)})_{1\\leq i\\leq d}\\in \\mathbb{R}^d$ such that $v^{(i)}\\geq 0$  for all $1\\leq i\\leq d$ and  ${\\displaystyle \\sum_{s=1}^dv^{(s)}=1}$. \\\\\nA {\\it null-sum vector} is a vector $v=(v^{(i)})_{1\\leq i\\leq d}\\in \\mathbb{R}^d$  such that  ${\\displaystyle \\sum_{s=1}^dv^{(s)}=0}$.\\\\\nA {\\it stochastic matrix} is a matrix $A=(a_{i,j})_{1\\leq i,j\\leq d}\\in M_d(\\mathbb{R})$ such that $a_{i,j}\\geq 0$ for all $1\\leq i, j\\leq d$, and ${\\displaystyle \\sum_{s=1}^da_{s,j}=1}$  for all $1\\leq j\\leq d$. \\\\\nThe inner product of two vectors  $v_1=(v_1^{(i)})_{1\\leq i\\leq d}$ and $v_2=(v_2^{(i)})_{1\\leq i\\leq d}\\in \\mathbb{R}^d$  is defined as \n$$\\langle v_1, v_2 \\rangle={\\displaystyle \\sum_{s=1}^dv^{(s)}_1v^{(s)}_2}.$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T10:51:11.470799+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e0d2ab8141660ba2ba0034c644b3bd9ef45b6b1afddf2648d60f6169c8dfc2b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 27 of arXiv:2609.02561, 'NON-NEF LOCI IN MIXED CHARACTERISTIC'] Let $f: X \rightarrow S$ be a projective surjective morphism of integral Noetherian schemes with $X$ normal.
\begin{enumerate}
\item 
For a Cartier divisor $D$ on $X$,
the base locus of $D$ over $S$ is defined as
\[\Bs|D/S| := \Supp \Coker (f^{*}f_{*} \sO_{X}(D) \rightarrow \sO_{X}(D)). \]
\item
For a $\Q$-Cartier $\Q$-divisor $D$ on $X$,
the stable base locus of $D$ over $S$ is defined as
\[\B (D/S) := \bigcap_{\substack{m \in \mathbb{Z}_{>0} \\ \text{$mD$ Cartier}}} \Bs|mD/S|.\]
\item
For an $\R$-Cartier $\R$-divisor $D$ on $X$,
the augmented base locus of $D$ over $S$ is define as
\[\Bp (D/S) := \bigcap_{A}  \B (D-A/S), \]
where $A$ runs through all $f$-ample $\R$-Cartier $\R$-divisors such that $D-A$ is $\Q$-Cartier, and the restricted base locus of $D$ over $S$ is defined as
\[\Bm (D/S) := \bigcup_{A}  \B (D+A/S), \]
where $A$ runs through all $f$-ample $\R$-Cartier $\R$-divisors such that $D+A$ is $\Q$-Cartier.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:58:40.876062+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e2c39ba19a7c615a5b9cd7d7fb7a7fb4cd64d6fe0374a7e9c9abf67837fcfc9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop.detailed_close_is_close of arXiv:2605.10911, 'The stochastic block model has the overlap graph property for modularity'] [\bf Partitions with near-optimal modularity are close to the planted] 

Fix $a>b>0$ and integer $k\ge 2$. Let $p=p(n)=\omega\; a / n$ and $q=q(n)=\omega \; b/n$. For any $\varepsilon>0$ and $\delta<\frac{a-b}{a+(k-1)b} \cdot \frac{2}{k^2}$, there exists $c=c(\varepsilon)$ such that, if $\omega>c$, then the following holds with probability at least $1-\varepsilon$ provided $n$ is large enough.

Let $G \in \mathcal{G}(n,k,p,q)$ with the planted partition $\mathcal{P}$. 

Then, $q_\mathcal{A}(G)>q^{\star}(G) - \delta $ for some $k$-part partition $\mathcal{A}$ implies $d(\mathcal{A}, \mathcal{P}) < \delta' + \varepsilon$,
where $\delta' =\delta'(\delta) \in \big(0,\frac{1}{k(k-1)}\big)$.

In fact, $\delta'=\delta'(\delta)$ is the unique value in the interval $\big(0,\frac{1}{k(k-1)}\big)$ that satisfies 
$$
\frac {a-b}{a+(k-1)b} h(\delta') =  \frac {a-b}{a+(k-1)b} h(0)-\delta,
$$
which is equivalent to 
$$
\delta = \frac {a-b}{a+(k-1)b} \Big( 2 \delta' ( 1 - \delta'(k-1)) \Big).
$$ (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:38:13.644942+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e39f279efa832a2f98c3fc986a9aabe2ce5898cb117d5b3f51e5c49435409cb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 3 of arXiv:2609.00719, 'On the Aleksandrov--Bakelman--Pucci estimates for the weighted $1$-Laplacian'] Let $u\in\operatorname{USC}(\R^n)$ be nonnegative with $\operatorname{supp}u\subseteq\overline\Omega$. Set $M:=\sup_{\R^n}u$ and
\[
c_\epsilon:=2\epsilon+\sqrt{2\epsilon M}.
\]
Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\renewcommand{\labelenumi}{(\roman{enumi})}
\item $u^\epsilon$ is $1/\epsilon$-semiconvex, i.e.
$u^\epsilon(\cdot)+|\cdot|^2/(2\epsilon)$ is convex.
\item $u^\epsilon$ is globally Lipschitz in $\R^n$.
\item
\[
\operatorname{supp}u^\epsilon\subseteq\Omega_{c_\epsilon}.
\]
\item Suppose that $F\in C(\R^n\times\mathcal S^n)$ satisfies $F(x,0)=0$ for every $x\in\R^n$ and is uniformly elliptic with constants $\lambda,\Lambda$, that $f\in C(\R^n)$, and that $u$ is a viscosity subsolution of \eqref{F} in $\{u>0\}$. Define, for $x\in\R^n$,
\begin{align*}
F_\epsilon(x,X)&:=\sup_{q\in B_{c_\epsilon}(x)}F(q,X),\\
f_\epsilon(x)&:=\inf_{q\in B_{c_\epsilon}(x)}f(q).
\end{align*}
Then $F_\epsilon\in C(\R^n\times\mathcal S^n)$, $f_\epsilon\in C(\R^n)$, $F_\epsilon(x,0)=0$, and $F_\epsilon$ is uniformly elliptic with the same constants $\lambda,\Lambda$. Moreover, $u^\epsilon$ is a viscosity subsolution of
\[
|\nabla u^\epsilon|^{(2-n)/(n-1)}
F_\epsilon\bigl(x,\widetilde D^2u^\epsilon\bigr)\geq f_\epsilon(x)
\qquad\text{in }\{u^\epsilon>0\}.
\]
\item For every sequence $x_\epsilon\to x$,
\[
\limsup_{\epsilon\to0}u^\epsilon(x_\epsilon)\leq u(x).
\]
\item For every $x\in\R^n$,
\[
u^\epsilon(x)\longrightarrow u(x)\qquad\text{as }\epsilon\to0.
\]
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

$$
\alpha_r\coloneqq r -\frac{d}{q} \in \left(0,\frac12\right),\quad

$$
\mathbb X_1(T)\coloneqq{_0H}^{1,p}_{\beta_1}\left([0,T];L^{q/2}(\mathbb T^d)\right)

$$

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:57:44.948427+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e5c6578b1b3675868c78395269b081487d6d565b96f816ee25ba31df6191adb","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 7 of arXiv:2606.24703, 'Scheduling jobs with unknown size distribution in a M/G/1 queue: the shifted empirical Git'] Consider a stable M/G/1 queue in which the scheduler does not observe individual
    job sizes. Assume that $f$ (the density of job size distributions) satisfies assumption \ref{ass:1}. Let $n$ be the number of samples, $\epsilon >0$, $1/2 > \alpha >0$ be two constants and let  $n \geq  \Delta^{2 +4\alpha} $.

      \[ \gamma_n  = \frac{1 + \frac{n^{-\alpha (1-2\alpha)}}{\ell}}{1 -
            \frac{n^{-\alpha (1-2\alpha)}}{L}} \frac{1 + \frac{L}{\Delta \epsilon
