{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.376759+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_8e61bd090f62d43a44ea41fdfc55f56cf5875d06c224e218013ae47a821947fe","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A family {e_i : i in I} in a Hilbert space H is orthonormal if <e_i, e_j> = 0 for i distinct from j and ||e_i|| = 1 for every i. An orthonormal basis (complete orthonormal system) of H is an orthonormal family whose closed linear span is all of H. Equivalent characterizations: the family is a maximal orthonormal set; the only vector orthogonal to every e_i is 0; every x in H has the expansion x = sum over i of <x, e_i> e_i, where at most countably many coefficients <x, e_i> are nonzero and the series converges in norm regardless of ordering. Every Hilbert space has an orthonormal basis (by Zorn's lemma), any two orthonormal bases of H have the same cardinality, and H is separable exactly when it has a countable orthonormal basis. An orthonormal basis of an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is not a vector-space (Hamel) basis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:43:37.235957+00:00","domain":"information theory","id":"claim_8e63ac7bc55bc701174da93f82cefc303f58472689e85a95cc07ff366d9ab954","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For two probability distributions P and Q on the same discrete set X, with pmfs p and q respectively, the Kullback-Leibler divergence from Q to P is D(P||Q) = sum_{x in X} p(x) * log( p(x)/q(x) ), with the conventions 0*log(0/q) = 0 for any q >= 0, and D(P||Q) = +infinity if there exists x with p(x) > 0 and q(x) = 0. D(P||Q) is in general not symmetric (D(P||Q) need not equal D(Q||P)) and does not satisfy the triangle inequality, so it is not a metric, but it is the standard measure of how much one probability distribution P differs from a reference distribution Q.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:38:04.499457+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e73064ae949e0f43ffe9e8bad99d2510e787565f2741b59a43bc8fe198fed1b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm1 of arXiv:2607.12459, 'Renormalisation of Inhomogeneous Random Graphs'] {\bf [Averaged homogeneous attractor]}

Suppose that
\[
(\Box) \qquad
\begin{aligned}
&0 < \mathbb{E}_X\big[g^{\neq}(X_1,X'_1)\big] < \infty,\\
&0 \leq \mathbb{E}_X\big[g^{=}(X_1)\big] < \infty,\\
&k^{-2} \sum_{i=1}^k g^{\neq}(X_i,X_i)  \xrightarrow[k\to\infty]{\mathbb P} 0,
\end{aligned}
\]
where \(X'_1\) is an independent copy of \(X_1\) and $(X_i)_{i\in\mathbb{N}}$ are i.i.d.\ copies of $X_1$. Put
\[
q^{\neq} = \mathbb{E}_X\big[g^{\neq}(X_1,X'_1)\big],
\qquad
q^{=}=\mathbb{E}_X\big[g^{=}(X_1)\big],
\]
and
\[
p^{\neq} = 1-\mathrm{e}^{-q^{\neq}},
\qquad
p^{=} = 1-\mathrm{e}^{-\frac12(q^{\neq}+q^{=})}.
\]
Then
\[
\lim_{\ell \to \infty} \sup_{L \geq \ell}\,\mathbb{E}_X\left[\Delta\Big(P(G^{(\ell)}[X]),P(G_{\ell,p})\Big)\right] = 0
\]
with \(p=(p^{\neq},p^{=})\). (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:03:59.344204+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e740087662d18f12fa36131c9b391a9af68266d37478de9b40072b5c65cbfd6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Satz thm:HigherOrder2 of arXiv:2507.08692, 'Some notes on higher order concentration of measure'] Given Assumptions (ass:Set2 of the paper) (1)--(3), let $f\colon \Omega \to {\mathbb R}$ be a suitable function with ${\mathbb E} f = 0$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:56:21.583970+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_8e75b91904bdb5b759def454bb57ea1f8753958b6e312b29e8e4e679f729c2cc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a smooth projective algebraic variety over the complex numbers. Its cohomology group H^{2p}(X,C) decomposes by the Hodge decomposition into subspaces H^{q,q'}; a rational Hodge class is a class of type (p,p) that also lies in the rational cohomology H^{2p}(X,Q). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:15:34.456704+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e7a75f8cda5d58a0c1d332c50ff3c6675b3e52790102e88ba7487f8e2ca44dd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 9 (Model nonuniqueness with identical multiplier ideals) of arXiv:2609.03296, 'Nonuniqueness of Model Potentials and Weak Geodesic Rays'] For every \(\rho\in(0,1)\), there exist distinct normalized positive-mass
model potentials
\[
 \phi,\psi\in\PSH(\CP^1,\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}),
\]
and a closed Fubini--Study disk \(C\subset\CP^1\) such that their
non-pluripolar Monge--Amp\`ere measures agree as Borel measures,
\[
 \left\langle\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}+\ddc\phi\right\rangle
 =
 \left\langle\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}+\ddc\psi\right\rangle
 =
 \one_C\omega_{\mathrm{FS}},
 \tag{4.1}
\]
with total mass \(1-\rho>0\). By
\cite[Corollary~3.4(ii)]{DNT21}, their zero-contact sets agree
\(\omega_{\mathrm{FS}}\)-almost everywhere:
\[
 \one_{\{\phi=0\}}
 =
 \one_{\{\psi=0\}}
 =
 \one_C
 \qquad \omega_{\mathrm{FS}}\text{-a.e.}
 \tag{4.2}
\]
Moreover,
\[
 \nu(\phi,x)=\nu(\psi,x)=0
 \qquad\text{for every }x\in\CP^1,
 \tag{4.3}
\]
and
\[
 \cI(c\phi)=\OO_{\CP^1}=\cI(c\psi)
 \qquad\text{for every real }c>0.
 \tag{4.4}
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.826148+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8e7e2ae6259e77ace12e0ff21362060b576b7092b58b90933ba8c56873fac78a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:spectral-rank of arXiv:2609.01690, 'Iterated-sumset spectra: The complete exponent law and its rank geometry'] For every $h\geq2$,
\begin{align}
 \mathcal R^{[0]}(h,4)&=\{M_h\},\\
 \mathcal R^{[1]}(h,4)&=
 \{M_h-M_{h-j}:2\leq j\leq h\},\\
 \mathcal R^{[2]}(h,4)&=
 \mathcal R(h,4)\setminus
 \bigl(\mathcal R^{[0]}(h,4)\cup\mathcal R^{[1]}(h,4)\bigr).
 
\end{align}
The first two layers have cardinalities $1$ and $h-1$ exactly.  As
$h\to\infty$, the third has cardinality
$|\mathcal R(h,4)|-h=\Theta(h^3)$; in particular, all but a
$\Theta(h^{-2})$ proportion of the distinct values have minimum rank two.
Moreover, as $h\to\infty$,
\[
 \left|\mathcal R^{[2]}(h,4)\cap
 \left[M_h-\frac{h^3}{250},M_h-\frac{h^3}{400}\right]\right|
 \gg h^3.
\]
For every rank-two cardinality, the realization count is an exact
quasipolynomial in $q-1$ of degree two and the normalized shape locus is
zero-dimensional.  Such a cardinality has no realization of normalized

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.546101+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8eb30b7c3068e3fdbf43852a973715a6c23ef0f8df140587e64f3865ac7fa501","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 28 of arXiv:2608.05185, '\large\bf ON THE HEAT FLOW CONJECTURE FOR RANDOM MATRICES'] There is a unique probability measure \(\mu\) whose Cauchy transform, in
the convention
\[
 \C_+=\{w\in\C:\Im w>0\},
 \qquad
 \C_-=\{w\in\C:\Im w<0\},
\]
satisfies
\[
 m(z)=\int_{\R}\frac{\dd\mu(x)}{z-x},
 \qquad z\in\C_+.
\]
This transform solves the Pastur equation
\begin{equation}
 m(z)=\int_{\R}\frac{\dd\mu_0(a)}{z-a-sm(z)}.
\end{equation}
Almost surely,
\[
 L_{\mathbf{B}_N}\overset{\mathrm{w}}{\longrightarrow}\mu.
\]
The deterministic mean measures satisfy
\[
 \mathbb{W}_1(\overline{\mu}_N,\mu)\longrightarrow0.
\]
The measure \(\mu\) is compactly supported, is absolutely continuous, and
has density at most \(1/(\pi\sqrt{s})\).  This measure is the additive free
convolution \(\mu_0\boxplus\mathfrak{sc}_s\).","status":"unverified"}

	\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.596581+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ee4dd5de42e80feffe1451d5a09d55a2345587de77359019efdfcb5df877027","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop eq:Ac of arXiv:2606.06187, 'How to Study Reflected Brownian Motion in a Quadrant via Kernel Functional Equations?\\ \m'] Let $(Z_t)_{t\ge 0}$ be a reflected Brownian motion in $\mathbb{R}_+^2$ satisfying
\[
Z_t = Z_0 + \mu t + B_t + R L_t,
\]
where the covariance matrix, the reflecting matrix and the drift are
\[
\Sigma =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_{11} & \sigma_{12}\\
\sigma_{12} & \sigma_{22}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
R =
\begin{pmatrix}
r_{11} & r_{12}\\
r_{21} & r_{22}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
\mu= \begin{pmatrix}
\mu_1 \\
\mu_2 
\end{pmatrix}.
\]
Define
\begin{equation}
A =
\begin{pmatrix}
\sigma_{11}^{-1/2} & 0\\
0 & \sigma_{22}^{-1/2}
\end{pmatrix},
\qquad
c = |A\mu|= \sqrt{
\frac{\mu_1^2}{\sigma_{11}} + \frac{\mu_2^2}{\sigma_{22}}
},

\end{equation}
and introduce the process
\[
\bar Z_t = c\, A\, Z_{t/c^2}.
\]
Then $(\bar Z_t)_{t\ge 0}$ is a reflected Brownian motion in $\mathbb{R}_+^2$ satisfying
\[
\bar Z_t = \bar Z_0 + \bar\mu t + \bar B_t + \bar R\, \bar L_t,
\]
where the covariance matrix, the reflecting matrix and the drift are
\[
\bar\Sigma =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 & \rho\\
\rho & 1
\end{pmatrix}
\text{ with }
\rho = \frac{\sigma_{12}}{\sqrt{\sigma_{11}\sigma_{22}}},
\quad
\bar R =
\begin{pmatrix}
1 &
\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{22}}{\sigma_{11}}} \frac{ r_{12}}{r_{22}}\\[1em]
\sqrt{\frac{\sigma_{11}}{\sigma_{22}}} \frac{ r_{21}}{r_{11}} &
1
\end{pmatrix},
\quad
\bar\mu = \frac{A\mu}{|A\mu|}
\text{ with }
|\bar\mu|=1,
\]
and
\[
\bar L_t^i = \frac{cr_{ii} }{\sqrt{\sigma_{ii}}}\; L_{t/c^2}^i,
\qquad i=1,2,
\]
is the local time of the process on the axes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["T_n is an ordered rooted tree, and its one-vertex fringe subtrees are leaves."],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8eeb93530b800f12c01ed104639a108b8119a9456beb5c141963fc3c2a9de5b8","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, author checked; depends on the companion memo on Problem 20.2] This is the negative part of the answer recorded for Svante Janson's Problem 20.4 in Simply generated trees, conditioned Galton-Watson trees, random allocations and condensation, Probability Surveys 9 (2012), arXiv:1112.0510. Problem 20.4 asks for a Gaussian extension of Theorem 7.12, the law of large numbers for fringe-subtree counts. Let T_n be the simply generated tree, equivalently the conditioned Galton-Watson tree, with n vertices. Let N_T be the number of vertices whose fringe subtree equals a fixed finite ordered rooted tree T, and let N_d be the number of vertices with d children. For the one-vertex tree bullet, N_bullet = N_0 exactly, since its occurrences are precisely the leaves. In both constructions of the companion memo on Problem 20.2, the subcritical law of its Theorem A (nu < 1) and the critical infinite-variance law of its Theorem B (nu = 1, sigma^2 = infinity), most vertices have degree 0 or 1, but N_0 = n - N_1 - sum_{d>=2} N_d and sum_{d>=2} N_d is of order n whenever pi_d > 0 for some d >= 2, so N_0 = n - N_1 + O(1) does not follow. Since N_0 - n pi_0 = -(N_1 - n pi_1) - sum_{d>=2} (N_d - n pi_d), N_bullet inherits, with the sign reversed, the non-Gaussian limit of (N_1 - n pi_1)/sqrt(n) (a two-point law in the first construction, a mixture of two Gaussians in the second) if sum_{d>=2} (N_d - n pi_d) = o(sqrt n) in probability, which is not shown; otherwise its limit depends on the joint fluctuations of all the degree counts. So the negative answer, that fringe-subtree counts are not asymptotically normal in general when nu < 1, nor when nu = 1 with sigma^2 = infinity, is not established by this reduction. The finite-variance critical case is resolved in the literature by Janson (Random Structures Algorithms 48, 2016, Theorem 1.5) and is not included here as own work. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

$$M_2=\frac{a^2+ab+b^2}{3}$$
$$M_3=\frac{a^3+a^2b+ab^2+b^3}{4}$$

 Let $(\bT \! , \boo)\! :\!  \Omega \! \rightarrow \!   \overline{\bbT}^\bullet\! $ be a

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:04:59.433341+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8f1af7d70cb7ded84d411c7497181baa6adc84c07b3325302dcc74ecf68ca73b","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:exp-decay-centered-moments of arXiv:2605.20697, 'Uniform-in-time propagation of chaos for \\ Second-Order Consensus-Based Optimization'] Let \(p\geqslant2\), and assume (assump:centered-decay of the paper) for this value of \(p\).
Assume also that
\[
    \mathbf{E}\left[
        \momentp{p}{\mu_{\mathcal X^J_{0}}}
        +
        \momentp{p}{\mu_{\mathcal V^J_{0}}}
    \right]
    <\infty.
\]
Define
\begin{equation}
    \lambda_{p}
    :=
    \begin{cases}
        \displaystyle
        \frac{\min\{v_1,v_3\}}{c_2^{(2)}},
        & p=2,\\[1.2em]
        \displaystyle
        \frac{p\mu_{\mathrm{gap},p}}{4\gamma},
        & p>2.
    \end{cases}
\end{equation}
Then the expected centered Lyapunov functional decays exponentially:
\begin{equation}
    \frac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm d t}\mathcal L_p(t)
    \leqslant
    -\lambda_{p}\mathcal L_p(t).
\end{equation}
Consequently,
\begin{equation}
    \mathcal L_p(t)
    \leqslant
    e^{-\lambda_{p}t}\mathcal L_p(0).
\end{equation}
Moreover, there exists a finite constant \(C_p>0\), depending only on the parameters
and on the norm-equivalence constants, such that
\begin{equation}
    \mathbf{E}\left[
        \mathfrak M_p(\mu_{X_t^J})
        +
        \mathfrak M_p(\mu_{V_t^J})
    \right]
    \leqslant
    C_p e^{-\lambda_{p}t}
    \mathbf{E}\left[
        \mathfrak M_p(\mu_{X_0^J})
        +
        \mathfrak M_p(\mu_{V_0^J})
    \right].
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

 \lct_x\bigl((X,\Delta);D\bigr)

\begin{align} \nonumber

We refer to $(\omega_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$  as the correlation decay functions for $\tilde \mathcal{P}$ and without loss of generality, we assume that the  collection $(\omega_k)_{k \in \mathbb{N}}$ is  an {\em increasing-decreasing family} of functions, by which we mean that for all $k \in \mathbb{N}$ we have $ \omega_k \leq \omega_{k + 1}$  and $\omega_k(s) \downarrow 0$ as $s \to \infty$.

\item   $\tilde\mathcal{P}$ has {\em 
 fast $\textnormal{BL}$-mixing correlations}  if in addition to  (equation e.mppmixing of the paper),

 \item  A {\em family of marked point processes}   $(\tilde\mathcal{P}_l)_{l \in \mathbb{N}},$

  and such that  (equation e.mppmixing of the paper) holds uniformly in
 $l \in \mathbb{N}$ with respect to the Palm distributions  of marks $\mathbb {E} _{\bk  x1{p+q}}
[f(\bk{U_l}1{p})g(\bk {U_l}{p+1}{p+q})]$ of $\tilde{\mathcal{P}}_l$.
  The family  $(\tilde\mathcal{P}_l)_{l \in \mathbb{N}}$ has 
  {\em  fast} $\textnormal{BL}$-mixing correlations, if

 \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:33:17.699198+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8f645675d660aa781bad62a7bfc7379268b6e1154d4329e2e230d8bd7738ec0b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 25 (Local paracontrolled solution) of arXiv:2607.10813, '2607.10813'] Let $K\Subset\R^3$ and $0<T\le T_0$.  Let $\Xi$ satisfy

quantity enters the fixed-point problem.  A triple $(u,v,\mathcal N)$ is a local paracontrolled solution associated with
$(\Theta,\Xi)$ on $[0,T]\times K$ if there exist an adapted localization pair
$(\chi,\rho)$ and a fixed point
$Z=(X_{\W},X_{\K},Y_{\W},Y_{\K})\in\mathcal Z_T$ of the map defined by

and
\begin{equation}
  \mathcal N
  =\Theta+\mathscr F_X^{\chi,\rho}(Z)
          +\mathscr F_Y^{\chi,\rho}(Z),
\end{equation}
where the source maps are defined in
\eqref{eq:localized-X-source} and \eqref{eq:localized-Y-source}.  Every localized component of $\Xi$, together with $\chi\Theta$, must be
formed using this same pair $(\chi,\rho)$; components constructed with

while

\[

in $\mathcal D'((0,T)\times K)$.  Two such solutions are identified if

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:31:57.882266+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8f660339e0fd30e3725d33b07a82f8b785fa6b5ccac73408673a5a4509ea3473","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2510.13659, 'On the energy image density conjecture of Bouleau and Hirsch'] Let $(X,d,\mu)$ be a metric measure space and $p \in (1,\infty)$. 
		For $f \in L^p(X,\mu)$, we define
		\[
		\norm{f}_{1,p}:=   \norm{f}_{L^p(\mu)}+  \inf_{(g_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}} \liminf_{i \to \infty} \norm{g_i}_{L^p(\mu)},
		\]
		where the infimum is taken over all sequences, $(g_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ such that there exists a
		sequence, $(f_i)_{i \in \mathbb{N}}$ with $f_i \xrightarrow{L^p(\mu)} f$
		and such that $g_i$ is an upper gradient for $f_i$ for all $i \in \mathbb{N}$. The Sobolev space $H_{1,p}:= H_{1,p}(X,d,\mu)$ is defined as $\{f \in L^{p}(X,\mu) \vert \norm{f}_{1,p} <\infty\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869663+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_8f8607701d73455e9027918fc0de4490c6352b1e7bbbba155cac2fa232328b3e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"FIRES WHEN a proof about a constrained operator bounds the constrained part and then treats the UNCONSTRAINED part as if it were also bounded. WHAT HAPPENED: the definition of a xi-QSO constrains only same-block pairs; cross-block pairs may have arbitrary coefficients P_{ij,k}. The first pass bounded the new empty-body mass by x_0' >= x_0^2 + (1/q)(1 - x_0)^2 and concluded convergence, but that last inequality quietly assumes the cross-block coefficients sum to at most one - which the definition permits but does not force - so the mass produced at states other than 0 is uncontrolled and can be recycled into cross-block pairs at the next step. Whether that recycling can sustain a nontrivial fixed point is exactly what the Cauchy-Schwarz bound does NOT decide. CONDITION OF FAILURE: any unconstrained coefficient block that the bound silently constrains. THE FIX that closed it: lower-bound x_0' by the contributions that MUST land on 0 under the definition - the pair (0,0), the pairs containing 0, and the same-block pairs - which gives 1 - x_0' <= (1 - 1/q)(1 - x_0)^2 with no assumption on the cross-block coefficients at all.","status":"unverified"}

\item $d(x,x) = 0$ for all $x \in E$,
\item  $d(x,z) \le d(x,y)  + d(y,z)$ for all  $x,y,z \in E$.
\end{enumerate}
The mapping $d$ is called a \emph{pseudo-metric}, if it satisfies in addition the property
\begin{enumerate}[resume*]
\item $d(x,y) = d(y,x)$ for all  $x,y \in E$,
\end{enumerate}
and the pseudo-metric is a \emph{metric}, if in addition
\begin{enumerate}[resume*]
\item $d(x,y) = 0$ if and only if $x=y$. 
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:25:35.633399+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8f8f6289835d0b02376abe7274aa2ed6289ebbd83068b16b6aa283e1b0bd69b2","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition1 weak_Markovian_halfplane of arXiv:2603.05491, '\textbf{Local limits of uniform triangulations with boundaries in high genus}'] A random triangulation of the half-plane $H$ is said to satisfy a weak spatial Markov property if there exists a function $a$ such that, for any $t$, we have
\[
\mathbb{P}(t \subset H) = a(|\partial^{*}t| - |\partial t|, |t_{\mathrm{in}}|).
\]
We say that $H$ is strongly Markovian if there exist constants $\beta,\lambda > 0$ such that, for any $t$, we have 
\[
\mathbb{P}(t \subset H) = \beta^{|\partial^{*}t| - |\partial t|}\lambda^{|t_{\mathrm{in}}|}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T18:57:59.663801+00:00","domain":"classical mechanics","id":"claim_8fa6c3924079e0840ec862d2b25961f423b7cc6c7a7e4556a39a003ec41c12a9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H(q,p,t) be a Hamiltonian on phase space with canonical coordinates (q,p), whose flow is generated by Hamilton's equations dq/dt = dH/dp, dp/dt = -dH/dq. Liouville's theorem states that the time-t flow map preserves phase-space (Lebesgue) volume: for every measurable region D, the volume of the image of D under the flow equals the volume of D, for all t; equivalently the flow's Jacobian determinant is identically 1. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:15:15.556267+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8fd213f2fa332824cd4b39a3ec8b892985263eb38b618f17d924bbf48cf623e9","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma L-Lip-d of arXiv:2507.01406, '{\Large On Iterated Lorenz Curves with Applications: The Multivariate Case }'] \noindent  For each $n\geq 1$, the map $L_{n}:[0,1]^{d}
\rightarrow \lbrack 0,1]$ is uniformly Lipschitz with respect to the $\ell
^{1}$--norm. More precisely, 
\begin{equation}
|L_{n}(x)-L_{n}(y)|\leq \frac{1}{c_{d}}\Vert x-y\Vert _{1},\qquad x,y\in
\lbrack 0,1]^{d}.  
\end{equation}

Consequently, the family $(L_{n})_{n\geq 1}$ is $\sqrt{d}/c_{d}$-Lipschitz
with respect to the Euclidean norm. Moreover, since under the standing
density assumptions $L_{0}\in C([0,1]^{d})$, the full family $(L_{n})_{n\geq
0}$ is relatively compact in $C([0,1]^{d})$ with the uniform topology.

\noindent In particular, for any sequence $n_{k}\rightarrow \infty $ there
exists a subsequence $n_{k_{\ell }}$ and a continuous distribution function $
L^{\ast }$ on $[0,1]^{d}$ such that 
\begin{equation}
\sup_{x\in \lbrack 0,1]^{d}}|L_{n_{k_{\ell }}}(x)-L^{\ast }(x)|\rightarrow
0\qquad \text{as }\ell \rightarrow \infty .  
\end{equation}
The marginals $L_{i}^{n_{k_{\ell }}}$ converge uniformly on $[0,1]$ to the
marginals $L_{i}^{\ast }$ of $L^{\ast }$. Each $L_{i}^{\ast }$ is a
continuous distribution function on $[0,1]$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:01:25.577298+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8fe108bf3cee057f6d4470f8ff0eea5837d7cf7475674eec753f33783ca5698f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:truncated-exploration-data of arXiv:2605.16086, 'Loop pruning and downward deviations for maximum local time of discrete-time simple random'] Let \(v\in V^{\partial}(W)\).

\[
W(\mathrm{par}(v))=(a_1,\ldots,a_r,0,0,\ldots).
\]
Set
\[
\bigl(W(\mathrm{par}(v))\bigr)_{<v}:=(a_1,\ldots,a_{\operatorname{pre}_W(v)}),
\]
with the convention that \(\bigl(W(\mathrm{par}(v))\bigr)_{<v}\) is the empty tuple when
\(\operatorname{pre}_W(v)=0\).
We further define
\[
\operatorname{Res}_v W
:=
\Bigl(W\big|_{V_{\mathrm{exp}}^{v,W}\setminus\{\mathrm{par}(v)\}},\,

\]

\[
\mathfrak H^{v,W}

\bigl(v,V_{\mathrm{exp}}^{v,W},\operatorname{Res}_v W\bigr).
\]

\(\mathrm{par}(v)\) it records only the prefix completed before the

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.678887+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8fe5327bfb5b1283abd6159ea83b09443b2d94c9fceda0cedcefe1b28c80e4e6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn def.stabilizing_marking of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] \

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:48:30.906326+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8fe607d61427707ba0efd51dbdcc7856354c49060886cad9077cd510ae3c1a1a","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 20 (Minimal $2$-spheres with constant Gauss curvature) of arXiv:2609.00922, 'The Morse Index, Nullity and Jacobi Fields of Constant-Curvature 2-Spheres in Complex Proj'] Let $\psi:S^2\to\CP^N$ be a minimal immersion whose induced metric has
constant Gauss curvature, and let $\CP^n\subset\CP^N$ be its projective span.
Then its curvature is positive, and there exist
$k\in\{0,\ldots,n\}$, an ambient isometry $F$ of $\CP^N$, and a conformal
diffeomorphism $h$ of $S^2$, possibly orientation-reversing, such that
\[
 F\circ\psi=\phi_{n-2k,n}^{N}\circ h.
\]
Consequently,
\[
 \Ind_{\CP^N}(\psi)=2k(n-k)(N+1),
 \qquad
 \Nul_{\CP^N}(\psi)=2\bigl((N+1)(n+1)-4\bigr).
\]
Moreover, every normal Jacobi field along $\psi$ is integrable through a
smooth family of minimal $2$-spheres.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:15:34.489227+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_8ffbf1c8bcf64dbf4cef7ad30e25746777867f975e0a66cd64af4c340c8615fb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 16 (The gradient Ricci soliton equation as an ODE system) of arXiv:2609.03332, 'Singularity Models of Finite-Time K\"ahler-Ricci Flows'] Let $\varphi : I \to \mathbb{R}$ be smooth and $\lambda \in \mathbb{R}$ a constant. For the metric \eqref{eq:ansatz-metric}, with $\nu = \partial_s$, $\xi^* = \xi/H$, and $X, Y \in \mathcal{H}_i$ basic horizontal:
	
	\emph{(i) The Hessian of a radial function.} $\mathrm{Hess}\,\varphi = \varphi''\, ds \otimes ds + \varphi'\, \mathrm{II}$, where $\mathrm{II}$ is the second fundamental form \eqref{eq:second-fundamental-form} of the leaves $P_s$; explicitly, in the adapted frame,
	
	\[
	\mathrm{Hess}\,\varphi(\nu, \nu) \;=\; \varphi'' \,, \qquad \mathrm{Hess}\,\varphi(\xi^*, \xi^*) \;=\; \frac{H'}{H}\, \varphi' \,, \qquad \mathrm{Hess}\,\varphi(X, Y) \;=\; \frac{F_i'}{F_i}\, \varphi'\; g(X, Y) \,,
	\]
	
	with every remaining component --- mixed vertical, mixed vertizontal, and cross-block horizontal --- equal to zero: $\mathrm{Hess}\,\varphi$ is block-diagonal, of exactly the shape of $\operatorname{Ric}$ (Proposition \ref{prop:ricci-ansatz}(ii)).
	
	\emph{(ii) The soliton equation as an ODE system.} The metric $g$ solves $\operatorname{Ric} + \mathrm{Hess}\,\varphi = \lambda\, g$ if and only if $( H, F_1, \dots, F_r, \varphi )$ satisfies, on $I$,
	
	\begin{equation*}
		\begin{gathered}
			\varphi'' \;+\; \operatorname{Ric}(\nu, \nu) \;=\; \lambda \,, \\
			\frac{H'}{H}\, \varphi' \;+\; \operatorname{Ric}(\xi^*, \xi^*) \;=\; \lambda \,, \\
			F_i\, F_i'\, \varphi' \;+\; \mathcal{R}_i \;=\; \lambda\, F_i^2 \quad ( i = 1, \dots, r ) \,,
		\end{gathered}
	\end{equation*}
	
	with $\operatorname{Ric}(\nu, \nu)$, $\operatorname{Ric}(\xi^*, \xi^*)$, $\mathcal{R}_i$ as in \eqref{eq:Ric-nu}--\eqref{eq:Ric-horizontal}; explicitly,
	
	\[
	\varphi'' \;-\; \frac{H''}{H} \;-\; \sum_{i=1}^r n_i \left( \frac{q_i H' + \kappa_i'}{F_i^2} \;-\; \frac{(q_i H + \kappa_i)^2}{2 F_i^4} \right) \;=\; \lambda \,,
	\]
	
	\[
	\frac{H'}{H}\, \varphi' \;-\; \frac{H''}{H} \;+\; \sum_{i=1}^r n_i \left( \frac{q_i^2 H^2}{2 F_i^4} \;-\; \frac{H'}{H}\, \frac{q_i H + \kappa_i}{F_i^2} \right) \;=\; \lambda \,,
	\]
	
	\begin{equation*}
		\begin{gathered}
			\frac{q_i H + \kappa_i}{2}\, \varphi' \;+\; p_i \;-\; \frac{q_i H' + \kappa_i'}{2} \;-\; \frac{H'}{2H}\,(q_i H + \kappa_i) \;+\; \frac{\kappa_i\,(2 q_i H + \kappa_i)}{2 F_i^2} \\
			\;-\; \frac{q_i H + \kappa_i}{2} \sum_{j=1}^r \frac{n_j\,(q_j H + \kappa_j)}{F_j^2} \;=\; \lambda\, F_i^2 \,, \\
			i = 1, \dots, r \,.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-09T06:55:03+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_901c0a8cd124bb8d518e1184c9227edfe32dcfdd9106fe5b7c65b23e17e91da4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 2.5 of arXiv:2512.19517v1, 'Spiking and Resetting' (Cédric Bernardin and Vsevolod Vladimirovich Tarsamaev); numbered Proposition 6 in the earlier card; corrected to the increment form]

## Proposition 2.5 (increment form)

Assume the standing hypotheses of Section 1: (f,h\in C^2([0,1])), (f(1)<0<f(0)), (h(1)=0), (h'(1)\ne0), and (h(x)>0) on ([0,1)). Let

\[
e_1^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge0:X_t^\varepsilon>y_*^\varepsilon\},\qquad
e_2^\varepsilon=\inf\{t\ge e_1^\varepsilon:X_t^\varepsilon=0\},
\]

and define the post-(e_1^\varepsilon) holding time

\[
d_2^\varepsilon:=e_2^\varepsilon-e_1^\varepsilon.
\]

Then, for every (t\ge0),

\[
\lim_{\varepsilon\downarrow0}\mathbb P(d_2^\varepsilon>t)=e^{f(1)t},
\]

so (d_2^\varepsilon\Rightarrow \operatorname{Exp}(-f(1))).

The proof in the paper restarts the deterministic flow at (e_1^\varepsilon) with local time (s=0); its displayed survival integral is therefore for (d_2^\varepsilon), not the absolute epoch (e_2^\varepsilon). The source says that after the stopping time “the process evolves deterministically until the next reset” (v1 HTML lines 252-257), which is precisely an increment statement.

## Later alternating holding-time sentence

For the recursively defined epochs (e_k^\varepsilon), the strong Markov property applies to the increments

\[
e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon-e_{2k}^\varepsilon,
\qquad
e_{2k+2}^\varepsilon-e_{2k+1}^\varepsilon,
\]

not to the increasing absolute epochs themselves. The alternating increments are the quantities that can be independent and have the two respective holding-time laws. Any downstream card should preserve this distinction.

## Why the absolute-time statement cannot hold as written

For every (\varepsilon), (e_2^\varepsilon\ge e_1^\varepsilon), hence

\[
\mathbb P(e_2^\varepsilon>t)\ge\mathbb P(e_1^\varepsilon>t).
\]

This stochastic order must persist at continuity points of any weak limits. Yet the paper permits (f(x)=1-3x) and (h(x)=1-x), for which (f(0)=1) and (f(1)=-2). Its two displayed absolute-time limits would require (e^{-2t}\ge e^{-t}) for (t>0), an immediate contradiction. No additional relation between (f(0)) and (f(1)) is present in the standing hypotheses.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["real or complex sequences","the Cesaro means are the (C,1) means; higher-order (C,k) means and Abel summation are stronger methods, also regular"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626125+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_902f46d4318754283aa93b9e5d2191dae27430be7baba15fb73b078490254ee2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"DEFINITION. The Cesaro means of a sequence (s_n)_{n >= 0} are sigma_n = (s_0 + s_1 + ... + s_n) / (n + 1). A series sum a_n with partial sums s_n is Cesaro summable (C,1) to L if sigma_n -> L. THEOREM (Cauchy; Cesaro). If s_n -> L then sigma_n -> L: convergence implies Cesaro convergence to the same limit (the method is regular). The converse fails: the series 1 - 1 + 1 - 1 + ... has partial sums 1, 0, 1, 0, ... and Cesaro means (m+1)/(2m+1) or 1/2 tending to 1/2, so it is (C,1)-summable to 1/2 without converging. Two further facts, cited: a (C,1)-summable series has a_n / n -> 0, so a series whose terms do not satisfy a_n = o(n) is not Cesaro summable at all; and Hardy's Tauberian theorem says that a (C,1)-summable series with a_n = O(1/n) converges. Cesaro means of Fourier series are the Fejer means, and Fejer's theorem is exactly this regularity turned into a positive summability kernel.","status":"unverified"}

# C016 v1: why fixed iid heads do not inherit the paired construction
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target: 1.
This is an obstruction to the existing witness route, not absence of epochwise
double descent in iid-initialized networks. Novelty is unestablished.

## 1. Precisely the precursor model considered
Let 0<e<1/4, D0=1+e^2+e^4, x_(s,t)=(1,es,e^2t)/sqrt(D0), s,t in {+1,-1}.
The population is uniform on these four points. Set
u_e=(0,e,1)/sqrt(1+e^2), c_e=e^2/sqrt(D0(1+e^2)), alpha=c_e/2.
The teacher g(x)=ReLU(u_e.x)-c_e/2 has Walsh coefficients
(theta_0,theta_s,theta_t,theta_st)=(0,alpha,alpha,alpha).
Here the name u_e denotes the teacher direction; nu below is a different,
fixed readout magnitude in (0,1]. Initialize m independent neurons with
W_j~N(0,I_3), a_j independently uniform on {+nu,-nu}, independently of W_j.
Let z_h^(m) be the Walsh coefficients of the random initial output.
Consider the deterministic FULL initial kernel H_nu from C009/C014,
including both trained layers, and real-time-interpolated kernel GD
with step gamma=1/2. If lambda_h are its normalized four-point eigenvalues,
put b_h=-log(1-lambda_h/2), q_h(t)=exp(-b_h t).
The phrase interpolation only means allowing real t in this exact spectral
formula; at integer t it is precisely discrete GD, not gradient flow.
Use centered independent effective label errors of Walsh variance alpha^2.
For instance, four independent errors +/-2alpha have exactly this property.
Balanced replication with fixed sigma and n chosen so sigma^2/n~alpha^2
also gives the same conclusions with rho_e= sigma^2/(n alpha^2)->1.

The noise-averaged clean risk, conditional on initialization, is exactly
 Q_e(t;z)=sum_h [q_h(t)^2(z_h-theta_h)^2
                         +alpha^2(1-q_h(t))^2].           (1)
No independence between noise Walsh modes is needed: Parseval removes
cross-mode terms. The derivative below refers to this interpolated FROZEN
risk, not derivatives of finite-width ReLU iterates.
We use the already recorded full-kernel clocks
 b_s~nu^2 e/(4pi), b_t~b_st~nu^2 e^2/(8pi),
 b_0 -> a positive constant, eta=(b_t+b_st)/b_s~e.
This is the four-point balanced precursor of C015, NOT its continuous,
iid-input-count, actual-network model. No automatic transfer of the negative
result to that stronger model is asserted.

## 2. Initial covariance on the correct signal scale
Let phi_h(W)=one-quarter sum_(s,t) h(s,t) ReLU(W.x_(s,t)).
For each fixed e, ordinary finite-dimensional iid CLT gives
 z^(m) => Z_e as m->infinity, a centered Gaussian four-vector with
 Var(Z_(e,h))=nu^2 lambda_h^RF, lambda_h^RF=E phi_h(W)^2.
The covariance is diagonal by invariance of W under coordinate sign flips.
One can get the vector CLT by applying the scalar finite-variance CLT to
every linear combination. Width is deterministic, not a stopped random list.
All moments used are finite since |phi_h|<=||W|| on the unit inputs.

For almost every W with W_0 !=0,
 phi_s(W)/e -> W_1 1{W_0>0}.
Group the two s values for each t and use ReLU's Lipschitz property to get
 |phi_s(W)|<=e |W_1|/sqrt(D0).
Dominated convergence therefore proves
 lambda_s^RF/e^2 -> E[W_1^2 1{W_0>0}]=1/2.              (2)
Grouping instead by the t coordinate similarly gives
 |phi_t(W)|, |phi_st(W)|<=e^2 |W_2|/sqrt(D0),
so their variances are O(e^4). The constant-mode variance is O(1).
Since alpha~e^2/2, the fast standardized initial output satisfies
 Var(Z_(e,s)/alpha)~2nu^2/e^2.                            (3)
Thus the initial fast prediction error is not negligible on the teacher's
scale. Let A_e=(Z_(e,s)/alpha-1)^2. For any fixed C>0, the Gaussian maximum
density bound gives
 P(eta A_e<=C) <= 2 sqrt(C/eta)/sqrt(2pi Var(Z_(e,s)/alpha))
                    =O(sqrt(Ce)/nu) ->0.                 (4)
Hence eta A_e diverges to infinity in probability. This uses no independence
between A_e and the other modes.

## 3. The old fast-minimum witness diverges on its normalized scale
Let k_1=floor(log(2)/b_s), the C010/C015 precursor's fast witness.
Then q_s(k_1)->1/2. From the single nonnegative term in (1), for any fixed C,
 P(Q_e(k_1;Z_e)/alpha^2<=C)
 <= P(|Z_(e,s)/alpha-1|<=sqrt(C)/q_s(k_1))=O(sqrt(C)e/nu)->0. (5)
Thus Q_e(k_1;Z_e)/alpha^2 ->infinity in probability, rather than 7/2.
This is an iterated width-then-e statement for the iid initialization;
finite-width convergence in distribution follows from the preceding CLT.
For an upper bound at a distributional event boundary one may enlarge C
arbitrarily and use Portmanteau; no uniform-in-e CLT rate is claimed.
The paired-initialization witness statement itself is unaffected.

## 4. The old central peak window is decreasing in the frozen model
Put B_e=log(1/eta), t_e(s)=(B_e+s)/b_s. For any fixed L<infinity,
q_s(t_e(s))=eta exp(-s). Differentiate (1), divide by
2 alpha^2(b_t+b_st), and separate the fast mode. Its contribution is exactly
 exp(-s)-eta(A_e+1)exp(-2s).                              (6)
For the two slow modes, (Z_h/alpha-1)^2 is tight by the O(e^4) covariance
bound. Their rate ratios b_h/(b_t+b_st) are bounded and q_h<=1, hence their
combined contribution is uniformly O_P(1) over |s|<=L.
The constant-mode contribution is o_P(1): b_0 is bounded away from zero,
Z_0=O_P(1), alpha^2~e^4/4, and q_0(t_e(s)) decays faster than every power
of e uniformly on this fixed s interval. Consequently

 sup_|s|<=L Q'_e(t_e(s);Z_e)/(2alpha^2(b_t+b_st))
 <= exp(L)-eta A_e exp(-2L)+O_P(1) -> -infinity
                                                        (7)
by (4). With probability tending to one this entire old peak window is
strictly decreasing in the frozen-risk interpolation. In particular, its
interval maximum lies at the left endpoint, not at the paired model's
interior peak. Tightness plus (4), rather than independence, is sufficient.
The same proof works when the effective noise factor rho_e tends to1:
replace exp(-s) in (6) by rho_e exp(-s) and1 by rho_e.

## 5. What this settles and what remains open
Merely replacing paired heads by fixed-variance iid heads while retaining
the unit-teacher scaling, noise scaling and peak witnesses does NOT preserve
C010/C015's precursor argument: the witness risk diverges and the old
central peak interval has the wrong derivative sign in the limiting frozen
model. This is the exact failure point, not a theorem of global monotonicity.
Other times, other teachers/noise scales, non-lazy learning, the continuous
iid-input model and the actual finite-width derivative pattern remain open.
In particular, C015's positive paired-initialization result is not retracted.
Next route: choose teacher/noise scales jointly with initial GP covariance
before proposing iid-head witnesses. Shrinking readout variance changes the
full-kernel clocks, so one cannot keep fixed-nu clock asymptotics silently.

{"assumptions":["H is a complex Hilbert space","the operator in question is densely defined and symmetric but its adjoint has a strictly larger domain"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771968+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory, quantum mechanics","id":"claim_90607036aaf6052e0e3969770549f68d2f6a3b0e0d151f0440b57246950ca254","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: self-adjointness requires the equality of domains D(T) = D(T*), not merely ⟨Tx, y⟩ = ⟨x, Ty⟩ on D(T). Everything that makes an operator usable - the spectral theorem, the Borel functional calculus, real spectrum, the unitary group e^{itT}, the resolvent bound 1/|Im z| - fails for a merely symmetric operator. What fails: a closed symmetric operator T that is not self-adjoint never has spectrum inside ℝ; its spectrum is all of ℂ when both n_+ ≥ 1 and n_- ≥ 1 (in particular whenever n_+ = n_- ≥ 1), and a closed half plane when exactly one of n_+, n_- is 0, so 'eigenvalue' and 'spectral decomposition' statements are void. Counterexample: on H = L²(0,1) let T = −i d/dx with D(T) = {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(0) = f(1) = 0}. T is densely defined, closed and symmetric, and T* = −i d/dx on all of H¹(0,1). Deficiency: ker(T* − i) = span{e^{−x}} and ker(T* + i) = span{e^{x}}, so n_+ = n_- = 1 and T is not self-adjoint. For every λ ∈ ℂ, Ran(T − λ)^⊥ = ker(T* − λ̄) = span{e^{iλ̄x}} ≠ {0}, so σ(T) = ℂ. Its self-adjoint extensions are the operators T_θ = −i d/dx on {f ∈ H¹(0,1) : f(1) = e^{iθ}f(0)}, θ ∈ [0, 2π), with spectrum {θ + 2πk : k ∈ ℤ} - a different physical momentum operator for each θ. Second counterexample, where no self-adjoint extension exists at all: S = −i d/dx on D(S) = {f ∈ H¹(0, ∞) : f(0) = 0} in L²(0, ∞) is closed and symmetric with ker(S* − i) = span{e^{−x}} and ker(S* + i) = {0}, so n_+ = 1, n_- = 0; S is maximal symmetric and has no self-adjoint extension in L²(0, ∞), so there is no unitary group it generates. Audit rule: whenever a proof invokes the spectral theorem, functional calculus, Stone's theorem, Kato-Rellich or 'the eigenvalues of T', check that self-adjointness (or essential self-adjointness plus passing to the closure) has actually been established, typically via Ran(T ± i) dense or a semibounded range condition.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:22:21.898623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_906087a4b65d975284a1bbb827852f65b954959298f237dcdd5e96b48ca2baae","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn of arXiv:2411.11408, 'Multidimensional specific relative entropy between continuous martingales'] Let $T>0$, $t \\in [0,T]$ and $l \\in \\mathbb{N}$. {"assumptions":["the target space has the approximation property (automatic in Hilbert spaces and in spaces with a Schauder basis)","in a general Banach space compactness alone does not give norm approximation by finite-rank operators"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573577+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Banach space theory","id":"claim_9063aacd7b762796789db5a4019c2eadcd50f3f3cee806ae5cdd905624995622","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In Hilbert space every compact operator is an operator-norm limit of finite-rank operators, and many arguments quietly reuse this in a Banach setting, where it can be false. A Banach space Y has the approximation property (AP) if the identity of Y is a limit of finite-rank operators uniformly on compact subsets of Y; Grothendieck proved that Y has AP if and only if, for every Banach space X, the finite-rank operators are norm dense in K(X,Y). Enflo (1973) produced a separable reflexive Banach space without AP, and Davie and Szankowski showed that l^p for p not equal to 2, and c_0, have closed subspaces without AP; consequently there are Banach spaces X, Y and a compact operator X -> Y that is not a norm limit of finite-rank operators. Szankowski further showed that B(l^2) itself fails AP. What breaks without AP: (a) proofs of Fredholm-type results that first replace a compact K by a finite-rank F with ||K - F|| small; (b) attempts to define a trace on nuclear operators (the trace is well defined on the nuclear operators of X exactly when X has AP; without it the same nuclear operator has representations with different 'traces'); (c) approximation-number arguments imported from Hilbert space. Safe hypotheses to state instead: the space is a Hilbert space, or has a Schauder basis, or has the (bounded) approximation property; classical spaces such as C(K), L^p(mu) for 1 <= p <= infinity, and c_0 all have AP, so the pitfall bites only in exotic settings - but the hypothesis must be present, not assumed silently.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:58:24.512564+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_90854d75e625b23facc605b7c39f86b84effa77c61befef449b817242b353ad3","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn sec:schwm of arXiv:2601.09537, 'Gene genealogies in haploid populations evolving according to sweepstakes reproduction'] {\bf A genomic Schweinsberg model}

In each generation   the $2N$ diploid individuals randomly
form $N$ pairs as follows. Each individual is assigned a unique label, we form
all  $(2N-1)N$ pairs of labels, and  draw from the pool of label pairs, uniformly at random without
replacement, $N$ pairs of labels. The  parent pairs thus formed
independently contribute  random numbers of  juveniles according to some given law. If the total number of juveniles thus formed is at least $2N$,   then   from the pool of juveniles   $2N$
juveniles are sampled  uniformly at random without replacement  to form a new set
of $2N$ reproducing individuals; otherwise the population is unchanged until the next  generation.    In this framework, in each generation
 each diploid individual pairs with at most one other diploid individual.  Each offspring of each parent pair is assigned  2{\ensuremath{\mathds h} } chromosomes  by  sampling, uniformly at random,   one chromosome of each homologous set from each parent;  each parent therefore contributes  {\ensuremath{\mathds h} } non-homologous chromosomes independently  to each of its offspring.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:55.642005+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_908af5f6c99570c2b635c1a83076be6161a608cee2196b7d846b452d5cb8308b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 1 ({\citet[Theorem 29.11, 29.13) of arXiv:2605.23659, '2605.23659'] {Kallenberg-third}}] 
There exist a measure \(n\) on \(D_0\), a Poisson point process \(N\) on \([0,\infty)\times D_0\) with intensity measure \(dt\otimes n\), a non-negative non-decreasing continuous adapted process \(L=(L_t)_{t\ge0}\), and a constant \(c\ge0\) such that the following hold:

n(\zeta > h) < \infty.
\]

N([0,t]\times\{\zeta>h\})<\infty

\]

Define a right-continuous strictly increasing process \(\eta=(\eta_s)_{s\ge0}\) by
\[
\eta_s
=
cs+\int_{[0,s]\times D_0}\zeta(e) N(du\,de)

\]

X_t=e_{t-\eta_{s-}}
\quad
\text{for } t\in[\eta_{s-},\eta_s),

\quad \text{for } u \in [0,\zeta(e)).
\]
\item

{"assumptions":["coordinates of X independent, mean zero, sub-Gaussian with psi_2 norms at most K","A an arbitrary real n by n matrix; no symmetry is required","c is an absolute constant"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628497+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_908badbf12a5ec45572dec14ab5daa9643b8baf082a5a148183ab488fa20801c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) be a random vector with INDEPENDENT, mean-zero, sub-Gaussian coordinates with sub-Gaussian norms bounded by K, and let A be an n by n real matrix. Then there is an absolute constant c > 0 such that for every t >= 0, P( | X^T A X - E[X^T A X] | > t ) <= 2 exp( - c min( t^2 / (K^4 ||A||_F^2) , t / (K^2 ||A||_op) ) ), where ||A||_F is the Frobenius norm and ||A||_op the spectral norm. The two regimes are the sub-Gaussian one governed by the Frobenius norm and the sub-exponential one governed by the operator norm; this is the quadratic-form analogue of Bernstein's inequality and reduces to it for diagonal A. The coordinates must be INDEPENDENT and sub-Gaussian: independence cannot be weakened to uncorrelatedness, and heavier tails change the shape of the bound. E[X^T A X] equals the trace of A when the coordinates have unit variance, but in general it is sum_i A_{ii} E[X_i^2]. A standard corollary is a concentration bound for the Euclidean norm of a random vector, ||BX||_2 concentrated around ||B||_F within K^2 ||B||_op scales. [Hanson and Wright (1971); modern proof in Rudelson and Vershynin, 'Hanson-Wright inequality and sub-gaussian concentration', arXiv:1306.2872]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:06.979839+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_908c3e765573e97f7bb10037e4991ae01a0ccf6ebf2bfee560449d996014634e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm2_2 of arXiv:2607.26169, 'Scaling and partial universality of the height zero probability in the 2D Abelian sandpile'] {LL2010}}]

    Assume $U$ is bounded. Fix \(\epsilon > 0\) and 
    let \(g : \partial U_\epsilon \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\). 
    There exists a unique function $u : U_\epsilon \cup \partial U_\epsilon\rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ that is discrete harmonic in \(U_\epsilon\) and that satisfies the Dirichlet boundary conditions \(u = g\) on \(\partial U_\epsilon\). Moreover, the solution is given by 
    \[
        u(z) = \sum_{f \in\partial U_\epsilon} H_{\partial U_\epsilon}(z,f) g(f), 
             \quad z \in U_\epsilon, \qquad\qquad u(f) = g(f), \quad f \in \partial U_\varepsilon.
    \]
    where \(H_{\partial U_\epsilon}(z, \cdot) : \partial U_\epsilon \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) denotes the exit distribution, or Poisson kernel, for the simple random walk on \(\epsilon\mathcal{V}\) started at \(z\in U_\epsilon\), stopped on first exiting \(U_\epsilon\). 
    That is, denoting the simple random walk by \((S_n)_{n\geq 0}\), and the stopping 
    time \(\tau_{U_\epsilon} = \inf\{n \geq 0 : E_n \in \partial U_\epsilon\}\), we have 
    \[
        H_{\partial U_\epsilon}(z,f) 
        = \mathbf{P}^z[E_{\tau_{\partial U_\epsilon}} = f ], \quad
          z\in U_\epsilon, \, f \in \partial U_\epsilon.
    \] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:58:40.873531+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_90b4bfe725187a007412944c05936ea7da93a79e8c86eb4da0fbde8eb97a048c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:CMT of arXiv:2605.10617, 'Logarithmic scaling of selective sweep curves:\\ from tents to houses'] Let $(Z^N(t))_{t\geq 0}$ be a binary branching process with individual birth rate $\lambda_N \geq 0$ and individual death rate $\mu_N \geq 0$. Further, let $\varphi_N$ and $b\in[0,1)$ as in Definition~(def:moderate-selection of the paper) and denote $b_N=-\log_N\varphi_N$. Lastly, let $\beta_N\geq b_N$ for all $N$, assume that $\beta:=\lim_{N\to\infty}\beta_N$ exists and let the initial conditions satisfy $Z^N(0) = \lfloor N^{\beta_N} \rfloor$.
\begin{enumerate}[a)]
    \item \emph{(Slightly supercritical case.)}   
    Assume that $\lambda_N = 1+a \varphi_N$ for some $a>0$ and some sequence $(\varphi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ of positive numbers, and $\mu_N=1$.
   
    In case $\beta=b$ assume additionally that $N^{\beta_N}\gg \varphi_N^{-1}$. Then, for any $T,\delta>0$
    \[
      \lim_{N\to\infty} \mathbb{P} \Big(  \sup_{t \leq T} \Big| \log_N(Z^N(t \varphi_N^{-1} \log N) ) - (\beta+at) \Big| >\delta \Big)
        = 0,
    \]
    i.e.\ $(\log_N(Z^N(t \varphi_N^{-1} \log N) ))_{t\in[0,T]}$ converges uniformly in probability to $(\beta+at)_{t\in[0,T]}$.
    \item \emph{(Slightly subcritical case.)}  Assume that $\mu_N = 1+a \varphi_N$ for some $a>0$ and for some sequence $(\varphi_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ of positive numbers, and $\lambda_N=1$.

    Let $\beta>b$ and $(\varepsilon_N)_{N\in\mathbb{N}}$ be a non-negative sequence tending to 0 such that $N^{-\varepsilon_N}\to0$ as $N\to\infty$.
    Then, for  $T_N := \frac{\beta_N-b_N-\varepsilon_N}{a}$ and for any $\delta>0$,
    \[ \lim_{N\to\infty}  \mathbb{P} \Big(  \sup_{t \leq T_N} \Big| \log_N(Z^N(t \varphi_N^{-1} \log N) ) - (\beta-at) \Big| >\delta \Big)=0. \]
    In particular, for any $s<\frac{\beta-b}{a}$, $(\log_N(Z^N(t\varphi_N^{-1}\log N)))_{t\in [0,s]}$ converges uniformly in probability to $(\beta-at)_{t\in [0,s]}$ as $N\to\infty$.
\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform measure","rho in [-1, 1]"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T09:12:41.903032+00:00","domain":"analysis of Boolean functions","id":"claim_90ceb417f6d0e3f62f0845d6f98fe521b17bdee29d921ddd39c72c3db9d79557","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"On the uniform cube {-1, 1}^n let f be real, f^(S) = E[f chi_S] its Walsh coefficients and W_k = sum over |S| = k of f^(S)^2. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:37:15.537251+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_90d7b93b3c6641a00d4fa2b50bbf7449f540fc5583f936f8365dd3eed505db77","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 13 of arXiv:2607.12384, '2607.12384'] Let $F=(F^{(1)},\ldots,F^{(m)})$ be a random vector such that
	$F^{(i)}=\delta(v^{(i)})$ for $v^{(i)}\in \operatorname{Dom}\delta$,
	$i=1,\ldots,m$. Assume $F^{(i)}\in \mathbb{D}^{1,2}$ for
	$i=1,\ldots,m$. Let $Z$ be an $m$-dimensional centered Gaussian vector
	with covariance matrix $(C_{i,j})_{1\leq i,j\leq m}$. For any $C^2$
	function $h:\mathbb{R}^m\to\mathbb{R}$ with bounded second partial
	derivatives, we have
	\[
	\left|
	\mathbb{E}h(F)-\mathbb{E}h(Z)
	\right|
	\leq
	\frac{1}{2}\|h''\|_{\infty}
	\sqrt{
		\sum_{i,j=1}^{m}
		\mathbb{E}\left[
		\left(
		C_{i,j}
		-
		\left\langle DF^{(i)},v^{(j)}\right\rangle_{\mathcal{H}}
		\right)^2
		\right]
	},
	\]
	where
	\[
	\|h''\|_{\infty}
	=
	\max_{1\leq i,j\leq m}
	\sup_{x\in\mathbb{R}^m}
	\left|
	\frac{\partial^2 h}{\partial x_i\partial x_j}(x)
	\right|.
	\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:54:12.531322+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_90de4829555074d7189951b34dddf149b2ff3ac8daf0e0c025dd817efa168211","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:couprLPP of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Let $I=\llbracket a,b\rrbracket$ for some $-\infty \le a < b \le \infty$. \begin{itemize}
    \item[(1)] $A_i\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\gamma_0+\beta_i)$, $B_i\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\gamma_1+\beta_i)$, $C_i\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\gamma_1+\beta_i)$, $D_i\sim \operatorname{Exp}(\gamma_0+\beta_i)$, where $\gamma_0<\gamma_1$ and $\{\beta_i\}_{i\in I}$ are real parameters, such that $\gamma_0+\beta_i>0$ for each $i\in I$; or

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.361725+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_90e7ebd4c16ea52a508520889df0b0e554f9fe85c000e52e36fa7ac975fea90c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:chaos of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Under the subcriticality condition~(equation eq:subcritical of the paper):
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\roman*), leftmargin=*]
			\item for every $z$, $D_{n}(z)$ is a mean-one martingale, and
			$\mu_{n} \to \mu$ almost surely weakly for a random Borel measure
			$\mu$ on $[0,1]$;
			\item the two-point function is log-correlated: uniformly in $n$
			and in pairs with $|z - z'| \le \tfrac12$,
			\begin{equation}
				\mathbb{E}\big[D_{n}(z)\,D_{n}(z')\big]
				\;\le\; C_{b,\lambda}\,|z - z'|^{-\bar\gamma^{2}},
				
			\end{equation}
			together with a power-law lower bound, uniform in $n$, governed by
			the complementary distortion constant $\ln b + \Lambda$; in the
			weak-tempering regime the lower exponent is
			positive and matches the
			exponent~(equation eq:effective-temperature of the paper) to leading order;
			\item $\sup_{n}\mathbb{E}[\mu_{n}(I)^{2}]
			\le C_{b,\lambda}\,|I|^{2-\bar\gamma^{2}}$ for every
			interval $I$, so the martingale $\mu_{n}(I)$ is uniformly
			integrable,
			$\mathbb{E}\,\mu(I) = |I|$ for every interval and
			$\mathbb{P}(\mu \neq 0) = 1$;
			\item almost surely $\mu$ has full support, no atoms, and vanishes
			on every Borel set of Hausdorff dimension less than
			$1 - \bar\gamma^{2}$;
			\item $S_{\infty}(z) := \mu([0,z])$ is almost surely a strictly
			increasing H\"older homeomorphism of $[0,1]$, with any exponent
			below $(1-\bar\gamma^{2})/2$.
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:09:43.712688+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_90ebaa5cea0e79cd0bb99ad06f39a21c26e825802c41c5f907c460706adc3971","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition p:covario-new of arXiv:2605.28430, 'Limit theory for Lipschitz-localized statistics in random geometric models'] Let $M=\{M(x)\}_{x\in\mathbb{R}^d}$ be a real-valued random field in $\mathbb{R}^d$ having fast $\mathbb{B} $-mixing correlations as in  Definition~(d.omegatmixing-field of the paper)(i.B-mixing-field of the paper)(i.mixing-field-fast of the paper).
Let $\mathcal{P}$ be a simple point process on $\mathbb{R}^d$ having fast mixing correlations as in Definition~(d.omegamixing of the paper)(i.mixing-ground-fast of the paper), bounded reduced  Palm intensity function~(equation bdedreduced of the paper), and independent of the random field $M$.
Consider empirical covariogram $\sigma_{n}^{\gamma}$ of $M$ based on $\mathcal{P}$, as in (equation e.sigma-covariogram-new of the paper), for some value $h$ and tolerance $\delta>0$ .
\begin{enumerate}[wide,label=(\roman*),labelindent=0pt]
\item 
If  $M$ has $p$-moment conditions for all $p>1$ (i.e., ~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) holds with  $\zeta(x,M(x))=M(x)$) then the central limit theorem holds  for
    $(\sigma_{n}^{\gamma}(f))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$, i.e., as $n \to \infty$

\[   ({\rm Var} \, \sigma_{n}^{\gamma}(f) )^{-1/2}\Big( \sigma_{n}^{\gamma}(f) - \mathbb {E}  \, \sigma_{n}^{\gamma}(f) \Big) \stackrel{d}{\Rightarrow} Z
  \]
for $f\in\mathbb{B} (W_1)$, provided the random    ${\rm Var} \, \sigma_{n}^{\gamma}(f) = \Omega(n^{\nu})$ for some $\nu > 0$.

\item 
Further, if the random field $M$ and the point process $\mathcal{P}$ are  stationary (necessarily jointly so, due to their independence), with $\rho$ the intensity  of $\mathcal{P}$,
then the  expectation and variance asymptotics and multivariate central limit
theorem hold {\em mutatis mutandis} for 
$(\sigma_{n}^{\gamma}(f))_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$
as in Proposition~(expvar of the paper) and Theorem (t:multcltmarkedpp of the paper)
under $p=(2+\epsilon)-$ or $p=(4+\epsilon)$--~moment condition for $M$ i.e.,~~(equation e:M-p-moment of the paper) with $\zeta(x,M(x))=M(x)$, respectively.
Precisely, the limiting expectation takes the form $\rho \, \bar\gamma(h)$
of~(equation e:covario-mean of the paper)
and the covariance of the empirical covariogram at two values  
$\sigma_{n}^{\gamma(h)}(f)$ and $\sigma_{n}^{\gamma(h')}(f)$, with $h,h'\in\mathbb{R}^d$, (and for the simplicity, we assume  the same tolerance $\delta>0$ such that $\delta<\min\{|h|, |h'|, |h-h|', |h+h'|\}$) takes the form

$$\lim_{n\to\infty}\frac 1n {\rm Cov}(\sigma_{n}^{\gamma(h)}(f)),\sigma_{n}^{\gamma(h')}(f)))=
\sigma^2(h,h')\int_{W_1}f(x)^2\,\mathrm{d} x\in (-\infty,\infty),$$

 where 

\begin{align}  
&\sigma^2(h,h') :=\\
&\quad \frac{\rho}{16\theta^2_d \delta^{2d}} \int_{B_\delta(\0\pm h)}\int_{B_\delta(\0\pm h')}\mathbb {E} \big[(M(\0) - M(y))^2(M(\0) - M(y'))^2\big]\rho^{(3)}(\0, y,y')\, \mathrm{d} y \, \mathrm{d} y' \nonumber\\
&\quad +
\int_{\mathbb{R}^d}\biggl(\frac1{16\theta^2_d \delta^{2d}}\int_{B_\delta(\0\pm h)\cap B_\delta(z\pm h')}\mathbb {E} \big[(M(\0) - M(y))^2(M(z) - M(y))^2\big] \rho^{(3)}(\0,z,y)\mathrm{d} y \nonumber\\
&\qquad +\frac1{16\theta^2_d \delta^{2d}}\int_{B_\delta(\0\pm h)}\int_{B_\delta(z\pm h')}\mathbb {E} \big[(M(\0) - M(y))^2(M(z) - M(y'))^2\big] \rho^{(4)}(\0,z,y,y') \, \mathrm{d} y \, \mathrm{d} y'  \nonumber\\
&\hspace{10cm} - \rho^2 \, \bar\gamma(h) \, \bar\gamma(h') 
\biggr) \mathrm{d} z \in (-\infty, \infty). \nonumber
\end{align}

\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

Theorem 1.1: an explicit subcritical offspring law with finite third moment and no exponential moment (pi_1 = 1/4, rare atoms at H_r +- sqrt(n_r), n_1 = 256, n_{r+1} = n_r^4) for which (N_1(T_{n_r}) - n_r/4)/sqrt(n_r) converges to the Gaussian mixture (1/2)N(-a, v) + (1/2)N(a, v) with a = 0.99990793915708 and v = 1.7283757730977e-5. Theorem 1.2: a critical offspring law of infinite variance with limit (1/2)N(-1, 3/16) + (1/2)N(1, 3/16). The centering n mu_A and the scale sqrt(n) are the right ones and the limit exists along the subsequence; it is not Gaussian. Mechanism: by the cycle lemma the outdegrees are i.i.d. conditioned on their sum being n - 1, and for a lacunary tail the condensation vertex takes one of two values 2 sqrt(n) apart, each with probability tending to 1/2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.178281+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_90f7773b72d6edac6816e01b8f4ed95f81f45b7bf4e7dd9ced217afdb694d7a3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 83 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $0<\epsilon < 1/2$ and any $x\in\R$,
    \[
    2\epsilon^{1/2}
    +\frac{2(|x|-1)^2}{\epsilon^{1/2}} \ge x^2-1\,.
    \]
\begin{proof}
We can suppose without loss $x\ge0$, and make the change of variables $y=x-1$. Then the desired inequality rearranges to
    \[
    \bigg(\frac{2}{\epsilon^{1/2}}-1\bigg) y^2
    - 2y+2\epsilon^{1/2}\ge 0\,.
    \]
The left-hand side is a quadratic function of $y$ which is strictly positive at $y=0$ and has negative discriminant for the range of $\epsilon$ given in the statement of the lemma. It follows that the left-hand side never reaches zero, and the claim follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Lemma~(lem:realize of the paper) realizes a whitened system in $\mathbb{R}^4$. It is a
rectangle system: its positive circuits are exactly
$\{0,1,2\}$, $\{3,4,5\}$, $\{1,4,6\}$, $\{2,5,7\}$, and no subset of at
most five directions positively spans. Its four circuit-plane energies are
$\frac49,\frac49,\frac13,\frac{167}{450}$, all below $\frac12$; and its
anchor costs satisfy
\[
\min_it_i=\tfrac{32003064046811}{144192302726400}\approx0.2219>\tfrac15,
\quad
\min_{i<j}t_{ij}\approx0.4439>\tfrac13,
\quad
\min_{i<j<k}t_{ijk}\approx1.1097>1 .
\]
Hence both branches of (equation eq:R of the paper) fail, and so do the single- and
triple-anchor variants. The system is nevertheless cheap for the selector:
the single point $0$ gives ratio about $1.2219$, and an explicit five-point
strictly convex objective on the support $\{0,4,5,6,7\}$ gives exact ratio
$\frac{2452861}{2000000}=1.2264\ldots<2$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T17:11:02.376083+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9132d1f74d4493b11d07d7ee4c84fcde7f1e1f15bdbda2b5580bf259a2641948","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition of arXiv:2507.10294, 'Guessing Strategies for Shelf-Shuffling Machines'] We have $S_2\lesssim e^{-2}\cdot (2\pi)^{-1/2}\cdot (n- \sqrt{n})^{1/2}$.
    \begin{proof}
        From the uniform upper bound in Lemma $(upper bound for s2 summand of the paper)$, we have
        \[S_2\leq\frac{(\frac{n}{2}-m-1)\binom{n-2m-4}{\frac{n}{2}+m+1}}{2^{n-2m-4}}\]
        We check that
        \[\frac{\frac{n}{2}+m+1-\frac{n-2m-4}{2}}{\sqrt{(n-2m-4)(\frac{1}{4}})}\]
        \[\frac{4m+6}{\sqrt{(n-2m-4)}}=\frac{2\,O(\sqrt{n})}{O(\sqrt{n})}\to 2\]
        so the conditions of Lemma $(de Moivre-Laplace of the paper)$ are satisfied. This means
        \[\frac{(\frac{n}{2}-m-1)\binom{n-2m-4}{\frac{n}{2}+m+1}}{2^{n-2m-4}}\sim\frac{(\frac{n}{2}-m-1) (e^{-2})}{\sqrt{2\pi(n-2m-4)(\frac{1}{4}})}\]
        \[\sim e^{-2}\cdot (2\pi)^{-1/2}\cdot (n- \sqrt{n})^{1/2}\]
        which establishes asymptotic control over $S_2$.
    \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is given by a differential expression on a domain with boundary or on a punctured space","essential self-adjointness on the chosen core is not verified"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.772085+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Schrodinger operators, boundary value problems","id":"claim_9144d6537a78e5261760c787afb10663c3eb5665068915709c8ea0cb0eddfa3a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: 'the operator −Δ' or 'the Schrodinger operator H = −Δ + V' is not defined by its formula; the domain is part of the data, and essential self-adjointness on a chosen core is a theorem, not a convention. What fails without it: two different self-adjoint operators can agree on a common dense domain, with different spectra, different semigroups and different dynamics; semiboundedness does not select a unique extension either. Counterexamples. (1) −d²/dx² on C_c^∞(ℝ) is essentially self-adjoint with closure the operator on H²(ℝ); but −d²/dx² on C_c^∞(0, ∞) in L²(0, ∞) has deficiency indices (1, 1), and its self-adjoint extensions are the Dirichlet realization {f ∈ H²(0,∞) : f(0) = 0} and the Robin family {f ∈ H²(0,∞) : f'(0) = α f(0)}, α ∈ ℝ. All extend a nonnegative symmetric operator, yet for α < 0 the Robin extension has the eigenvalue −α² with eigenfunction e^{αx}: the lower bound 0 valid on C_c^∞(0,∞) is not inherited by every self-adjoint extension. The Friedrichs extension (here the Dirichlet realization) is the one that always inherits the lower bound; the Robin extensions with α ≥ 0 happen to stay nonnegative as well, so the lower bound alone singles out nothing. (2) −d²/dx² on C_c^∞(0, 1) has deficiency indices (2, 2); the Dirichlet, Neumann and periodic realizations are distinct self-adjoint extensions with eigenvalues {(kπ)² : k ≥ 1}, {(kπ)² : k ≥ 0} and {(2πk)² : k ∈ ℤ} respectively. (3) −Δ on C_c^∞(ℝⁿ ∖ {0}) is essentially self-adjoint if and only if n ≥ 4; for n ≤ 3 removing a single point changes the operator, and the extensions in n = 3 are the point-interaction ('delta potential') Hamiltonians. Audit rule: a claim 'H is self-adjoint' must name the domain or the core, and a claim that a computation on smooth compactly supported functions determines the operator must cite an essential self-adjointness theorem (Kato-Rellich, Faris-Lavine, Nelson's analytic vectors, or a limit-point analysis).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:01:25.650277+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_914b75bf45a2e9b1646758f8529f22191011958c84da050d2d4feef4142adaae","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:pruning_times of arXiv:2605.16086, 'Loop pruning and downward deviations for maximum local time of discrete-time simple random'] Let \(I=[I^-,I^+]\subset\mathbb{Z}\) be an integer interval and let \(j\in(I^-,I^+]\).
If the step \((S_{j-1},S_j)\) is pruned in \(\mathsf{Prune}(S(I),E)\), we define its forward and backward pruning times by
\begin{align*}
\zeta^+(j)=\zeta^+(j,I)
&:=\inf\Big\{i\in [j,I^+]:\ (S_{j-1},S_j)\text{ is pruned in }\mathsf{Prune}(S[I^-,i],E)\Big\},\\
\zeta^-(j)=\zeta^-(j,I)
&:=\sup\Big\{i\in (I^-,j]:\ (S_{i-1},S_i)\text{ is retained in }\mathsf{Prune}\big(S[I^-,\zeta^+(j,I)],E\big)\Big\},
\end{align*}
where \(\sup\emptyset:=I^-\).

If \((S_{j-1},S_j)\) is not pruned in \(\mathsf{Prune}(S(I),E)\), we set \(\zeta^+(j):=+\infty\) and \(\zeta^-(j):=-\infty\).
\smallskip
\noindent We will also use the shorthand
\[
\zeta(j)=\zeta(j,I):=\bigl[\zeta^-(j),\,\zeta^+(j)\bigr]
\]
for the associated pruning interval.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.895397+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9151569c7bfe21f7dd9d6f2063a19c588248543a890a45ab0c42594294897ce1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:scalimRW of arXiv:2607.09946, 'Statistics on Yau's conjecture: Variance asymptotics'] Let $M$ be either a compact Riemannian manifold of dimension $n$, or $M=\mathbb{R}^n$. Let $\dist \cdot \cdot$ denote the Riemannian distance function on $M\times M$.
Let $I_\ell\subset [0,+\infty)$ be an interval such that $\ell=\max I_\ell\in \mathbb{R}$ and let $\alpha\in [0,1]$.
We will refer to the following scaling bound for $\phi^M_{I_\ell}$ as the \emph{$\mathcal{C}^k$ Scaling Bound of Random Waves of type $\alpha$ in range $[\rho_\ell',\rho_\ell]$}:
\begin{gather}
E_{I_\ell}^M(x,y)=\ell^{n-1}{|I_\ell|} \left( 
{E^n_{\mathsf U(\alpha,1)}}\left( \ell\cdot \dist x y \right)
+
R_{\alpha,I_\ell}^{M}(x,y)
\right), \quad \text{and define}
\\
\sup_{ \rho_\ell'\le \mathrm{dist}(x,y)\le \rho_\ell}\sup_{|a|,|b|\le k} \frac{\| \nabla^a \nabla^b R_{\alpha,I_\ell}^{M}(x,y)\|}{\ell^{|a|+|b|}}\sqrt{n}^{|a|+|b|}=: \delta_{I_\ell}^{M}(\alpha,\mathcal{C}^k,[\rho_\ell',\rho_\ell])
    \end{gather} 
where $0\le\rho_\ell'\le \rho_\ell$ and $k\in \mathbb{N}$. We call the number $\delta_{I_\ell}^{M}(\alpha,\mathcal{C}^k,[\rho_\ell',\rho_\ell])$ the 
\emph{$\mathcal{C}^k$ Scaling error of Random Waves of type $\alpha$ in range $[\rho_\ell',\rho_\ell]$}. 

\textbf{Notation:} in what follows, to keep a lighter notation, we shall write $\delta_{I_\ell}^M \equiv \delta_{I_\ell}^{M}(\alpha,\mathcal{C}^k,[\rho_\ell',\rho_\ell])$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:57:28.219570+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91738d2faee9a1d6025b40b8176e9ad323a9fc0a591b0f25a48036dfc96a2875","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 5 (discrete R\'enyi and Tsallis entropies) of arXiv:2607.17576, 'How much randomness is needed to symmetrize a random variable?'] Let $X$ be a discrete random variable with the probability mass function $\{f(k)\}_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}$. For $\alpha\in (0, 1)\cup (1, \infty)$, the R\'enyi entropy $H_\alpha(X)$ of order $\alpha$ is defined by
$$
H_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\log \sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}f(k)^\alpha
$$
and the Tsallis entropy $T_\alpha(X)$ of order $\alpha$ is defined by
$$
T_\alpha(X) = \frac{1}{1-\alpha}\left(\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}f(k)^\alpha-1\right).
$$
Taking the limit $\alpha\to 1$, both entropies are reduced to Shannon entropy 
$$
H(X)=-\sum_{k\in\mathbb{Z}}f(k)\log f(k).
$$","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.168080+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_917501103e3120230731cde7a8230b436257d03fc77d1053d4287fe8c93416f9","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 61 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $q_0 \in [0,1)$, we have $\sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0) \subseteq \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0)$. 

\begin{proof}
    This is a consequence of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}.
    Consider any $\mu \in \cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)$. Then, there exists
    \[
        (q_*,b,\sigma,w,p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising) \in \Adm^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)
    \]
    such that $\mu(q_*,b,\sigma,p,\zeta) = \mu$.
    Let $\tilde p$ denote the restriction of $p$ to $[q_*,1] \subseteq [q_0,1]$.
    We will argue that $(b,\sigma,w,\tilde p,\zeta,\zeta^\Ising)$ satisfies the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered} with $q_*$ in place of $q_0$.
    Indeed, conditions~\ref{it:1.1}, \ref{it:2.1}, \ref{it:3.1}, \ref{it:4.2}, \ref{it:5.1}, and \ref{it:6.1} exactly correspond to assumptions~(\ref{i:IAMP-main-coefs}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-diffusivity}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-p}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-budget}), (\ref{i:IAMP-main-endpt}), and (\ref{i:IAMP-main-init}) of Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}, while condition~\ref{it:1.1} also provides the additional assumption in Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered} that $w(t,\cdot)$ is even and $\zeta^\Ising$ is symmetric. By Theorem~\ref{thm:IAMP-main}\ref{i:IAMP-main-centered}, there exists $\iota = \iota(\epsilon)$ with $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \iota(\epsilon) = 0$ such that for all (sufficiently large) $N$, there exists a $C(L,\epsilon)$-Lipschitz algorithm $\cA_N$ with
    \[
        \max\Big(
            \bbW_2(\mu(\cA_N), \mu),
            \bbW_2(\mu^{\Ising}(\cA_N), \cP(\{\pm 1\}))
        \Big) \le \iota
    \]
and
    $\bbE[\cA_N(\bG,\bg^\aux)] = \bzero$.
    This implies $\chi_{\cA_N}(0) = 0$.
    Recalling the definition \eqref{e:cM.Lip.q0}, we have $\mu \in \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))$.
    We have thus shown
    \[
        \cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon) \subseteq \cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\,.
    \]
    Thus, for $\cB_\epsilon$ as defined in \eqref{e:W2.ball.notation},
    \[
        \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \subseteq \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;C(L,\epsilon),\iota(\epsilon))\Big)\,.
    \]
    Taking a union over $L>0$ shows
    \[
        \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \subseteq \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\iota(\epsilon))\Big)
        \subseteq \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\tilde\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\tilde\epsilon)\Big)\,,
    \]
    where $\tilde\epsilon = \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon) = \max(\epsilon,\iota(\epsilon))$.
    Since $\lim_{\epsilon\rightarrow 0} \tilde\epsilon(\epsilon) = 0$, taking an intersection over $\epsilon$ yields
    \begin{align*}
        \sM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0)
        &\stackrel{\eqref{e:measure.classes.simplification.without.L0}}{=}
        \adjustlimits
        \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\IAMP}(\alpha,q_0;L,\epsilon)\Big) \\
        &\,\,\subseteq
        \adjustlimits \bigcap_{\epsilon>0} \bigcup_{L>0} \cB_{\epsilon}\Big(\cM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0;L,\epsilon)\Big)
        \stackrel{\eqref{e:sM.Lip.q0}}{=} \sM^{\Lip}(\alpha,0)\,. \qedhere
    \end{align*}
  \end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:49:17.498171+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91763d7e7ddba1fc113bf6f0a989656647029ef37637c448f76b876ca807ca87","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 4 of arXiv:2605.29469, 'Multiscale Asymptotic Analysis of Kernel-Smoothed Solutions to Fractional Riesz-Bessel Equ'] Assume that the kernel function $g(\cdot,\cdot)$ has a finite Sobolev norm of order~$-\alpha$ with respect to the first variable, and assume that this norm is H\"older continuous of order $\theta \in (0,1]$ with respect to the second variable, that is,

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:04:55.822399+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9191a593c842b7606d58fabc334655d0bfab4a260f6eb013c885dbf3edf271be","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary c:markov-holonomy-elementary of arXiv:2607.24640, 'The Yang-Mills measure on surfaces via Morse theory'] Let $\gamma,\tilde{\gamma}$ be two elementary curves which are both of type $\operatorname{I}$ or $\operatorname{II}_\pm$ such that $\tilde{\gamma}\preccurlyeq\gamma$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:36:44.556390+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9192dca46735c29d22cbbec600fc24a5d8af31b812f4b54ee0626c24f8ebaf35","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 29 (Tightness) of arXiv:2604.02312, 'A weak transport approach to the Schrödinger--Bass bridge'] Let $\beta>0$ and $\mu, \nu \in \cP_2(\Rd)$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:51:11.953880+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91bdcd997adca9bb438363c57b1d7d97f25528afc3a7d2892cbd366118e120e4","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 11 (Three-point representation of four centered moments) of arXiv:2608.07820, 'Linear Spectral Statistics for Entrywise-Transformed Spiked Wigner Matrices under Shifted '] Let \(X\) be a real random variable satisfying
\begin{equation}
 \E X=0,
 \qquad
 \E X^2=v>0,
 \qquad
 \E X^4<\infty.
\end{equation}
Put
\begin{equation}
 a:=\frac{\E X^3}{v^{3/2}},
 \qquad
 b:=\frac{\E X^4}{v^2},
 \qquad
 c:=b-a^2.
\end{equation}
Then \(c\ge1\).  Define
\begin{equation}
 \alpha:=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+4c}-a}{2},
 \qquad
 \beta:=\frac{\sqrt{a^2+4c}+a}{2},
\end{equation}
and
\begin{equation}
 p_-:=\frac{1}{\alpha(\alpha+\beta)},
 \qquad
 p_+:=\frac{1}{\beta(\alpha+\beta)},
 \qquad
 p_0:=1-\frac1c.
\end{equation}
These numbers are nonnegative and sum to one.  If \(Q\) has the three-point
law
\begin{equation}
 \mathbb P(Q=-\alpha)=p_-,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P(Q=0)=p_0,
 \qquad
 \mathbb P(Q=\beta)=p_+,
\end{equation}
then \(\widehat X:=\sqrt v\,Q\) satisfies
\begin{equation}
 \E\widehat X^q=\E X^q,
 \qquad q=1,2,3,4.
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
 |\widehat X|
 \le2\sqrt{\frac{\E X^4}{v}}.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:04:39.212219+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91e1404fa676dacdf7afde8eadcf87cffc2f007ea5413a3135ec9cae901ac54c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 11 (Subgaussian Kahane--Khintchine inequality) of arXiv:2608.13687, 'Multiplicative chaos from random multiplicative functions'] Let $H$ be a real or complex Hilbert space and fix $(f_i)_{i\in\N}\subset H$.
If $H$ is a real Hilbert space, let $(A_i)_{i\in\N}$ satisfy Case \caseR, and if $H$ is a complex Hilbert space, let $(A_i)_{i\in\N}$ satisfy \caseS.
For any $m\in\N$, 
define  
\[
S_m\coloneqq\sum_{k=1}^m A_k f_k \qquad \text{and} \qquad \sigma_m^2\coloneqq\E\|S_m\|_H^2 =  \sum_{k=1}^m \|f_k\|_H^2 \,.
\]
There exist $c,C>0$ such that for all $m \in \N$ such that  $\sigma_m >0$,
and for all $u\geq 0$,
\begin{align}
        \P(\|S_m\|_H>u)
        \le
        Ce^{-cu^2/\sigma_m^2}\,.
\end{align}
\begin{proof}
A version of the Kahane--Khintchine inequality stated explicitly for Rademacher, Steinhaus, and Gaussian coefficients can be found in \cite[Proposition~6.2.7]{kahane-khintchine-source}\footnote{They call Steinhaus random variables ``complex Rademacher'' random variables.}, which states the bound $\E e^{\delta\|S_m\|_H^2} \leq (1- 2e \delta \E\|S_m\|_H^2)^{-1}$ for all $\delta \in (0, (2e\sigma_m^2)^{-1})$. Equation~\eqref{eq:subgaussian-kahane-khintchine-tail} now follows from taking $\delta = 1/4e\sigma_m^2$ and the Markov inequality.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:40:26.974631+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91ee8b8e2026ec4c6d69cb7db395331740b99982a3d8db781cb4a648f2a8afa4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Zk of arXiv:2604.10602, 'Fractional Navier-Stokes Equations with Caputo Derivative Driven by Hermite Noise'] Assume $0<\alpha<1$, $H\in(1/2,1)$, $0\le\nu<1$, and $\alpha(1-\nu)+2H>2$. Then for any $p\ge2$ and $t\in[0,T]$,
\[
\|Z_k(t)\|_{L^p(\Omega;\dot{H}^\nu)} \le C_{p,k} \, t^{\frac{\alpha(1-\nu)+2H-2}{2}},
\]
with $C_{p,k}=(p-1)^{k/2}C_0$. Moreover, for $0\le t_1<t_2\le T$,
\[
\|Z_k(t_2)-Z_k(t_1)\|_{L^p(\Omega;\dot{H}^\nu)} \le C_{p,k} (t_2-t_1)^{\gamma},
\]
where $\gamma = \min\bigl\{\frac{2-(2-\nu)\alpha}{2},\ \frac{\alpha(1-\nu)+2H-2}{2}\bigr\}$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T18:32:23.615892+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_91efc8bf944186c7b00b2f551ba2f42bac3d353a901586a29dcce476b21d4ca0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:neighbourhood of arXiv:2603.16824, 'Age-dependent random connection models with arc reciprocity: clustering and connectivity'] Let \(\beta>0\), \(\gamma\in(0,1)\), \(\delta>1\), and \(\Gamma\geq 0\). Almost surely, the root \(\0\) in \(\mathscr{D}_o\) has finite degree. More precisely, for \(k\in\mathbb{N}_0\), we have 
    \begin{enumerate}[(i)]
        \item 
    	   for the indegree
    	   \begin{equation*}
    		  \begin{aligned}
    		      & \mathbb{P}_o\big(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{in}}=k\big)\asymp k^{-1-\nicefrac{1}{\gamma}}. 
    		  \end{aligned}	
    		\end{equation*}
    	\item 
            For the outdegree, we have, 
            \begin{enumerate}[(a)]
            	\item
            		if \(\Gamma>\gamma\), then \(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{out}}\) is Poisson distributed with parameter \(\lambda\asymp \tfrac{\omega_d \delta \beta}{\delta-1}(\tfrac{1}{(\Gamma-\gamma)}+\tfrac{1}{\gamma})\), where \(\omega_d\) denotes the volume of the \(d\)-dimensional unit ball.
            	\item 
            		If \(\Gamma=\gamma\), then
            			\[
            		        \mathbb{P}_o\big(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{out}}=k\big) \asymp \int_0^1 \frac{u \log(1/u)^k}{k!} \,\mathrm{d} u = 2^{-(k+1)}.
            			\]
            	\item 
            		If \(\Gamma<\gamma\), then 
            		\[
                		\begin{aligned}
               	    			& \mathbb{P}_o\big(\sharp\mathscr{N}^{\text{out}}=k\big)\asymp k^{-1-\nicefrac{1}{(\gamma-\Gamma)}}.
               	 		\end{aligned}
            		\]
            \end{enumerate} 		
    \end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
