{"assumptions":["T is measure-preserving on a probability space","A is measurable","integrability of log^+ ||A|| is the standing hypothesis for the multiplicative ergodic theorem"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438394+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, Lyapunov exponents","id":"claim_920354a52c00e42c3e25c80f9069506badd8e398097645124d1386fa4d04f5aa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $(X, \\mathcal{B}, \\mu, T)$ be a probability-preserving system and $A: X \\to M_d(\\mathbb{R})$ a measurable matrix-valued function. The linear cocycle generated by $A$ over $T$ is $A^n(x) = A(T^{n-1}x) \\cdots A(Tx)\\,A(x)$ for $n \\ge 1$, $A^0 = I$; it satisfies the cocycle identity $A^{n+m}(x) = A^m(T^n x) A^n(x)$. (If $T$ is invertible and $A(x) \\in GL_d$, one also sets $A^{-n}(x) = A^n(T^{-n}x)^{-1}$.) The cocycle is (forward) integrable if $\\log^+ \\|A\\| \\in L^1(\\mu)$, where $\\log^+ t = \\max(\\log t, 0)$ and $\\|\\cdot\\|$ is any matrix norm; it is two-sidedly integrable if also $A(x)$ is invertible a.e. and $\\log^+\\|A^{-1}\\| \\in L^1$. For $v \\in \\mathbb{R}^d \\setminus \\{0\\}$ the (forward) Lyapunov exponent of $v$ at $x$ is $\\lambda(x, v) = \\lim_{n\\to\\infty} \\frac1n \\log \\|A^n(x) v\\|$ when the limit exists (in $[-\\infty, \\infty)$); more generally $\\bar\\lambda(x, v) = \\limsup$. The function $v \\mapsto \\bar\\lambda(x, v)$ takes finitely many values and satisfies $\\bar\\lambda(x, u + v) \\le \\max(\\bar\\lambda(x,u), \\bar\\lambda(x,v))$, so for each $x$ the sets $\\{v : \\bar\\lambda(x, v) \\le c\\} \\cup \\{0\\}$ are linear subspaces and form a filtration of $\\mathbb{R}^d$. The prototype is the derivative cocycle $A(x) = Df_x$ of a smooth map $f$ on a manifold (trivialised bundle), whose exponents measure exponential rates of divergence of nearby orbits. Warning: $\\|A^n(x)\\|^{1/n}$ and $|\\text{eigenvalues of } A^n(x)|^{1/n}$ are different things; Lyapunov exponents are the growth rates of SINGULAR values of $A^n(x)$, not eigenvalues, and for non-commuting products the two can differ.","status":"unverified"}

 \frac1N\sum_{i=1}^N\delta_{(\sigma_i,\tau_i)}.

{"assumptions":["the axiom of choice (used in step 3 to select orbit representatives; the result is not a theorem of ZF alone)","n >= 3 for the paradox; rigid motions of R^n (isometries); 'pieces' are arbitrary sets, necessarily non-measurable"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.480173+00:00","domain":"measure theory and geometry","id":"claim_926a5872eb18b627a0e7fd10743a1293421bfa6309bdf99c41e9eb5a25b9a1d1","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Assuming the axiom of choice, the closed unit ball B in R^3 can be partitioned into finitely many pieces which can be reassembled by rigid motions (rotations and translations) into two disjoint copies of B; five pieces suffice (Robinson), and four do not. More generally (the strong form) any two bounded subsets of R^n, n >= 3, with nonempty interior are equidecomposable: one can be cut into finitely many pieces and moved by isometries onto the other. The pieces are necessarily non-measurable, so no contradiction with Lebesgue measure arises - the theorem shows that no finitely additive, isometry-invariant measure defined on ALL subsets of R^3 and normalising the ball can exist. In dimensions 1 and 2 the paradox fails: Banach showed that Lebesgue measure on R and R^2 extends to a finitely additive isometry-invariant measure on all subsets, because the isometry groups of R and R^2 are amenable (solvable), while SO(3) contains a free group on two generators, which is the source of the paradox (Hausdorff, 1914). Tarski's theorem (1929) makes this exact: a group action admits a paradoxical decomposition if and only if it carries no finitely additive invariant probability measure, i.e. it is non-amenable. With choice the result is a theorem; in ZF plus the axiom of determinacy, or in Solovay's model, every set of reals is measurable and the decomposition does not exist.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.360189+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92a1d9662fc1cdf4d1b67078367c48365ebd49b68fc0e169dce8c66a0fd60926","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 252 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] If $\bX:\R^{N'}\to\R^N$ is $L$-Lipschitz, $\bg$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^{N'}$, and $\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] = N$, then for any $\delta > 0$, there exists $c(\delta) > 0$ such that 
    \[
    \P\bigg(
    \bigg|\frac{\|\bX(\bg)\|^2}{N} - 1\bigg|
    \ge \delta\bigg)
    \le e^{-c(\delta)N}\,.\]

\begin{proof}
    Since $\bg \mapsto \|\bX(\bg)\|$ is $L$-Lipschitz, it follows from Lemma~\ref{l:lip.subgaus} that $\|\bX(\bg)\|-\E\|\bX(\bg)\|$ is subgaussian with variance proxy $2L^2$, and satisfies the concentration bound \eqref{e:lip.subgaus}:
    \[
    \P\bigg( \Big|
    \|\bX(\bg)\| - \E\|\bX(\bg)\|\Big| \ge t
    \bigg) \le 2\exp\bigg\{-\frac{t^2}{2L^2}\bigg\}\,.
    \]
It follows that $\|\bX(\bg)\|$ has variance $O(L^2)$, which implies
    \[
     \frac{O(L^2)}{N}
     \ge
    \frac{\E[\|\bX(\bg)\|^2] - ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}
    =1- \frac{ ( \E\|\bX(\bg)\|)^2}{N}\,.
    \]
Combining the last two displays gives the claim.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Definition of the specific source model; beta>1,s>0,uniform power-law comparison constants.","Fresh independent Gaussian features and independent Gaussian constant-order label noise; averaged minibatch gradients.","Zero initial iterate and zero initial momentum for the scaling-law protocol."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T15:47:26.804438+00:00","domain":"Kernel regression and stochastic optimization","id":"claim_92bc45c903189bf192adf6404c4679485e5e9b8150fad2524367d7a2833ca314","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"The model used by Wang-Huang-Li-Wu in arXiv:2609.02728 is Gaussian-feature, online least-squares regression. In the covariance eigenbasis, a feature vector phi has centered Gaussian law N(0,H) with H=diag(lambda_1,lambda_2,...) positive trace class, lambda_1>=lambda_2>=...>0. A label is y=<phi,theta_star>+epsilon with epsilon~N(0,sigma^2) independent of phi. The target has finite prediction energy sum_j lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2<infinity; the pairing can equivalently be read as its mean-square-convergent Gaussian series. The population risk is R(theta)=E(<phi,theta>-y)^2/2, and the excess risk is Ecal(theta)=sum_j lambda_j*|theta_j-theta_star_j|^2/2=R(theta)-sigma^2/2. Their source/capacity assumptions are beta>1,s>0, lambda_j asymp j^(-beta) and lambda_j*|theta_star_j|^2 asymp j^(-(1+s*beta)), where asymp means upper and lower bounds by fixed positive constants, uniform in j. The label-noise standard deviation sigma is bounded above and away from zero by fixed constants (the constant-order noisy setting). At iteration k a fresh IID batch of B examples, independent of all past batches, gives the AVERAGED gradient g(theta;batch)=B^(-1)*sum_i phi_(k,i)*(<phi_(k,i),theta>-y_(k,i)). For a constant eta>0 and constant rho in[0,1), SGD uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch); Polyak uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k-eta*g(theta_k;batch)+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)); Nesterov first sets theta_k_la=theta_k+rho*(theta_k-theta_(k-1)) and uses theta_(k+1)=theta_k_la-eta*g(theta_k_la;batch). The source scaling-law analysis takes theta_0=theta_-1=0. For a one-pass data budget D, take T=D/B updates (or integer rounding at the exponent level), and B=D^(b+o(1)) with fixed b in[0,1). Hyperparameters can depend on D but are constant within each run. This protocol concerns final expected excess risk; it is not a finite-data repeated-epoch protocol, nor a theorem giving explicit constants in the critical-batch trade-off.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T14:09:34.494853+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92d321365a35e1fdb09d2d7b3b0cda3acab6c8d20c455e3b4fa61147909dfbf1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn rational SLE0 of arXiv:2505.14762, 'Multiple radial SLE($\kappa$) and quantum Calogero-Sutherland system'] In the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$, let $e^{i\theta} \in \partial \mathbb{D}$ be the growth point, and let $u_1, u_2, \dots, u_m \in \overline{\mathbb{D}}$ be marked points. A symmetric double divisor $(\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+, \boldsymbol{\sigma}^-)$ assigns a charge distribution on $e^{i\theta}$ and $\{u_1, \dots, u_k\}$, where
\[
\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+ = a \cdot e^{i\theta} + \sum_{j=1}^{k} \sigma_j \cdot u_j,
\quad \text{and} \quad
\boldsymbol{\sigma}^- = \overline{\boldsymbol{\sigma}^+}|_{\mathbb{D}},
\]
and the total charge satisfies the neutrality condition $\int\boldsymbol{\sigma}=-2$.

We define the rational $\mathrm{SLE}_0[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ Loewner chain as a normalized conformal map $g_t(z)$ with initial conditions $g_0(z) = z$ and $g_t'(0) = e^{-t}$. The evolution of $g_t$ is governed by the Loewner differential equation:
\[
\partial_t g_t(z) = g_t(z) \frac{e^{i\theta(t)} + g_t(z)}{e^{i\theta(t)} - g_t(z)}, \quad g_0(z) = z.
\]

In the angular coordinate, let $h_t(z)$ be the covering map of $g_t(z)$ defined by $e^{i h_t(z)} = g_t(e^{i z})$. Then $h_t(z)$ evolves according to
\[
\partial_t h_t(z) = \cot\left( \frac{h_t(z) - \theta(t)}{2} \right), \quad h_0(z) = z.
\]

The driving function $\theta(t)$ evolves according to
\[
d\theta(t) = \frac{\partial \log \mathcal{Z}(\boldsymbol{\theta})}{\partial \theta} \, dt.
\]

where the Coulomb gas partition function is
\begin{equation} 
\mathcal{Z}(\boldsymbol{\theta}) = \prod_{j < k} \sin\left( \frac{\theta_j - \theta_k}{2} \right)^{\sigma_j \sigma_k} 
\cdot \prod_j e^{\frac{i}{2} \sigma_j (\sigma_0 - \sigma_\infty)\theta_j}.
\end{equation}

The flow $g_t$ is well-defined up to the first time $\tau$ at which $w(t) = g_t(w)$ for some $w$ in the support of $\boldsymbol{\sigma}$. For each $z \in \overline{\mathbb{D}}$, the process $t \mapsto g_t(z)$ is well-defined up to $\tau_z \wedge \tau$, where $\tau_z$ is the first time such that $g_t(z) = e^{i\theta(t)}$. Denote
\[
K_t = \left\{ z \in \overline{\mathbb{D}} : \tau_z \leq t \right\}
\]
as the hull associated with the Loewner chain.

Furthermore, the rational $\mathrm{SLE}_0$ Loewner chain is invariant under Möbius transformations in $\mathrm{Aut}(\mathbb{D})$ (up to a time reparameterization), due to the conformal invariance of the Coulomb gas correlation. Consequently, rational $\mathrm{SLE}_0[\boldsymbol{\sigma}]$ in any simply connected domain $\Omega$ is defined by pulling back via a conformal map $\phi: \Omega \rightarrow \mathbb{D}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:52.741850+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92d6dc6b75a73de5b6da57156d4090247c485e21e10393b54e7c0079fd8270ae","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 40 of arXiv:2506.10494, 'Geometric Jensen-Shannon Divergence Between Gaussian Measures On Hilbert Space'] [\cite{Minh:2022KullbackGaussian}, Theorem 11]
	
	Let $0 \leq \alpha \leq 1$.
	Let $A\in \Sym(\Hcal) \cap \HS(\Hcal)$, $I+A > 0$. Then
	\begin{align}
		0 &\leq \log\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}] 
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\leq \alpha(1-\alpha)||(I+A)^{-1}||\;||A||^2_{\HS}.
	\end{align}
	Let $B\in \Sym(\Hcal) \cap \HS(\Hcal)$, $I+B > 0$. Then
	\begin{align}
		&\left|\log\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}] \right.
		\nonumber
		\\
		&\left. -\log\det[(1-\alpha)(I+B)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+B)^{1-\alpha}]]\right| 
		\\
		&\leq \alpha (1-\alpha)||(I+A)^{-1}||\;||(I+B)^{-1}||
		\nonumber
		\\
		& \quad \times [||A||_{\HS} + ||B||_{\HS} + ||A||_{\HS}||B||_{\HS}]||A-B||_{\HS}.
	\end{align}
	Consequently, let $\{A_k\}_{k\in \Nbb} \in \Sym(\Hcal) \cap \HS(\Hcal)$, $I+A_k > 0$ $\forall k \in \Nbb$, be such that
	$\lim_{k \approach \infty}||A_k - A||_{\HS} = 0$. Then
	\begin{align}
		&\lim_{k \approach \infty}\log\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A_k)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A_k)^{1-\alpha}]
		\nonumber
		\\
		&=
		\log\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}].
	\end{align}
	Let $\beta \in \R$ be fixed but arbitrary. Then
	\begin{align}
		&\lim_{k \approach \infty}\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A_k)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A_k)^{1-\alpha}]^{\beta}
		\nonumber
		\\
		&=
		\det[(1-\alpha)(I+A)^{-\alpha} + \alpha (I+A)^{1-\alpha}]^{\beta}.
	\end{align} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:33:11.960027+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92e48b9ac631443a82725ec1a098daec22d5d19518ce2027cad21957ceb2ec69","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:romiksniady-main of arXiv:2607.24018, 'Jeu de taquin forests \\ and the inverse infinite RSK correspondence'] \begin{enumerate}

\item The Plancherel measure $P$ is the push-forward of the
infinite-dimensional Lebesgue measure $\Lambda$ on
$[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ under the map $\RSK(\cdot)$.

\item The jeu de taquin map $J$ is a measure-preserving
transformation on the Plancherel measure space $(\Omega,
\mathcal{F}, P)$.

\item The jeu de taquin map is intertwined with the shift map $S$
on $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$ (defined by $S(z_1,z_2,\ldots)=(z_2,z_3,\ldots)$)
by the map $\RSK(\cdot)$, in the sense that the
relation
\[
J \circ \RSK = \RSK\circ S
\]
holds $\Lambda$-almost surely on $[0,1]^\mathbb{N}$. 

\item The RSK map $\RSK(\cdot)$ is an isomorphism between
the two measure-preserving dynamical systems $([0,1]^\mathbb{N},
\mathcal{B}, \Lambda, S)$ and $(\Omega, \mathcal{F}, P, J)$.

\item The inverse map $\RSK^{-1}(\cdot)$ is given explicitly by
\begin{equation} 
\RSK^{-1}(T) = ( \zeta(T), \zeta\circ J(T), \zeta \circ J^2(T), \ldots)
\quad \textrm{for $P$-almost every }T\in \Omega,
\end{equation}
where
\begin{equation}

\zeta(T) =
1 - F\left(\lim_{n\to\infty} \frac{x_n-y_n}{\sqrt{T_{x_n,y_n}}} \right),
\end{equation}
where $((x_n,y_n))_{n=0}^\infty$ denotes the jeu de taquin
path associated with $T$ as in (equation eq:jdt-path of the paper) and
$F(u)$ is given by
\begin{equation}

F(u) = \frac{1}{2\pi} \int_{-2}^u \sqrt{4-s^2} \, ds
\qquad (-2 \le u \le 2).
\end{equation}
(This statement includes the assertion that the limit in
(equation eq:inverse-rsk-firstcoord of the paper) exists and takes a value in $[-2,2]$
$P$-almost surely.)

\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

every $t\in[t_0,t_1]$. An event is \emph{increasing} if it is preserved by adding particles, in
the sense of (prop:mono of the paper)(ii). For an increasing event $E$ restricted to $X$ and $[0,t]$, we
write $\nu_E(\zeta,X,X',t)$ for the probability that $E$ holds when the particles in $X$ at time

{"assumptions":["Finite E, orthogonal subspaces H_1, H_2","Evidence is computational on |E| <= 8 only"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T07:36:18.299044+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_92f80e4dcf39be1b9857d932b15ffa66cb7d95ccb79f0a2e9b16609e2935e314","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"PRIVATE NUMERICAL EVIDENCE, not a proof. Lyons (ICM 2014, Question 2.8) asks whether for H = H_1 (+) H_2 orthogonal in l^2(E) there is a coupling of the determinantal projection measures P_{H_1}, P_{H_2} whose union has law P_H. Since the cardinalities are dim H_1, dim H_2 and dim H almost surely, the union must be disjoint, and the question is the nonemptiness of the transportation polytope with the three marginals. Exact LP (HiGHS, minimum total violation) on 1360 random pairs of orthogonal subspaces with |E| in {3,...,6} over all dimension splits, on generic instances with |E| = 7 and 8, on Fourier-mode subspaces of cycles of length 5..8, and on star-space splits in the edge space of K_4 found a feasible coupling with zero violation every time (intake raw/C_lyons_q28_lp_check.json and _structured.json). A structural observation: the naive rule 'sample X_1 from P_{H_1} conditioned on X_1 subset C, set X_2 = C minus X_1' does NOT reproduce the P_{H_2} marginal in general (checked on |E| = 4), so the coupling, when it exists, is not the conditional splitting. Open: a general construction.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.884753+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9369e826c029893f2b7aa18022a1f63e3ba97cc35b75364890d62fd0adab6c4c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition boundarydef of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let $(T, d, \rho)$ be a rooted complete $\mathbb{R}$-tree. 
 
 \smallskip
 
\begin{compactenum}
\item[$(a)$] A \emph{ray with endpoint $\rho$} is a subset $\mathbf r\! \subseteq\! T$ such that $\mathbf r\! = \!  c(\mathbb{R}_+)$ where 
$c\colon\mathbb{R}_+ \! \to \! T$ is a geodesic arc of infinite length necessarily, such that $c(0)\! = \!  \rho$. 

 \smallskip
 

\item[$(b)$] The \emph{boundary} of $(T,d , \rho)$ is the set  
$\partial T\! = \!  \big\{ \mathbf r \, ; \textrm{$\mathbf r$ is a ray whose endpoint is $\rho$} \big\}$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(c)$] $(T, d, \rho)$ is said to be \emph{boundaryless} if $\partial T\! = \!  \emptyset$. 

\smallskip

\end{compactenum}
{\noindent}
Let $\sigma \! \in \!  T$ and let $\mathbf r_1, \mathbf r_2\! \in \!  \partial T$. Let 
$c\colon [0, d(\rho, \sigma) ] \! \to \! T$, $c_i\colon \mathbb{R}_+ \!\! \to \! T$, $i\! \in \!  \{ 1, 2\}$, be geodesics such that $ c(0)\! = \!  \rho$, 
$c([0, d(\rho, \sigma)])\! = \!  [\![ \rho, \sigma ]\!]$ and $c_i(\mathbb{R}_+)\! = \!  \mathbf r_i$, $i\! \in \!  \{ 1,2\}$. We next introduce the following. 
 
\medskip
 
\begin{compactenum}
\item[$(d)$] For all $i\! \in \!  \{ 1, 2\}$, we set $d(\rho, \mathbf r_i)\! :=\!  \infty$ and $\underline{\mathbf r}_i(s)\! :=\!  c_i(s)$, for all $s\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(e)$] For all $s\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+$ we set $\underline{\sigma} (s) \! :=\! c(s\wedge d(\rho, \sigma))$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(f)$] We set $\mathbf r_1\! \wedge \mathbf r_2\! :=\!  c_1(s_0)$ where $s_0\! = \!  \max \{ s\! \in \!  \mathbb{R}_+ \! : \! c_1(s)\! = \!  c_2(s) \}$ if $\mathbf r_1\!\neq \! \mathbf r_2$, otherwise we set  $\mathbf r_1\! \wedge \mathbf r_2 \! :=\! \mathbf r_1$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:24:34.431279+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_93741d6f1b0c359b5c8c9407f443757629a23a1157b2ce3128d2e672b1715298","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 15 (Boolean-polynomial description) of arXiv:2608.31157, 'Sharp Approximation Rates for Neural Networks with Affine Latent Parameterizations'] Let $d,r,s,d_{\mathrm{pol}}\in\N^+$, let $X\subseteq\R^{d}$, and let
\[
 \calF:=\{g_{\bmmu}:X\to\R:\bmmu\in\R^r\}.
\]
Its joint truth set is
\begin{equation}
 \calS
 :=\left\{(\bmx,t,\bmmu)\in X\times\R\times\R^r:
 g_{\bmmu}(\bmx)>t\right\}.
\end{equation}

Choose a number of leaf occurrences $s_0$ with $1\le s_0\le s$.
For each occurrence $j=1,\ldots,s_0$, choose a polynomial
\[
 p_j\in\R[x_1,\ldots,x_{d},t,\mu_1,\ldots,\mu_r]
\].
We use the standard convention that the zero polynomial has degree
$-\infty$; thus identically zero atoms are covered by every nonnegative
degree bound below.
The $j$th atom produces the bit
\begin{equation}
 A_j(\bmx,t,\bmmu)
 :=\one_{\{p_j(\bmx,t,\bmmu)>0\}}.
\end{equation}
Finally, choose one Boolean formula tree
$\mathfrak{B}(Z_1,\ldots,Z_{s_0})$ as described above, and let
$\mathsf{B}:\{0,1\}^{s_0}\to\{0,1\}$ be the map obtained from its recursive
evaluation.  We say that $\calS$
has an $(s,d_{\mathrm{pol}})$ Boolean-polynomial description in the parameter
$\bmmu$ when, for every $(\bmx,t,\bmmu)$,
\begin{equation}
 \one_{\calS}(\bmx,t,\bmmu)
 =\mathsf{B}\bigl(
 A_1(\bmx,t,\bmmu),\ldots,
 A_{s_0}(\bmx,t,\bmmu)\bigr),
\end{equation}
and, for each fixed $(\bmx,t)$,
\begin{equation*}
 \deg_{\bmmu}p_j(\bmx,t,\cdot)\le d_{\mathrm{pol}},
 \qquad j=1,\ldots,s_0.
\end{equation*}
The integer $s$ is only an upper bound; $s_0$ is the number of leaf
occurrences actually used after all comparisons have been written in the
strict-positivity form of \eqref{eq:atom-truth-value}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["finitely many events"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:45:21.040786+00:00","domain":"moment methods and bounds for unions and counts of events","id":"claim_938cc5709ca51cd2eff44ea69b8ef941b28e850d88c3bd0fd567adad0df10d11","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let A_1, ..., A_m be events, X_i = 1_{A_i}, U their union, V = span{X_1, ..., X_m} in L2(P), alpha_i = P(A_i) and Sigma_ij = P(A_i and A_j). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:15:16.652674+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_93c501d1ba2e2cdeebc1ab59cb29325cbc6ba95e7d96b351198776f7118d36e2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 5 of arXiv:2608.30752, '2608.30752'] With the notation above, the normalized energy is nonincreasing and satisfies
\begin{equation}
  e^{-2t}E_{u_0}(X_t)
  \searrow
  \mathscr V_q(Y)

\begin{equation}
  \lim_{t\to\infty}

\(
  0<\mathscr V_q(Y)<\infty.

foliation of the ray, let
\(
  C_1,\ldots,C_r
\)
be its maximal flat cylinders. Write
\(
  C_i

Consequently,

If P/N->alpha and M/N->beta lie in (0,infinity), then for each fixed s>0, limsup_N [I(A_N;sqrt(s)A_N+G_N)-I(B_N;sqrt(s)B_N+G_N)]/(NP)<=0, with independent standard Gaussian observation noise and natural logarithms. Neither MI limit is assumed to exist. All dimension orderings and a positive mass of zero signal singular values are allowed. The proof uses a conditional rank-two Lindeberg resolvent estimate, concentration, moment bounds giving expected singular-value Wasserstein coupling, and Haar-mixture entropy concavity. It does not prove unconditional all-SNR product-MMSE extremality or a uniform small-SNR expansion.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.677034+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_93dfe83a5708a85cb4b64e857e7640c90b68aaee3be989a70fa0314c4c8054a0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 13 (Program refinement and the enhancement criterion) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $\mathfrak R$ be a causally calibrated response program on a descended

\item the map in \eqref{eq:program-refinement-canonical-map} is the unique

{"assumptions":["f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} Boolean, uniform product measure","c is a universal constant","the conclusion bounds only the MAXIMUM influence, not any specific coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-10-12T15:09:50+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_94198fd805d1f2269bd7bd89b92062349f91be394349788a2f4df1ea2bf88af8","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} be a Boolean function on the uniform product measure, and define the influence of coordinate i as Inf_i(f) = P( f(X) != f(X^{(i)}) ) where X^{(i)} flips the i-th coordinate. Then there is a universal constant c > 0 with max_{i <= n} Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n / n, where Var(f) = p(1-p) with p = E[f]. This does not bound the TOTAL influence by c Var(f) log n: a dictator f(x) = (1 + x_1)/2 has total influence 1 and Var(f) = 1/4 for every n. The total-influence form of the theorem is sum_i Inf_i(f) >= c' Var(f) log(1/max_i Inf_i(f)) for nonconstant f, with c' > 0 universal, and the maximum bound follows from it. The bound is SHARP up to the constant: the tribes function, a read-once DNF on blocks of size about log_2 n - log_2 log_2 n, is balanced and has all influences of order log n / n. The theorem is about the uniform measure on the cube; the analogous statement for p-biased measures carries an extra factor and is the Friedgut-Kalai sharp-threshold machinery. Note what it does NOT say: it does not bound the influence of any PARTICULAR coordinate, only the maximum, and it says nothing when Var(f) is 0, that is when f is constant. [Kahn, Kalai and Linial (1988); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Dimension3; arbitrary initialization-independent law of unit centers Z.","Independent uniform unit-ball perturbation V; 0<tau<=1/4, 0<nu<=1, integer width m>=1.","Iid Gaussian hidden weights, iid independent symmetric +/-nu readouts; shared initialization at both input locations."],"created_at":"2026-10-21T18:18:10.547540+00:00","domain":"learning theory","id":"claim_94221ebcc39878e74082e75a20abd5f3fda700c26ecaed2492893abafc4c9023","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft: proof (unaudited), kind route-failure, Target1. Independent correctness and novelty review pending. This obstructs the current comparison, not epochwise double descent.

# C024 v2: fixed-radius thickening fails the vanishing initial-function comparison
Status: proof (unaudited). Kind: route-failure. Target:1.
General T267 OPEN. This is a precise obstruction to one proof route, not a
counterexample to nonlinear epochwise double descent. Novelty unestablished.

1. Statement
Let Z have ANY initialization-independent probability law on unit vectors in R^3,
and let V be uniform on the unit three-dimensional ball, independent of Z.
Fix 0<nu<=1, 0<tau<=1/4 and any integer m>=1. Independently initialize
 f_m(x;0)=m^(-1/2)sum_(j=1)^m a_j ReLU(W_j.x),
where W_j are iid N(0,I_3), a_j are iid uniform {-nu,nu}, and all are independent.
The SAME network is evaluated at Z+tau V and Z. Conditional on its initialization
put Y_m=E_(Z,V)|f_m(Z+tau V;0)-f_m(Z;0)|^2.
Define the strictly positive Gaussian-box probability
 p=P(1<=G_0<=2, |G_1|<=1, |G_2|<=1)
  =(Phi(2)-Phi(1))*(2Phi(1)-1)^2, for independent standard normals G_i.
Then, uniformly in m and the law of Z,
 E_init Y_m >=nu^2 tau^2 p/5,
 E_init Y_m^2 <=3nu^4 tau^4,
 P_init(Y_m>=nu^2 tau^2 p/10)>=p^2/300.                 (1)
In particular, at a FIXED positive tau the coupled initial-function discrepancy
cannot vanish in probability as width increases, even though initializations
are shared exactly. No training, Gram approximation or kernel-width limit is
needed for this conclusion.

2. Gaussian active-region lower bound
Fix a unit z and choose orthonormal coordinates with first axis z. Rotational
invariance of N(0,I_3) gives the same probability p to
 A_z={1<=W.z<=2, absolute values of the two orthogonal coordinates <=1}.
On this event ||W||<=sqrt(6). For EVERY ||v||<=1 and tau<=1/4,
 W.z>=1 and W.(z+tau v)>=1-tau sqrt(6)>0,
since 6/16<1. Thus both ReLUs are active and their difference is EXACTLY
 tau W.v. Uniform-ball covariance is E VV^T=I_3/5: its radial density is
3r^2 on [0,1], so E||V||^2=3/5, and symmetry divides this equally among axes.
Consequently
 E_(W,V)[ReLU(W.(z+tau V))-ReLU(W.z)]^2
 >=tau^2 E_W[1_(A_z)||W||^2/5]>=tau^2 p/5.            (2)
The integrand is nonnegative, so restriction to A_z is legitimate. This
bound is uniform in z; the orthonormal coordinates need not be chosen jointly
measurably because the pointwise bound is already independent of z.

3. Independent centered heads and the second moment
For fixed z,v put delta_j=ReLU(W_j.(z+tau v))-ReLU(W_j.z), T_j=a_j delta_j.
The T_j are independent centered variables; centering follows from the
independent head sign, without requiring delta_j itself to be centered.
Therefore
 E_init |m^(-1/2)sum_j T_j|^2=nu^2 E_W delta_1^2.
Integrate over (Z,V) and apply (2), using Tonelli, to obtain the first
inequality in (1). There is no 1/m decay in this initial output fluctuation:
the summation has scale 1/sqrt(m), whereas a kernel sample mean has scale 1/m.
The conclusion does not apply to paired antithetic initialization with
identical hidden weights and opposite heads; that violates the iid hypothesis
and can make the initial function identically zero.

4. Fourth moment and a probability lower bound
ReLU is 1-Lipschitz, hence |delta_j|<=tau |W_j.v|. For fixed z,v, write
mu_2=E T_1^2 and mu_4=E T_1^4. Gaussian second and fourth moments give
 mu_2<=nu^2 tau^2 ||v||^2,
 mu_4<=3nu^4 tau^4 ||v||^4.
These Gaussian moments follow by rotating v to a coordinate axis and using
E G^2=1, E G^4=3 (integration by parts for the standard normal density).
In the expansion of E(sum_j T_j)^4, a term survives only if every index
occurs an even number of times. There are m all-equal terms and
6*binom(m,2) two-pair terms. Thus exactly
 E_init |m^(-1/2)sum_j T_j|^4
 =mu_4/m+3(1-1/m)mu_2^2
 <=3nu^4 tau^4 ||v||^4<=3nu^4 tau^4.                 (3)
Jensen on the (Z,V) probability space gives Y_m^2<=E_(Z,V)|D_m(Z,V)|^4,
where D_m is the same initial prediction difference. Integrating (3) proves
the second inequality in (1). All moments are finite by the displayed bounds.

For completeness, the one-sided moment step does not assume concentration.
Set a=nu^2 tau^2 p/5, b=3nu^4 tau^4 and E={Y_m>=a/2}. Then
 E Y_m<=a/2+E[Y_m 1_E]<=a/2+sqrt(b P(E))
by splitting at a/2 and applying Cauchy-Schwarz. Since E Y_m>=a,
P(E)>=a^2/(4b)=p^2/300. This is precisely the last inequality in (1).
It is a probability lower bound, not a conclusion from mean error alone.

5. Consequence for the C022/C023 transfer route
In those constructions Z is uniform on four unit centers. At initialization,
the coupled center-to-ball population L2 error is sqrt(Y_m). It is part of
D_m(T)=max_(0<=k<=T)||F_ball,k(Z+tau V)-F_center,k(Z)||_2,
so D_m(T)>=sqrt(Y_m) for every horizon T, regardless of subsequent updates.
The bound (1) therefore holds for an initial discrepancy inside exactly the
same coupling used there, for every e, every width, and every fixed tau>0.
Directly replacing tau=e^20 by a positive constant cannot retain the
vanishing prediction comparison D_m(T)=o_P(1), let alone o_P(e^5).
More generally, with fixed nu>0 and tau=tau_e<=1/4, any argument that requires
D_m(T)=o_P(e^5) in width-before-scale limits must have tau_e=o(e^5): if not,
a subsequence has tau_e/e^5 bounded below, and (1) gives a fixed positive
probability of D_m(T)/e^5 being bounded away from zero. This is only a
necessary condition for THAT prediction-error route; C022's e^20 radius
satisfies it. It says nothing about optimal radius exponents.

This does NOT prove that actual population-risk differences cannot cancel,
that no alternative nonshrinking-geometry proof exists, or that double descent
fails for fixed-radius input laws. A proof for such laws must analyze their
nonconstant initial function and population dynamics directly, or use an
alternative comparison. The obstruction identifies why the present center
comparison cannot simply be thickened.

6. Finite checks and audit scope
The accompanying exact Fraction script enumerates independent head signs
for several deterministic increment vectors and widths1 through8. It checks
second and fourth moment expansions and detects a deliberately omitted
mixed fourth-moment term. Its paired-head negative control yields zero
initial difference where the independent-head computation is positive.
These checks concern the finite combinatorial step only; they are not an
independent audit of the Gaussian, population or limiting arguments. No Lean
certificate or literature-priority claim is made. Reviewer PASS is pending.

Brain use: q022 returned the standard second-moment technique; its warning
against drawing a probability conclusion from a mean alone is addressed in
Section4. The population Jensen step assumes no independence across inputs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["gamma the standard Gaussian measure on R^n","f locally Lipschitz (or weakly differentiable) with f and grad f in L^2(gamma)","the constant 1 is sharp; there is no dimension dependence"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628017+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_947309ec928615f9dbb7adf2e8d0772e4ada248270d9924e007bfa120575ef81","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let gamma be the standard Gaussian measure on R^n and let f be locally Lipschitz with f and its gradient in L^2(gamma). Then Var_gamma(f) <= E_gamma[ |grad f|^2 ]. The constant 1 is SHARP and is attained exactly by the affine functions: for f(x) = a . x + b both sides equal |a|^2. The inequality is DIMENSION-FREE - the same constant 1 for every n - which is what makes it useful in high dimension, and it follows from the one-dimensional case by tensorization of the variance. It is strictly weaker than the Gaussian logarithmic Sobolev inequality, which implies it by applying the log-Sobolev inequality to 1 + eps f and expanding to second order in eps. Note the direction: the inequality bounds the variance by the gradient energy, so it gives concentration only at the level of variance, not exponential tails; exponential tails require the log-Sobolev inequality and the Herbst argument. [standard; e.g. Boucheron, Lugosi and Massart, Concentration Inequalities, Theorem 3.20]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T15:32:35.575534+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9478ddfb282b0c4b45f5621233d70db8a29cdb34a6bcbbdbcef010aa05a80e8b","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:projected.Stein.Wishart of arXiv:2606.04859, 'Stein's method for the Wishart distribution'] Suppose that the true scale matrix $\Sigma\in \mathcal{S}_{++}^d$ admits the linear representation
\[
\Sigma = \Sigma(\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star}) = \sum_{j=1}^p \beta_j^{\star} B_j
\]
for some $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star}\in \mathbb{R}^p$ and fixed symmetric templates $\smash{\{B_j\}_{j=1}^p \subseteq \mathcal{S}^d}$. Let $\{U_m\}_{m = 1}^{M} \subseteq \mathcal{S}^{d}$ be given, and for the corresponding linear probes $f_{U_m}(S) \vcentcolon= \mathrm{tr}(U_m S)$, form the structured Stein moment equations
\begin{equation}
\mathrm{tr}\{\Sigma(\boldsymbol{\beta}) U_m\} = y_{n,m}, \qquad y_{n,m} \vcentcolon= \frac{1}{\alpha n} \sum_{k=1}^n \mathrm{tr}(\mathfrak{W}^{(k)} U_m), \qquad m\in \{1, \ldots,M\}.
\end{equation}
Let $C\in \mathbb{R}^{M\times p}$ be the design matrix with entries $C_{mj} \vcentcolon= \mathrm{tr}(B_j U_m)$, and let $\boldsymbol{y}_n \vcentcolon= (y_{n,1}, \ldots,y_{n,M})^{\top}$. If $C$ has full column rank, then the least-squares solution
\[
\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_n = \arg\min_{\boldsymbol{\beta}\in \mathbb{R}^p} \|C \boldsymbol{\beta} - \boldsymbol{y}_n\|_2^2 = (C^{\top} C)^{-1} C^{\top} \boldsymbol{y}_n
\]
is strongly consistent for the true coefficient vector $\boldsymbol{\beta}^{\star}$, as $n\to\infty$. In particular, the structured estimator $\widehat{\Sigma}_n \vcentcolon= \Sigma(\widehat{\boldsymbol{\beta}}_n) = \sum_{j=1}^p \hat{\beta}_{n,j} B_j$ converges almost surely to $\Sigma$ and solves the projected Stein moment equations (equation eq:structured.Wishart.moments of the paper) in the least-squares sense. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:31:02.811441+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_947c73e249e3c16b4ba85a93d391778b391a654e36644ede293b24c7a11230a0","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm Sing of arXiv:2609.01501, 'Singularities of star cluster algebras'] The singular locus of $ X $ is described as follows:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:53:54.918881+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_948106c370cb23beb6b3fd107f5468cf67d690647b6c60259a3f1e417113a05d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 3 of arXiv:2607.17192, 'Geometric Regime--Switching Diffusions on Stratified Riemannian Spaces with an Application'] Suppose Assumptions~\assref{ass:diffusions} and~\assref{ass:jumps} hold.
		Then for every starting point $x\in E$ there exists a filtered
		probability space $(\Omega,\cl F_t^x,\P_x)$ and an
		$E$--valued càdlàg process $(X_t)_{t\ge 0}$ such that:
		\begin{enumerate}[label=(\roman*),ref=\roman*]
			\item $X_0=x$ $\P_x$--a.s.;
			\item between its jump times, the process remains in a single stratum:
			if $X_{t-}\in S_\alpha$ and $X_t=X_{t-}$, then $X_s\in S_\alpha$
			for all $s$ in a neighborhood of $t$; on each such interval,
			$X$ evolves as the diffusion with generator $L_\alpha$;
			\item the jumps of $X$ are governed by the structural kernels and rates:
			whenever $X_{t-}=x\in S_\alpha$, jumps of type $e\in\cl E$ with $\alpha(e)=\alpha$
			occur with conditional intensity $\lambda_e(x)$, and conditional on such a jump of type $e$,
			the post-jump location has law $K_e(x,\cdot)$;
			\item for every $f\in\cl D_0$, the process
			\[
			M_t^f=f(X_t)-f(X_0)-\int_0^t A f(X_s)\,ds
			\]
			is an $(\cl F_t^x)$--martingale. In particular, the law of $X$
			on $D([0,\infty);E)$ is a solution of the martingale problem for
			$(A,\cl D_0)$ with initial condition $x$.
		\end{enumerate}
		Moreover, $X$ is non-explosive and the map $ x \mapsto \P_x$ is Borel.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:35:05.831365+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9488b635a566371b19be454001c26a1a0affb4fdca178d76b3f121ac2c935e83","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:MO-service-Markovianity of arXiv:2606.24881, 'Queues with Correlated Service Times --- the $M/M_D/c$ Model'] Consider a time-homogeneous queueing system with finitely many servers

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:19:42.461901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_949428d2e7cfbaa98de6f5b6566cdc779f4bf7fb3aa2731414dba88301ac8dcc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 3 ({\cite[Th.~5.10, Th.~6.4) of arXiv:2609.03455, '2609.03455'] {KKtheta}}]
The map
\[
 \Theta_\tau:\C/(\Z+\tau\Z)\longrightarrow\P^6,
 \qquad
 z\longmapsto
 (\theta_0(z):\theta_1(z):\cdots:\theta_6(z))
\]
is an elliptic normal embedding of degree $7$.
Its image is cut out by fourteen quadrics.
If
\[
 S=\Theta_\tau(\tau/7),\qquad T=\Theta_\tau(1/7),
\]
then $S$ and $T$ are points of order $7$, and translation by them is
given respectively by cyclic permutation and diagonal multiplication
by powers of $\zeta_7=e^{2\pi i/7}$.

 \left\{

 a_2a_3x_i^2&=a_1^2x_{i+3}x_{i-3}-a_3^2x_{i+1}x_{i-1},
 \end{aligned}
 \right.
 \qquad i\in\Z/7\Z,
\end{equation}
together with the Klein relation \eqref{eq:Klein-a}.
The origin and a pair of $7$-torsion points are
\begin{align*}
 O&=(0:a_1:a_2:a_3:-a_3:-a_2:-a_1),\\
 S&=(-a_1:0:a_1:a_2:a_3:-a_3:-a_2),\\
 T&=(0:a_1\zeta_7^{-1}:a_2\zeta_7^{-2}:a_3\zeta_7^{-3}:
       -a_3\zeta_7^{-4}:-a_2\zeta_7^{-5}:-a_1\zeta_7^{-6}).

So the wall is a two-sided sandwich on the block-increment scale - a fixed-point equation whose solution is chi - and a one-directional induction cannot reach a fixed point, which is why it does not start. Proposed escape: carry a window [L, U] on the variance instead of a single value. The ratio R = U/L can contract (the upper leg lowers U given L, the lower leg raises L given U, neither proved about itself), which removes the circularity and reduces the difficulty to one missing ingredient: the lower leg as a per-scale contraction rate rho_L, a restricted-minimum anticoncentration statement weaker-looking than a full variance lower bound. and assume $A+B\geq2$. Define

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T11:11:44.421680+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_94d912b2a6e567b9d91bbc5e8bb1a73335f183ebe281b685778686f5ea5e8410","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theo 7 of arXiv:2609.03188, 'Some generalizations of Oort's conjecture'] Let $w\in \tW$.
Assume that $\supp_\sigma(w)=\tS$ and there exists $v\in \LP(w)$ such that $v^{-1}p(w)v$ is a Coxeter element with $\supp(v^{-1}p(w)v)=\bS$.
Let $\tau\in\Omega$ be the unique element such that $w\in W_a\tau$.
Then $X_w(\tau)\neq \emptyset$.
Moreover, there exist elements $w=w_0,w_1,\ldots,w_r\in \tW$ satisfying the following conditions:
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For each $0\leq k<r$, there exists $s\in \tS$ such that $w_{k+1}=sw_ks$ and $\ell(w_{k+1})\leq \ell(w_k)$.
Moreover, $\ell(w_r)<\ell(w_{r-1})$.
\item For each $0\leq k<r$ with $\ell(w_{k+1})=\ell(w_k)-2$, the element $s$ in (i) satisfies $X_{sw_k}(\tau)=\emptyset$ and $X_{sw_ks}(\tau)\neq \emptyset$. In particular, if $k=r-1$, then $s\notin\supp_\sigma(w_r)$.
\item The element $w_r$ is a $\sigma$-Coxeter element and $\J_\tau\cap P_{\supp_\sigma(w_r)}$ is a very special parahoric subgroup of $\J_\tau$.
In particular, $\supp_\sigma(w_r)\subsetneq\tS$ and $w_r$ is of minimal length in its conjugacy class.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently, there are $\J_\tau$-equivariant morphisms
$$X_w(\tau)=X_{w_0}(\tau)\longrightarrow X_{w_1}(\tau)\longrightarrow\cdots\longrightarrow X_{w_r}(\tau),$$
each of which is a universal homeomorphism or a Zariski-locally trivial $\A^1$-fibration up to a universal homeomorphism.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-13T03:42:25.818267+00:00","domain":"probability, trees, ergodic theory","id":"claim_94db0dee1d2ddaa48514c8d55f228d27c4d573e1cf1e757815403f5e1e40d56c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked, unrefereed] Lyons and Peres, Probability on Trees and Networks (version 19 August 2026), Question 17.18 (p. 575) asks whether a consistent equivariant flow rule admitting a stationary measure EQUIVALENT to Galton-Watson measure must induce an ergodic Markov chain; their Proposition 17.17 proves it when all child weights are strictly positive, and Exercise 17.22 gives a non-ergodic example whose stationary measure is only absolutely continuous, so equivalence is the point of the question. Galton-Watson measure is stationary, the root colour is invariant along the chain and takes each value with probability 1/2 - a non-constant invariant function, hence no ergodicity - and the stationary measure equals Galton-Watson measure, trivially equivalent to it. Verification as the source words it: the step the proof leaves implicit, and which was checked, is that Galton-Watson really is stationary - it holds because, conditioned on the children's colours, the child subtrees are independent, each distributed as Galton-Watson conditioned on its own colour, so the chosen subtree is exactly GW given colour = c, the uniform choice adds no bias, and mixing over c returns GW. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:22:59.720553+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_94eb48cd5885c214c7e906e1e3c0d3e7f9c6ff68df59a44ccfcf343278a45d3f","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition of arXiv:2608.29708, 'Intuitionistic and Constructive Modal Logics for Classical Modal Logicians'] We say $\mathfrak{F} = (W, \leq)$ is an \emph{intuitionistic frame (i-frame)} if $W$ is a non-empty set and $\leq$ is a preorder on $W$.
  We say $\mathfrak{M} = (\mathfrak{F}, V)$ is an \emph{intuitionistic model (i-model)} if $\mathfrak{F}$ is an i-frame and $V: \mathord{\mathrm{PropVar}} \to \mathcal{P}(W)$,
  where each $V(p)$ is upward closed with respect to $\leq$ (i.e. $\forall x, y\, (x \leq y \mathrel{\text{\&}} x \in V(p) \mathrel{\Rightarrow} y \in V(p))$).
  Such $\mathfrak{M}$ is said to be \emph{based on} $\mathfrak{F}$.
  For $\mathfrak{M} = (W, \leq, V)$, we define a \emph{satisfaction relation} $\Vdash_\mathfrak{M}$ on $W \times \mathscr{L}_p$ by:
  \begin{enumerate}
    \item $x \nVdash_\mathfrak{M} \bot$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} p \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} x \in V(p)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \land \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} (x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\text{\&}} x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \lor \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} (x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\text{or}} x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
    \item $x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \to \psi_2 \mathrel{\;\ratio\Longleftrightarrow\;} \forall x' \geq x\, (x' \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_1 \mathrel{\Rightarrow} x' \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \psi_2)$
  \end{enumerate}
  We write $\mathfrak{M} \vDash \varphi$ (``$\varphi$ is \emph{valid in} $\mathfrak{M}$'') to mean $\forall x \in W\,(x \Vdash_\mathfrak{M} \varphi)$,
  and $\mathfrak{F} \vDash \varphi$ (``$\varphi$ is \emph{valid on} $\mathfrak{F}$'') to mean that $\mathfrak{M} \vDash \varphi$ for every $\mathfrak{M}$ based on $\mathfrak{F}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is an open subset of R^N","u belongs to W^{1,p}(Omega) for the chain rule to apply","k > 0"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T01:59:23.250886+00:00","domain":"elliptic PDE, Sobolev spaces, truncation method","id":"claim_94ec221464adf6dc620b348214224d1a08fe5b06010d5e14cd92e3e805a01a53","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"For $k > 0$ the truncation at level $k$ is $T_k(s) = \\max(-k, \\min(k, s))$, $s \\in \\mathbb{R}$: it equals $s$ for $|s| \\leq k$ and $\\pm k$ outside. $T_k$ is Lipschitz with constant 1, odd, and $T_k(0) = 0$. Chain rule (Stampacchia): if $\\Omega \\subset \\mathbb{R}^N$ is open and $u \\in W^{1,p}(\\Omega)$, $1 \\leq p \\leq \\infty$, then $T_k(u) \\in W^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ with $\\nabla T_k(u) = \\nabla u \\cdot \\mathbf{1}_{\\{|u| < k\\}}$ almost everywhere; if $u \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$ then $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}(\\Omega)$, and $|T_k(u)| \\leq \\min(|u|, k)$. In particular $\\nabla u = 0$ a.e. on every level set $\\{u = c\\}$. Companion functions: the positive part $u^+ = \\max(u,0)$ and $G_k(u) = u - T_k(u)$ (the part of $u$ beyond level $k$); all such compositions satisfy the same chain rule $\\nabla(\\phi \\circ u) = \\phi'(u)\\nabla u$ a.e. for piecewise $C^1$ Lipschitz $\\phi$ with finitely many corners (with $\\phi(0) = 0$ to stay in $W_0^{1,p}$). The truncation method uses $T_k(u)$ (or $G_k(u)$) as a test function in a weak formulation; because it is bounded by $k$ it is admissible against $L^1$ right-hand sides, and $\\int_\\Omega |\\nabla T_k(u)|^p$ measures the energy of $u$ on the set where $|u| < k$. Sharp edges: the chain rule needs $\\phi$ Lipschitz (a merely continuous or unbounded-derivative $\\phi$ can leave $W^{1,p}$); for a function that is only in $L^1_{loc}$ with no Sobolev regularity, $T_k(u) \\in W_0^{1,p}$ for all $k$ is a genuine extra hypothesis, and this is exactly the class in which entropy solutions of $L^1$-data problems live.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["A small parameter: bubble (SAW), triangle (percolation) or square (lattice trees) diagram small at criticality","Above the upper critical dimension: d > 4 (SAW), d > 6 (percolation), d > 8 (lattice trees)","Nearest-neighbour models need d >= 5 (SAW) or d >= 11 (percolation) with current methods"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.968648+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9508af6f4f512cf74f16f4606c7b7ceb7dd262c959d7295040f6340ccc642962","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). The lace expansion writes the two-point function of self-avoiding walk, Bernoulli percolation, oriented percolation or lattice trees as a renormalised random-walk Green function plus a correction series: for SAW, c_n(x) = sum_y D(y) c_{n-1}(x - y) + sum_{m=2}^{n} sum_y pi_m(y) c_{n-m}(x - y), with pi_m the alternating-sign lace coefficients obtained by inclusion-exclusion over self-intersections (for percolation the analogous expansion is in terms of pivotal bonds and sausages). The expansion is an exact identity; its use requires a bootstrap showing the coefficients are small in a norm controlled by a random-walk diagram: the bubble diagram for SAW (finite for d > 4), the triangle diagram for percolation (finite for d > 6) and the square diagram for lattice trees (d > 8). Proved regimes: nearest-neighbour SAW for d >= 5 (Hara-Slade), spread-out SAW for d > 4, nearest-neighbour percolation for d >= 11 (Fitzner-van der Hofstad) and spread-out percolation for d > 6 (Hara-Slade). Conclusions there: mean-field exponents (gamma = 1, eta = 0, beta = 1 and delta = 2 in bounded-ratio senses), Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limits, and asymptotic expansions of critical points. It gives nothing at or below the upper critical dimension, and for nearest-neighbour percolation in 7 <= d <= 10 there is no small parameter, so the expansion holds only as an identity, not as a bound. Typical failure: Applying the expansion's mean-field conclusions (eta=0, Gaussian or super-Brownian scaling limit) to a model at or below its upper critical dimension without re-verifying the triangle or bubble condition; the coefficients pi_m are not shown small there, the bootstrap can fail to close, and the diagrammatic control silently assumed at the outset is exactly the open problem, which is why four-dimensional nearest-neighbor percolation mean-field behavior remains open despite the spread-out and high-dimension cases being resolved. Canonical reference: Hara and Slade, 1990, Communications in Mathematical Physics; Madras and Slade, The Self-Avoiding Walk, 1993, Birkhauser.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:57:59.865878+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_953a496a048652be83bbe87d69db22f3ae062db383f89b8c1b3e7fc604fb4b6d","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:c4-witness-block of arXiv:2607.05384, 'Well-invertible column subsets of sparse matrices are rare'] In this section a root, or candidate root, is a right vertex $j_\star\in J$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.162901+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9566de8788a2dd2f4f3bf959669521d315f4faf5a42e798e2177a0b45ef154f2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Ppn 22 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Recall $F^{\rii}$ from \eqref{e:F.rii}
    and $F^{\riii}$ from \eqref{e:F.iii}. 
    For sufficiently large $N$, for all $t\in \R$,
    \[
        \P(F^{\rii}(k) \ge t)
        \le \P
        \bigg(
        F^{\riii}(k,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
         + \frac{\epsilon'}{5} \ge t
        \bigg) + e^{-cN} \,.
    \]
That is, $F^{\riii}(k)$ approximately stochastically dominates
$F^{\rii}(k)$.

\begin{proof} Condition on any realization of $\bG$. Recall that
$F^\rii(k)$ is defined by \eqref{e:F.rii}
as the average of $F^\ri$ over $k$ orthogonal replicas, maximized over $S_\perp(k)$. Recall moreover that $F^\ri$ is defined by summing \eqref{e:F.B}--\eqref{e:F.w}, where we rewrote \eqref{e:F.B} and \eqref{e:F.U} in \eqref{e:F.B.rewrite} and \eqref{e:F.U.rewrite} above.
\begin{itemize}
\item Considering \eqref{e:F.U.rewrite}, 
note that $\bXi^\ell \hat{\bx} / \sqrt{N}$ is a standard gaussian in $\R^M$, independent of the gaussian process $\{\bXi^\ell \by^\ell : (\hat{\bx}, \by^\ell) = 0\}$.
Thus, the quantity inside
the maximum defining $F^\rii(k)$
(see \eqref{e:F.rii}),
as a process indexed by $\by^{1:k}$, remains distributionally unchanged if we replace each $\bXi^\ell \hat{\bx} / \sqrt{N}$ with $\bz^\ell$, which corresponds to replacing $F_U$ with $\bar{F}_U$. 
\item Considering \eqref{e:F.B.rewrite}, we can set
     \[
        \tbmeta^j
        = \frac{1}{|B_j|^{1/2}}
        \sum_{a\in B_j}
        \bmeta^{\ell,a}\,,
    \]
and note that the $\tbmeta^j$ are i.i.d.\ standard gaussian vectors in $\R^N$.
\end{itemize}
This shows that
    \begin{align*}
    F^{\rii}(k)&
       \stackrel{d}{=}
       \sup\bigg\{
       \frac{1}{k} \sum_{\ell=1}^k
     \bigg[
       \bar{F}_B(\tbmeta^\ell,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
       +F_v(\bG,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)) \\
 &\qquad\qquad\qquad\qquad 
       +\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N}
       \bar{F}_U(\bG,\bz^\ell,\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega))
       +F_w(\by^\ell,\hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)) \bigg]
        : \by^{1:k}
    \in S_\perp(k)
       \bigg\} \,.
    \end{align*}
Enlarging the domain from $S_\perp(k)$ to $S_+(k)$ can only decrease the above supremum. Finally, the difference between the quantity inside the above supremum, versus the quantity inside the supremum \eqref{e:F.iii} (with $\cB = \hat{\cB}(\bG,\omega)$),
is upper bounded by
    \baln
        &\lt|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \rt|
        \frac{1}{k}
        \sum_{\ell=1}^k
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hU_j}{MN|B_j|}
        \bigg(
            \sum_{a\in B_j}
            (\bz^\ell)_a \barbg^a,
            \by^\ell
        \bigg)^2 \\
        &\le \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \bigg|
        \frac{1}{k}
        \sum_{\ell=1}^k
        \sum_{j=1}^r
        \frac{\hU_j}{MN|B_j|}
        \|\bz^\ell(B_j)\|^2
        \|\bG^{B_j}\|_{\op}^2
        \|\by^\ell\|^2\,.
    \ealn
    By standard estimates, we have $\|{\bz^\ell(B_j)}\|^2 \le 2|B_j|$ with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$.
    Combined with the estimate $\|\bG^{B_j}\|_{\op} \le C\sqrt{N}$ from \eqref{e:wishart.bound.repeated}, and $\|\by^\ell\| = \sqrt{N}$, we find that the last display is
        \[
    \le O(1)
    \bigg|\frac{\|\bar{\bx}\|^2}{N} - 1 \bigg|
    \le \frac{\epsilon'}{5}\,,
    \]
where the last inequality holds with probability at least $1-e^{-cN}$ by
 Lemma~\ref{l:fp-gc}.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.484475+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_957806d6f03e715f9c5ecbca1dc39f420ba095ac39fd06be4554a39af6eb3d69","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma Euclidean spherical condenser of arXiv:2606.23025, 'Spectral-Capacitary Bounds for Homological Recovery from Reflected Brownian Trajectories'] Let
\(0 < \varepsilon < R\), and let \(u\) be the capacitary
potential of the spherical condenser
\(\left( \overline{B(0,\varepsilon)},\,\mathbb{R}^{d}\backslash B(0,R) \right)\),
that is, the harmonic function on
\(B(0,R)\backslash\overline{B(0,\varepsilon)}\) with \(u = 1\)
on \(\partial B(0,\varepsilon)\) and \(u = 0\) on
\(\partial B(0,R)\). Then

\[\int_{B(0,R)\backslash B(0,\varepsilon)}^{}|\nabla u|^{2}\, dx = \left\{ \begin{matrix}
\frac{2\pi}{\log(R/\varepsilon)}, & d = 2, \\
\frac{(d - 2)\,\omega_{d - 1}}{\varepsilon^{2 - d} - R^{2 - d}}, & d \geq 3.
\end{matrix} \right.\ \]

ball is
\(cap\left( B(0,\varepsilon) \right) = (d - 2)\,\omega_{d - 1}\,\varepsilon^{d - 2}\),

\(\varepsilon \rightarrow 0\),
\(\int|\nabla u|^{2}\, dx = (d - 2)\,\omega_{d - 1}\,\varepsilon^{d - 2}\left( 1 + O\left( (\varepsilon/R)^{d - 2} \right) \right)\)
for \(d \geq 3\) and
\(2\pi/\log(1/\varepsilon)\,\left( 1 + O\left( 1/\log(1/\varepsilon) \right) \right)\)

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:49:24.957478+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_95980b40a00251e003ea6b61f30ccd9b6e30055fd216ba882b165df1ffd031ef","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:certified-music-landscape of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Let
		$$
		X=\{\bm{x}_1,\dots,\bm{x}_s\},\quad s\ge 2
		$$
		be an  $s$-point cloud and 
			\[
	\delta_X:=\min_{j\ne k}\abs{\bm{x}_j-\bm{x}_k}
	\]
	be its minimum separation.  
	

Suppose		$$
		\bigcup_{j=1}^s\overline{B_\rho(\bm{x}_j)}
		\subset B_1(\bm{0})\subset\mathbb R^3, \quad\rho\le \frac{\delta_X}{2}.	$$
 Define two  fundamental dimensionless constants:
		\begin{eqnarray}
		
	\gamma:=\rho{\kappa}, \qquad \mu_X
		:=
		\frac{9}{2}
		\frac{s^{2/3}}{\kappa\delta_X}<1
\end{eqnarray}
with  $\kappa>0$ 
	and four other derived constants
	\begin{eqnarray}
\nu_X
		&:=&
	 \frac{64c_\nu^2}{27}
\frac{\mu_X^2}{s} = 	48c_\nu^2
		\frac{s^{1/3}}{\kappa^2\delta_X^2} ,\qquad c_\nu:=\sup_{t>0}\left|t\cos t -\sin t\right|/t \,\,\approx 1.0631,\\
				\nonumber	C_1&:=&
			\frac{\gamma^2}{9}
			+
			\nu_X+\sqrt{1+\nu_X}
			\sqrt{				\left(
				\frac{1}{3}+\frac{\gamma^2}{10}
				\right)^2
				+
				4\nu_X
			}\\
			\nonumber 	C_2&:=& \frac{8}{15} \gamma^2 +6\nu_X+ \frac{2\mu_X}{1-\mu_X} C_1.
\end{eqnarray}
Let \(\widetilde{\mathcal U}\) be any $s$-dimensional subspace of $\mathcal{H}$ 
satisfying
\[
    \|P_{\widetilde{\mathcal U}}-P_{\mathcal U_X}\|_2 =\varepsilon_{\rm sub}.
\]
Assume 
\begin{eqnarray}
 
 A_\gamma& :=& \frac{b_\gamma-\mu_X-\nu_X}{1-\mu_X}>0,\quad b_\gamma
		:=
		1-\sup_{t\ge \gamma} \operatorname{sinc}^2(t)
 \end{eqnarray}
			and 	\begin{eqnarray} C_2<\frac23,\qquad
\varepsilon_{\rm sub}
	< \min\left\{ \frac{\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\gamma
            \left(\frac23-C_2\right)
       }{1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\gamma \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt5}+\frac23\right)},\,\,   \sin\left(
        \frac12\arcsin\sqrt{A_\gamma}.
    \right)\right\},
		\end{eqnarray}
		Define
\begin{eqnarray}

\tau_0:=\varepsilon_{\rm sub}^2,\qquad    \tau_1
    :=
    \sin^2\left(
        \arcsin\sqrt{A_\gamma}-\arcsin\varepsilon_{\rm sub}
    \right).
\end{eqnarray}
Then  \(\tau_0<\tau_1\) and:

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
\item
For every \(j\),
\begin{eqnarray}

    C_0^-\kappa^2I_3
    \preceq
    \nabla^2\widetilde q({\bm z})
    \preceq
    C_0^+\kappa^2I_3,
    \qquad
    {\bm z}\in\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}
\end{eqnarray}
where
\begin{eqnarray}
C^-_0&:=&	\frac23
			-
			C_2
			-
			\left(
			\frac{2}{\sqrt5}+\frac23\right) 	\varepsilon_{\rm sub} > \frac{
            \frac23-C_2
       }{1+\frac{\sqrt3}{2}\gamma \left(\frac{2}{\sqrt5}+\frac23\right)},\\
    C_0^+
    &:=&\frac23+C_2
      +\left(\frac2{\sqrt5}+\frac23\right)\varepsilon_{\rm sub}.
\end{eqnarray}

\item
Every point outside the certified wells satisfies
\begin{eqnarray}
    \widetilde q({\bm z})\geq\tau_1,
    \qquad
    {\bm z}\in
    B_1(0)\setminus
    \bigcup_{j=1}^sB_\rho({\bm x}_j).
\end{eqnarray}
\item
Each \(B_\rho({\bm x}_j)\) contains exactly one critical point
\(\widetilde{\bm x}_j\), which is its unique minimizer, and
\begin{eqnarray}

    |\widetilde{\bm x}_j-{\bm x}_j|   \le  \frac{2\varepsilon_{\rm sub}}{\sqrt3\,C_0^-\kappa}<\rho,
    \qquad
    \widetilde q(\widetilde{\bm x}_j)\leq\tau_0.
\end{eqnarray}

\item 	If the  fill distance of  a finite set \(G\subset B_1(0)\)
	\begin{equation}
	
		{\rm mesh}_{B_1}(G)
		:=
		\sup_{{\bm z}\in B_1(0)}
		\min_{\bm g\in G}|{\bm z}-\bm g|
	\end{equation}
 satisfies
\[
    \operatorname{mesh}_{B_1}(G)
    <
    \min\left\{
        \rho- \frac{2\varepsilon_{\rm sub}}{\sqrt3\,C_0^-\kappa},
        \,
        \frac{\sqrt3}{2\kappa}(\tau_1-\tau_0)
    \right\},
\]
then
\[
    G_{\tau_1}:=
    \{{\bm g}\in G:\widetilde q({\bm g})<\tau_1\}
\]
contains at least one point in every certified well and no point
outside their union.

\item
For
\[
    0<h\leq
    \frac{2}{(C_0^-+C_0^+)\kappa^2}
    =
    \frac{3}{2\kappa^2},
\]
the gradient map
\[
    T_h({\bm z}):={\bm z}-h\nabla\widetilde q({\bm z})
\]
maps every \(\overline{B_\rho({\bm x}_j)}\) into \(B_\rho({\bm x}_j)\) and is
a contraction there with factor
\[
    r_h:=1-hC_0^-\kappa^2<1.
\]
Consequently, every accepted initialization converges geometrically
to the unique minimizer in its well. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:31:49.843414+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_95c8eb97cc793a026e9fc3756ec316b3c9bada3ec052a47044df71b770c7bd13","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 21 of arXiv:2506.13913, '2506.13913'] {}{}
Let \(\{X_t\}_{t \geq 0}\) be an Itô diffusion in \(\mathbb{R}^d\) satisfying the SDE
\[
\mathrm{d}X_t = b(X_t)\,\mathrm{d}t + \sigma(X_t) \,\mathrm{d}W_t.
\]
Assume that \(b(x) \in C^1( \mathbb{R}^d; \mathbb{R}^d)\) and \(\sigma(x) \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^n; \mathbb{R}^{d \times m})\). If \(p(t, x)\) is the probability density of \(X_t\), that is, 
\[ \mathbb{P}(X_t \in A) = \int_A p(t, x)\,\mathrm{d}x, \quad \forall A \in \mathcal{B}(\mathbb{R}^d), 
\]
and satisfies \( p(t, x) \in C^{1,2}((0, \infty) \times \mathbb{R}^d) \), with \( p_0(x) \in C^2(\mathbb{R}^d) \) and sufficient decay as \( \|x\| \to \infty \), that is, 
\[
p_0(x) \leq \frac{C}{(1 + \|x\|)^\alpha}, \quad \text{for some } C > 0, \alpha > 0.
\]
Then \( p(t, x) \) satisfies the \textbf{Fokker–Planck equation}
\[
\begin{cases}
\frac{\partial p}{\partial t}(t, x) = \mathcal{L}^* p(t, x), & t > 0, \, x \in \mathbb{R}^d, \\
p(0, x) = p_0(x), & x \in \mathbb{R}^d,
\end{cases}
\]
where the adjoint operator is
\[
\mathcal{L}^* p = - \sum_{i=1}^{n} \frac{\partial}{\partial x_i} \left( b_i(x) p \right) + \frac{1}{2} \sum_{i,j=1}^{n} \frac{\partial^2}{\partial x_i \partial x_j} \left( a_{ij}(x) p \right),
\]
where \(a(x) = \sigma(x) \sigma^\top(x)\) is the diffusion tensor. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space","T is continuous","the supremum is over T-invariant Borel probability measures; it need not be attained"],"created_at":"2026-09-13T02:00:35.438290+00:00","domain":"ergodic theory, topological dynamics, entropy","id":"claim_95cd3f5a581ee5b3b33c5ba6ef9422e6da7205ab57a2fb35db6f9be50cdf92b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let $T: X \to X$ be a continuous map of a COMPACT metric space and let $M(X, T)$ be the (nonempty, by Krylov-Bogolyubov) set of $T$-invariant Borel probability measures. Then
$$h_{top}(T) = \sup\{ h_\mu(T) : \mu \in M(X, T) \},$$
and the supremum may be restricted to ERGODIC invariant measures. The inequality $h_\mu(T) \le h_{top}(T)$ for every invariant $\mu$ is Goodwyn's half; the existence, for every $c < h_{top}(T)$, of an invariant $\mu$ with $h_\mu(T) > c$ is the Dinaburg-Goodman half (Misiurewicz's proof below). Both sides may be $+\infty$. A measure attaining the supremum is a measure of maximal entropy; it need NOT exist for a general continuous $T$ (there are continuous maps, and even homeomorphisms, with $h_{top} < \infty$ and no measure of maximal entropy), but it exists whenever $\mu \mapsto h_\mu(T)$ is upper semicontinuous, e.g. for expansive maps and for $C^\infty$ maps of compact manifolds. The variational principle is the case $\varphi = 0$ of the variational principle for topological pressure, $P(T, \varphi) = \sup_\mu \{ h_\mu(T) + \int \varphi\,d\mu \}$.

WHERE IT FAILS OR NEEDS CARE. (1) Non-compact $X$: the statement depends on which notion of topological entropy is used; for the Bowen metric entropy on a non-compact space the supremum over invariant measures can be strictly smaller, and $M(X,T)$ may be empty (translation on $\mathbb{R}$). (2) The supremum need not be a maximum (see above). (3) Restricting to a non-invariant measure is meaningless: $h_\mu(T)$ is defined only for invariant $\mu$. (4) The principle relates ENTROPY to entropy; it does not say that a generic point has orbit-growth rate $h_{top}$, nor that the measure of maximal entropy is unique (uniqueness = intrinsic ergodicity, a much stronger property that holds e.g. for topologically mixing shifts of finite type but fails for many systems).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:53:11.419060+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_95d10da435aa09244b9cddc64ed5486c89a34cf070cb402796cf8285753d7eea","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 19 (Skorohod integral) of arXiv:2606.08776, 'Approximation of certain stochastic integrals with anticipating integrands'] \
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
            \item We let $\dom(\delta)$ be the set of $u \in L_2([0,1]\times\Omega)$ such that
            \[
                  \left|\mathbb{E}\int_{0}^{1} D_tF u_tdt\right|^2 \leq C_u \E |F|^2
            \]
            for all $F \in \mathbb{D}_{1,2}$, where $C_u\ge 0$ is a constant depending on $u$.

            \item If $u\in \dom(\delta)$, then $\delta(u)$ is the element of $L_2(\Omega)$ characterized by
            \[
            \mathbb{E}(F\delta(u)) = \mathbb{E}\int_0^1 (D_t F) u_t dt \sptext{1}{for}{1} F \in \mathbb{D}_{1,2}.
            \]
           
      \end{enumerate}
The operator $\delta$ is called the {\normalfont divergence operator} and the divergence $\delta(u)$ is called the {\it Skorohod integral} of the process $u$, denoted by
      \[
            \delta(u) = \int_0^1 u_t \delta W_t.
      \]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:52:51.767581+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_95d5f733f7cb3ac9c5ceb76fd5b072b01f0b9a5bcc32bfce306ea391742c7ccd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:marked-isometry of arXiv:2605.02104, '\textbf{Chart-Generated Probability Geometry\\and Kolmogorov Expectations}'] For any two probability coordinate charts $G$ and $H$ on $I$, the map
\[
\Phi_{G,H}:=H^{-1}\circ G
\]
is an isometry from $(I,d_G)$ onto $(I,d_H)$. More precisely,
\[
d_H\bigl(\Phi_{G,H}(x),\Phi_{G,H}(y)\bigr)=d_G(x,y).
\]

\[
(I,d_G,P_X)

(I,d_H,(\Phi_{G,H})_{\#}P_X),
\]
but not in general to $(I,d_H,P_X)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:56:17.350956+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_96027ba99f974b0687326acd85db9973cfc6afa77a4001809717ec87c7567825","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop P:only-easy-consequences of arXiv:2604.10020, 'The directed landscape in half-space'] Take any half-space pre-landscape $\mathcal{M}^\rho$ continuously extended to $\mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$. Let $\mathcal{K}^\rho(x, s; y, t) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(x, s; y, t) + \frac{(x-y)^2}{(t-s)}$ for any $(x,s;y,t)\in \mathbb{H}^2_\uparrow$.
\begin{enumerate}
\item \textup{(Modulus of continuity, analogue of [DOV]).} For any $b \ge 2, \epsilon \le 1$, define
$$
K^\epsilon_b = \{(x, t; y, t + s) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow : s \in [\epsilon, b], \text{and } |t|, x, y \le b \}.
$$
For two points $u_i = (x_i, t_i; y_i, s_i)\in K^\epsilon_b$, $i = 1, 2$, let 
\begin{align*}
    \tau &= \tau(u_1, u_2) = \|(t_1, s_1) - (t_2, s_2)\|_2, \\
    \xi &= \xi(u_1, u_2) = \|(x_1, y_1) - (x_2, y_2)\|_2.
\end{align*}
Then if $\tau^{1/3} + \xi^{1/2} \le \min(\epsilon/b, 1/(\rho \vee 0))$, we have
$$
|\mathcal{K}^\rho(u_1) - \mathcal{K}^\rho(u_2)| \le M \left(\tau^{1/3}\log^{2/3}(\tau^{-1}) + \xi^{1/2}\log^{1/2}(4b\xi^{-1}) \right),
$$
with a random variable $M$  satisfying
$\mathbb{P}(M > a) \le b^{4}[(b/\epsilon)^{10} + (\rho \vee 0)^{10}] \exp(-ca^{3/2})$
for all $a > 0$. Here $c>0$ is a universal constant.
\item \textup{(Shape bound, analogue of [DOV]).} Fix $\rho_0 > 1$ and assume $\rho < \rho_0$. Then there exists $c > 0$ depending on $\rho_0$ such that the following holds. For all $u = (x, t; y, t + s) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ with $s \le \rho_0$, we have
$$
\left|\mathcal{K}^\rho(u) \right|\le M s^{1/3} \log^2\left(\frac{2\|u\|_2}{s}\right),
$$
where $M > 0$ is a random variable satisfying
$\mathbb{P}(M > a) \le 2\exp(-ca^{3/2})$
for all $a > 0$.
\item \textup{(Metric composition holds everywhere, analogue of [DOV])}
For each $u = (x, r;y, t) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ and $s \in (r, t)$, define
	$f_{u, s}(z) = \mathcal{M}^\rho(x,r;z,s)+\mathcal{M}^\rho(z,s;y,t)$. Then on an event of probability $1$, $\mathcal{M}^\rho$ satisfies the metric composition law
	\begin{equation}
	
	\mathcal{M}^\rho(u)=\max_{z \in \mathbb R} f_{u, s}(z)
	\end{equation}
	for every $u = (x, r;y, t) \in \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$ and $s \in (r, t)$. Moreover, for any compact set $K \subset \mathbb H^2_\uparrow$, there exists a random variable $B_K$ such that for all $u = (x, r;y, t) \in K$ and $s \in (r, t)$, the set where $f_{u, s}$ attains its maximum is contained in the interval $[-B_K, B_K]$.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

where $f_r:=1_{B(x,r)}:F\to [0,1]$ and $\overline{P_{\varepsilon}f_r}$ is a McShane extension with exponent $\kappa$, and

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.015256+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_961301c9988f1d7803cdd6f132918f73772ab3a0731fd279b623e4d56a5cf815","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 6 (Extended determinantal kernel for arbitrary complex Gaussian growth) of arXiv:2608.15137, '2608.15137'] Let $(z_{ij})_{i,j\geq1}$ be independent centered circular complex Gaussian variables with $\E\abs{z_{ij}}^2=1$. Let $((m_t,n_t))_{t=0}^T$ be an elementary up-right path with $T\geq1$ and $(m_0,n_0)=(1,1)$. Put
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 X_t&=(z_{ij})_{\substack{1\leq i\leq m_t\\1\leq j\leq n_t}},
 &p_t&=\min(m_t,n_t),\\
 q_t&=\max(m_t,n_t),
 &r_t&=q_t-p_t,
 &\epsilon_t&=p_{t+1}-p_t,
 \end{aligned}
\]
and $P=p_T$. Let
\[
 \lambda_1^{(t)}>\cdots>\lambda_{p_t}^{(t)}>0
\]
be the positive squared singular values of $X_t$. Define
\[
 \kappa_0=0,
 \qquad
 \kappa_t=\epsilon_{t-1}(r_{t-1}-1)-\epsilon_tr_t
 \quad(1\leq t<T),
\]
and
\[
 \kappa_T=\epsilon_{T-1}(r_{T-1}-1).
\]
Put
\[
 w_t(x)=x^{\kappa_t}\quad(t<T),
 \qquad
 w_T(x)=\ee^{-x}x^{\kappa_T}.
\]

Let $v_1,\ldots,v_P$ be distinct formal virtual states and define
\[
 E_t=(0,\infty)\sqcup\{v_{p_t+1},\ldots,v_P\},
\]
with Lebesgue measure on $(0,\infty)$ and counting measure on the virtual states. Define
\[
 \phi_1(x)=1\quad(x>0),\qquad
 \phi_i(v_i)=1\quad(2\leq i\leq P),
\]
with all other values zero, and define
\[
 \psi_i(y)=y^{P-i},\qquad y>0.
\]

For $0\leq t<T$, define $B_t\colon E_t\times E_{t+1}\to\R$ as follows. If $\epsilon_t=0$, let
\[
 B_t(x,y)=\ind_{\{y>x\}}
\]
for real $x,y$, let $B_t(v_k,v_l)=\ind_{\{k=l\}}$, and set all real-virtual cross terms to zero. If $\epsilon_t=1$, use the same real-real entry, set
\[
 B_t(v_{p_t+1},y)=1\quad(y>0),
 \qquad
 B_t(v_k,v_l)=\ind_{\{k=l\}}\quad(k,l\geq p_t+2),
\]
and set all remaining entries to zero. Define
\[
 W_t(z,y)=
 \begin{cases}
  B_t(z,y)w_{t+1}(y),&y>0,\\
  B_t(z,v_k),&y=v_k.
 \end{cases}
\]
Let $W_{s,t}$, $F_i^{(t)}$, $G_j^{(t)}$, and $M$ be as in Lemma~\ref{lem:fixed-particle-em}.

At level $t$, augment the positive squared singular values by the deterministic points
\[
 v_{p_t+1},\ldots,v_P.
\]
The resulting point process is determinantal. The matrix $M$ is finite and invertible, and an exact correlation kernel is
\[
 K(s,z;t,y)
 =
 -\ind_{\{s<t\}}W_{s,t}(z,y)
 +
 \sum_{i,j=1}^P
 G_j^{(s)}(z)(M^{-1})_{ji}F_i^{(t)}(y).
\]
Restricting this kernel to real arguments gives the complete multi-time process of positive squared singular values. The same conclusion holds for a finite path starting from any positive rectangle: prepend a path from $(1,1)$ and restrict the resulting determinantal process to the prescribed levels.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:42:39.104574+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_9670192abcf83e623593e5969093b1bf2c0802f9e7628b47434b26b5e2aa7740","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma LM61 of arXiv:2412.08886, 'On domination for (non-symmetric) Dirichlet forms'] Let $({\mathscr A},\mathcal{D}({\mathscr A}))$ be a Dirichlet form on $L^2(E,m)$ satisfying ${\mathscr E}'\preceq {\mathscr A}\preceq {\mathscr E}$,  where $({\mathscr E}',{\mathscr F}')$ is assumed to be quasi-regular.  Then, there exists a locally compact separable metric space $\widehat{E}$ and a measurable map $j:E\rightarrow \widehat{E}$ such that,  by defining $\widehat{m}:=m\circ j^{-1}$,  the operator $j^*$ is a unitary map from $L^2(\widehat{E},\widehat{m})$ onto $L^2(E,m)$,  and the following hold:

{"assumptions":["p, q probability mass functions on one finite set","p(A) > 0 and q(A) > 0","total variation is half the L1 distance"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:13:40.804747+00:00","domain":"total variation and couplings of finite probability laws","id":"claim_96788e32b7dc3e972356e5ee47f8562428e089141e06a6ce5f93c02ce9f3d9b2","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let p and q be probability mass functions on a finite set S and A a subset of S with a = p(A) > 0 and b = q(A) > 0. Let c be the total variation distance between the conditional laws p(.|A) and q(.|A), d = d_TV(p, q), M = max(a, b) and m = min(a, b). {"assumptions":["k algebraically closed; the curves are projective and have no common component","intersection multiplicity is the local-ring dimension (equivalently Fulton's axiomatic multiplicity)","over non-closed fields or in affine coordinates only the upper bound mn on the number of points holds"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.626765+00:00","domain":"algebraic geometry","id":"claim_9689091d3f27a70eb1bd6d2e53f2f98d9030885135749952fef3396e0d0e9bcd","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let C and D be projective plane curves over an algebraically closed field k, defined by homogeneous polynomials F, G in k[X, Y, Z] of degrees m and n with no common factor (the curves share no component). Then C and D meet in exactly mn points of the projective plane P^2(k) when each intersection point P is counted with its intersection multiplicity I_P(C, D) = dim_k O_P / (F, G) (the local ring at P modulo the ideal of the two curves); in particular they meet in at least one and at most mn distinct points. The multiplicity is at least m_P(C) m_P(D), the product of the multiplicities of the two curves at P, with equality exactly when the curves have no common tangent at P. {"assumptions":["K is a compact metric space","F is a uniformly bounded family in C(K)","F is equicontinuous on K"],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:15:45.377034+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_969621bacd8c4d8d1d18dc91064c5582eb98fa2cd21ef76831aadd2757e586da","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let K be a compact metric space and let F be a family of real- or complex-valued continuous functions on K. Suppose F is (i) uniformly bounded: there is M with |f(x)| <= M for all f in F and all x in K, and (ii) equicontinuous: for every epsilon > 0 there is delta > 0 such that d(x, y) < delta implies |f(x) - f(y)| < epsilon for every f in F simultaneously. Then every sequence in F has a subsequence converging uniformly on K (to a continuous limit); equivalently, F is relatively compact in C(K) with the supremum norm. Conversely, a relatively compact subset of C(K) is uniformly bounded and equicontinuous. (Pointwise boundedness plus equicontinuity already implies uniform boundedness on compact K; the classical statement on K = [a,b] is the special case.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:01:25.649893+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_96bbed7751e3ed953fef49d275b74566f04d110ec77de5fe72cf34e0d36e96e0","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:return_pattern_subset of arXiv:2605.16086, 'Loop pruning and downward deviations for maximum local time of discrete-time simple random'] Fix a nonempty subset \(J\subset [|I|]=\{1,\ldots,|I|\}\) (in later applications, mainly \(J\subset [m]\)), and write its elements in increasing order as
\[
J=\{j_1<j_2<\cdots<j_{\# J}\}.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Return patterns.}
A forward return pattern on \(J\) is a vector \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_{\# J})\in\mathbb{N}^{\# J}\) such that
\begin{equation}
\sum_{k=1}^{\ell} a_k\le \ell K \qquad \text{for all } \ell=1,\ldots,\# J.
\end{equation}
We denote the set of all such forward patterns by \(\mathcal P^{+}(J)\).

A backward return pattern on \(J\) is a vector \(\mathbf a=(a_1,\ldots,a_{\# J})\in\mathbb{N}^{\# J}\) such that the reversed sequence
\[
\check{\mathbf a}:=(a_{\# J},a_{\# J-1},\ldots,a_1)
\]
satisfies (equation eq:pattern_J_forward of the paper). We denote the set of all such backward patterns by \(\mathcal P^{-}(J)\).

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Priority orders.}
We order index pairs \((p,q)\in [m]\times[K]\) by
\[
(p,q)\succ_+(p',q')
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl(p>p'\bigr)\ \text{or}\ \bigl(p=p'\ \text{and}\ q>q'\bigr),
\]
and
\[
(p,q)\succ_-(p',q')
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\bigl(p<p'\bigr)\ \text{or}\ \bigl(p=p'\ \text{and}\ q>q'\bigr).
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Forward realization.}
The following definition is somewhat involved; the stack interpretation in Remark~(rem:urgent-file-stack of the paper) gives an intuitive explanation of the forward realization rule below.
Let \(J\subset [m]\) and \(\mathbf a\in\mathcal P^{+}(J)\).
We define lists \(\Lambda^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a)\) recursively via used-index sets \(\mathcal V^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a)\).
Set \(\mathcal V^{+}_0(\mathbf a):=\varnothing\). For each \(\ell=1,\ldots,\# J\), given \(\mathcal V^{+}_{\ell-1}(\mathbf a)\), define
\[
\mathcal I^{+}_\ell:=\{(p,q):\ p\in J,\ p\le j_\ell,\ 1\le q\le K\},
\qquad
\mathcal U^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a):=\mathcal I^{+}_\ell\setminus \mathcal V^{+}_{\ell-1}(\mathbf a),
\]
and let \(\Lambda^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a)\) be the ordered list consisting of the first \(a_\ell\) elements of \(\mathcal U^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a)\)
when \(\mathcal U^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a)\) is arranged in decreasing order \(\succ_+\).
Finally, set
\[
\mathcal V^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a):=\mathcal V^{+}_{\ell-1}(\mathbf a)\cup \{\text{elements appearing in }\Lambda^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a)\}.
\]

Recall the right rod sub-segments \(R^{+}_{pq}\).
We say that \(S\) realizes \(\mathbf a\) on \(J\) in the forward sense, and denote this event by \(\mathsf{Ret}^{+}_J(\mathbf a)\), if for every \(\ell=1,\ldots,\# J\),
writing
\[
\Lambda^{+}_\ell(\mathbf a)=\bigl((p^{(\ell)}_1,q^{(\ell)}_1),\ldots,(p^{(\ell)}_{a_\ell},q^{(\ell)}_{a_\ell})\bigr),
\]
there exist times \(u^{(\ell)}_1\le \cdots\le u^{(\ell)}_{a_\ell}\) with
\[
u^{(\ell)}_k\in(\rho_{j_\ell}+L,\rho_{j_{\ell+1}}+L],
\quad\text{for }k=1,\ldots,a_\ell,
\qquad \rho_{j_{\# J+1}}:=+\infty,
\]

such that
\[
S_{u^{(\ell)}_k}\in S\!\left(R^{+}_{p^{(\ell)}_k\,q^{(\ell)}_k}\right),
\qquad k=1,\ldots,a_\ell.
\]

\smallskip
\noindent\textbf{Backward realization.}
Let \(\mathbf a\in \mathcal{P}^-(J)\), and define the time-reversed path
\[
\check S_n := S_{-n},\qquad n\in\mathbb{Z}.
\]
Then the points
\[
\check\rho_i:=-\rho_{m+1-i},\qquad i=1,\ldots,m,
\]
form the corresponding sequence of rod points for \(\check S\) (along the \(-x_0\) direction) on the time interval $-I$.
We say that \(S\) realizes \(\mathbf a\) on \(J\) in the backward sense, and we denote this event by \(\mathsf{Ret}^{-}_J(\mathbf a)\), if the time-reversed path \(\check S\) realizes \(\check{\mathbf a}\) on the index set \(\check J:=\{m+1-j:\ j\in J\}\) in the forward sense.

Under this time reversal, the right rod sub-segments for \(\check S\) correspond to the left rod sub-segments for \(S\), namely
\[
R^{+}_{pq}(\check S)=R^{-}_{(m+1-p)\,q}(S),
\]
and the forward priority order \(\succ_+\) for \(\check S\) matches the backward priority order \(\succ_-\) for \(S\).","status":"unverified"}
