{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T02:39:12.167259+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a63777394c2ea4625a6dcc05aaf5845678eb8d5bd84c7635c800e4167c5c6aaa","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def_gen_perm_model of arXiv:2412.07258, 'Permuton limit of a generalization of the Mallows and $k$-card-minimum models'] Assume given a strictly decreasing $C^1[0,1]$ function $g$ satisfying $g(0)=1$ and $g(1)=0$.
For each $n \in \mathbb{N}_+$ and $i \in [n]$ let $\nu^{(n),i}_{g}$ denote the probability distribution supported on $[n-(i-1)]$ with probability masses
\begin{equation}
    \nu^{(n),i}_{g}( \{ l \} ):= \frac{g\left(\frac{(i-1)+(l-1)}{n}\right)-g\left(\frac{(i-1)+l}{n}\right)  }{g\left( \frac{i-1}{n} \right)}, \qquad l=1,\dots, n-(i-1).
\end{equation}
We say that a random element $\sigma_n$ of $S_n$ is a $g$-random permutation, or briefly write $\sigma_n \sim \mathrm{PERM}(g,n)$, if it can be generated as follows. We write the number $i$ on the $i$'th card of the original deck (counted from the bottom up).
$\sigma_n(i)$ will denote the number written on the card that is at position  $i$  in the new deck (counted from the bottom up). We build the new deck by picking a card from the remaining old deck  in each step and placing it at the top of the new deck.
\begin{itemize} \item  Let $C^{(n),i}, \, i \in [n]$ denote independent random variables with distribution \begin{equation*} C^{(n),i} \sim \nu^{(n),i}_{g}.\end{equation*}
\item For any $i \in [n]$ we will denote by $D^{(n)}_i$ the set of cards remaining in the old deck before the $i$'th step. Note that $|D^{(n)}_i|=n-(i-1)$.
\item
Let us define $D^{(n)}_i$   and $\sigma_n(i)$ for $i \in [n]$  recursively. Let $D^{(n)}_1 = [n]$.
\item If $D^{(n)}_i$ is already defined,  we pick the $C^{(n),i}$-th card of $D^{(n)}_i$ (counted from the bottom of $D^{(n)}_i$) and let $\sigma_n(i)$ be the number written on this card. We remove this card from the old deck, i.e., we let $D^{(n)}_{i+1} = D^{(n)}_i \setminus \{\sigma_n(i)\}$, and we place it on the top of the new deck.
\item We continue this procedure until there are no cards left in the old deck.
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T00:41:11.650989+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a64cf7e6408816fb0d1491dd7b47309217f1fe8391795753ce1e4823d8a86492","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition Discrete-discrete coupling of arXiv:2411.13964, 'Long-time analysis of a pair of on-lattice and continuous run-and-tumble particles with ja'] \label
 {def:discrete_discrete_coupling}

  Let $Y^L_0 = (y^L_0, (\sigma^1_0, \sigma^2_0))$ and
  $\tilde Y^L_0 = (\tilde y^L_0, (\tilde \sigma^1_0, \tilde
  \sigma^2_0))$ in $\{1, \ldots, L\} \times \Sigma$ be given. Now turn to
  constructing a coupling between two discrete processes $Y^L$ and
  $\tilde Y^L$ with respective initial states $Y^L_0$ and
  $\tilde Y^L_0$. Let $s^1, s^2, \tilde s^1, \tilde s^2$ be four

parameter $\gamma_L = (L-1) / \ell$ independent of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:57:28.711363+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a65450d189093bef9f2d3c1a5a5c068b2b949650b7d0168866b13dea802aea5c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 13 (Flow through one initial half-tile) of arXiv:2609.01143, 'The voter model on the hyperbolic graph'] Fix a sufficiently large constant $h_*>0$ and a terminal level $j_*$ with $h_{j_*}=h_*+O(1)$.  Let $H$ be a level-$j$ half-tile with $j\leq j_*$, and put
\[
k:=j_*-j,\qquad m:=\exp\{(1-\alpha)(h_j-h_{j_*})\}.
\]

Suppose that a prescribed point $v$ lies outside $H$ and all its descendants through level $j_*$, and is adjacent to every point of $H$. Under the Palm law obtained by adding $v$, with asymptotically positive probability one can construct a collection $\mathcal L_H$ of occupied level-$j_*$ descendants of $H$ and a unit flow $\Gamma_H$ on the component of $v$, supported on $v$ and the points in the descendant half-tiles between levels $j$ and $j_*$.  The collection contains at least a fixed positive proportion of the $2^k$ terminal descendants and, with $Z_H:=|\mathcal L_H|$,
\[
\operatorname{div}\Gamma_H=\mathbbm{1}_v- \frac1{Z_H}\sum_{L\in\mathcal L_H} \mathrm{unif}_{\mathcal P_n\cap L},
\]
while $\cE_{\cG}(\Gamma_H)\leq C/m$ for a fixed $C<\infty$.

The construction uses only the Poisson points in these half-tiles. Success events for initial half-tiles with disjoint descendant regions are therefore independent.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:33:21.475247+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a66546df5d6e9d57f4c98b8d050ab0f062f2e05e8740353ba4f22bf3cf98da14","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:dyadic-maximal of arXiv:2606.21006, 'Law of the Iterated Logarithm for Weighted Sums of Functionals of Long-Memory Gaussian Seq'] Let $N\ge2$, and let $Z_{N+1},\ldots,Z_{2N}$ be centered square-integrable random variables.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:03:35.763720+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a66a5b1c6834129f294b0c9379489ec36176befe65804002cd99f4852655d951","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop finiteNAdjointDuality of arXiv:2609.02743, 'Sharp mean-field estimates for diffusive log/Riesz gases in the Hilbert--Schmidt regime'] For $t\in[0,T]$ and $\phi\in\mathscr D_T$, let $f^r=\mathsf{U}^{r,t}\phi$ denote the classical solution of the backward adjoint problem (equation eq:backwardAdjointEquation of the paper).  Then
\begin{align}
S_N^t(\phi)
=S_N^0(\mathsf{U}^{0,t}\phi)
+\sqrt N\,M_N^t[f]
-\frac{\sqrt N}{2}\int_0^t
\mathsf A_1(\nabla f^r,X_N^r,\mu^r)\,\mathop{}\!\mathrm d r,
\end{align}
where
\begin{align}

By the boundedness of $\nabla f$, $(M_N^\tau[f])_{0\le\tau\le t}$ is a continuous square-integrable martingale.  The last term in (equation eq:finiteNAdjointDuality of the paper) converges to zero in $L^1$ at rate $O(N^{-1/2})$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T12:43:43.439053+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a68b582c4fb1191f736f62405f7c0ee1d2dcc96706d969bc025c306fa329c14b","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:SSS of arXiv:2509.04155, 'An Approach to Sub-Gaussian Heat Kernel Estimates via Analysis on Metric Spaces'] Let $p \geq 1$.
    A \emph{$p$-energy structure} on a metric measure space $(X,d,\mu)$ is a triplet $(\mathcal{F}_p,\Gamma_p,\Psi)$ consisting of the following data.
    \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\arabic*)}, leftmargin=*]
    \vspace{3pt}
    \item $\mathcal{F}_p$ is subset of $L^p(X,\mu)$ which we call a \emph{Sobolev space}.
    The members of $\mathcal{F}_p$ are called \emph{Sobolev functions}. 
    \vspace{3pt}
    \item $\Gamma_p$ assigns to every $f \in \mathcal{F}_p$ a non-negative finite Borel measure denoted $\Gamma_p\Span{f}$. We call the measure $\Gamma_p\Span{f}$ the \emph{energy measure} of $f$. To emphasize that these are Dirichlet type $p$-energies in many practical cases, we will frequently use the notation
    \[
         \int_{A} \, d\Gamma_p\Span{f} = \Gamma_p\Span{f}(A).
    \]
    \item $\Psi : X \times (0,\infty) \to (0,\infty)$ is a scale function such that the pair $(\mathcal{F}_p,\Gamma_p)$ satisfies both the Poincar\'e inequality (eq:PI of the paper) (Definition (def:PI of the paper)) and the upper capacity estimate (eq:UCap of the paper) (Definition (def:Ucap of the paper)).
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-08-02T17:09:44.799493+00:00","domain":"harvested overview (Wikipedia lead)","id":"claim_a69b4271c80fa20aa2fea9d95ad80807bc72e1765e618476cb1e679b00be37b2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"In the mathematical field of graph theory, the Erdős–Rényi models are two closely related models for generating random graphs and the evolution of a random network. These models are named after Hungarian mathematicians Paul Erdős and Alfréd Rényi, who introduced one of the models in 1959. Edgar Gilbert introduced the other model contemporaneously with and independently of Erdős and Rényi. In the model of Erdős and Rényi, all graphs on a fixed vertex set with a fixed number of edges are equally likely. In the model introduced by Gilbert, also called the Erdős–Rényi–Gilbert model, each edge has a fixed probability of being present or absent, independently of the other edges. These models can be used in the probabilistic method to prove the existence of graphs satisfying various properties, or to provide a rigorous definition of what it means for a property to hold for almost all graphs.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["U ⊂ C is open and connected","f is holomorphic on U","f is not constant on U"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:42.482048+00:00","domain":"complex analysis","id":"claim_a6b99002ecb79eae7c982d9fde341aac0683db46b4f620776ddcbf4a03879dbe","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let U be a connected open subset of C and f : U → C holomorphic and not constant. Then f(V) is open for every open V ⊂ U. More precisely, if z0 is in U and f - f(z0) has a zero of order m ≥ 1 at z0, then for every sufficiently small r > 0 there is δ > 0 such that every w with 0 < |w - f(z0)| < δ has exactly m preimages (counted with multiplicity, in fact m distinct simple preimages when r is small enough) in the disk |z - z0| < r. Consequences: a nonconstant holomorphic function on a connected open set cannot have locally constant modulus, real part, or argument, and an injective holomorphic map has nonvanishing derivative and holomorphic inverse. Connectedness can be replaced by: f is nonconstant on every connected component of U.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["H is a Hilbert space (complete)","a is sesquilinear and bounded on all of H × H","a is coercive: Re a(u,u) ≥ α‖u‖² with α > 0, on the whole space H","F is a continuous (conjugate-)linear functional on H"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:42.771728+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, elliptic PDE, variational methods","id":"claim_a6ce6929f12d5ce7339c07a63e3bc2c50cf5e81c49bcf05a5a388b1517ad79ba","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let H be a real or complex Hilbert space and a: H × H → K (K = ℝ or ℂ) a sesquilinear form (bilinear in the real case, linear in the first and conjugate linear in the second argument in the complex case) such that: (boundedness) |a(u, v)| ≤ C‖u‖‖v‖ for all u, v ∈ H with C < ∞; (coercivity) Re a(u, u) ≥ α‖u‖² for all u ∈ H with α > 0. Then for every continuous conjugate-linear functional F on H (equivalently every f ∈ H via F(v) = ⟨f, v⟩) there is a unique u ∈ H with a(u, v) = F(v) for all v ∈ H, and ‖u‖ ≤ ‖F‖/α. The solution map F ↦ u is bounded with norm at most 1/α. No symmetry of a is assumed; if a is Hermitian and coercive, the statement is exactly the Riesz representation theorem for the equivalent inner product a. The weaker hypothesis |a(u, u)| ≥ α‖u‖² also suffices. Standard use: for a bounded Lipschitz domain Ω, the form a(u, v) = ∫_Ω (A∇u·∇v̄ + b·∇u v̄ + c u v̄) on H = H_0^1(Ω) is bounded and coercive under uniform ellipticity of A, bounded b, c, and a smallness or sign condition making Re a(u,u) ≥ α‖u‖_{H^1}²; then the weak Dirichlet problem has a unique solution.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:48:17.127109+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6dcda708eb0fbc045b609129d84b5d2be7d00ab29f70f2635dce589f23fbe9c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Dfn 17 ({\cite[Definition 2.3.1) of arXiv:2605.27974, 'Discrete approximation of semi-Dirichlet forms with non-symmetric perturbations of resista'] {kigami2001analysis}}]
Let $X$ be a set, $\mathcal{F}$ a subspace of $l(X)$ containing all the constant functions on 
$X$, and $\mathcal{E} \colon \mathcal{F} \times \mathcal{F} \rightarrow \R$ a bilinear form. 
Then, $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ is called a resistance form on $X$ if the following hold:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[$\mathrm{(RF1)}$]
$\mathcal{E}(g,f)=\mathcal{E}(f,g)$ and $\mathcal{E}(f,f) \geq 0$ for $f,g \in \mathcal{F}$. 
Also, $\mathcal{E}(f,f)=0$ if and only if $f$ is a constant function.
\item[$\mathrm{(RF2)}$]
$\left( \mathcal{F}/ {\sim}, \mathcal{E} \right)$ is a Hilbert space, where 
$\sim$ is an equivalence relation on $\mathcal{F}$ defined by 
$f \sim g$ if $f-g$ is a constant function.
\item[$\mathrm{(RF3)}$]
For any finite subset $V \subset X$ and $f^{\prime} \in l(V)$, there exists some
$f \in \mathcal{F}$ such that $f \lvert_{V} =f^{\prime}$ holds.
\item[$\mathrm{(RF4)}$]
For any $x,y \in X$, we have 
\begin{align}
    R(x,y) \coloneqq \sup \left\{\frac{\abs{f(x)-f(y)}^{2}}{\mathcal{E}(f)} \middle |
    f \in \mathcal{F},f \, \text{is not constant}\right\} < \infty.
\end{align}
\item[$\mathrm{(RF5)}$]
For any $f \in \mathcal{F}$, we have $0 \vee f \wedge 1 \in \mathcal{F}$ and 
$\mathcal{E}(0 \vee f \wedge 1)\leq \mathcal{E}(f)$.
\end{enumerate}
Then, $R$ in $\mathrm{(RF4)}$ is a metric on $X$, called the resistance metric associated 
with $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$.

In what follows, $(\mathcal{E},\mathcal{F})$ is a resistance form on $X$ and $V$ is a non-empty finite subset of $X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:12:46.885561+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6e51db7d2b66af2382575b58c092ccc0296aa94a38051a99fd36a3d358222d4","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition projdef of arXiv:2608.09856, '\bf Mass erasure on measured $\bbR$-trees,\\ applications to L\'evy forests'] Let $(T,d, \rho, \mu)$ be a rooted finitely measured Polish $\mathbb{R}$-tree. Let $\rho \! \in \!  \mathtt{t}\! \subset \! T $ 
be a closed subtree. Let $C_i$, $i\! \in \!  I$, be the connected components of the open set $T\backslash \mathtt{t}$ (here, the $C_i$ are non-empty open subsets and $I$ is countable since $T$ is separable). 
Then the following holds true. 
\begin{compactenum}

\smallskip

\item[$(i)$] For all $i\! \in \!  I$, there is $\sigma_i\! \in \!  \mathtt{t}$ such that $C_i$ is a connected component of $T\backslash \{ \sigma_i\}$, and $C_i\cup \{ \sigma_i\} $ is the closure of $C_i$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(ii)$] For all $\sigma\! \in \!  T$, either $\sigma \! \in \!  \mathtt{t}$ and $f_\mathtt{t} (\sigma)\! = \!  \sigma$ or there exists $i\! \in \!  I$ such that $\sigma \! \in \!  C_i$ and $f_\mathtt{t} (\sigma) \! = \!  \sigma_i$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(iii)$] $f_\mathtt{t}$ is 1-Lipschitz with respect to $d$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(iv)$] Let $\mathtt{t}_0$ and $\mathtt{t}_1$ be two closed subtrees of $T$ that contain $\rho$. Then, $\mathtt{t}_0\! \cap \! \mathtt{t}_1$ is a closed subtree of $T$ and  $f_{\mathtt{t}_0} \!\circ\! f_{\mathtt{t}_1}\! = \!  f_{\mathtt{t}_0\cap \mathtt{t}_1}$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(v)$] We define the \emph{projection $\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}} \mu$ of $\mu$ onto $\mathtt{t}$} as the push-forward  
measure of $\mu$ via $f_\mathtt{t}$. Then, 
\vspace{-0.5mm}
\begin{equation}

\textstyle\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}} \mu = \mu (\cdot \cap \mathtt{t}) + \sum_{{i\in I}}\,  \mu (C_i)\delta_{\sigma_i} \; .
\end{equation}

Consequently we get $d_{\mathtt{var}} (\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}}\mu, \mu) := \sup_{B\in \mathscr B (T)} |\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}} \mu (B)\! -\! \mu(B)| \! \leq \!  \mu (T\backslash \mathtt{t})$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(vi)$] Let $\sigma \! \in \!  T$. If $ \sigma \! \in \!  \mathtt{t}$, then $\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}}\mu (\theta_\sigma T)\! = \!  \mu (\theta_\sigma T)$ and if $ \sigma \! \notin\!  \mathtt{t}$, then $\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}}\mu (\theta_\sigma T)\! = \!  0$. 

\smallskip

\item[$(vii)$] Let $(T^*\! ,d^*\! , \rho)$ be the bordification of $(T,d,\rho)$. Then $\mathtt{t}$ is also a closed subtree of $T^*$. We denote by $f_{\mathtt{t}}^*\colon T^* \! \to \! \mathtt{t}$ and $\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}}^*\colon \mathcal{M}_f(T^*)\! \to \! \mathcal{M}_f(\mathtt{t})$ the projections onto $\mathtt{t}$. Then $f_{\mathtt{t}}^*$ and $f_{\mathtt{t}}$ coincide on $T$ and $\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}}^*$ and $\mathtt{P}_{\!\mathtt{t}}$ coincide on $\mathcal{M}_f(T)$. 
\end{compactenum} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent (product) Bernoulli measure, possibly with coordinate-dependent parameters","A is a monotone (increasing) event depending on finitely many coordinates","differentiability in p, automatic for finite-dimensional product measures"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.974074+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6e95b98b55e5073a7f62110341ac5fe86d89ae81b909d71bb1c753c13feb7de","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For the product measure mu_p on {0,1}^E with each coordinate independently open with probability p and an increasing event A depending on finitely many edges, Russo's formula states d/dp mu_p(A) = sum_{e in E} mu_p(e is pivotal for A), where e is pivotal for A at a configuration omega if flipping the state of e changes the indicator of A. When different edges carry different parameters p_e, the analogous statement is d/dp_e mu(A) = mu(e is pivotal for A). This identity converts questions about how quickly an event's probability crosses a threshold into questions about counting or bounding pivotal edges, which is the basic engine behind sharp-threshold theorems when combined with the Margulis-Russo framework and tools such as hypercontractivity, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm influence bound, or the OSSS inequality. Russo's formula does not by itself give sharp thresholds; it requires monotonicity of A, since non-monotone events need a more complex signed-pivotal generalization; and it is stated for independent-coordinate measures, so applying it to dependent measures such as the random-cluster model requires a separate Glauber-dynamics-based generalization rather than the naive product-measure formula. Typical failure: Using Russo's formula on a non-monotone event without its signed-pivotal generalization, or applying the plain product-measure version of the formula to a dependent measure such as a random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure, where the correct analogue requires the generator of an associated Glauber dynamics rather than a simple coordinatewise derivative; both errors produce a derivative formula that looks structurally similar but is simply wrong. Canonical reference: Russo, 1981, Zeitschrift fur Wahrscheinlichkeitstheorie und verwandte Gebiete; Margulis, 1974, Problemy Peredachi Informatsii; Grimmett, Percolation, second edition, 1999, Springer, Chapter 2.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:57:30.994065+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6f0f9ae991e501982155aabb678eeaf75543488ad65d2195e541dec2e32c168","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 39 (Identification of the Hilbert--Stein and primitive--Fock splittings) of arXiv:2608.12492, 'Weak Limits of Wiener Chaos: Primitive--Fock Classification and Hilbert--Stein Extraction'] Let
\[
 X_{n,a}=I_q(f_{n,a}),
 \qquad
 \sup_n\sum_{a=1}^{d}q!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2<\infty,
\]
choose $R>0$ with
$R^2\ge\sup_n\sum_aq!\norm{f_{n,a}}^2$, and run the spectrally reduced
feedback on $x_{n,a,q}=\sqrt{q!}\,f_{n,a}$ from the zero module.  Along every
subsequence on which the covariance and all the finitely many proper
self-contraction norms converge, one may extract a further subsequence
and choose a sufficiently slow diagonal $J(n)\to\infty$ such that, with
the corresponding active and
residual Wiener polynomials $A_n^{[J(n)]},B_n^{[J(n)]}$,
\[
 (A_n^{[J(n)]},B_n^{[J(n)]})
 \Longrightarrow(A_{\mathrm{FF}},G_{\mathrm{prim}}),
 \qquad X_n\Longrightarrow A_{\mathrm{FF}}+G_{\mathrm{prim}},
 \qquad
 G_{\mathrm{prim}}\indep A_{\mathrm{FF}}.
\]
If $\xi_a=[f_{n,a}]_{\mathcal U}\in\cH_q$, then, in the terminal
primitive--Fock representation,
\begin{align}
 A_{\mathrm{FF},a}
 &=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cD_q}\xi_a,
 \\
 G_{\mathrm{prim},a}
 &=\mathbb U_q^{-1}P_{\cK_q}\xi_a.
 
\end{align}
The second term belongs to the first Gaussian chaos over $\cK_q$; the
first is the orthogonal sum of all weighted sectors containing at least
two primitive particles.  In particular the split is intrinsic relative
to the represented packet and ultrafilter, and
\begin{equation}
 \Cov(G_{\mathrm{prim}})_{ab}
 =\ip{P_{\cK_q}\xi_a}{P_{\cK_q}\xi_b}_{\cH_q}
 =q!\,\Ulim\ip{p_{n,a}}{p_{n,b}},

where $(p_{n,a})$ is any bounded representative of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.346929+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a6f272d3910a1bb420699733275bf3581af0d5decfbc48ff611189fbbd7e6037","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:sine-gordon of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] Let $w$ be a kernel and
		$\varphi_{w} := A_{w} - \mathrm{id}$ its reaction.
		\begin{enumerate}[label=\normalfont(\roman*), leftmargin=*]
			\item If $f$ solves the diffusive
			equation~(equation eq:flow-diffusion of the paper) with kernel $w$ and integrable
			data, then $F$ solves the local semilinear equation
			\begin{equation}
				\partial_{t}F = D\,\partial_{xx}F + \varphi_{w}(F),
				\qquad
				\varphi_{w}(u) = \int_{0}^{u}\big(w(s) - 1\big)\,ds,
				
			\end{equation}
			and conversely; for the canonical kernel
			$\varphi(u) = -\sin(2\pi u)/(2\pi)$, so the angular variable
			$v = 2\pi F$ solves the overdamped sine--Gordon equation
			$\partial_{t}v = D\,\partial_{xx}v - \sin v$.
			\item For every $F_{0} \in \mathcal{M}$ the
			equation~(equation eq:cdf-equation of the paper) has a unique global solution,
			smooth for positive times, monotone in $x$ with values in $[0,1]$
			and limits $0, 1$ preserved for all time: laws evolve to laws, mass
			and positivity being conserved automatically.
			\item The dynamics is monotone for first-order stochastic
			dominance: $F_{0} \le G_{0}$ pointwise implies
			$F_{t} \le G_{t}$ for all $t$, the diffusive extension of the
			order-preservation of the operators themselves, which is the
			monotonicity of the transport maps $A_{w}$.
			\item As $D \to 0$, solutions converge locally uniformly on
			compact time intervals to the diffusionless flow; for the canonical
			kernel, to the exact solution~(equation eq:exact-solution of the paper).
		\end{enumerate} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:34:33.538197+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a70f390a87961bef2641fa26487d376ea5658643a1a53cf70e854f913929d4c7","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 2 of arXiv:2603.28702, 'Distribution of the magnetization of the critical Ising model on sparse random graphs'] Consider the Ising model on a graph $G\sim G(n,d/n)$ (for $d>1$) at the critical temperature, $\beta_c=\tanh^{-1}(d^{-1})$. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:49:17.487365+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a71199f33b6d47496c9fc4a90aae350201e9e53a7a804dd465decd6dcd5f6c54","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 21 of arXiv:2605.28377, 'Geometric functionals of Brownian motion on Hermitian symmetric spaces of non-compact type'] Let $k_1\ge 1, k_2\ge0$ and $k_3 \in \mathbb{R}$ be such that $k_2+k_3\ge 1$, then for any $\tau,\eta\in\bar{\mathcal{C}}$ we can write
    \[
        p_{t}^{k}(\tau, \eta)
        =
        p_{t}^{k, \text{cont}}(\tau, \eta)
        +
        \sum_{j=1}^{r} p_{t}^{k,  j}(\tau, \eta)
    \]
    where
    \[
        p_{t}^{k, \text{cont}}(\tau, \eta) 
        = 
        \int_{i \mathbb{R}^{r}} e^{-\frac{t}{2}\left(|\lambda|^{2}+|\rho(k)|^{2}\right)} F_{\lambda}(k ; \tau) F_{\lambda}(k ;-\eta) 
        \frac{C d \lambda}{\left|c_{k}(\lambda)\right|^{2}}
    \]
    and 
    \[
        
        p_{t}^{k, j}(\tau, \eta)
        =
        
        \sum_{\xi \in D_{k,j}} 
            d_{j}(\xi, k) 
            \int_{i a^j}
                e^{
                    \frac{t}{2}\left(\langle\xi+\lambda, \xi
                    +
                    \lambda \rangle
                    -
                    |\rho(k)|^{2}\right)
                } 
                F_{\xi+\lambda}( k ; \tau) 
                F_{\xi+\lambda}(k ;-\eta) 
                \frac{C_jd\lambda}{\left|c_{k}^{j}(\xi+\lambda)\right|^{2}}
    \]
    for some constants $C,C_1,\dots,C_r\in\mathbb{C}$ that do not depend on the multiplicities and such that each integral is real-valued---we refer to \cite[Equation~5.8]{honda2024inversion}. In particular, when $k_3\ge-2$, the sum term in $p_t^k$ vanishes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T05:30:36.761711+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a72df9ee1d4f857552cb5a7d7d78037933794d24db69d1999e2bcc1b367ad13e","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 6 (Log-convexity classification for the product of two correlated normal random variables) of arXiv:2607.09499, 'Log-convexity and log-concavity of noncentral gamma sums and differences'] The density $p_Z$ of the product $Z = XY$ is log-convex on $(0,\infty)$ if and only if
\[
\frac{\mu_X}{\sigma_X} + \frac{\mu_Y}{\sigma_Y} = 0.
\]
The density $p_Z$ is log-convex on $(-\infty,0)$ if and only if
\[
\frac{\mu_X}{\sigma_X} - \frac{\mu_Y}{\sigma_Y} = 0.
\]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:33:06.543530+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7552c7039dad5f3094d54a8424605004a9ad5684a9b54f6db870238e0846452","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 24 (Estimates for the standard replacement) of arXiv:2608.25971, 'Positive \texorpdfstring{$\tau$}{tau}-bi-Ricci curvature and Mean curvature flow with surg'] Fix $0<\eta<1$ and an integer $m_0\geq2$.  After fixing
  $\alpha_0^*$ and the surgery parameters in
  Lemma~\ref{lem:surgery-taubiric-preservation}, the neck quality may be
  improved and the surgery radius decreased, without changing
  $\alpha_0^*$, so that there exist
  \begin{equation*}
  \eps_s>0,\qquad
  k_s\geq m_0+2,\qquad
  L_s\geq L_b,\qquad
  r_s>0,
  \end{equation*}
  and constants $c_s>0$, $C_m<\infty$, $0\leq m\leq m_0$, with the
  following property.

  If surgery is performed on an $(\eps,k,L)$-neck of radius $r$ satisfying
  \begin{equation*}
  \eps\leq\eps_s,\qquad
  k\geq k_s,\qquad
  L\geq L_s,\qquad
  r\leq r_s,
  \end{equation*}
  and if \eqref{eq:incoming-surgery-taubiric} holds on the incoming neck,
  then every changed point satisfies
  \begin{align}
    \widetilde P_{ij}^{(\tau)}
    &\geq
    \alpha_0^*\widetilde H
    |\widetilde\lambda_p-\widetilde\lambda_q|,
    \\
    \widetilde P_{ij}^{(\tau)}
    &\geq c_sr^{-2},
    \qquad
    \widetilde H\geq c_sr^{-1},
    \\
    |\widetilde A|^2-
    \left(\frac1{n-1}+\eta\right)\widetilde H^2
    &\leq
    -c_s\widetilde H^2,
    \\
    r^{m+1}|\widetilde\nabla^m\widetilde A|
    &\leq C_m,
    \qquad
    0\leq m\leq m_0.
    
  \end{align}
  The area removed from each changed neck is at least $c_sr^n$, and the
  replacement may be chosen so that
  \begin{equation}
    \min_{\widetilde M}\widetilde H
    \geq
    \min_MH.
  \end{equation}

  If $0<R\leq1$ and
  \begin{equation}
    r\leq\frac{c_sR}{n+\alpha_2},
  \end{equation}
  then the replacement preserves
  $\CC_\tau(R,(\alpha_0^*,\alpha_1,\alpha_2))$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:17:17.101831+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7752a8cfe7368faf53c08fda26a3942a5af5b3bcdbeb8955f3edfc5fd1b0c33","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 9 (Lopatto--Otto Poisson approximation) of arXiv:2608.20101, '\bfseries Largest bulk gap of the complex Ginibre ensemble'] Fix \(\kappa>0\), \(\varepsilon\in(0,1/16)\), and a Borel set

{"assumptions":["X is a compact metric space and T : X -> X is continuous","M(X,T) carries the weak-star topology and is nonempty (guaranteed by Krylov-Bogolyubov)","h*(T) = 0 (asymptotic h-expansiveness); h-expansiveness and expansiveness are sufficient special cases","h_mu(T) is the Kolmogorov-Sinai entropy of the measure-preserving system (X, mu, T)","the existence corollary uses the variational principle, which itself needs only compactness and continuity"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:20:07.090700+00:00","domain":"topological dynamics, entropy, measures of maximal entropy","id":"claim_a77bafb383fb156acf97fdf0ec6338f3cdb7ec81469c4cf42ee27a80550d59df","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a compact metric space, T : X -> X continuous, and let M(X,T) be the set of T-invariant Borel probability measures with the weak-star topology, a nonempty compact convex metrisable set. Suppose T is ASYMPTOTICALLY h-EXPANSIVE, i.e. its tail entropy h*(T) = lim as eps -> 0 of sup over x of h(T, Gamma_eps(x)) vanishes; this holds in particular when T is h-expansive, and a fortiori when T is expansive. THEN the entropy map mu -> h_mu(T) is upper semicontinuous on M(X,T): whenever mu_k -> mu weak-star inside M(X,T), limsup_k h_{mu_k}(T) <= h_mu(T). CONSEQUENCES: an upper semicontinuous function on a nonempty compact set attains its supremum, so by the variational principle a measure of maximal entropy exists and h_top(T) = max over mu in M(X,T) of h_mu(T); the entropy function is then a bounded, affine, upper semicontinuous function on a Choquet simplex, which is what makes the theory of maximal measures and of symbolic extensions run. WHERE IT FAILS: (i) some hypothesis of this kind is necessary. For a general continuous map the entropy map need not be upper semicontinuous and a measure of maximal entropy need not exist; this is why smoothness matters - Newhouse proved that C^infinity diffeomorphisms of compact manifolds are asymptotically h-expansive and therefore always carry maximal measures, while for finite smoothness there are counterexamples. (ii) The conclusion is strictly one-sided and cannot be improved to continuity even for expansive systems: in a mixing shift of finite type the periodic-orbit measures, all of entropy 0, are weak-star dense, so they converge to the measure of maximal entropy and the entropy map is not lower semicontinuous. (iii) Compactness of X (hence of M(X,T)) is what converts upper semicontinuity into existence of a maximiser; on a noncompact space the existence conclusion fails even when the map is upper semicontinuous. (iv) The implication is stated in one direction only: upper semicontinuity of the entropy map is a strictly weaker property than asymptotic h-expansiveness, so do not run the criterion backwards.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:11:57.293553+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a77fb2b8939555101b220306284f1781070ca246e3f2be6a24c056811906d234","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 (Probabilistically weak and strong solutions) of arXiv:2607.22470, 'A Logarithmic Fluctuation Hierarchy for Sequential Interacting Diffusions'] We call
\[
(Y,\mathcal M)
=
\bigl((Y^n)_{n\ge0},(\mathcal M^n)_{n\ge0}\bigr)
\]
a probabilistically weak solution of the limiting logarithmic hierarchy if
there exists a stochastic basis
\[
(\Omega,\mathcal F,(\mathcal F_t)_{t\in[0,T]},\mathbb P)
\]
such that, on this basis, \(Y\) and \(\mathcal M\) have the following
properties.
\begin{enumerate}
\item[(i)] For every \(n\ge0\), \(Y^n\) is a continuous
\((\mathcal F_t)\)-adapted process with values in \(H^{-\beta,-m}\) and has
weakly continuous paths in \(H^{-\beta_\ast}\). Moreover, for some
\(q\in(0,1/4)\),
\begin{equation}
\sum_{n=0}^\infty
q^n
\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}\|Y_t^n\|_{H^{-\beta_\ast}}^2
<\infty.
\end{equation}

\item[(ii)] For every \(n\ge0\), \(\mathcal M^n\) is a continuous
\((\mathcal F_t)\)-adapted process with values in \(H^{-\beta,-m}\), and
\(\mathcal M\), viewed as an \(E^{\mathbb N_0}\)-valued random element, is
centered Gaussian. For every \(n\ge0\) and
\(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\R^d)\),
\[
M_t^n(\varphi):=\langle\mathcal M_t^n,\varphi\rangle
\]
is a continuous \((\mathcal F_t)\)-martingale, and
\begin{equation}
\langle M^n(\varphi),M^k(\psi)\rangle_t
=
\frac{(n+k)!}{n!\,k!}
\int_0^t
\langle
\bar\rho_s,
\nabla\varphi\cdot\nabla\psi
\rangle\,\dd s
\end{equation}
for all \(n,k\ge0\), \(t\in[0,T]\), and
\(\varphi,\psi\in C_c^\infty(\R^d)\).

\item[(iii)] For every \(n\ge0\) and
\(\varphi\in C_c^\infty(\R^d)\), the following identity holds
\(\mathbb P\)-almost surely for all \(t\in[0,T]\):
\begin{align}
\langle Y_t^n,\varphi\rangle
={}&
\langle Y_0^n,\varphi\rangle
+
\int_0^t
\langle Y_s^n,L_s\varphi\rangle\,\dd s\notag\\
&+
\int_0^t
\left\langle
\bar\rho_s,
(K*Y_s^{n+1})\cdot\nabla\varphi
\right\rangle\,\dd s
+
\langle\mathcal M_t^n,\varphi\rangle.

\end{align}
\end{enumerate}

We call \(Y\) a probabilistically strong solution if there exist a stochastic
basis and a process \(\mathcal M\) on it such that \((Y,\mathcal M)\) is a
probabilistically weak solution and \(Y\) is adapted to
the normal filtration generated by
\((Y_0^n)_{n\ge0}\) and \(\mathcal M\).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:48:17.126824+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a785141bc285e5049c06b2b1622193be74bc6e17504a376de2b2a7d4b5ae4cb5","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prp 13 ({\cite[Theorem 2.41) of arXiv:2605.27974, 'Discrete approximation of semi-Dirichlet forms with non-symmetric perturbations of resista'] {Jtolle}}]

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T23:41:03.265807+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a78cb25e0801f2be5999acd2252a87933ab44f745d96f3ade833bdec7c79be36","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm1 of arXiv:2411.08303, 'The discrepancy in min-max statistics between two random matrices with finite third moment'] Let $X$,$X^{\prime}$ be $n \times m$ independent random matrices defined before. Then for every $\beta > 0$, $\delta > 0$ and $\tau >\frac{1}{\beta(1+\delta)}$, we have 
		$$\begin{aligned}
			&\mathbb{P}(|\min_{1 \leq i \leq n}\max_{1 \leq j \leq m}X_{i,j}-\min_{1 \leq i \leq n}\max_{1 \leq j \leq m}X_{i,j}^{\prime}|>2(\frac{\log n}{\beta\delta}\vee \frac{\log m}{\beta})+3\tau)\\		
			\leq& \dfrac{\varepsilon +C\beta(1+\delta)\tau^{-1}(B_1+B_1^{\prime}+B_3+\beta(1+\delta)(B_2+B_2^{\prime}))}{1-\varepsilon}.

		Moreover, if $X$ and $X^\prime$ are Gaussian random matrices, we have $$\begin{aligned}

		\end{aligned}$$

		\begin{align}

		$$\begin{aligned}
			&B_1=\mathbb{E}[\max\limits_{i_1,j_1,i_2,j_2}|X_{i_1,j_1}X_{i_2,j_2}-\mathbb{E}[X_{i_1,j_1}X_{i_2,j_2}]|],\\

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:24:20.608642+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a79aa3af72e46b9f5d2bef562310d08dd0693725a290c10af6529ab7d0a758d9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] Given an element $a\in A$ of a $C^*$-algebra, define its spectrum as:
$$\sigma(a)=\left\{\lambda\in\mathbb C\Big|a-\lambda\notin A^{-1}\right\}$$
The following spectral theory results hold, exactly as in the $A=B(H)$ case:
\begin{enumerate}
\item We have $\sigma(ab)\cup\{0\}=\sigma(ba)\cup\{0\}$.

\item We have $\sigma(f(a))=f(\sigma(a))$, for any $f\in\mathbb C(X)$ having poles outside $\sigma(a)$.

\item The spectrum $\sigma(a)$ is compact, non-empty, and contained in $D_0(||a||)$.

\item The spectra of unitaries $(u^*=u^{-1})$ and self-adjoints $(a=a^*)$ are on $\mathbb T,\mathbb R$.

\item The spectral radius of normal elements $(aa^*=a^*a)$ is given by $\rho(a)=||a||$.
\end{enumerate}

{"assumptions":["two independent centered Gaussian fields on a common finite or suitably truncated index set","existence and enough regularity of the covariance functions to differentiate the interpolated expectation under the integral","a consistent-sign comparison, or specific structural relation, between the two covariance kernels","the test functional F smooth with the correct sign of mixed partial derivatives for the interpolation identity to yield a useful inequality rather than an uncontrolled remainder"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.986351+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7b6b7b2b6ff3d35232e25a83c85018f52e970e60f45507e62d94c80f06513bc","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For two independent centered Gaussian fields X, Y indexed by a common finite (or suitably truncated) set T with covariance functions C_X, C_Y, Kahane's interpolation forms Z(t,u) = sqrt(u) X(t) + sqrt(1-u) Y(t) for u in [0,1] and computes d/du E[F(Z(.,u))] for a smooth test function F, obtaining an integral expression involving (C_Y(s,t) - C_X(s,t)) times a mixed second derivative of F, evaluated against the law of Z(.,u). When C_X <= C_Y pointwise (or the relevant difference has a consistent sign) and F is chosen with matching sign of mixed partials, this yields a comparison inequality between functionals of X and Y, an approach that both generalizes Slepian-type comparisons and, in the Gaussian multiplicative chaos literature, is used to show that different regularizations of a log-correlated field, such as the two-dimensional Gaussian free field, converge to the same limiting chaos measure regardless of the approximation scheme, a key technical step in constructing Liouville quantum gravity measures. It does not apply to non-Gaussian fields, it requires the two fields being compared to be independent for the interpolation construction itself, and the sign or convexity conditions on F needed to obtain a clean inequality must be verified case by case rather than assumed. Typical failure: Applying the interpolation to fields that are not independent, or to a family of regularizations whose covariance difference does not have a consistent sign across the whole index set, which is common when comparing regularizations of a log-correlated field near its singular set; either error breaks the monotonicity the interpolation is meant to exploit, and the resulting comparison can go in the wrong direction with no explicit error term to control it. Canonical reference: Kahane, 1986, Annales des Sciences Mathematiques du Quebec; Robert and Vargas, 2010, Comptes Rendus Mathematique; Berestycki, 2017, Electronic Communications in Probability.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["uniform (or explicitly known-bias) product measure on {-1,1}^n or {0,1}^n","f in the relevant L^p space, typically boolean or bounded","the noise parameter rho within the sharp Bonami-Beckner range 0<=rho<=sqrt((p-1)/(q-1))","a well-defined Fourier-Walsh expansion, i.e. finite n or a suitable limiting argument"],"created_at":"2026-09-07T08:44:20.984732+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7cdeeca3ae5af431b85d8b03bcd9758e011331b5617840dca263851d2163174","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"TECHNIQUE CARD (drafted from a spec by a helper model, every card read and seven corrected by the Fable agent on 2026-09-07; canonical statements only, no original claim). For f: {-1,1}^n -> R with Fourier-Walsh expansion f = sum_S hat{f}(S) chi_S and the noise operator T_rho, which independently resamples each coordinate to a fresh uniform sign with probability (1-rho)/2, the Bonami-Beckner inequality states ||T_rho f||_q <= ||f||_p whenever 1 <= p <= q and 0 <= rho <= sqrt((p-1)/(q-1)). Equivalently, T_rho f = sum_S rho^{|S|} hat{f}(S) chi_S, and the inequality forces the Fourier weight of f on high-degree levels to decay geometrically once rho<1, giving sum_S rho^{2|S|} hat{f}(S)^2 <= (E[|f|^p])^{2/p} for suitable p. This is the central tool converting L^2 Fourier information into higher-moment (typically L^4) control, and it underlies the Kahn-Kalai-Linial theorem on the existence of an influential coordinate, the Benjamini-Kalai-Schramm noise-sensitivity theorems, and Friedgut's junta theorem for low-influence functions. It does not directly give influence bounds without further combination with such machinery, and the sharp constant and range of rho given here hold for the uniform measure on {-1,1}^n; biased-p product measures or non-product (dependent) measures require different, generally weaker, p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractive inequalities. Typical failure: Applying the sharp uniform-measure {-1,1}^n hypercontractive constant to a biased-p product measure or to a dependent measure such as the random-cluster or Ising Gibbs measure without switching to the correct p-biased or dependency-adjusted hypercontractivity inequality, whose constants generally degrade as p approaches 0 or 1; this silently invalidates quantitative noise-sensitivity conclusions claimed for critical percolation at p != 1/2 or for genuinely non-product models. Canonical reference: Bonami, 1970, Annales de l'Institut Fourier; Beckner, 1975, Annals of Mathematics; O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, 2014, Cambridge University Press.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} Boolean, uniform product measure","c is a universal constant","the conclusion bounds only the MAXIMUM influence, not any specific coordinate"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:37.628283+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7d3fa81d9e828619a0897ad9b5e1de549e37211c93fe093b3a6f7e2f0ac728c","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let f : {-1,1}^n -> {0,1} be a Boolean function on the uniform product measure, and define the influence of coordinate i as Inf_i(f) = P( f(X) != f(X^{(i)}) ) where X^{(i)} flips the i-th coordinate. Then there is a universal constant c > 0 with max_{i <= n} Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n / n, where Var(f) = p(1-p) with p = E[f]. Equivalently the TOTAL influence satisfies sum_i Inf_i(f) >= c Var(f) log n. The bound is SHARP up to the constant: the tribes function, a read-once DNF on blocks of size about log_2 n - log_2 log_2 n, is balanced and has all influences of order log n / n. The theorem is about the uniform measure on the cube; the analogous statement for p-biased measures carries an extra factor and is the Friedgut-Kalai sharp-threshold machinery. Note what it does NOT say: it does not bound the influence of any PARTICULAR coordinate, only the maximum, and it says nothing when Var(f) is 0, that is when f is constant. [Kahn, Kalai and Linial (1988); see O'Donnell, Analysis of Boolean Functions, Chapter 9]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T16:53:30.575601+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7d6391b3fbc0bd6a5210a42a61abaeb229f2ed2ea70c7c8a749750754005fcf","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def-point function of arXiv:2505.24043, 'Weak solutions of Navier-Stokes Equation with purely discontinuous L\'evy Noise'] Suppose that $X $ is a non-empty set. A point function on $X $ is a partial function, \textit{i.e.},\ a functional binary relation,
$$ p \subset (0,\infty) \times X .$$
which is  at most a countable set.\\
If $p$ is a point function on $X $ then we define
\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm{Dom}(p)&=\mathrm{D}_p:=\bigl\{ t \in (0,\infty): p \cap (\{t\} \times X) \not= \emptyset\}
\\&
=\bigl\{ t \in (0,\infty):  \mbox{ there exists an element } x\in X: (t,x) \in  p \}.
\end{aligned}
\]
 \\
If $t\in \mathrm{Dom}(p)$, then we will denote by $p(t)$ the value of $p$ at $t$, i.e.\ the unique element $x\in X$ such that $ (t,x) \in  p $.\\
Moreover, when we will write $p(t)$ we will implicitly understand   that  $t\in \mathrm{Dom}(p)$. 

The family of all point functions on $X$ will be denoted by $\Pi_X$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["No finiteness, countability or uniformity assumption on the family;","values in the extended reals are allowed."],"created_at":"2026-09-12T14:01:51.298864+00:00","domain":"real analysis, topology","id":"claim_a7d6b373429f32266ad5157b4e9a016da414a695cb09150843502c65cad89b8f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and let (f_i) be an arbitrary family of functions on X with values in the extended reals. If every f_i is upper semicontinuous - in particular if every f_i is continuous - then the pointwise infimum inf_i f_i is upper semicontinuous. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:06.979709+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7f23fe4bfd112e666c94a47b34a15aaccf1ff90a8f4e1df9b66b94c53217f09","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def2_2 of arXiv:2607.26169, 'Scaling and partial universality of the height zero probability in the 2D Abelian sandpile'] Let $U\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ be a connected region with boundary \(\partial U\), satisfying
    Assumption (a:U of the paper). Fix \(\epsilon > 0\).
    \begin{itemize}
        \item Let $f : \epsilon\mathcal{V} \rightarrow \mathbb{R}$ and let $e = (z,w)$ be an oriented edge of $(\varepsilon\mathcal{V}, \varepsilon \mathcal{E})$. 
        Define the discrete derivative $\partial_e$ to be the operator given by 
            \[
                (\partial_e f)(x) = f(w) - f(z) 
                = f(z+e) - f(z), \quad x \in \varepsilon\mathcal{V}.
            \] 
        \item We define the discrete Laplace operator $\Delta$
            \[
                (\Delta f)(z) = \sum_{e \in \varepsilon\mathcal{E} : e_- = z} (f(z)-f(e_+)) 
                = -\sum_{e} \partial_e f(z), \quad z\in\varepsilon\mathcal{V}.
            \]
        \item A function \(f : U_\epsilon \cup \partial U_\epsilon \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\) is said to be discrete harmonic in \(U_\epsilon\) if it satisfies \(\Delta f = 0\) in \(U_\epsilon\). (For the purposes of computing $(\Delta f)(z)$ when $z \in U_\varepsilon$ 
        and $e \in \partial U_\varepsilon$ with $e_- = z$, the value of $f$ at $e_+$ is taken to be $f(e)$.)
        \item For a given function \(g : \partial U_\epsilon \rightarrow \mathbb{R}\), $f$ is said to be the solution to the discrete Laplace equation with Dirichlet boundary condition \(g\) if, in addition, \(f = g\) on \(\partial U_\epsilon\).
        \end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149018+00:00","domain":"elliptic partial differential equations, maximum principles","id":"claim_a7ff9de16f2bbefc6c4fe4f5adbe349d50f8611965c390800f138c4833c83567","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: c <= 0 in the nondivergence convention Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu (equivalently c >= 0 in the divergence convention -div(A grad u) + b.grad u + cu). Second, finer point: even with c <= 0 the conclusion is only sup u <= sup over the boundary of u^+ and not sup u <= sup over the boundary of u. Example: on (-1,1), u(x) = -cosh x satisfies u'' - u = 0 (so c = -1 <= 0), u(0) = -1 while u(-1) = u(1) = -cosh 1 which is about -1.543; the interior supremum strictly exceeds the boundary supremum, and only the truncation at 0 saves the statement. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-28T01:29:08.782564+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a7ff9e6e768db2042daa88a08e9773bc148ad4eca5417690be72deb9a539e69a","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn subexp of arXiv:2412.00593, 'A new approach to strong convergence II.\\The classical ensembles'] An \emph{operator space} is a closed subspace of a 
$C^*$-algebra. A finite-dimensional operator space $\mathbf{W}$ is called
\begin{enumerate}[$\bullet$]
\itemsep\smallskipamount
\item 
\emph{exact} if for every $C>1$, there exists $S\in\mathbb{N}$ and a
linear embedding $u:\mathbf{W}\to\mathrm{M}_S(\mathbb{C})$ such that
for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $x\in \mathbf{W}\otimes\mathrm{M}_N(\mathbb{C})$, we have
$$
	\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\| \le
	\|x\| \le C\|(u\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|;
$$
\item \emph{$C$-subexponential} if there exists
$D_N\in\mathbb{N}$ with $D_N=e^{o(N)}$ and a linear embedding 
$f_N:\mathbf{W}\to\mathrm{M}_{D_N}(\mathbb{C})$ such that
for every $N\in\mathbb{N}$ and $x\in \mathbf{W}\otimes\mathrm{M}_N(\mathbb{C})$, we have
$$
	\|(f_N\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\| \le
	\|x\| \le C\|(f_N\otimes\mathrm{id})(x)\|.
$$
\end{enumerate}
An operator space $\mathbf{W}$ is called exact or $C$-subexponential if 
every finite-dimensional subspace of $\mathbf{W}$ is exact or 
$C$-subexponential, respectively. The subexponential constant of an
operator space
$\mathbf{W}$ is $C(\mathbf{W}) := \inf\{C:\mathbf{W}\text{ is }C\text{-subexponential}\}$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:36:23.146881+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a80b2ba814ada8069fb5068dd32102538e407ed20565459878e45f27ddbe622c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition definition131 of arXiv:2507.05417, 'Invertibility for non-Hermitian and symmetric random band matrices with sublinear bandwidt'] Consider a random matrix $A_n=V\odot W$, where $V$ is a $n\times n$ deterministic matrix with non-negative entries, and $W$ is an $n\times n$ random matrix with real or complex entries. The symbol $\odot$ denotes entrywise product, or Hadamard product, so that $a_{ij}=v_{ij}w_{ij}$ where we write $A=(a_{ij}),B=(b_{ij})$, $W=(w_{ij})$. 
    
    
    Let $d_n\in\mathbb{N}$ be a sequence of integers with $1\leq d_n\leq n$. We assume the following conditions on the randomness $W$:
        \begin{enumerate}
        \item The entries $w_{ij}$ of $W$ are independent random variables with mean 0, variance 1. 
        \item The entries  $w_{ij}$ of $W$ are uniformly anticoncentrated in the following sense: we can find some $\beta\in(0,1)$ such that 
        \begin{enumerate}\item When $w_{ij}$ is real-valued, then $\mathcal{L}(w_{ij},1)\leq \beta$ for each $i,j=1,\cdots,n$. \item  When $w_{ij}$ are complex valued, then its real and complex parts, denoted by $w_{ij}^\Re,w_{ij}^\Im$, are independent random variables satisfying that $\mathcal{L}(w_{ij}^\Re,\frac{1}{2})\leq \beta$ and $\mathcal{L}(w_{ij}^\Im,\frac{1}{2})\leq \beta$ for each $i,j=1,\cdots,n$.
        \end{enumerate}
    \end{enumerate}

    We assume the following conditions on the variance $V$: we can find positive constants $C_V^1,C_V^2,C_V^3$ independent of $n$ such that 
    \begin{enumerate}
        \item The entries close to diagonal are bounded from below and above:
        $$
C_V^1\leq v_{ij}\leq C_V^2\quad \forall 1\leq i,j\leq n:|i-j|\leq d_n.
        $$
        \item Bounded norm for each row: for each $i=1,\cdots,n$ we have
        $$\sum_{j=1}^n v_{ij}^2\leq C_V^3 \cdot d_n.
        $$
    \end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:53:00.818877+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a8241f9b7631cea869b291347fb6b5111f2053452f8e10f19ee65b153dfd3046","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition eqn: Gaussian kernel of arXiv:2607.17393, 'Optimal Covariance Estimates for Schr\"odinger Semigroups with White Noise in $d=1,2$'] Throughout the paper, we denote the $d$-dimensional
Gaussian kernel as
\begin{align}

p_t(x)=\frac{e^{-|x|^2/2t}}{(2\pi t)^{d/2}},\qquad t>0,~ x\in\mathbb R^d.
\end{align}
Then, for every $\epsilon>0$, we define
$\xi_\epsilon=\xi*p_{\epsilon/2}$,
where $*$ denotes the convolution. Since the Gaussian
kernel is smooth, so is $\xi_\epsilon$. Moreover,
given that $p_s*p_t=p_{s+t}$ and $p_t(x)=p_t(-x)$ is even,
for every $\epsilon_1,\epsilon_2>0$, we have the
covariance identity
\begin{align}

\mathbb E[\xi_{\epsilon_1}(x)\xi_{\epsilon_2}(y)]=p_{(\epsilon_1+\epsilon_2)/2}(y-x),
\qquad x,y\in\mathbb R^d.
\end{align}
In particular, $\xi_\epsilon$ is a centered Gaussian process with covariance kernel $p_\epsilon$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:11:11.713563+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a828e587eef79b836d42cdb561655494d14049b00ffe01133cf0085d00e7fc7e","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:singular-exponent-ledger of arXiv:2609.00698, 'Kinetic Wedge Layers and Diffusive Limit of Neutron Transport in Polygonal Domains'] Let $\mathsf d$ be an admissible hierarchy depth and fix a vertex $V_m$. The \emph{singular-exponent index set} $\mathscr I_m(\mathsf d)$, together with auxiliary sets $\mathscr D_{m,k}$ of \emph{order-$k$ differentiated slots}, is the smallest pair of families of entries $\mathfrak l=(m,k,\lambda,b;\mathsf t)$, with $0\le k\le N$, $b\in\mathbb N_0$ and $\mathsf t\in\mathscr T$, satisfying the clauses below. Every clause is monotone in the pair, so the intersection of all pairs satisfying them is again one, and the smallest pair exists.

\begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(L\arabic*)},leftmargin=*,itemsep=0.3em]

\item \emph{Primitive endpoint seeds.} For $0\le k\le2$, $i=1,2$ and every integer $n\ge0$, the entry $(m,k,n,0;e_i)$.

\item \emph{Positive pencil seeds.} For $0\le k\le N$ and every $n\in\mathbb N$ with $\lambda_{m,n}=n\pi/\omega_m<\mathsf d-k$, the entry $(m,k,\lambda_{m,n},0;\rho)$.

\item \emph{Differentiation.} If $(m,k-1,\lambda,b;\mathsf t)$ is an entry with $\mathsf t\in\{U,\mathrm{SL}_1,\mathrm{SL}_2\}$, then so are $(m,k,\lambda-1,b;\mathsf t)$ and, when $b\ge1$, $(m,k,\lambda-1,b-1;\mathsf t)$. Both are placed in $\mathscr D_{m,k}$ as well.

\item \emph{End state.} If $(m,k,\lambda,b;U)\in\mathscr D_{m,k}$ or $(m,k,\lambda,b;\mathrm{SL}_i)\in\mathscr D_{m,k}$, then $(m,k,\lambda,b;e_i)$ is an entry.

\item \emph{Ray lift and resonance.} If $(m,k,\lambda,b;e_i)$ is an entry, then so is $(m,k,\lambda,c;\rho)$ for every $0\le c\le b+\iota_{\rm res}(\lambda)$.

\item \emph{Total interior profile.} If $(m,k,\lambda,b;\rho)$ is an entry, then so is $(m,k,\lambda,b;U)$.

\item \emph{Side layer.} If $(m,k,\lambda,b;U)$ is an entry, or $(m,k,\lambda,b;e_i)$ is a seed of \textup{(L1)}, then $(m,k,\lambda,b;\mathrm{SL}_i)$ is an entry.

\item \emph{Truncation.} An entry is retained only when $\alpha(\mathfrak l)=k+\lambda<\mathsf d$. A clause whose output violates this bound creates no entry, and the truncation creates none.

\item \emph{Duplicates.} Entries are tuples, so coincident tuples arising from different clauses are one entry, with their contributions added. Nothing is retained with multiplicity.

\item \emph{Padding.} A tuple present at one tag, one ray or one order and absent at another is read in every coefficientwise comparison as present there with coefficient zero, as in (equation eq:mellin-ray-data-comp of the paper). All objects of index $-1$ are zero.
\end{enumerate}
The two families are related as follows. Clause \textup{(L3)} is the only one that writes into $\mathscr D_{m,k}$, and it writes each output into both families, so
\begin{align}
 \mathscr D_{m,k}
 \subseteq
 \bigl\{\mathfrak l\in\mathscr I_m(\mathsf d):
 \text{$\mathfrak l$ has order }k,\
 \mathsf t(\mathfrak l)\in\{U,\mathrm{SL}_1,\mathrm{SL}_2\}\bigr\},
 
\end{align}
and the inclusion is in general strict. An order-$k$ entry created by \textup{(L6)} from a $\rho$ slot, or by \textup{(L7)}, belongs to $\mathscr I_m(\mathsf d)$ but is recorded in $\mathscr D_{m,k}$ only if \textup{(L3)} produces it as well. So $\mathscr D_{m,k}$ isolates provenance rather than value. It holds the slots that reach order $k$ by differentiating order-$(k-1)$ slots, as against those created within order $k$ by the solves themselves. In particular $\mathscr D_{m,k}$ is determined by the order-$(k-1)$ part of $\mathscr I_m(\mathsf d)$ alone, so it is fixed before any order-$k$ solve is performed, and $\mathscr D_{m,0}=\varnothing$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X integrable with X in an open interval I almost surely","phi convex on I","E[phi(X)^-] < infinity, so that E[phi(X) | G] is defined"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752623+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a82c08a702478464e662ccbbaeeea30b77120ba9b85679d10ca8d340f884bc36","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be an integrable random variable taking values almost surely in an open interval I of R, let phi : I -> R be convex, and let G be a sub-sigma-algebra. If phi(X) is integrable, or more generally if E[phi(X)^-] < infinity so that E[phi(X) | G] is well defined in (-infinity, +infinity], then phi(E[X | G]) <= E[phi(X) | G] almost surely. Taking G trivial recovers the unconditional Jensen inequality. Two hypotheses do real work: X must lie in the interval where phi is convex, and some one-sided integrability of phi(X) is needed for the right-hand side to be defined. Convexity cannot be weakened to midpoint convexity without measurability, and the inequality REVERSES for concave phi. A standard consequence is that for a convex phi and a martingale (M_n), the process phi(M_n) is a submartingale whenever it is integrable. [standard; e.g. Durrett, Probability: Theory and Examples, 5th ed., Theorem 4.1.10]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:32:28.993192+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a8373ad786cbe44d360b50a6afe09e7c460c8cd264d584d81b990bdca4028aa2","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Problem prob:planar of arXiv:2608.23545, 'Eulerian walkers on $\Z^2$ have range exponent $2/3$'] For which doubly periodic plane graphs does Theorem~(thm:main of the paper) hold? {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.039011+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a84116062dfde697eb4950949c21dc5cb21c39c4bad0177193c37aed3b478650","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 25 (Three involutions, and which one acts on
starting sites) of arXiv:2608.15805, 'Spectral duality structures and the Fisher--Rao geometry of reset distributions'] Let $O=\{z,\sigma(z)\}$ be an orbit and write
$\alpha=\kappa(z)^{1/4}$, $\beta=\kappa(\sigma(z))^{1/4}$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item[\textup{(i)}] The site involution $\sigma$ acts on
$\mathbb R^m$ by the permutation matrix exchanging the coordinates
of each orbit; it is defined on all of $\Delta_{m-1}$, maps
vertices to vertices, $e_z\mapsto e_{\sigma(z)}$, and on the orbit
plane is the reflection across the diagonal $\mathbb R(1,1)$.
\item[\textup{(ii)}] The spherical reflection $R_L$ is defined on
all of $S^{m-1}(2)$ and fixes $\Phi(\Sigma^\circ)$ pointwise; on
the orbit plane it is the reflection across
$\mathbb R\,\mathbf e_O$, with matrix
\[
\frac1{\alpha^2+\beta^2}
\begin{pmatrix}\beta^2-\alpha^2 & 2\alpha\beta\\
2\alpha\beta & \alpha^2-\beta^2\end{pmatrix}.
\]
\item[\textup{(iii)}] The induced simplex map
$\iota=\Phi^{-1}R_L\Phi$ is defined only on the open set
$U\subseteq\Delta^\circ_{m-1}$ of
Proposition~\ref{prop:reflective}\textup{(ii)}. In particular it is
\emph{not defined at the vertices}, which lie on
$\partial\Delta_{m-1}$.
\item[\textup{(iv)}] $R_L$ and $\sigma$ agree on the orbit plane if
and only if $\alpha=\beta$, that is $\kappa(z)=\kappa(\sigma(z))$
--- in the canonical realisation, precisely the unbiased walk
$p=q$. Moreover they are not conjugate by any diagonal weighting:
$D\sigma D^{-1}$ has vanishing diagonal on the orbit plane for
every diagonal $D$, whereas the diagonal of $R_L$ is
$\pm(\beta^2-\alpha^2)/(\alpha^2+\beta^2)$.
\end{enumerate}
Consequently every statement in this section about starting sites
is a statement about $\sigma$ alone. The reflection $\iota$ plays
no role here; what $D$ relates is not the two involutions but their
eigenspace data, $D\Sigma\subseteq E^{+}$ and $D^{-1}V=E^{-}$
\textup{(}Remark~\ref{rem:sectors}\textup{)}.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:38:37.403343+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a846b8468b125845887a8b7a2039c5031569c5ea5176313bbdb4f380293ca852","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Defn 3 of arXiv:2605.15501, 'Well-posedness of the obstacle problem for generalized Dean--Kawasaki equation\thanks{ The'] Let $u_{\mathrm{init}}\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$
be nonnegative and $\mathcal{F}_{0}$-measurable.
A stochastic kinetic solution of the obstacle problem for \eqref{eq:main} is a pair $(u,\nu)$, where $u\in L^{1}(\Omega\times[0,T];L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))$ is a nonnegative, $L^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d})$-valued $\mathcal{F}_{t}$-predictable function, and $\nu$ is a predictable Radon measure on $Q_T$ satisfying the following properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] Almost surely $u\leq \psi$, and $\mathbb{E}[\nu(Q_T)]<\infty$.

\item[(ii)] Preservation of mass: almost surely for every $\phi\in C_c^{\infty}([0,T))$,
\begin{align}
    -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u(x,s)\partial_s\phi(s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s+\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(s)\mathrm{d}\nu(x,s)=\phi(0)\int_{\mathbb{T}^d} u_{\mathrm{init}}\mathrm{d}x.
\end{align}
\item[(iii)] The initial condition: almost surely
\begin{align}
\lim_{\tau\to0}\frac{1}{\tau}\int_0^{\tau}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}|u(x,t)-u_{\mathrm{init}}(x)|\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}t=0.
\end{align}
\item[(iv)]  $\sigma(u)\in L^{2}(\Omega;L^{2}(Q_T))$, \quad $g(u)\in L^{1}(\Omega;L^{1}(Q_T;\mathbb{R}^d))$.

\item[(v)] For every $K\in\mathbb{N}$,
\[
[(u\land K)\lor(1/K)]\in L^{2}(\Omega\times[0,T];H^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}))).
\]
\end{itemize}
Furthermore, there exists a kinetic measure $q$ satisfying the following three properties.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(vi)] Almost surely as a nonnegative measure, $q$ satisfies
\[
\delta_{0}(\xi-u)\Phi^{\prime}(\xi)|\nabla u|^{2}\leq q\quad\text{on}\quad\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T].
\]
\item[(vii)] (Vanishing)
\[
\lim_{N\to\infty}\mathbb{E}\big[q(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times[N,N+1]\times[0,T))\big]=0.
\]
\item[(viii)] For every $\phi\in C_{c}^{1}(\mathbb{T}^{d}\times(0,\infty)\times[0,T))$, the kinetic function $\chi$ of $u$ almost surely satisfies
\begin{align}
& -\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\chi(x,\xi,s)\partial_s\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi\mathrm{d}s\\
 & =\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\bar{\chi}(u_{\mathrm{init}},\xi)\phi(x,\xi,0)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}\xi-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Phi^{\prime}(u)\nabla u\cdot(\nabla\phi)(x,u,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\big(F_{1}(x)[\sigma^{\prime}(u)]^{2}\nabla u+\sigma(u)\sigma^{\prime}(u)F_{2}(x)\big)\cdot(\nabla\phi)(x,u,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber\\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\partial_{\xi}\phi(x,\xi,s)\mathrm{d}q(x,\xi,s)-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^d}\phi(x,u,s)\nabla\cdot g(u)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad+\frac{1}{2}\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\Big(\sigma(u)\sigma^{\prime}(u)\nabla u\cdot F_{2}(x)+\sigma^{2}(u)F_{3}(x)\Big)(\partial_{\xi}\phi)(x,u,s)\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}s\nonumber \\
 & \quad-\int_{0}^{T}       \int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,\psi,s)\mathrm{d}\nu(x,s)-\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{T}^{d}}\phi(x,u,s)\nabla\cdot(\sigma(u)f_{k})\mathrm{d}x\mathrm{d}B_{s}^{k}.\nonumber
\end{align}
\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X and Y are Banach spaces over the same field","T is a bounded linear operator from X to Y"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.571248+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Fredholm theory","id":"claim_a8d654dd18a265403bd8a3b84aa51c1024872fabf26f962e91167e35b5920dca","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X and Y be Banach spaces and T in B(X,Y) a bounded linear operator. T is a Fredholm operator if (a) its kernel ker T is finite-dimensional and (b) its range ran T has finite codimension, i.e. the quotient vector space Y / ran T is finite-dimensional. The index of a Fredholm operator is the integer ind T = dim ker T - dim(Y / ran T). The range of a Fredholm operator is automatically closed (a bounded operator between Banach spaces whose range has finite algebraic codimension has closed range), so texts that add 'ran T is closed' to the definition define the same class. For Fredholm T one has dim(Y / ran T) = dim ker T', where T': Y' -> X' is the Banach-space adjoint, so ind T = dim ker T - dim ker T'. Examples on l^2: an invertible operator has index 0; the unilateral shift S(x_1, x_2, ...) = (0, x_1, x_2, ...) is injective with range of codimension 1, so ind S = -1, and its adjoint (the backward shift) has index +1; I + K with K compact has index 0. The set of Fredholm operators X -> Y is written Phi(X,Y).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["R associative with identity; 'semisimple' means semisimple as a left module over itself (equivalent to the right-module version)","the division rings need not be commutative (the real quaternions H occur, e.g. in R[Q_8])"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:31:12.479831+00:00","domain":"ring theory and representation theory","id":"claim_a8dff8cc7fd1ebc995d2f1c2cd5a96f7c66d395874540b73e9f3e7c21eab6fcc","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"A ring R (associative, with 1) is semisimple - every left R-module is a direct sum of simple modules, equivalently R is a finite direct sum of simple left modules, equivalently R is left Artinian with zero Jacobson radical - if and only if R is isomorphic to a finite product of matrix rings over division rings: R = M_{n_1}(D_1) x ... x M_{n_r}(D_r). The integers r and n_i and the division rings D_i (up to isomorphism) are determined by R: r is the number of isomorphism classes of simple left R-modules, and the simple module S_i = D_i^{n_i} has End_R(S_i) = D_i (opposite conventions aside). A simple left Artinian ring is a single matrix ring M_n(D). Consequences: for a finite group G and a field k of characteristic not dividing |G| (Maschke), the group algebra k[G] is semisimple, so k[G] = prod M_{n_i}(D_i); over an algebraically closed field the D_i are k itself, the n_i are the degrees of the irreducible representations, r is the number of conjugacy classes, and |G| = sum n_i^2. A commutative semisimple ring is a finite product of fields. Wedderburn's little theorem (finite division rings are fields) then gives: a finite semisimple ring is a product of matrix rings over finite fields.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:30:24.619813+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a8eb4256b0023a963321ef3f509435f3f05676eb92ad77aba4a4d19ff24ecbfd","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 20 (Rough weak solution) of arXiv:2506.09637, 'Nonlinear Stochastic Filtering with Volterra Gaussian Noises'] A finite measure-valued path
\(
    \varkappa:[0,T]\to\mathcal M_f(\mathbb R)
\)
is called a rough weak solution of the rough Zakai equation if for every \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\), the path
\(\varkappa^\epsilon\), constructed using smooth approximating paths of $\hat J$, satisfies the weak Zakai equation
\begin{equation}
\begin{aligned}
    \varkappa_t^\epsilon(\phi)
    &=
    \varkappa_0^\epsilon(\phi)
    +
    \int_0^t
        \varkappa_s^\epsilon\bigl(A_{Y_s^\epsilon}\phi\bigr)\,
        dc^\epsilon(s)        \\
    &\quad
    +
    \int_0^t
        \varkappa_s^\epsilon
        \bigl(\mathscr f(\cdot,Y_s^\epsilon)\phi\bigr)\,
        d\hat Y_s^\epsilon
    -
    \frac12
    \int_0^t
        \varkappa_s^\epsilon
        \bigl(f(\cdot,Y_s^\epsilon)^2\phi\bigr)\,ds 
\end{aligned}
\end{equation}
and for every \(\phi\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\),
\[
    \sup_{t\in[0,T]}
    \left|
        \varkappa_t^\epsilon(\phi)-\varkappa_t(\phi)
    \right|
    \to 0 .
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.349462+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a92498367fe58854a9a798399bcf45fca47089064441a3fc5204baf9947d404f","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Cor 170 (quenched second moment bounds for $Y^{\RomI}$ and $Y^{\RomI,\frozen}$) of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For $N$ large enough, we have
	\beq
	\max\bigg\{
	\bE\Big[\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big]
	: 0 \le d\le \dmax-1
	\bigg\}
    \le L^{O(1)} \delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2
    \,,
    \eeq
with $\MAX_N$ as in Proposition~\ref{p:Y.kolmogorov}. The same bound holds with $\vY^\frozen$ in place of $\vY$. 

\begin{proof} It follows using
Lemma~\ref{l:X.Y.discrep} that
	\[\bE\Big(
	\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big)
	\le \bE\Big( \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))^2\Big)
	+ O(\eta)\bigg\{ \bE\Big| \Delta X^{\trunc,\RomI}(q_d,a(q_{d+1}))\Big|
	+ \eta\bigg\}\,.\]
From the spatial rerandomization (Definition~\ref{d:rerand}), the index $a(q_{d+1})$ is a uniformly random sample from $[M]$, even if we condition on the gaussian disorder. Thus we can apply Proposition~\ref{p:X.second.mmt.quenched} with $a(q_{d+1})$ in place of $\hat{a}$. Together with Jensen's inequality and \eqref{e:deriv.p.bound}, it implies
	\[
	\bE\Big[\Delta Y^{\RomI}(q_d)^2\Big]
    \le L^{O(1)}\Big\{ \delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2
    + \eta^2\Big\}
    \le L^{O(1)}\delta^2 (\MAX_N)^2\,,
	\]
using that $\MAX_N\ge1$ and $\eta\ll\delta$ from Assumption~\ref{a:params}. This proves \eqref{e:Y.I.second.quenched}, and the analogous bound for $Y^{\frozen,\RomI}$ follows by the same argument.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:02:34.838012+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a93177c98fdc12003afe78d16a072fe14eedaff0d0f718f16ee64c65c2ee1f71","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 6 (Configuration-space factorization of the Palm-cell volume) of arXiv:2607.20680, 'Exact Scale--Shape Factorization of the Typical Poisson--Voronoi Cell Volume in Arbitrary '] Let \(K=N(C_0)\). Then the quantities defined in \eqref{eq:p-def} are the facet-number probabilities:
\begin{equation*}
  \mathbb P(K=k)=p_{d,k},
  \qquad k\geq d+1.
\end{equation*}

For every \(k\) with \(p_{d,k}>0\), let \(\bfx\) have distribution \(\mathsf P_{d,k,\lambda}\), and define
\begin{equation*}
  T_k=Q(\bfx),
  \qquad
  U_k=Q(\bfx)^{-1/d}\bfx\in\Sigma_{d,k}.
\end{equation*}
Then their joint distribution is the product measure
\begin{equation}
  
  \mathsf P_{d,k,\lambda}
  \{T_k\in\dd t,U_k\in\dd\bfu\}
  =
  \frac{\lambda^k}{\Gamma(k)}
  t^{k-1}e^{-\lambda t}\,\dd t\,
  \nu_{d,k}(\dd\bfu).
\end{equation}
In particular,
\begin{equation*}
  T_k\sim
  \operatorname{Gamma}\bigl(k,\operatorname{rate}=\lambda\bigr),
  \qquad
  U_k\sim\nu_{d,k},
  \qquad
  T_k\perp U_k.
\end{equation*}

Writing
\[
A_k=\alpha(U_k)=\frac{G(U_k)}{Q(U_k)}=G(U_k),
\]
the conditional Palm-cell volume satisfies
\begin{equation}
  
  V_{d,\lambda}\mid\{K=k\}
  \overset{\mathrm d}=T_kA_k,
\end{equation}
where
\[
A_k\sim\eta_{d,k},
\qquad
T_k\perp A_k.
\]

Equivalently, for the intensity-normalized cell volume
\[
Y_d=\lambda V_{d,\lambda},
\]
one may construct \(K\) with \(\mathbb P(K=k)=p_{d,k}\) and, conditionally on \(K=k\), independent random variables
\[
A_k\sim\eta_{d,k},
\qquad
Z_k\sim\operatorname{Gamma}(k,\operatorname{rate}=1),
\]
such that
\begin{equation}
  
  Y_d\overset{\mathrm d}=A_KZ_K.
\end{equation}
Values assigned on strata with \(p_{d,k}=0\) are immaterial.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:58:10.026338+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a93392eb07a1410824caa99228b57f8b70681a835ecefc6187a512eead4d3a52","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:cesaro of arXiv:2607.19844, 'Binomial probabilities at a fixed distance from the mode:\\ size-biasing and the complete '] Let $0<p<1$ and $h_N=\lceil Np\rceil-Np$.

Then the following identities hold:

=\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ii}^2+2\sum_{i<j}P_{ij}^2.

\item[(ii)]
\[
\mathsf{Tr}[P]^2=\Big(\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ii}\Big)^2
=\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ii}^2+2\sum_{i<j}P_{ii}P_{jj}.
\]
Equivalently,
\[
\sum_{i<j}P_{ii}P_{jj}=\frac12\Big(\mathsf{Tr}(P)^2-\sum_i P_{ii}^2\Big).
\]

\item[(iii)]
\[
\mathsf{Tr}[PDP]=\sum_{i,j=1}^n P_{ij}D_{jj}P_{ji}
=\sum_{j=1}^n D_{jj}\sum_{i=1}^n P_{ij}^2
=\mathsf{Tr}(P)+\sum_{j=1}^n D_{jj}\sum_{i\neq j}P_{ij}^2.
\]
Therefore,
\begin{equation}
\mathsf{Tr}[PDP]-\mathsf{Tr}[P]=\sum_{j=1}^n D_{jj}\sum_{i\neq j}P_{ij}^2
=\sum_{i<j}(D_{ii}+D_{jj})P_{ij}^2.
\end{equation}
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

\]

\[
\theta_{n}(t)
:=
\frac{
\#\{1\le k\le\lfloor nt\rfloor:\ k = r \, ({\rm mod}\, q)\}}{\Theta_n
},
\,\,   t\in[0, 1].

0.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:22:08.474853+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a9783454000d961a7316e47a691fe9b7835f4345aa631bc50430782d1eda293a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary of arXiv:2607.29020, 'Entropic Symmetrization Resistance'] Let $X = (X_1, \dots, X_d) \in_R \{\pm1\}^d$ with asymmetric coordinates $X_i$. 
Let $Y = (Y_1, \dots, Y_d) \in \Sym(X)$ with independent coordinates $Y_1, \dots Y_d$. 
Then, $H(Y) \ge H(X)$, with equality if and only if the following conditions are both satisfied: 

\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item For all $i \in [d]$, $f_{Y_i} = f_{-X_i}$,
\item the random variables $X_i$ are mutually independent. 
\end{enumerate}

Also, if $X_1 = \pm X_2 = \dots = \pm X_d$ (with any choice of signs), then $H(Y) \ge dH(X)$ with equality if and only if (i) is satisfied. 
\begin{proof}
Clearly 
\[ H(Y) 

= \sum_{i \in [d]} H(Y_i)
\ge \sum_{i \in [d]} H(X_i)
\ge \sum_{i \in [d]} H(X_i \mid X_1, \dots X_{i-1})
= H(X). \]

Equality conditions are clear from the analysis in the proof of (thm:hypercube_entropy of the paper). 
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:43:16.156210+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a97ca19ddb5fb919add071486d38c457f3dbdd5dd0b08cc0c20360ead5f05a30","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 4 of arXiv:2604.13845, 'Minkowski content construction of\\ the CLE gasket measure'] Let $D \subsetneq \C$ be a simply connected domain.  Fix $N \in \N_0$ and let $\ul{x} = (x_1,\ldots,x_{2N})$ be a collection of distinct prime ends which are ordered counterclockwise.
\begin{enumerate}[(i)]
\item We call $(D;\ul{x})$ a \emph{marked domain}. Let $\markeddomain{2N}$ be the collection of marked domains with $2N$ marked points.
\item Suppose that $(D;\ul{x}) \in \markeddomain{2N}$, and we have a non-crossing collection of paths $\ul{\gamma} = (\gamma_1,\ldots,\gamma_N)$ outside of $D$ where each $\gamma_i$ connects a distinct pair of marked points. The paths $\ul{\gamma}$ induce a planar link pattern $\beta$ on the exterior of $D$, formally described by a partition of the marked points into pairs $\beta = \{\{a_1,b_1\},\ldots,\{a_N,b_N\}\}$ where $\{a_1,b_1,\ldots,a_N,b_N\} = \{1,\ldots,2N\}$, $a_r<b_r$, and such that the configuration $a_r<a_s<b_r<b_s$ does not occur. We let $\eldomain{2N}$ be the collection of exterior link pattern decorated marked domains.
\item Suppose that $(D;\ul{x}) \in \markeddomain{2N}$, and we have a non-crossing collection of paths $\ul{\eta} = (\eta_1,\ldots,\eta_N)$ in~$D$ where each $\eta_i$ connects a distinct pair of marked points. We consider similarly the planar link pattern $\alpha$ on the interior of $D$ induced by the paths $\ul{\eta}$. We let $\ildomain{2N}$ be the collection of interior link pattern decorated marked domains.
\end{enumerate}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.356775+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a995d06274ddf557e5d3170e4d4483f83f08209bad25e038d38c0297bc13eb05","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 236 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] For all $1\le \fq < \fp$ and $C > 0$, the spaces $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ and $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, endowed with the $\bbW_\fq$ metric,
are compact.

\begin{proof}
	We will show compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$, as compactness of $\cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$ is proved analogously.
	It suffices to show that every sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$ in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ has a subsequence converging in $\bbW_\fq$ to a measure in $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$.
	Consider any such sequence $(\mu_n)_{n\ge 1}$.
	The set of measures $\cP_\fp(\R,C)$ is clearly tight, so by Prohorov's theorem there exists a weakly convergent subsequence $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$. 
Let $\mu$ be its weak limit. By Skorokhod's theorem, we can find a coupling of random variables $X_j\sim\mu_{n_j}$ and $X\sim\mu$ such that
$X_j\to X$ almost surely. Then, by Fatou's lemma, we have
	\[
		\|\mu\|_{L^\fp}^\fp 
	=\E[|X|^p]^{1/p}
		\le
		\liminf_j \E[|X_j|^p]^{1/p}
		= \liminf_{j\to\infty} \|\mu_{n_j}\|_{L^\fp}^\fp
		 \le C\,,
	\]
	so $\mu \in \cP_\fp(\R,C)$. 
	It remains to show $(\mu_{n_j})_{j\ge 1}$ converges to $\mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
	 Note that for any $\nu \in \cP_\fp(\R_{\ge0},C)$, Markov's inequality implies
	\[
	\nu(|x|>K) 
	\le \frac{1}{K^\fp}\int
		|x|^\fp \,d\nu
		 \le \frac{C}{K^\fp}\,.
	\]
Combining this with H\"older's inequality gives
	\beq
		\int_{|x|>K} |x|^\fq \,d\nu
		\le \nu(|x|>K)^{1 - \fq/\fp} \bigg(
			\int |x|^\fp \,d\nu
		\bigg)^{\fq/\fp}
		\le \frac{C}{K^{\fp - \fq}}\,.
	\eeq
	By \eqref{e:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq.tail} and the weak convergence $\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$,
	\begin{align*}
		\limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\bigg|
		&\le \limsup_{j\to\infty} \bigg|
			\int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			\,d\mu_{n_j}
			- \int
			\max\{|x|,K\}^\fq
			 \,d\mu
		\bigg|\\
		&\qquad + \limsup_{j\to\infty} \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		+ \int_{|x| > K} |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		\le \frac{2C}{K^{\fp-\fq}}\,.
	\end{align*}
	Since $K$ was arbitrary, we infer the convergence of $\fq$-th moments
	\[
		\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\E[|X_j|^p]
		=\lim_{j\to\infty} 
		\int |x|^\fq \,d\mu_{n_j}
		= \int |x|^\fq \,d\mu
		= \E[|X|^p]\,.\]
This implies that the random variables $\{X_j\}$ are uniformly integrable, so
	\begin{align*}
	&\bbW_\fq(\mu_{n_j}, \mu)^\fq
	\le \E[|X_j-X|^\fq]\\
	&\le\E\Big[
	\max\{|X_j-X|,2K\}^\fq\Big]
	+\E\Big[|X_j| ; |X_j|\ge K\Big]
	+ \E\Big[|X| ; |X|\ge K\Big]
	\\
	&\le o_j(1) + o_K(1)+ o_K(1)\,.
	\end{align*}
Since the left-hand side does not depend on $K$, we conclude that
$\mu_{n_j} \rightarrow \mu$ in the $\bbW_\fq$ metric.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}
