{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:51:12.739547+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a9b021e1b84cf296affb1ec09aef80d87ff2c5c2cfae7fe3259cc1511984c9c4","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 2 of arXiv:2605.02430, '\textbf{Scaling limit of the range of tree-valued branching random walks in random environ'] \textbf{(Rooted ordered trees, subtrees, forests)}
$(\textbf{a})\, $ A \textit{rooted ordered tree} is a subset $ \fftree\! \subset \! \bbU$ satisfying the following conditions: 
\begin{compactenum}
\item[] \textbf{(1):} $\varnothing \ino \fftree$. \textbf{(2):} If $u\ino  \fftree\backslash \{ \varnothing\}$ 
then $\overleftarrow{u}\ino  \fftree$. \textbf{(3):} For all $u\ino  \fftree$, there exists $k_u ( \fftree)\ino \bbN\cup \! \{ \infty\}$ such that: $u \! \ast \!  (j)\ino  \fftree$  if and only if  $1\! \leq \! j \! \leq \! k_u ( \fftree)$. 
\end{compactenum}
Here, $k_u ( \fftree)$ is interpreted as the \textit{number of children of $u$} and if 
$1\! \leq \! j \! \leq \! k_u ( \fftree)$, then $u\ast (j) $ is the \emph{$j$-th child of $u$.}
We denote by $\bbT$ the set of rooted ordered trees.

\smallskip

\noindent
$(\textbf{b})\, $
Let $ \fftree\ino \bbT$ and $u\ino t$. Then 
$\theta_u  \fftree\!  = \! \{ v\ino \bbU: u\ast v\ino  \fftree \}$ is the \emph{subtree of $ \fftree$ stemming from $u$}. 
Note that $\theta_u t\ino \bbT$. 

\smallskip

\noindent
$(\textbf{c})\, $ A \emph{fores}t is a sequence of trees 
$(t^{_{(k)}}_{^{\,}} )_{k\in \bbN^*}$. It is sometimes convenient to view it as a single tree $t\ino \bbT$ with $k_\varnothing(t)\eqo\infty$ such that 
$t^{_{(k)}}_{^{\,}}$ is the subtree stemming from the $k$-th child of $t$: $t^{_{(k)}}_{^{\,}}\eqo \theta_{(k)}t$. \cq","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:28:04.856569+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a9ddf98859cd49e93578c284471d46b6789e4499c8c40221348908710d5e2c9b","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 102 of arXiv:2511.20322, 'Dissertation'] Let $T > 0$ and $B, l\in \N$.

\begin{align*}
F(h,t,\thet,z) := &  -\frac{u_t} B\sum_{k=0}^{B-1}\nabla R_{z(k)}(\thet), \quad h\in (0,1),t\in [0,T], \thet \in \R^d, z = (z_0,\dots, z_{B-1})\in \cZ^B,\\
Z_n := & (\bz(0 + Bn),\dots, \bz((B-1) + Bn)), \quad n\in \N,\\
f_t^h(\thet) := & F(h,t,\thet, Z_{\floor{t/h}}), \quad h\in (0,1),t\in [0,T], \thet \in \R^d.

Then

\[\bar f_t(\thet) := -u_t \nabla \cR(\thet), \quad \Si_t(\thet) := \frac{u_t^2}{B}\E[(\nabla R_{\bz(0)}(\thet) - \nabla \cR(\thet))^{\otimes 2}],\]
for all $\thet\in \R^d$ and $t\in [0,T]$, we have $\bar f\in \Lip^l([0,T]\times \R^d, \R^d), \Si \in \wC l 2([0,T]\times \R^d, \R^{d\times d})$, and
\[\bar f_t(\thet) = \E[f_t^h(\thet)], \quad  \Si_t(\thet) = \Cov f_t^h(\thet),\]

{"assumptions":["the semicircle law normalised to [-2,2], corresponding to Wigner matrices with entry variance 1/n","the convention m(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} d mu(x); the opposite sign convention changes the equation"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:38.544103+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_a9f9a8f598dab28e0957ae56e87073ce26d8a3b6d7df827c75290aa5f4b04b18","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let mu_sc be the semicircle law with density (1/(2 pi)) sqrt(4 - x^2) on [-2, 2]. Its Stieltjes transform m(z) = integral (x - z)^{-1} mu_sc(dx) satisfies the self-consistent equation m(z)^2 + z m(z) + 1 = 0 for every z in C^+, equivalently m(z) = -1/( z + m(z) ), and is the UNIQUE solution of that equation with Im m(z) > 0 for z in C^+; explicitly m(z) = ( -z + sqrt(z^2 - 4) )/2 with the branch of the square root chosen so that m(z) is asymptotic to -1/z as |z| tends to infinity. This equation is the fixed point that resolvent proofs of Wigner's theorem converge to: the Schur complement identity applied to the resolvent of a Wigner matrix gives (1/n) tr (H - z)^{-1} approximately equal to -1/(z + (1/n) tr (H - z)^{-1}) up to errors that vanish as n grows, and stability of the fixed point then forces the empirical Stieltjes transform to converge to m. For the Marchenko-Pastur law the analogous equation carries the aspect ratio and reads m(z) = 1/( 1 - y - y z m(z) - z ), a different fixed point that must not be substituted for this one. [standard; e.g. Anderson, Guionnet and Zeitouni, An Introduction to Random Matrices, Section 2.4]","status":"unverified"}

# Target 1: scalar three-token self-attention under joint training

Version 1, unaudited. Own work; novelty not established globally.
This extends the scalar family, not arbitrary vector-valued token geometry.

## Data, model and conclusions

For each i=1,...,n, n>=2, take a label y_i in {-1,+1} and three distinct
signed token values c_ij. Their minimum m_i is negative, maximum M_i positive,
and the FIRST token c_i1 is positive. Let raw tokens x_ij=y_i c_ij and use
the actual first token x_i1 as the self-attention query. With jointly trained
scalar head v and scalar attention weight p, signed prediction is v h_i(p),

 h_i(p)=sum_j c_ij exp(zeta_i c_ij p)/sum_j exp(zeta_i c_ij p),
 zeta_i=c_i1>0.

The loss is average logistic loss. Let
 H=max_i max(|m_i|,|M_i|), D=max_i zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2,
 eta_*=min(2/H^2,1/(2D)).

For every fixed eta in (0,eta_*], simultaneous GD in (v,p) has precisely
three possible limits: the unique finite saddle (0,p_bar), where
mean_i h_i(p_bar)=0; matching-positive escape v,p->+infinity; or
matching-negative escape v,p->-infinity. The saddle's global stable set is
planar null. Both escaping basins are open and nonempty. Their hard selections
are respectively the maximum signed token in EVERY example and the minimum
signed token in EVERY example. No interior token, or mixed pattern of extrema,
is a hard-selection limit in this scalar model. On escaping trajectories
p=O(log |v|), loss->0 and the normalized joint directions are (+1,0),(-1,0).
The corresponding minimum signed margins, normalized by sqrt(v^2+p^2),
are Gamma_+=min_i M_i and Gamma_-=min_i(-m_i).

In addition, for EVERY eta>0 the regions
 Q_+={v>0,p>max_i rho_i}, Q_-={v<0,p<min_i rho_i},
where h_i(rho_i)=0, are forward invariant and satisfy the same respective
escape/margin conclusions. Thus if Gamma_+>Gamma_-, the inferior basin is
open and positive measure even without a step-size restriction. A sufficient
strict inequality is M_i+m_i>0 for every example.

## Scalar softmax link estimates

Write alpha_ij(p) for the three softmax weights. Direct differentiation gives
h_i'=zeta_i[sum alpha_ij c_ij^2-h_i^2]
     =zeta_i sum_{j<l} alpha_ij alpha_il(c_ij-c_il)^2>0.
Also |h_i|<=H, h_i'<=zeta_i(M_i-m_i)^2<=D, and h_i tends to m_i,M_i
at the two infinities. Thus each root rho_i exists uniquely.

Let delta be the minimum over i of zeta_i times either adjacent gap of its
sorted three token values. It is strictly positive. For p>=0, the total
softmax mass on nonmaximum tokens is <=2 exp(-delta p).
Variance is no larger than the second moment about the maximum token,
so h_i'(p)<=2D exp(-delta p). Reflecting yields the same upper bound
2D exp(-delta |p|) for p<=0. Every h_i is real analytic, strictly increasing,
bounded, and has exponentially decaying derivative.

## Full-plane trapping and escape

For g_i=(1+exp(v h_i(p)))^-1 put F=mean g_i h_i and G=mean g_i h_i'>0.
GD is v_+=v+eta F, p_+=p+eta vG. The following estimates are identical
to those needed in proof 005, now established for genuine three-token links:

 -H^2/4<=F_v<=0,
 F(0,p)=mean h_i(p)/2=:F_0(p), 0<F_0'<=D/2, G<=D.

There is a unique mean root p_bar. Set u=p-p_bar, A=H^2/4.
In v,u>0, v_+>=(1-eta A)v+eta F_0(p)>0 and p increases; reflecting gives
invariance in v,u<0. In a bad quadrant v>0,u<0, v decreases and u increases
until it exits or converges to the saddle. Double crossing would require

 (1-eta A)v<=eta(D/2)|u|<=eta^2 D^2 v/2,

impossible since eta A<=1/2 and eta D<=1/2. The other bad quadrant is the
reflection. An axis point other than the saddle enters a good quadrant after
one step. A bad-quadrant orbit staying there is bounded and monotone; continuity
of increments gives vG=F=0 at its limit, hence the saddle.

Consider a positive good-quadrant orbit. If p had a finite limit P and v were
bounded, compactness would give G bounded below; Delta p->0 would force v->0,
but F_0(P)>0 contradicts convergence of v to zero. If v were unbounded and
P<=R:=max rho_i, an example with root R has h_j(p)<=0 and therefore g_j>=1/2.
On the compact p interval its derivative is bounded below, so
Delta p>=eta d v/(2n), contradicting finite P. If P>R, eventually all links
are >=c>0; v then increases without bound and
Delta p/Delta v>=d v/H again contradicts finite P. Thus p->infinity.
Eventually all h_i>=c, forcing v->infinity (bounded v would keep the g_i
uniformly positive). Negative escape follows by reflection using -h_i(-p).

This proof also applies directly within Q_+ or Q_- at any eta>0: both
coordinates are monotone from the start and all signed links are positive
after reflection. Only the full-plane trapping argument uses eta_*.

## Rates, margin, and the null exceptional set

On a positive escaping trajectory, h_i>=c>0 eventually, so
Delta p<=eta D v exp(-cv)->0. Moreover
Delta p/Delta v<=2D v exp(-delta p)/c.
Once Delta p<=1, the mean value theorem gives
Delta exp(delta p)<=C v Delta v. Telescoping against v^2 gives
exp(delta p)<=C'(1+v^2), so p=O(log v). Reflection proves the other branch.
Loss and normalized margin limits now follow. For any parameter pair,
the endpoint bounds and sqrt(v^2+p^2)>=|v| show the normalized minimum
margin cannot exceed max(Gamma_+,Gamma_-); the larger branch attains it.

At the saddle, the update Jacobian is
[[1-eta A_s,eta B_s],[eta B_s,1]],
where A_s=mean h_i(p_bar)^2/4<=A and B_s=mean h_i'(p_bar)/2 in (0,D/2].
Its determinant >=7/16 and det(DT-I)<0: one eigenvalue lies in (0,1),
the other exceeds 1. The analytic update map has a Jacobian determinant
not identically zero; the zero set is null. Away from that set its local
inverse maps preserve null sets. By a countable cover, preimages of null
sets are null. The local stable-manifold theorem and countably many iterated
preimages therefore give a null global stable set. Each escaping basin is
the union of preimages of its open good quadrant, hence open. This is the
same null-preimage argument detailed in proofs/003 and 005, not an assumption
that the GD map is globally invertible.

## Which locally optimal selections, and comparison with prior art

For p->+infinity only the largest signed c_ij can dominate; for p->-infinity
only the smallest can dominate. Because all zeta_i>0 these choices must be
consistent across examples. At finite p all weights are strictly positive,
so an interior token cannot become a hard selection. For a fixed v>0, the
maximum-token pattern is the only locally optimal feasible hard selection;
for fixed v<0 the minimum-token pattern is the only one. Both are stable
under joint training, by the open basins above. The minimum pattern can
nevertheless be inferior when comparing the two JOINT normalized margins.

Tarzanagh et al., 2306.13596, Definition 2 (PDF p.5) compares the chosen token
score only to its active SVM neighbors, with a FIXED head. Their Theorem 3
(PDF p.6) gives convergence from cones C_{mu,R} around such locally optimal
directions. It already includes a three-token illustration immediately after
the theorem. The present scalar result is not the discovery of that phenomenon:
it classifies the scalar joint-head basins and excludes mixed/interior hard
patterns in this stated geometry. General vector-valued three-token locally
optimal selections and their joint-head basins remain open here.

## Explicit distinct mixed-label witness

Take signed triples (3/2,1/4,-1/2) and (3/2,1/8,-1), with labels +1,-1.
Raw triples are (3/2,1/4,-1/2),(-3/2,-1/8,1); actual first-token queries
are 3/2,-3/2. Both zeta_i=3/2. H=3/2, D=75/8, eta_*=4/75.
Gamma_+=3/2 and Gamma_-=1/2. The conditions are strict and persist in an
open neighborhood of these data. This witness is illustrative; the theorem
covers the whole family above rather than just this isolated case.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:06:18.018284+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aa4cc6d487ee620971b9e8b534804605d15b51e6147edb90e1d0f7569d387a1d","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Thm 14 (Two-level kernel for orientation-reversing nested rectangles) of arXiv:2608.15137, '2608.15137'] Suppose one physical side has size $p$ at the earlier rectangle and $Q$ at the later rectangle, while the other has size $q$ earlier and $P$ later, where
\[
 p<q\leq P<Q.
\]
Put
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 r_0&=q-p,
 &C&=P-q,
 &B&=Q-q,\\
 A&=P-p=r_0+C,
 &r&=Q-P=B-C.
 \end{aligned}
\]
Define $\mathcal L_{d,\alpha}$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:fixed-orientation-kernel}.

Set $W(x,z)=0$ for $z\leq x$. If $C=0$, put
\begin{equation}
 W(x,z)
 =
 \ee^{-z}\frac{(z-x)^{r_0+B-1}}{(r_0+B-1)!}.
\end{equation}
If $C\geq1$, put
\begin{equation}
 W(x,z)
 =
 \ee^{-z}z^r
 \int_x^z
 \frac{(u-x)^{r_0+B-1}u^{-B}(z-u)^{C-1}}
 {(r_0+B-1)!(C-1)!}\,\dd u.
\end{equation}

The two-level positive squared-singular-value process is determinantal, with one exact kernel
\begin{align}
 K_{00}(x,y)
 &=
 \ee^{-x}x^{r_0}\mathcal L_{p,r_0}(x,y),
 \\
 K_{11}(x,y)
 &=
 \ee^{-y}y^r\mathcal L_{P,r}(x,y),
 \\
 K_{10}(x,y)
 &=
 \left(\frac{\dd}{\dd y}\right)^A
 (rI+E_y)^{\mathrm{fall}\,B}
 \mathcal L_{P,r}(x,y),
 \\
 K_{01}(x,y)
 &=
 -W(x,y)+
 \int_0^\infty W(x,z)K_{11}(z,y)\,\dd z.
 
\end{align}
The same statement holds with rows and columns interchanged.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:45:05.439425+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aa56bd5d69f8f7d8c83882e579a5c5eff0b5ff662f4cb1dcfa4d56a97843d13f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 142 (Fixed-interface, fixed-driver response-completion extension) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Fix the law family $\cP$, one backward-compatible continuation interface
$(\mathcal E_{s,t})$, and one admissible driver $F$ in the sense of
\Cref{def:admissible-backward-driver}.  Let $\mathscr D_0$ be a
response-quotiented operational data core for this fixed triple and suppose
every $d\in\mathscr D_0$ carries a backward first-jet trajectory with terminal
response $\xi^d$.  Assume that $d\mapsto\xi^d$ is part of the declared data
metric and is Cauchy-continuous into $\mathcal L_{\cP}^2$.  If the
operational solution map
\[
 \Phi_{\rm bw}^{\rm op}:d\longmapsto(Y^d,Z^d)
\]
is Cauchy-continuous from the declared data metric into
$\mathscr W_{Q,\cP}^{1,2}$, then it extends uniquely to the metric completion
$\overline{\mathscr D_0}$:
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{\rm bw}:\overline{\mathscr D_0}
 \longrightarrow\mathscr W_{Q,\cP}^{1,2}.
\end{equation}
Assume also that $\mathscr D_0$ carries declared truncations
$\rho_u^{\mathscr D}$ which preserve $\mathscr D_0$, are Cauchy-continuous
for the data metric, and form a truncation system:
\[
 \rho_T^{\mathscr D}=I,
 \qquad
 \rho_u^{\mathscr D}\rho_v^{\mathscr D}
 =\rho_{u\wedge v}^{\mathscr D},
 \qquad u,v\in[0,T].
\]
Assume, moreover, that
\begin{equation}
 \Phi_{\rm bw}^{\rm op}(\rho_u^{\mathscr D}d)
 =\rho_u^{\mathscr W}\Phi_{\rm bw}^{\rm op}(d),
 \qquad d\in\mathscr D_0,\quad u\in[0,T].
\end{equation}
Then the truncations and the displayed compatibility extend to the two
completions; the extended maps still satisfy the truncation identities.
The terminal response extends simultaneously; writing its extension again as
$d\mapsto\xi^d$, continuity of terminal evaluation gives
$Y_T^d=\xi^d$ on $\overline{\mathscr D_0}$.  Thus the limit is independent of
the operational approximation in the declared data metric and retains the
terminal condition.  The running sources $B^F[Y^d,Z^d]$, common stochastic integrals,
and intrinsic defects converge as continuous readouts, and the limiting defect
remains in $\mathbb K_{\cP}^{2,\uparrow}$.  For every declared seam $s\le t$
put

 :=\{G_{s,t}[Y^d,Z^d]:d\in\mathscr D_0\}.

\eqref{eq:backward-response-law} passes to the limit and remains

 \mathscr S_{\rm sol}
 :=\overline{\Phi_{\rm bw}(\overline{\mathscr D_0})}
 ^{\,\mathscr W_{Q,\cP}^{1,2}}.

first-jet truncations.

realization
\[
 \Phi_{\rm bw}(d)
 =\bigl(Y^d,\mathcal Z_{\rm sol}(Y^d)\bigr).
\]
Only when the solver range is a closed linear relation does this reduce to the
vertical-space and closed-value-domain criterion of

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:35:04.164461+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aa7ee49186ba658d9c910cdec1f29ecb659b7af0bd7ea0dc6a4fb81c9c4eb808","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 27 of arXiv:2608.30059, 'Multihomogeneous Measures and Stochastic Polar Representations'] For the fixed admissible gauge \(\tau\), with
\(C_\star=(1,2]^q\) and \(d_\alpha=m_\alpha(C_\star)\), set  
\begin{equation}

s_\tau
:=
\varsigma_\tau(\Sigma_\tau)
=
\frac{1}{d_\alpha}
\int_{\{\tau\in C_\star\}}
\chi_\alpha(\tau(x))\,\nu(dx)
=
\frac{\nu\{\tau\in C_\star\}}
{\vartheta_\alpha(C_\star)}
\in(0,\infty].
\end{equation}
Every stochastic representer \(Z\) of \(\nu\) satisfies
\[
\E{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}=s_\tau.
\]
The following are equivalent:
\begin{enumerate}[\rm(i)]
\item
Some stochastic representer \(Z\) has \(R_Z\perp Y_Z\).

\item
\(s_\tau<\infty\).

\item
\(\nu\{\tau\in C_\star\}<\infty\).
\end{enumerate}

If \(s_\tau<\infty\), put
\[
\bar\alpha:=\sum_{i=1}^q\alpha_i,
\qquad
a_\tau:=s_\tau^{1/\bar\alpha}\boldsymbol1 
\]
and  for any stochastic representer \(Z\)  define
\begin{equation}

\frac{d\mathbb P_Z^\tau}{d\mathbb P}
:=
\frac{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}{s_\tau},
\end{equation}
\begin{equation}

Z_\tau^\circ
:=
S_{a_\tau}Y_Z
=
S_{a_\tau R_Z^{-1}}Z.
\end{equation}
Under \(\mathbb P_Z^\tau\),
\[
Y_Z\sim\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau},
\qquad
\tau(Z_\tau^\circ)=a_\tau,
\qquad
\nu_{Z_\tau^\circ}=\nu,
\]
and
\[
\mathcal L(Z_\tau^\circ)
=
(S_{a_\tau})_\#
\left(\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau}\right).
\]
Consequently, every stochastic representer \(W\) satisfying
\(\tau(W)=a_\tau\) almost surely has this law.

Finally, for \(Z\) concentrated on \(E_\tau\) with \(R_Z\perp Y_Z\),
\[
\nu_Z=\nu
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
Y_Z\sim\frac{\varsigma_\tau}{s_\tau}
\ \text{ and }\
\E{\chi_\alpha(R_Z)}=s_\tau.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T09:13:18.496794+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aaa8a596621b7a47c5612730d379560e677a253d50c05ba961f09180b666b053","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop 10 of arXiv:2608.30578, 'Compactly Supported Solutions near a Nehari Critical Value'] Let $\lambda_0$ belong to a compact subinterval of
$(\lambda_{1,\Omega},\lambda^*)$ for the branch $u_\lambda^-$, or of
$(-\infty,\lambda^*)$ for the branch $u_\lambda^+$. Then there exist
$\delta>0$ and
$r_i^\pm(\lambda,\lambda_0)=o(|\lambda-\lambda_0|)$, $i=1,2$, such that,
whenever $0<\lambda-\lambda_0<\delta$,
\begin{align}
	-\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_\lambda^-\|_2^2+r_1^-(\lambda,\lambda_0)
	&\leq E_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)-E_{\lambda_0}(u_{\lambda_0}^-)
	\notag\\
	&\leq -\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_{\lambda_0}^-\|_2^2
	+r_2^-(\lambda,\lambda_0).
	
\end{align}
and
\begin{align}
	-\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_\lambda^+\|_2^2+r_1^+(\lambda,\lambda_0)
	&\leq E_\lambda(u_\lambda^+)-E_{\lambda_0}(u_{\lambda_0}^+)
	\notag\\
	&\leq -\frac{\lambda-\lambda_0}{2}\|u_{\lambda_0}^+\|_2^2
	+r_2^+(\lambda,\lambda_0).
	
\end{align}
Moreover, for every fixed
$\lambda_0\in(\lambda_{1,\Omega},\lambda^*)$, there exist
$\delta,c_0,C_0>0$ such that, whenever $|\lambda-\lambda_0|<\delta$,
\[
|H_\lambda(u_\lambda^-)|\geq c_0,
\qquad
\|u_\lambda^-\|\leq C_0.
\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T20:06:06.293688+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aaac5ecf4f3ed00ef053216afdb53d23adfd0cf929c4e712c1d9a91d228d6ce1","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition def:mucs of arXiv:2605.22787, 'Invariant measures for half-space geometric LPP: classification and the one force--one sol'] We define the following family of measures.
 For $c \in [0,q^{-1})$ and $r_c \le s < q^{-1}$, let $\mu_{c,s}$ denote the law of the following function $f:\mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{R}$:

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:04:07.031970+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aad1c342f4931e8eb7d7fd673ef23041a1a43e6d0cbdf8ded2c58958e4e4c86c","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:one-point-gaussian-regression of arXiv:2607.29330, 'Large deviations for the maximum of\\ the generalized TAP free energy'] Under the hypotheses and notation of
		Proposition~(prop:one-point-conditional-hessian of the paper), whenever
		\(m=\partial_x\Phi_\zeta(r,x)\), write
		\[
		u(r,m):=\partial_{xx}\Phi_\zeta(r,x)
		=\frac1{\partial_{mm}h_\zeta(r,m)}.
		\]
		Set \(e=\mathbf{m}/\sqrt{Nq}\), and let \(P\) be the orthogonal
		projection onto \(\mathbf{m}^\perp\). Define
		\[
		z_i
		:=
		\xi''(q)\left(
		\frac{b_i}{\xi'(q)}-\partial_m u(q,m_i)
		-2\zeta(\{0\})m_i
		\right).
		\]
		There exist a GOE matrix \(W_N\), with off-diagonal entries of
		variance \(N^{-1}\), and a standard Gaussian vector \(g_N\) in
		\(\mathbf{m}^\perp\), independent of \(W_N\), such that, under
		\(\mathbb{P}_{\mathbf{m},f_N}\) and relative to
		\(\mathbb R e\oplus\mathbf{m}^\perp\),
		\begin{equation}
			\nabla_-^2F_{\mathrm{TAP},\zeta}(\mathbf{m})
			=
			\begin{pmatrix}
				a_N&y_N^{\mathsf T}P\\
				Py_N&C_N
			\end{pmatrix}
			+o(1),
		\end{equation}
		where the error converges to zero in operator norm in probability,
		and
		\begin{equation}
			C_N
			=
			P\left(
			\sqrt{\xi''(q)}\,W_N
			-\operatorname{diag}\left(
			\frac1{u(q,m_i)}
			+\frac{\xi''(q)}N\sum_{j=1}^Nu(q,m_j)
			\right)_{i\le N}
			\right)P\big|_{\mathbf{m}^\perp},
		\end{equation}
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			y_N={}&
			\frac1{\sqrt N}\left(
			-\frac{m_i}{\sqrt q\,u(q,m_i)}+\sqrt q\,z_i
			+\sqrt q\,\zeta(\{0\})\xi''(q)m_i
			\right)_{i\le N}\\
			&+\left(
			\frac{\xi''(q)+q\xi'''(q)-q\xi''(q)^2/\xi'(q)}N
			\right)^{1/2}g_N,
		\end{aligned}
		\]
		and
		\[
		\begin{aligned}
			a_N={}&
			-\frac1{Nq}\sum_{i=1}^N\frac{m_i^2}{u(q,m_i)}
			-\frac{\xi''(q)}N\sum_{i=1}^Nu(q,m_i)
			+\frac2N\sum_{i=1}^Nm_iz_i\\
			&+q\left(
			-\frac{\xi'''(q)}N\sum_{i=1}^Nu(q,m_i)
			+\zeta(\{0\})\xi''(q)
			-\frac{2\xi''(q)}N\sum_{i=1}^N\partial_q u(q,m_i)
			\right).
		\end{aligned}
		\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:42:47.752482+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aade0c56360e82e81a44b947e6f162dfd65386ccec1bb8f2058583e3c8d8222c","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 6 of arXiv:2604.11682, 'Semilocalization for inhomogeneous random graphs'] A \emph{path} $\gamma$ in a graph $G$ is a sequence of vertices

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:46:26.249146+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aae02d5d5f4748fcdce1a2c859ec21634c029017d76a2a35babdc1c1f75ea3f6","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 1 of arXiv:2605.22445, 'Generalized specific entropy on Wiener space with application to Martingale Optimal Transp'] Given $\Sigma(t,x)  \in \mathbb S^d_{+}$, a probability measure \(\mathbb P\) on the c\`adl\`ag path space

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.774470+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_aaf5b9b1b62827a32ec6f5199485e2d1de8f146393db87469eb999cb20440202","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Corollary 29 (Careless uniform exponential tails and moments) of arXiv:2605.14511, 'Clumsy and Careless:\\ Stationary-Entry Flux in Non-monotone Coupon Collectors'] Let $Y_n:=\mu_nT_{n,p}$ in the fixed-$p$ careless collector started from the empty collection, where
\[
        \mu_n=\Pbb_{\nu_n}(K_0<n,K_1=n)
\]
is the stationary-entry flux into the post-loss completion state.  There are constants $C,c\in(0,\infty)$, depending only on $p$, such that
\[
        \Pbb(Y_n>x)\le C e^{-cx},
        \qquad x\ge0,
\]
for all sufficiently large $n$.  Consequently, for every fixed $r\ge1$,
\[
        \Ebb Y_n^r\longrightarrow \Ebb Z^r=r!,
        \qquad Z\sim\Exp(1).
\]
In particular,
\[
        \Ebb T_{n,p}\sim \frac{1}{\mu_n},\qquad
        \Var(T_{n,p})\sim \frac{1}{\mu_n^2}.
\]
Together with Theorem~\ref{thm:careless-sharp-constant}, this gives the explicit constant
\[
        \mu_n\sim \frac{1}{(q;q)_\infty}
        \frac{n!}{n^n}q^{n(n+1)/2}.
\]
Consequently,
\[
        \Ebb T_{n,p}
        \sim (q;q)_\infty\frac{n^n}{n!}q^{-n(n+1)/2},
\]
and
\[
        \Var(T_{n,p})
        \sim (q;q)_\infty^2\left(\frac{n^n}{n!}\right)^2q^{-n(n+1)}.
\]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["independent coordinates with finite ranges","f real valued"],"created_at":"2026-10-06T08:50:16.134109+00:00","domain":"Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition on finite product spaces","id":"claim_ab09a2c6051a4049fa8a2429dd73e7b3cd9ba24b6ee241a42e79d2fdc03080e9","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X = (X_1, ..., X_n) have independent coordinates with finite ranges, f a real function of X, and f = sum over S of f_S its Hoeffding (ANOVA) decomposition over subsets S of {1, ..., n}: f_S depends only on X_S, f_empty = E f, and E[f_S | X_T] = 0 unless S is inside T. Put w_S = E[f_S^2] and W_k = sum over |S| = k of w_S, the variance at interaction order k. With R_r the block conditional variances, put D_m = (-1)^(m+1) Delta^m R_0 for 1 <= m <= n, and let H_<m be the functions whose Hoeffding components of order m or more vanish. Then D_m = binom(n, m)^(-1) sum_{k=m}^n binom(k, m) W_k and D_m <= dist_2(f, H_<m)^2 <= binom(n, m) D_m; so D_m = 0 if and only if f lies in H_<m. With nonzero tail, the left inequality is an equality exactly when all the tail mass sits at order n, and the right one exactly when it sits at order m. The same holds with Q_r, the average over |A| = r of E[(f(X) - f(X^(A)))^2], since Q_r = 2 R_r: for m = 1 it reads Var(f) <= (1/2) sum_i E[(f(X) - f(X^(i)))^2].","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:56:11.132821+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ab164c5977382e3eb8693db5b617908cbc028bb1c54fc2ddd7d2059bda4789b0","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 27 of arXiv:2608.10183, '2608.10183'] Fix a time-independent reinforcement environment $\eta$. Assume that, for
every $M\geq 2$, the frozen $M$-replica process admits an invariant probability
measure $\pi_M^\eta$ with the exponential integrability required below.
Assume moreover that $\pi_M^\eta$ is exchangeable with respect to
permutations of the replica labels.

Assume further that the Poisson Hypothesis holds.

Let
\begin{align*}
\beta_i
&:=
\mathbb E_\eta[X_i+z_i].
\end{align*}

Assume moreover that, as $M\to\infty$,
\begin{align*}
\beta_i^M
&\longrightarrow
\beta_i,
\\
\Lambda_i^{M,m,\eta}(u)
&\longrightarrow
\Lambda_i^\eta(u),
\\
\Theta_i^{M,m,\eta}(u,v)
&\longrightarrow
\Theta_i^\eta(u,v),
\end{align*}
for $u$ in a common open interval $I$ containing $0$.

Assume in addition that, for every compact set $K\subset I$, there exists
$\delta_K>0$ such that $u+2\delta_K\in I$ for every $u\in K$ and
\begin{align*}
\sup_{M\geq 2}
\sup_{u\in K}
\mathbb E_{\pi_M^\eta}
\left[
e^{(u+2\delta_K)(X_i^m+z_i)}
\right]
&<\infty.
\end{align*}

Then, for every $u\in I$,
\begin{align}
0
=&
-(1+a_i u)
\bigl(\Lambda_i^\eta\bigr)'(u)
+
a_i u z_i\Lambda_i^\eta(u)
+
\beta_i e^{u(r_i+z_i)}+
\\
\nonumber +
&\sum_{j\in\mathcal P_i}
\beta_j Q_i^\eta(+1)
\bigl(e^{u w_{ji}}-1\bigr)
\Lambda_i^\eta(u)
+
\sum_{j\in\mathcal P_i}
\beta_j Q_i^\eta(-1)
\left[
\Theta_i^\eta(u,v_{ji})
-
\Lambda_i^\eta(u)
\right].
\end{align}

Moreover,
\begin{align*}
\beta_i
&=
\bigl(\Lambda_i^\eta\bigr)'(0).
\end{align*}

If $r_i=0$, the contribution arising from the reset mechanism before
combination with the deterministic drift is
\begin{align*}
\beta_i e^{u z_i}
-
\bigl(\Lambda_i^\eta\bigr)'(u).
\end{align*}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:51:33.317889+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ab26e7af558d3607ec9756b0f749a126b8f6a42d9b10d10bb293c9376652c31c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Prop the-horrible-proof-we-dont-talk-about of arXiv:2608.28504, 'Global $\bm\infty$-categories and global Thom spectra'] The $T$-$\infty$-category ${\mathcal{C}}_{/Y}^\circ$ is a $T$-$\infty$-groupoid, and there exists an equivalence $\smash{{\textup{Hom}}(\Upsilon(-),Y)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\mathcal{C}}_{/Y}^\circ}$ sending a map $a_!a^*1=\Upsilon(A)\to Y$ to the object in the slice given by its adjunct $a^*1\to a^*Y$.
    \begin{proof} 
        Throughout, we will abbreviate ${\mathcal{U}}\coloneq\textup{Un}^\textup{ct}({\mathcal{C}})$ for ease of notation. The adjunction equivalence ${\textup{Hom}}_{{\mathcal{C}}(1)}(\lambda s(-),Y)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\textup{Hom}}_{{\mathcal{U}}}(s(-),Y)$ is natural, so it will suffice to construct an equivalence ${\textup{Hom}}_{{\mathcal{U}}}(s(-),Y)\xrightarrow{\;\smash{\raisebox{-0.25ex}{\ensuremath{\scriptstyle\sim}}}\;}{\mathcal{C}}_{/Y}^\circ$ given on objects by factoring a map $s(A)\to Y$ into a fiberwise map followed by a cartesian edge. We will do so by working on the level of cartesian unstraightenings.

        \smallskip
        \textit{Step 1.} Let us describe the cartesian unstraightening of the target first. In the proof of Theorem~(thm:criterion-spc-T of the paper) we explained that the cartesian unstraightening of $\Ar({\mathcal{C}})$ is given by $\Ar^\text{fw}({\mathcal{U}})$, with evaluation maps corresponding to the obvious maps to ${\mathcal{U}}$. As unstraightening preserves limits, we conclude that the cartesian unstraighening of ${\mathcal{C}}_{/Y}^\circ$ is given by the iterated pullback
        \[
            \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=0ex]
                T\arrow[dr, "s"'] && \arrow[dl,"\ev_0"{description}]\Ar^\text{fw}({\mathcal{U}})\arrow[dr,"\ev_1"{description}] && \arrow[dl,"s_Y"]T\rlap,\\
                & {\mathcal{U}} && {\mathcal{U}}
            \end{tikzcd}
        \]
        where $s_Y$ denotes the unique map of cartesian fibration with $s_Y(1)=Y\in{\mathcal{C}}(1)\subset{\mathcal{U}}$.

        \smallskip
        \textit{Step 2.} On the other hand, we can also describe the cartesian unstraightening of the source quite easily: taking the usual description of the unstraightening of the contravariant hom-functor, it is given by the iterated pullback
        \[
            \begin{tikzcd}[row sep=0ex]
                T\arrow[dr, "s"'] && \arrow[dl,"\ev_0"{description}]\Ar({\mathcal{U}})\arrow[dr,"\ev_1"{description}] && \arrow[dl,"Y"]1\rlap.\\
                & {\mathcal{U}} && {\mathcal{U}}
            \end{tikzcd}
        \]

        \smallskip
        \textit{Step 3.} We will now massage the description from Step 1. {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869212+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_ab403eae02babe283bdaed7631d179880589c9cff81d8649db11e29a3ce1de2c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: candidate_full_solution - author-checked with a scope caveat; NO independent review - the parent that reviewed it had itself supplied two of the argument's steps, so its review does not certify the amended proof; no Lean] van Handel, The strong convergence phenomenon, arXiv:2507.00346v2 (11 February 2026), Section 6.9, pp. 69-70, asks whether strong convergence of a family of random matrices forces the empirical complex-eigenvalue measures of every noncommutative polynomial to converge to the corresponding limiting Brown measure. Then V_j U_j = omega_j U_j V_j, U_j^{q_j} = I, V_j^{q_j} = -I, and det(z I - U_j - V_j) = z^{q_j} exactly, so A_j = U_j + V_j is nilpotent and every empirical eigenvalue measure is delta_0, while the Brown measure of u + v for the limiting irrational-rotation pair is Haar measure on the unit circle (Fang, Jiang, Lin and Xu, arXiv:1210.4771, Theorem 12.2 - a literature dependency, not proved here). {"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:33:01.753254+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ab44bddca90c995f912e92cf910d2083e736574934b0f5e966f17663146713e6","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 29 (Mean) of arXiv:2605.14206, 'The clumsy coupon collector's problem'] The first moment of $T_{m, p}$ is
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m \, H_m + 
      \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}

      \right]
  \]
  where $H_m$ is the $m^\text{th}$ harmonic number
  and $L(x) \coloneqq x + (1-x) \log(1-x)$.
  If $p = p_m$ is an $o(1/m)$ sequence then this becomes
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m\,H_m
    + p\,m^2 + \frac{1}{4} \, p^2 \, m^3
    + O\left(p^2 \, m^2\right) + O\left(p^3 \, m^4\right).
  \]
  as $m \to \infty$. If $p \sim c/m$ then
  \[
    \E T_{m, p} = m\,H_m + \left(1 + o(1)\right)
      m \left[ c + c^2 \int_0^1 e^{-cx} \, L(x) \, dx\right].
  \]
  If $p = \omega(1/m)$ then
  \[
    \E T_{m,p} = m\,H_m + \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p} \left(1
    + O\left(\frac{1}{p\,m}\right)\right).
  \]
  In particular, for $p$ constant,
  \begin{align*}
    \E T_{m,p}
    = m \, H_m
    + \frac{(1-p)^{-m}}{p}&\Bigg\{
      1 + \left(-6p + 5 + \frac{1}{p}\right) m^{-1}\\
    &\phantom{\Bigg\{} {} + \left(45\,p^2 - 62\,p + 8 + \frac{7}{p} + \frac{2}{p^2} \right) m^{-2}
      + O\left(m^{-3}\right)
    \Bigg\}.
  \end{align*}
  \begin{proof}
    The difference $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$ has \textsc{mgf}
    $I_{m, p}(t)$. Corollary~\ref{thm:mgf} implies
    the \textsc{mgf} of $T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}$

    $\E [T_{m, p} - T_{m, 0}] = \lim_{t \uparrow 0} I_{m,p}'(t)$.

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T07:19:00.888410+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ab64b124ea7005b3fecc671d337de434b702f50ff275126dd6c8478819fae6a3","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 46 (Mixture supermartingales) of arXiv:2608.20337, 'Information on trajectories:\\ martingales and random times'] Suppose that for every $\lambda \in \Lambda$ (a measurable parameter space), $E_t(\lambda)$ is a nonnegative supermartingale with $E_0(\lambda) \leq 1$.
Let $\mu$ be a prior probability measure on $\Lambda$ and define $\overline E_t := \int E_t(\lambda)\,\mu(\dd\lambda)$.
Then $(\overline E_t)$ is a nonnegative supermartingale.
Moreover, for every adapted posterior $\rho_t \ll \mu$ (possibly data-dependent) with $\rho_t(\{\lambda : E_t(\lambda) = 0\}) = 0$, the mixture log-wealth is a Donsker--Varadhan identity,
\begin{equation}
  \log \overline E_t
  = \int_\Lambda \log E_t(\lambda)\,\rho_t(\dd\lambda)
       - \KL(\rho_t \| \mu) + \KL(\rho_t \| \rho^*_t)
\end{equation}
with $\dd\rho^*_t/\dd\mu \propto E_t(\cdot)$; dropping the nonnegative residual $\KL(\rho_t\|\rho^*_t)$ gives the PAC-Bayes lower bound $\log \overline E_t \ge \int_\Lambda \log E_t(\lambda)\,\rho_t(\dd\lambda) - \KL(\rho_t\|\mu)$.
In particular, if $E_t(\lambda) = \exp(\lambda Y_t - \overline\Psi_t(\lambda))$,
\begin{equation}
  \PP\!\left(
    \exists\,t :
    \int_\Lambda [\lambda Y_t - \overline\Psi_t(\lambda)]\rho_t(\dd\lambda)
    - \KL(\rho_t\|\mu) \geq x\right)
  \leq e^{-x}.
\end{equation} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["the operator is compact on a Hilbert space","self-adjointness or normality is what the eigenbasis conclusion needs","for a general compact operator only the Riesz-Schauder conclusions and the singular value decomposition are available"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:46.573312+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, spectral theory of compact operators","id":"claim_ab876a6af8757c91d5eb78a56fd013d6691bfc416c7fa2ac4c3ae96614531a82","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"The spectral theorem for compact self-adjoint operators (an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors, real eigenvalues tending to 0, ||T|| = max |eigenvalue|, min-max characterisation of eigenvalues) requires self-adjointness or at least normality. Compactness alone gives only the Riesz-Schauder picture: the nonzero spectrum consists of eigenvalues of finite algebraic multiplicity accumulating only at 0, and the set of such eigenvalues may be empty. The standard counterexample is the Volterra operator on L^2([0,1]), (V f)(x) = integral from 0 to x of f(t) dt, which is Hilbert-Schmidt (kernel k(x,t) = 1 for t < x, 0 otherwise) hence compact, but has no eigenvalues at all: V f = lambda f with lambda nonzero forces f to be absolutely continuous with f' = f/lambda and f(0) = 0, so f = 0; and V f = 0 forces f = 0 a.e. Thus sigma(V) = {0}, spectral radius 0, while ||V|| = 2/pi; the singular values of V are 1/((n + 1/2) pi), n >= 0, so V is Hilbert-Schmidt but not trace class, and the moduli of its eigenvalues (all zero) are nowhere near its singular values. Consequences for an auditor: (a) 'compact, so expand in eigenfunctions' is invalid without normality; the right substitute is the Schmidt decomposition in singular values, which always exists; (b) 'compact, so the spectral radius equals the norm' is false; (c) Rayleigh-quotient and min-max formulas for eigenvalues are statements about self-adjoint operators and become statements about singular values otherwise; (d) Mercer-type positivity conclusions require a self-adjoint positive kernel, not just an L^2 kernel.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:49:24.957384+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_abcdec1b02f8bee7f067c1c0e1ac0a8f410eb98eae9def7cf092c7c76e109b4f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition prop:music-chordal-residual of arXiv:2609.03264, 'Certified Spherical MUSIC for 3D Localization under Adversarial Subspace Perturbations'] Let \(Z=\{{\bm z}_1,\ldots,{\bm z}_s\}\) be a configuration for which

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T13:59:53.346360+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac19dfd4b613b7d8e5ad4725d566f3e48c6752e9bc5220b4fc92e6b09d22ac91","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem thm:torsor of arXiv:2607.24705, 'Derangetropy Operators'] For every open interval $I$, the subgroup of $\mathcal{G}$ of
		distortions with continuous positive derivative on $(0,1)$ acts
		freely and transitively on the laws of $\mathcal{D}_{+}$ with support
		$\overline{I}$, and the full group $\mathcal{G}$ acts so on the
		enlargement of $\mathcal{D}_{+}$ by all laws whose restricted
		distribution function is an absolutely continuous homeomorphism with
		absolutely continuous inverse: for two such laws $f, g$ the unique
		$A \in \mathcal{G}$ with $\alpha_{A}f = g$ is
		\begin{equation}
			A = F_{g}\circ Q_{f}.
			
		\end{equation}
		Consequently, for a reference law $f_{0} \in \mathcal{D}_{+}^{2}$
		with support $\overline{I}$, the potential map is the coadjoint
		orbit map $A \mapsto \operatorname{Ad}^{*}_{A}U_{f_{0}}$, and its
		fibers are the cosets of the stabilizer, which by
		Theorem~(thm:fibers of the paper) is the conjugated M\"obius group
		\begin{equation}
			\operatorname{Stab}_{\mathcal{G}}(U_{f})
			= \big\{\, F_{f}\circ M\circ Q_{f} \;:\;
			M \ \text{an increasing M\"obius self-map of } I \,\big\}.
			
		\end{equation}
		For $f, g \in \mathcal{D}_{+}^{2}$ the torsor
		map~(equation eq:torsor-map of the paper) is automatically a $C^{3}$-diffeomorphism
		of $(0,1)$, and the coadjoint formula, which involves only three
		derivatives, extends verbatim to $C^{3}$ distortions with the same
		cocycle law; the orbit-map statement is understood in this extended
		sense, on the $C^{3}$-regular part of the fiber.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Complete graph; rate-one simple walks; one initial particle at every vertex."],"created_at":"2026-10-10T06:51:51.364811+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac19fb17f8b6202fe9d73b38375403bae5da6d4e0abac576f7e143cb733f1608","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign result 2026-09-14, Author-checked, no independent read.] This is an elementary special case recorded alongside Open Problem 14.12 in David Aldous and James Allen Fill's Reversible Markov Chains and Random Walks on Graphs, unfinished monograph (2002, recompiled 2014; official source https://www.stat.berkeley.edu/~aldous/RWG/book.html). Let K_n be the complete simple graph with n>=2 vertices and start one particle per vertex. Each particle jumps independently at rate one to a uniformly chosen different vertex; particles merge on meeting. If T_coal is the time until one particle remains, then E[T_coal]=sum_{k=2}^n (n-1)/(k(k-1))=(n-1)^2/n. The discrete-time simple-walk matrix has n-1 nonconstant eigenvalues all equal to -1/(n-1), so its spectral mean hitting-time sum K=sum_{j=2}^n 1/(1-lambda_j) is also (n-1)^2/n. This is an unrefereed campaign result.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T06:39:11.680442+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac208104cf8fb7c637f2c01f9fe8040b7a98415d3a6f002a72c760d80f5ead1e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 40 (Universal factorization of finite-dimensional triangular tests) of arXiv:2608.04993, '2608.04993'] Let $m\in\mathbb N$, let $C\in\mathcal L(H,\mathbb R^m)$, and let
$B\in\mathcal L(\mathfrak I(H),\mathbb R^m)$.  For an accessible type, the
restarted finite-dimensional triangular system
\begin{equation}
 \dd Y_r^{P,s}=C\,\dd X_r+B\bigl(U_r^{P,s}\otimes\dd X_r\bigr),
 \qquad Y_s^{P,s}=0,
\end{equation}
where $U^{P,s}$ solves the first equation in
\eqref{eq:primitive-triangular-system}, has the coordinatewise It\^o solution
\begin{equation}
 Y_{s,t}^{P,s}=C X_{s,t}+B V_{s,t}^{P,s}.
\end{equation}
Consequently its complete restarted response is a stable-causal
readout of $\mathcal J_\tau Z_\tau$.  Thus every coefficient-defined
finite-dimensional triangular It\^o test whose second-order coefficient
extends continuously to $\mathfrak I(H)$ factors through the single
operator-valued step-two signature response.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:26:47.199182+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac3b35e8d69c8916a75f31a260dd4f7e833a3c597539ff4b35fbe5e35e24ce2c","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 130 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Let $X^1$ and $X^2$ be solutions to SDEs
    \[
    dX^i(t)
    =
    b^i(t,X^i(t))\,dt
    +
    \sigma^i(t,X^i(t))\,dB_t\,,
    \]
such that $X^1(q_*)$ and $X^2(q_*)$ are equidistributed.
Suppose for some finite constant $\oL$ that the SDE coefficients $b^i$ and $\sigma^i$ are uniformly bounded by $\oL$, and moreover are $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate. Lastly suppose
	\[
    \sup_{(t,x)\in [q_*
    ,1]\times \mathbb R}
    \bigg\{
    \Big|b^1(t,x) - b^2(t,x)\Big|
    +
 	\Big|\sigma^1(t,x)-\sigma^2(t,x)\Big|
    \bigg\}
    \le \epsilon\,.
    \]
Then the marginal laws of $X^1$ and $X^2$ are close in $L^2$-Wasserstein distance for all time: more precisely, there is a coupling of $X^1$ with $X^2$ under which
	\[
	\sup\bigg\{
	\E\bigg[\Big(X^1(t)-X^2(t)\Big)^2\bigg] 
	: t\in[q_*
        ,1]
	\bigg\} \le 
	C(\oL) \epsilon^2\,,
	\]
where $C(\oL)$ denotes a constant depending only on $\oL$.

\begin{proof}
Couple $X^1$ and $X^2$ with the same Brownian motion $B$, and same initial value (almost surely). For this coupling let $Z(t) = X^1(t)-X^2(t)$, and $E(t) = \E[Z(t)^2]$. By It\=o's formula, for any
$0\le t\le t'\le1$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	=\E \int_t^{t'} \bigg\{
		2 Z(s)
		\Big(b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)
	+\Big( \sigma^1(s,X^1(s))
		-\sigma^2(s,X^2(s))
		\Big)^2
		\bigg\}\,ds\,.
	\]
For $s\in[q_*,1]$, using that $b^1$ and $b^2$ are $\epsilon$-close to one another, and $\oL$-Lipschitz in the space coordinate, gives
	\[
	\Big|b^1(s,X^1(s))-b^2(s,X^2(s))
	\Big|
	\le \oL\Big| X^1(s)-X^2(s)\Big|
		+ \epsilon
	=\oL |Z(s)|
		+ \epsilon\,.
	\]
A similar bound holds with $\sigma^i$ in place of $b^i$. It follows that 
for $[t,t']\subseteq[q_*,1]$, we have
	\[
	E(t')-E(t)
	\le 3
	\E \int_t^{t'}
	\Big(\oL |Z(s)| + \epsilon\Big)^2\,ds
	\le 6 \bigg\{
	\oL^2 \int_t^{t'} E(s)\,ds
	+ \epsilon^2 (t'-t)
	\bigg\}\,.
	\]
The claimed bound follows from Gr\"onwall's inequality. More precisely, we can use the form stated in \cite[Lem.~6.1]{MR1071170} which says that if for all $t\in[q_*
    ,1]$ we have
	\[
	E(t) \le a(t) +\int_{q_0}^t b(s) E(s)\,ds
	\]
with $a,b$ continuous nonnegative functions, then it holds that
	\[
	E(1)
	\leq 
	E(q_*)
	+
	\int_{q_*
        }^1
	a(s)b(s)
	\exp
	\lt(
	\int_s^1 b(r)\,dr
	\rt)\,ds.
	\]
In our setting $E(q_*)=0$, $b(t)=6\oL^2$, and $a(t)=6\epsilon^2(t-q_*)$. Therefore
$a(1) \le 6\epsilon^2$, and the claimed bound follows.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["N>=3,K>=2,1<=r<K,0<=s,t<=r integers","One arbitrary and one systematic context, remaining contexts known S; source uniform contexts then uniform truths","Known truth identities from actual untagged factual samples and optional verifier; all compatible supports/orientations allowed","Robust source exact-level zero miscalibration; arbitrary generators"],"created_at":"2026-10-21T21:03:49.822810+00:00","domain":"statistical learning; robust calibration; truth support identification","id":"claim_ac4030be2b43ae3f012bf4d5561467d93512ee60948bd24529927d6d06add842","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"Own-work draft; proof (unaudited); independent mathematical, priority and target-scope audit pending. # Neutral truth/false bundles defeat the smaller-count hypothesis

T379-C016 v2, proof (unaudited), exact checks PASS; independent audit pending.
Targets 1/2: auxiliary-route failure, no target score claimed.

For every integer m>=5 and N>=3 set K=3m,r=3(m-1),d=1. In the two
variable contexts L,R suppose the known truth unions have sizes
s=2(m-1),t=r, respectively. There are N-2 fixed known S contexts.
No partition tags are supplied. Both orientations remain compatible:
if L is A its r-support contains C_L of size s; if R is A its support
is exactly C_R of size r. Such unions have positive probability from
actual untagged factual samples with ell=0, e.g. one occurrence of
every known truth, n=s+r. The identities can be permuted within each
context without affecting the construction or source probabilities.

Put lambda=1/(NK). Partition the variable-context atoms as follows:

* B: all K-s=m+2 atoms outside C_L and two atoms outside C_R;
* T: all s known L truths and any s of the known R truths;
* Z: the remaining m-1 known R truths and its one remaining outside atom.

B has m+4 atoms; T has 4(m-1); Z has m. In either orientation and
for EVERY compatible residual L support, their source masses are

 p(B)=lambda*(m+2),
 p(T)=lambda*(4m-2),
 p(Z)=lambda*m.

For B, if L is A its residual true count is r-s=m-1, so
p(B)=(m-1)/(Nr)+2/(NK)=lambda*(m+2). If R is A the same mass comes
from K-s systematic L atoms and no R truths. T's mass is always
s/(Nr)+s/(NK). Z's mass is (m-1)/(Nr)=m/(NK) when R is A and is
also m/(NK) when R is S. This checks invariance directly from p.

Define g as the uniform coarsening of these groups:

 g(B atom)=lambda*(m+2)/(m+4)=q,
 g(T atom)=lambda*(2m-1)/(2(m-1)),
 g(Z atom)=lambda,
 g(fixed S atom)=lambda.

The total is one and all probabilities are nonnegative. Equal lambda
scores merge Z and fixed S; their source masses remain invariant.
Thus g is source Mis_infinity=0 for every compatible world, not just
on average or conditional on a correct orientation prediction.

If L is A all three false atoms lie in B, giving H_L=3q.
If R is A two false atoms lie in B and one in Z, giving H_R=2q+lambda.
Since q<lambda, the worst-world false mass is

 max H=lambda*(3m+8)/(m+4).                              (1)

C016 v1 conjectured that the smaller known count alone gives the exact
value. Here h=s yields that conjectured value

 V_small=3lambda*(m+1)/(m+2).

The actual feasible worst risk (1) is strictly smaller, by

 V_small-max H=lambda*(m-4)/((m+2)(m+4))>0.               (2)

For m=5,N=3 these are 2/35 versus 23/405, gap 1/2835.
This refutes the entire proposed smaller-count formula; it does not
establish the optimal risk in this family. In particular the nine
complete small-alphabet score-partition checks were consistent with
the conjecture but insufficient to prove it. No general lower bound
was promoted from those computations.

The neutral Z group contains truths and possible falsehoods in exactly
the systematic true-density ratio. Its p mass is orientation-invariant
even though the known truth counts are unequal. This mechanism is
invisible to a rule that discards all surplus known truths. A general
unequal-count frontier must account for invariant weighted count
identities, not merely the minimum count or posterior risk ordering.
This is a route obstruction, not a solution of the unrestricted target.
Primary calibration basis: Kalai--Vempala 2311.14648v3 Definitions 1--2.

calibration checks. It exhausts residual L supports for m=5,6,7;

representative support, without claiming exhaustive enumeration there.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T22:55:27.167274+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac418b64a1d00975e0dcee610dbd15477608d1e7aa9dac471f34ff6bfff58f56","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem Th2 of arXiv:2609.04080, 'On radicals in differential invariants: \\ global theory vs moving frames'] Let $\ell$ be the order of stabilization of singularities of the $G$ action on $\mathcal{E}$. Assume that stabilizers of generic points
of $\mathcal{E}^\ell$ belong to the same conjugacy class in $G$. Then there exists a quasi-section that is a $\Gamma$-section

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-03T17:05:27.627182+00:00","domain":"real analysis","id":"claim_ac75738e8e3dabce1159fdd76643746f5142db1f8704a7114eee97125f9e99b8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"A function f: [a, b] -> R has bounded variation if its total variation V(f; [a, b]) = sup over all partitions a = x_0 < x_1 < ... < x_n = b of sum_{i=1}^{n} |f(x_i) - f(x_{i-1})| is finite; the space of such functions is BV[a, b]. Facts (Jordan, Lebesgue): (1) f is of bounded variation if and only if f = g - h with g and h nondecreasing on [a, b] (Jordan decomposition; one may take g(x) = V(f; [a, x]), the variation function, and h = g - f, both nondecreasing); (2) a BV function is bounded, has one-sided limits at every point, has at most countably many discontinuities, all of them jumps, and is differentiable Lebesgue-almost everywhere with f' integrable and integral_a^b |f'(x)| dx <= V(f; [a, b]), with equality if and only if f is absolutely continuous; (3) monotone functions and Lipschitz functions are BV (a Lipschitz function with constant L has V <= L (b - a)), while a continuous function need not be: x sin(1/x) on (0, 1] (extended by 0) has infinite variation, and the Cantor function is continuous, nondecreasing, BV, yet has f' = 0 almost everywhere with total variation 1 (so it is not absolutely continuous); (4) BV[a, b] is a Banach space under ||f|| = |f(a)| + V(f; [a, b]); (5) f is BV exactly when the Riemann-Stieltjes integral integral_a^b g df exists for every continuous g, and then g -> integral g df is a bounded linear functional on C[a, b] of norm V(f; [a, b]) - the Riesz representation of the dual of C[a, b] (normalised BV functions correspond to finite signed Borel measures). In higher dimensions BV functions are those whose distributional gradient is a finite vector measure.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:53:46.149510+00:00","domain":"elliptic regularity, L^p theory","id":"claim_ac7bfef65ba08df89da6d269b48b216132d2600e11e7ada5844f2602810376eb","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"Load-bearing hypothesis: in the Calderon-Zygmund theory for Lu = sum a^{ij}D_{ij}u + b.Du + cu the leading coefficients must be continuous (uniform continuity on the relevant compact set), or at least of vanishing mean oscillation; only then does the freezing-and-absorption step work for every 1 < p < infinity. Mere measurable uniform ellipticity is not enough, and the failure is not a technicality: both the estimate and uniqueness fail. Counterexample (Gilbarg-Serrin type): on the unit ball B_1 in R^n, n >= 2, fix lambda in (0,1) and set a^{ij}(x) = delta^{ij} + beta x_i x_j/|x|^2 with 1 + beta = (n-1)/(1 - lambda) > 0. These coefficients are bounded, symmetric, uniformly elliptic (eigenvalues 1 with multiplicity n-1 and (n-1)/(1-lambda)) and continuous except at the origin. For radial u, D_{ij}u = u''(r) x_i x_j/r^2 + (u'(r)/r)(delta_{ij} - x_i x_j/r^2), hence Lu = (1 + beta) u'' + (n-1) u'/r, and u(x) = |x|^lambda gives Lu = r^{lambda - 2} [ (1 + beta) lambda(lambda - 1) + (n-1) lambda ] = 0. Now w = |x|^lambda - 1 lies in W^{2,p}(B_1) for every p < n/(2 - lambda), lies in W^{1,p}_0(B_1) for those p, satisfies Lw = 0 almost everywhere, and is not identically zero (w(0) = -1). Consequences: the Dirichlet problem is not uniquely solvable in W^{2,p} intersect W^{1,p}_0 for p < n/(2 - lambda), so no global estimate ||w||_{W^{2,p}} <= C ||Lw||_{L^p} can hold there; the maximum principle also fails for such strong solutions (w attains its minimum -1 at an interior point while Lw = 0 and w = 0 on the boundary). Note n/(2 - lambda) < n and lambda may be taken as close to 1 as desired, so the failure reaches every exponent below n. What survives with only measurable coefficients: the Aleksandrov-Bakelman-Pucci estimate and Krylov-Safonov theory, both of which require the solution to be in W^{2,n}_loc - which is exactly the class this example escapes.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T08:33:12.357576+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ac81b303f3d1341ca273c97542be91edbaf419690548b6ea7476e7328eb55d4a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lem 242 of arXiv:2608.29416, 'Algorithmic threshold for high-dimensional projection pursuit I: general theory'] Fix any $\phi \in C_b(\R,\R)$ and define the domain
	\[
		\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha) = \Big\{
			\mu \in \cP_2(\R,C'(\alpha)) : \bbW_1(\mu, \ocM^{\Ising}(\alpha)) \le 1
		\Big\}\,.
	\]
	Then the function
	\[
		f_\phi(\mu) \equiv \int \phi\,d\mu
	\]
	is uniformly continuous on $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ equipped with the $\bbW_1$ metric.

\begin{proof}
The set $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ is clearly closed with respect to the $\bbW_1$ metric. By Lemma~\ref{l:confinement.cPp.compact.Wq}, the space $\cP_2(\R,C'(\alpha))$ endowed with the $\bbW_1$ metric is compact, so $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ is also compact. It thus suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is continuous. In fact, since we are on a metric space, it suffices to show that $f_\phi$ is sequentially continuous. To this end,  consider any sequence $\mu_n$ in $\ocM^{\Ising+}(\alpha)$ converging to $\mu$ in $\bbW_1$. Then $\mu_n$ also converges weakly to $\mu$. Since $\phi$ was assumed to be a bounded continuous function, we obtain 
	 \[\lim_{n\to\infty} f_\phi(\mu_n) = f(\mu)\,.\]
Therefore $f_\phi$ is indeed continuous, which concludes the proof.
\end{proof} (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["homogeneous marked Poisson grain field with ballistic grain motion","K_1 and K_2 are balls; the general reduction holds for arbitrary compact targets and arbitrary motion","the Brownian version is NOT settled"],"created_at":"2026-09-23T13:15:27.869001+00:00","domain":"probability","id":"claim_ac9d0f5c4d8213c77e0334fb4d69467ea3ed32400779d34cbe5dfab472c47b2f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[campaign status: settled_inertial_balls - author-checked, verification unreviewed; the two-ball instance was not separately simulated - the ball-and-point instance of E0105 is its validation] Let K_1 and K_2 be two compact targets in a moving Boolean model, with detection times S_1 and S_2. GENERAL EXACT REDUCTION, valid for any grain motion: writing A_i(t) for the set of grain initial conditions that detect K_i by time t, the Poisson void probability gives P(S_1 > s, S_2 > t) = exp(-lambda |A_1(s) union A_2(t)|), so P(S_1 < S_2) is an explicit integral of |A_1(s) union A_2(s)| against the intensity. The whole content of the problem is the volume of the union of two swept regions. CLAIM: for two BALLS of radii r_1 and r_2 in the homogeneous INERTIAL model, P(S_{K_1} < S_{K_2}) = P(S_{K_1} = 0 < S_{K_2}) + integral_0^infinity (d/dt Lambda)(u,u) exp(-Lambda(u,u)) du, with Lambda the void exponent of the union of two parallel capsules of radii R_i = r_i + r about the two centres, h being the perpendicular offset of b_2 - b_1 from the track - the same formula as E0105 with the point replaced by the second ball. NESTED CASE, worth stating because the naive answer is wrong: if K_1 contains K_2 then S_{K_1} <= S_{K_2} almost surely, but ties have POSITIVE probability, so the honest statement is P(S_{K_1} < S_{K_2}) = P(the first grain to touch K_1 does not simultaneously touch K_2), computable from the Palm calculus of the grain field. DISJOINT TARGETS ARE NOT INDEPENDENT: one grain path can detect both, and the dependence is exactly the Poisson two-set inclusion-exclusion above.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:20:33.736259+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_acb7c83ade502e0e860e2824a2f326ff6d59511999024a91240571512ee348da","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 14 (Structure of $g_{A,B}$ via Hadamard products and Abelian evaluation) of arXiv:2601.16580, 'Coin flipping and waiting times paradoxes \\ Why fair coins are exceptional'] There exist coprime polynomials $N_{A,B},D_{A,B}\in\mathbb{Z}[p]$ such that
\[
g_{A,B}(p)=\frac{N_{A,B}(p)}{D_{A,B}(p)}\qquad\text{for }p\in(0,1),
\]
with
\[
\deg_p N_{A,B},\ \deg_p D_{A,B}\ \le\ S_A+S_B
\ \ \le\ \ \frac{L_A(L_A+1)}{2}+\frac{L_B(L_B+1)}{2}.
\]
All coefficients are integers. Moreover, there is a polynomial $P(L_A,L_B)$ such that

\[
\|N_{A,B}\|_1,\ \|D_{A,B}\|_1\ \le\ P(L_A,L_B)\cdot 2^{\,S_A+S_B}.
\]
We record these endpoint limits because they give quick sign information (and will be useful as simple ``filters'' in computations).
As $p\downarrow 0$ and $p\uparrow 1$ the endpoint limits satisfy
\[
\lim_{p\downarrow 0} W^{\mathrm{rtb}}_{A,B}(p)=
\begin{cases}
1,& h(A)<h(B),\\
0,& h(A)>h(B),\\
\tfrac12,& h(A)=h(B)>0,\\
\mathbf{1}_{\{L_A<L_B\}}+\tfrac12\,\mathbf{1}_{\{L_A=L_B\}},& h(A)=h(B)=0,
\end{cases}
\]
\[
\lim_{p\uparrow 1} W^{\mathrm{rtb}}_{A,B}(p)=
\begin{cases}
1,& t(A)<t(B),\\
0,& t(A)>t(B),\\
\tfrac12,& t(A)=t(B)>0,\\
\mathbf{1}_{\{L_A<L_B\}}+\tfrac12\,\mathbf{1}_{\{L_A=L_B\}},& t(A)=t(B)=0.
\end{cases}
\]
Let $\Delta_h=|h(A)-h(B)|$ and $\Delta_t=|t(A)-t(B)|$. Then the first nonzero terms near the endpoints have orders
\[
\bigl|W^{\mathrm{rtb}}_{A,B}(p)-\mathbf{1}_{\{h(A)<h(B)\}}\bigr|=\Theta\bigl(p^{\Delta_h}\bigr)\quad (p\downarrow 0),
\]
\[
\bigl|W^{\mathrm{rtb}}_{A,B}(p)-\mathbf{1}_{\{t(A)<t(B)\}}\bigr|=\Theta\bigl((1-p)^{\Delta_t}\bigr)\quad (p\uparrow 1),
\]
and if $h(A)=h(B)\ge 1$ (resp.\ $t(A)=t(B)\ge 1$) then
\[
g_{A,B}(p)=O(p)\quad(p\downarrow 0),\qquad
g_{A,B}(p)=O(1-p)\quad(p\uparrow 1).
\]
In particular, if $(h(A)-h(B))(t(A)-t(B))<0$ then $g_{A,B}$ has at least one zero in $(0,1)$.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T20:58:53.193852+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_acbce9fb6240111ab0a4e688c3ae2425f85bb1ad052738787989095fdd4d4f42","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition 25 of arXiv:2606.31455, 'Discrete time-multidimensional renewal theory and applications'] Let $\lambda_1,\lambda_2>0$ and $\rho\in[-1,1]$.
Let
\[
F_X(x_1)=1-e^{-\lambda_1 x_1},\qquad
F_Y(x_2)=1-e^{-\lambda_2 x_2},\qquad x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+.
\]
The FGM bivariate exponential distribution is defined by the joint cdf

\begin{equation}
F(x_1,x_2)
=
F_X(x_1)F_Y(x_2)\Big[1+\rho\,(1-F_X(x_1))(1-F_Y(x_2))\Big],
\qquad (x_1,x_2)\in\mathbb{R}_+^2,
\end{equation}

whose joint density is

\begin{equation*}
f(x_1,x_2)
=
\lambda_1\lambda_2\,e^{-(\lambda_1 x_1+\lambda_2 x_2)}
\Big[1+\rho\,(1-2e^{-\lambda_1 x_1})(1-2e^{-\lambda_2 x_2})\Big],
\qquad x_1,x_2\in\mathbb{R}_+.
\end{equation*}
Equivalently, \eqref{eq:fgm-cdf} is obtained by combining the exponential marginals
with the FGM copula \cite{morgenstern1956einfache,nelsen2006introduction}.
The case $\rho=0$ corresponds to independence.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X a normed space; no completeness of X is needed","for metrizability and sequential compactness of the ball: X separable","Tychonoff (hence a form of the axiom of choice) in the general case"],"created_at":"2026-09-03T13:20:36.752423+00:00","domain":"functional analysis","id":"claim_ad0f3a207b3c5379410429f086bcbbeb1babd7dfb64560bd3c03ab098d3b5d3e","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a normed vector space over R or C. The closed unit ball B of the dual space X^* is COMPACT in the weak-* topology, that is the topology of pointwise convergence on X. Two refinements matter. (a) If X is SEPARABLE then the weak-* topology restricted to B is metrizable and B is weak-* SEQUENTIALLY compact, so bounded sequences of functionals have weak-* convergent subsequences; without separability compactness need not give sequential compactness. (b) The general theorem uses Tychonoff's theorem for a product of compact scalar discs and therefore, in ZF, is not provable without some choice; the separable case needs only a diagonal argument. The theorem does NOT say the ball is norm-compact: by Riesz's lemma the closed unit ball of a normed space is norm-compact if and only if the space is finite-dimensional. Nor does it say the ball of X itself is weakly compact - that characterises reflexivity (Kakutani). [standard; e.g. Rudin, Functional Analysis, 2nd ed., Theorem 3.15]","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T19:26:26.807268+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ad2577d53d461574b2aa13e7c5473ca3510eb25e4462f7d955d961221f62d0ed","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma lem:read-k of arXiv:2608.06159, 'Majority Dynamics on Resampled Sparse Erd\H{o}s--R\'enyi Graphs:\\[0.5ex] Gaussian Winner '] {gavinsky2015tail}}]
    
     Let \(\{\rY_j\}_{j\in[r]}\) be a read-\(k\) family of indicator random variables with \(p_j \coloneqq\P(\rY_j=1)\), and denote their average by \(\bar p \coloneqq r^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^r p_j\).
    If \(0<\bar p<1\), then
    \begin{subequations}
    \begin{align}
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\ge (\bar p+\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p+\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le1-\bar p,
    \\
    \P\bigg(
    \sum_{j=1}^r \rY_j\le (\bar p-\varepsilon)r
    \bigg)
    &\le
    \exp\bigg(
    -\frac{r}{k}\D_{\mathrm{KL}}(\bar p-\varepsilon\|\bar p)
    \bigg),
    &&0<\varepsilon\le\bar p.
    \end{align}
    \end{subequations}
    where the Kullback-Leibler divergence is defined as
    \[
    \D_{\mathrm{KL}}(u\|v)\coloneqq
    u\log(u/v)+(1-u)\log((1-u)/(1-v)).
    \]
    We use the standard convention \(0\log0=0\) at \(u\in\{0,1\}\).
    If \(\bar p\in\{0,1\}\), all the indicators are almost surely constant and
    the corresponding tail statements are trivial. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:45:38.358413+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ad3216dc0eaed1044c645b89a8d6e19f0c258394f0c30a035a2a53411ee40401","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Proposition 4 (McDiarmid's inequality) of arXiv:2604.21143, 'Quantitative homogenization for the critical long-range random conductance model'] Let $\lambda \in (0,1]$, let $X_1, \ldots, X_n$ be independent random variables taking values in $[\lambda, \lambda^{-1}]$, and let $f : [\lambda, \lambda^{-1}]^n \to \R$ be Borel measurable.
		Assume that there exist constants $a_1, \ldots, a_n \ge 0$ such that, for every $1 \le i \le n$,
		\[
		\sup_{\substack{x_1, \ldots, x_n \in [\lambda, \lambda^{-1}] \\ x_i' \in [\lambda, \lambda^{-1}]}} \left| f(x_1, \ldots, x_n) - f(x_1, \ldots, x_{i-1}, x_i', x_{i+1}, \ldots, x_n) \right| \le a_i\,.
		\]
		Then, for every $t > 0$,
		\[
		\P\left( \left| f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - \E[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n)] \right| > t \right) \le 2\exp\left( -\frac{2t^2}{\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2} \right).
		\]
		In particular, there exists a universal constant $C < \infty$ such that
		\[
		\left| f(X_1, \ldots, X_n) - \E[f(X_1, \ldots, X_n)] \right| \le \mathcal{O}_2\left( C\Bigl(\sum_{i=1}^n a_i^2\Bigr)^{1/2} \right).
		\] (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

Let $(X_n',Y_n')$ be an independent copy of $(X_n,Y_n)$. 
Suppose further that the limits
\begin{equation}
    \lim_{n\to\infty}\mathbb{E}h(X_n\mid Y_n)
    \quad\text{and}\quad

exist, and that, for some $\lambda\in(0,1)$,

    =

    -

    \right],
\end{equation}
where

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:05:37.767829+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ada6bb71336f4aa0c91cf431aef1484ec65aaca39e0ec609d1a09018c2f84dc8","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Definition regulated process of arXiv:2607.29548, 'Generalized reflected BSDEs with irregular obstacles driven by RCLL increasing processes o'] \begin{itemize}
			\item A process
			\[
			\mathcal{X}:\Omega\times[0,T]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
			\]
			is called a \emph{regulated process} if, for
			$\mathbb{P}$-almost every $\omega\in\Omega$, the mapping
			\[
			t\longmapsto\mathcal{X}_t(\omega)
			\]
			admits a finite right limit at every $t\in[0,T)$ and a finite
			left limit at every $t\in(0,T]$.
			
			\item Let $\mathcal{X}$ be a process with regulated trajectories.
			For $s\in(0,T]$, we define its left limit and left jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s-}
			:=
			\lim_{u\uparrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_s-\mathcal{X}_{s-},
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_-\mathcal{X}_0=0$.
			
			For $s\in[0,T)$, we define its right limit and right jump by
			\[
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}
			:=
			\lim_{u\downarrow s}\mathcal{X}_u,
			\qquad
			\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_s
			:=
			\mathcal{X}_{s+}-\mathcal{X}_s,
			\]
			with the convention $\Delta_+\mathcal{X}_T=0$.
			
			The trajectories of a regulated process have at most countably
			many discontinuities; see
			[DudleyNorvaisa2011].
			
			\item Let
			\[
			\mathsf{K}:\Omega\times[0,T]\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}
			\]
			be a regulated process of finite variation. Then $\mathsf{K}$
			admits the decomposition
			\[
			\mathsf{K}
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d+\mathsf{K}^g,
			\]
			where $\mathsf{K}^c$ is continuous, the càdlàg pure-jump process
			$\mathsf{K}^d$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^d_t
			:=
			\sum_{0<s\leq t}\Delta_-\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			and the càglàd pure-jump process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is defined by
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^g_t
			:=
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T].
			\]
			The above sums converge absolutely along each trajectory since
			$\mathsf{K}$ has finite variation.
			
			In particular,
			\[
			\mathsf{K}_t
			=
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}_t
			+
			\sum_{0\leq s<t}\Delta_+\mathsf{K}_s,
			\qquad t\in[0,T],
			\]
			where
			\[
			\mathsf{K}^{\ast}
			:=
			\mathsf{K}-\mathsf{K}^g
			=
			\mathsf{K}^c+\mathsf{K}^d
			\]
			is the càdlàg, or right-continuous, part of $\mathsf{K}$.
			The process $\mathsf{K}^g$ is the left-continuous pure-jump part
			of $\mathsf{K}$.
		\end{itemize}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["(X, Sigma, mu) is a measure space","1 <= p < infinity (the statement is false for p = infinity)","for p = 1: mu sigma-finite (or localizable) for surjectivity; mu semifinite for isometry","scalars real or complex"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T09:49:36.552519+00:00","domain":"functional analysis, Lp spaces","id":"claim_adee9ce43c73105fd97da47f2239ef349918c1fc447cc025fb6cb07edd000262","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (X, Sigma, mu) be a measure space and 1 <= p < infinity with conjugate exponent p'. For g in L^{p'}(mu) define Lambda_g(f) = int_X f g dmu. (a) If 1 < p < infinity, then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^{p'}(mu) onto the dual space (L^p(mu))*, for an arbitrary measure space. (b) If p = 1 and mu is sigma-finite (more generally, localizable), then g -> Lambda_g is an isometric isomorphism of L^infinity(mu) onto (L^1(mu))*. In particular L^p is reflexive for 1 < p < infinity. For 1 < p < infinity the map is isometric over every measure space; for p = 1 it is isometric as soon as mu is semifinite, and without sigma-finiteness (or localizability) it need not be surjective. The case p = infinity is genuinely different and is NOT covered: the analogous map L^1(mu) -> (L^infinity(mu))* is isometric when mu is semifinite but in general not surjective, so (L^infinity)* is in general strictly larger than L^1 (see the pitfall).","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["Omega is a compact metric space and T: Omega -> Omega is a homeomorphism","(Omega, T) is minimal","V: Omega -> R is continuous","H_omega is the discrete Schrodinger operator with potential n -> V(T^n omega) on l^2(Z) (equivalently, the continuum Schrodinger operator over a minimal flow)","E is a real energy","uniform hyperbolicity is understood with constants uniform over all of Omega"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814897+00:00","domain":"spectral theory of ergodic Schrodinger operators, hyperbolic cocycles","id":"claim_ae02788a467b182215c0322bd89b1ed9531f9fb0c3a5dbf18d877ba74f12ef05","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let (Omega, T) be a MINIMAL topological dynamical system, Omega a compact metric space and T a homeomorphism, and let V: Omega -> R be continuous. For each omega in Omega let H_omega be the discrete Schrodinger operator on l^2(Z) given by (H_omega u)(n) = u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega) u(n). By minimality the spectrum sigma(H_omega) is one and the same compact set Sigma contained in R for every omega. For an energy E in R define the Schrodinger cocycle (T, A^E) over (Omega,T), where A^E(omega) is the SL(2,R) matrix with rows (E - V(omega), -1) and (1, 0); its iterates are A^E_n(omega) = A^E(T^{n-1}omega) ... A^E(omega), and they transfer solutions of the difference equation u(n+1) + u(n-1) + V(T^n omega)u(n) = E u(n). The cocycle is UNIFORMLY HYPERBOLIC if there is a continuous T-invariant splitting R^2 = E^s(omega) + E^u(omega) and constants C > 0, lambda > 1 with ||A^E_n(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^s(omega) and ||A^E_{-n}(omega)v|| <= C lambda^{-n}||v|| for v in E^u(omega), for all n >= 0 and all omega; equivalently (for SL(2,R) cocycles over a compact base) ||A^E_n(omega)|| >= C lambda^n for all omega and all n >= 0. THEOREM (R. Johnson): E belongs to R \\ Sigma if and only if the cocycle (T, A^E) is uniformly hyperbolic. Equivalently, Sigma is exactly the set of real energies at which the Schrodinger cocycle fails to be uniformly hyperbolic. The same statement holds in the continuum setting for Schrodinger operators -u'' + V(T_t omega)u on the line with a minimal flow, which is Johnson's original formulation, and it is the standard dictionary between spectral theory and the dynamics of the transfer-matrix cocycle. SHARP EDGES. (a) UNIFORM hyperbolicity is far stronger than a positive Lyapunov exponent, and this is the single most often misused point. In the supercritical almost Mathieu operator, and more generally in the localisation regime, the Lyapunov exponent L(E) is positive at EVERY energy of the spectrum; those energies are in Sigma, so the cocycle there is non-uniformly hyperbolic. 'Positive exponent' therefore does NOT imply 'in the resolvent set'; only uniformity does. (b) Minimality of the base is used twice: to make sigma(H_omega) independent of omega, and to propagate the exponential dichotomy from one orbit to all of Omega. For a non-minimal base the spectrum can genuinely depend on omega and the statement must be reformulated (typically with the union of the spectra over the support of an ergodic measure, or over the whole base), so do not apply the equivalence verbatim outside minimality. (c) The theorem characterises the RESOLVENT set, which is open; correspondingly uniform hyperbolicity is an open condition in E and in the cocycle, whereas positivity of the Lyapunov exponent is not open. (d) The statement is for real E; for non-real E the operator is invertible anyway and the associated cocycle is not an SL(2,R) cocycle.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":["X is a topological space","f takes values in the extended reals (-infinity, +infinity]","for the liminf characterisation, X is first countable (e.g. metric)","for the attainment-of-the-infimum statement, X is compact","for the approximation by Lipschitz functions, X is metric and f is bounded below"],"created_at":"2026-09-12T19:07:38.814277+00:00","domain":"general topology, real analysis, calculus of variations","id":"claim_ae0d76cf084a3679aa5c60bc21a5f1aa5a7d55e81a31da780dbc20178aa9cae5","kind":"definition","schema_version":1,"statement":"Let X be a topological space and f: X -> (-infinity, +infinity] an extended-real function. f is lower semicontinuous (lsc) at a point x0 if for every real a < f(x0) there is a neighbourhood U of x0 with f(x) > a for all x in U. f is lsc on X iff any one of the following equivalent conditions holds: (i) the superlevel set {x : f(x) > a} is open for every real a; (ii) the sublevel set {x : f(x) <= a} is closed for every real a; (iii) the epigraph {(x,t) in X x R : t >= f(x)} is closed in X x R. If X is first countable (in particular metric), lower semicontinuity at x0 is equivalent to liminf_{x -> x0} f(x) >= f(x0). f is upper semicontinuous iff -f is lsc, and f is continuous iff it is both. Standard facts, each of which is the reason lsc is worth naming: (1) the pointwise SUPREMUM of an arbitrary family of lsc functions is lsc; (2) a sum of finitely many lsc functions is lsc provided no (+infinity) + (-infinity) occurs, and a nonnegative multiple of an lsc function is lsc; (3) a nondecreasing pointwise limit of continuous functions is lsc, and conversely on a METRIC space every lsc function bounded below is the pointwise nondecreasing limit of a sequence of Lipschitz functions (Baire); (4) the indicator 1_A is lsc iff A is open; (5) WEIERSTRASS FORM: if X is compact and f is lsc then f attains its infimum on X, because the sublevel sets {f <= a} are closed and have the finite intersection property. This is the form in which lsc is used in the direct method of the calculus of variations: coercivity plus lsc on a compact (or weakly compact) set yields a minimiser. SHARP EDGES, i.e. what is NOT true. (a) lsc buys you MINIMA only, never maxima: on the compact space [0,1] the function f(x) = x for x < 1, f(1) = 0 is lsc (every superlevel set {f > a} is (a,1) or [0,1] or empty), its supremum is 1 and it is not attained. (b) The supremum of lsc functions is lsc but the INFIMUM of infinitely many lsc functions need not be: on R the continuous functions f_n(x) = max(0, 1 - n|x|) have pointwise infimum the indicator of {0}, whose superlevel set {f > 1/2} = {0} is not open. (c) 'lsc at every point' is genuinely weaker than continuity; an lsc function may be discontinuous on a dense set. (d) Statement (3) uses metrizability of X; on a general topological space an lsc function need not be a pointwise limit of continuous functions (it is a supremum of continuous functions on compact Hausdorff or, more generally, normal spaces, by Urysohn/Katetov-Tong, but for arbitrary X no such representation is available). (e) In integration theory the useful instance is Fatou's lemma, which says exactly that f -> integral f is lsc along pointwise convergence of nonnegative measurable functions; no upper semicontinuity holds there without a domination hypothesis.","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T21:02:38.607107+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae2f62daa02f830834a94395dafeac40a3fe4f5f5f4c4e48dd98095791eb2a7a","kind":"concept","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem 2 of arXiv:2607.08242, 'Convergence of random sums in non-commutative probability'] Suppose $(\mathcal{A}, \varphi)$ is an NCP. 

Let $\{a_i\}$ be self-adjoint variables such that, $\varphi(a_i)=0, \varphi(a_i^2)=1$, and  $\sup_i|\varphi(a_i^m)| < \infty$ for every positive integer $m$. 
Then the following hold for $S_n:=a_1+\cdots +a_n$.\vskip5pt

\noindent (i) If $\{a_i\}$ are free, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} s$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (ii) If $\{a_i\}$ are independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}\stackrel{*}{\to} z$.

\vskip5pt

\noindent (iii) If $\{a_i\}$ are half-independent, then $S_n/\sqrt{n}
\stackrel{*}{\to} r_S$.

\vskip3pt

\noindent In other words, $\varphi(S_n/\sqrt{n})^m$ in (i), (ii) and (iii) respectively, equal $\varphi(s^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(z^m)+o(1)$, $\varphi(r_S^m)+o(1)$. (Proof in the paper; no proof environment follows the statement in the TeX.)","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-26T19:49:02.090002+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae325f24040744b8f8cf7d064e76b80897dacb51b2bfa623c2b875071b1074db","kind":"lemma","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Lemma 25 (Amplification via many macroscopic subtrees) of arXiv:2604.25877, 'Asymptotic height of Plancherel random trees'] Fix $\theta>0$ and let $H_n$ denote the height of the Ewens tree $\mathcal T_n$.
Assume that there exist constants $p_0\in(0,1)$ and $m_0\ge 1$ such that
\begin{equation}
\inf_{m\ge m_0}\Pp\left(H_m\ge h(m)\right)\ \ge\ p_0,
\end{equation}
for some function $h:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N$.
Fix any $\delta\in(0,1)$ and set $m:=n-1$ and the macroscopic threshold
\[
t_n := \lceil m^{1-\delta}\rceil,
\qquad
h_{\min}(n):=\min(\{h(j):\ t_n\le j\le m\}).
\]
Then, for all $n$ large enough so that $t_n\ge m_0$,
\begin{equation}
\Pp\left(H_n \ge 1+h_{\min}(n)\right)
\ \ge\
1-\E\left[(1-p_0)^{N_0}\right].
\end{equation}
Moreover,
\begin{equation}
\E[(1-p_0)^{N_0}]\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}0
\qquad\text{and therefore}\qquad
\Pp\left(H_n \ge 1+h_{\min}(n)\right)\xrightarrow[n\to\infty]{}1.
\end{equation}","status":"unverified"}

{"assumptions":[],"created_at":"2026-10-27T21:18:54.368193+00:00","domain":"probability theory","id":"claim_ae4a6f0afb2be571fce696816d9421636504f419dfcd2fc0cefa6b443279fe2f","kind":"theorem","schema_version":1,"statement":"[Theorem of arXiv:2608.10415, 'Continuous random variables'] The chi law of parameter $n\in\mathbb N$, appearing as
